pages.text:
No 10
Brushy Wednesday Night
April 15th /63
Dear Brother:
Again I take my pen to write, though I will not promise to be very interesting. Laura received your letter of 21st March last Saturday, the first letter we had got for three weeks. Lou got Joda’s letter last Sunday with yours of the 12th inst. enclosed which gave us great satisfaction; as we did not know whether you had left Galveston or not. I hope your new situation will prove a healthy, and agreeable one, though, fear it will not be so much so as the one you left. I fear you will not remain there long, but be ordered along untill you get to the Mississippi and there be trapped up like the Post prisoners were or perhaps receive a worse fate.

pages.family_text:
Brushy, Wednesday night, April 15, 1863. Letter No. 10.
Dear Brother,
I am writing again, although I cannot promise anything very interesting. Last Saturday Laura received your March 21 letter—the first we had received for three weeks. On Sunday Lou received Joda’s letter with your April 12 letter enclosed. We were very glad, because we did not know whether you had left Galveston.

I hope your new posting is healthy and pleasant, though I fear it will be less so than the one you left. Do you think you could be attacked so far inland? It seems a curious place for soldiers. I fear you will not stay there long, but will keep being sent onward until you reach the Mississippi, where you might be trapped like the prisoners at the Post, or suffer a worse fate.

You cannot imagine how worried we were when we had no news. We thought of so many reasons why letters had not arrived. Perhaps someone had read some of your letters, or some of—
pages.family_note: The sentence continues on the next scan page. Lizzie’s fears and predictions describe her state of mind; they do not establish George’s orders or what actually happened.

pages.title: Mother’s fears, Lizzie’s request to burn letters, and farm work
pages.text:
mine to you, and something dreadful been done to you; for you may have been careless with them, leave them lying about, and who knows how much treason might be found in some of our uncongenial ideas. So reasoned Mother and what truthfulness there was in her logic time alone could determine. I know you will smile when you read this, but you must remember how scary we allways are when any thing unusual happens. Moreover, Mother has enjoined upon me, to be careful what I put on paper, in these perilous times: and, by the by just while I think of it, Beck told us she found several of my old letters in Warrens trunk. had, nt you better, after you have perused them to your hearts content, just commit them to the flames of your camp fire; they will only raise the blaze a little higher and then settle down and be out of mischief.

After hoeing so hard all day, and then brought a buckett of water from the head spring and then milked the cows (we have six young calves in the pen) I feel right smartly fatigued so for the present, hopeing you are not on guard to night, I make my best bow and retire.

16th This is a very pretty evening, the clouds that obscured the Sun for a while this morning, have been driven away by a strong southern breeze.

[[separate block: closing written upside down above the main text]]
This leaves all well on Brushy
no more at present Affectionately
Lizzie

—my letters to you, and perhaps something dreadful had happened to you. You might have carelessly left them lying around. Who knows how much treason someone might find in our unpopular ideas? That was Mother’s reasoning; only time could show whether she was right. I know you will smile at this, but remember how easily frightened we become when anything unusual happens.

Mother has also warned me to be careful what I write in these dangerous times. While I remember, Beck told us she found several of my old letters in Warren’s trunk. After you have read my letters as much as you like, would it not be better to burn them in your campfire? They will make the fire burn a little higher, then settle down and cause no trouble.

After hoeing hard all day, carrying a bucket of water from the main spring and milking the cows—we have six young calves in the pen—I feel very tired. Hoping you are not on guard tonight, I will say goodnight and retire.

April 16. It is a beautiful evening. A strong southern breeze has blown away the clouds that hid the sun this morning.

Closing written in the upper margin:
Everyone here on Brushy is well. No more for now. Affectionately, Lizzie.

pages.title: Lizzie reports Mrs. Payne’s death and worries over the mail
pages.text:
Saturday Night April 4
Dear George:
Warrens stay is about over with us, as he starts tomorrow; and I thought I would write you a few lines to let you know we are all stirring. We have not received a line from you for about two weeks, I cant tell why it is we dont get letters unless they have stopped you from writing; yet I hope this is not the case. We were filled with sadness this evening by hearing of the death of Mrs Payne. Poor woman to die and leave her little children to meet the worlds cold frowns without a mothers kind and tender care there is five of them one an infant of one week old. Preston is at home now though as a matter of course he will have to go back to the army soon
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 07-009. Year not written; the later slip suggests 1863.

pages.family_title: Lizzie reports Mrs. Payne’s death and worries over the mail
pages.family_text:
Saturday night, April 4 [year not stated; possibly 1863].
Dear George,
Warren’s visit is nearly over, since he leaves tomorrow. I thought I would write a few lines to tell you that we are all up and about. We have had no letter from you for about two weeks. I cannot understand why, unless you have been stopped from writing; I hope that is not the case.

This evening we were saddened to hear that Mrs. Payne has died. Poor woman, leaving her little children to face an unkind world without a mother’s loving care. There are five children, including a one-week-old baby. Preston is home now, though of course he will soon have to return to the army.
pages.family_note: The letter reports the death and children but does not give Mrs. Payne’s first name. Preston’s relationship to her is not explicitly stated in this passage.

pages.title: Cotton socks, medicine, and longing for the family to reunite
pages.text:
We send you two pairs of socks and some pills and a fine [[deleted: comb?]] comb. I wish we could send something else but I have been studying and can think of nothing else that would be of any benefit to you; as you seemed to like the cotton socks Ellen gave you we thought we would knit some more thinking they would be more pleasant for summer. If you do not like them I suppose you have woollen socks enough to do you till we can send you more. Sister is over and Warren being here it only lacks your presence and Jodas to make us seem as we used to seem. Oh! I do hope the time will come when you can again be with us; but if you have gone east I fear it will be a long time first. As I wrote you a long letter by last yesterdays mail I can write no news of interest to nite.
Your Sister Lizzie
pages.editorial_notes: Concludes the letter on 07-008. The first comb appears crossed out and repeated.

pages.family_text:
We are sending you two pairs of socks, some pills and a fine comb. I wish we could send something else, but I have thought about it and cannot think of anything else that would help you. You seemed to like the cotton socks Ellen gave you, so we knitted more, thinking they would be more comfortable in summer. If you do not like them, I suppose you have enough wool socks until we can send more.

Sister is visiting, and Warren is here. With you and Joda here too, things would feel as they used to. I hope the time comes when you can be with us again, but if you have gone east, I fear it will be a long wait. I sent you a long letter in yesterday’s mail, so I have no more interesting news tonight.
Your sister, Lizzie.

pages.title: Lizzie waits for letters and reports deaths near Brushy
pages.text:
Brushy Tex.
Jan. 22nd /1863
Dear Brother.
Again I take my pen to write you a few lines, though I dont promise to be very interesting. I have written you four letters, and never have received a line from you yet. We have been looking anxiously for letters for the last week and none have come. Laura went to the Post Office this evening and I thought sure we would get a letter but as usual we were disappointed. I attribute not getting letters partly to the mail for I think surely you do write. The last date we have is the 7th, your letter to Mary Orr.

This leaves all well on Brushy, except Father he has a spell of the headache. But Death has again visited our neighbourhood. Eliza [[Andrews?]] died last Sunday morning. Lizzie D. is still mending slowly. I forgot to mention in my last the death of Dr. Burkhart; he has been dead about

[[separate block: side margin]]
Dont you get enough to eat? Your health is always better as if you were hungry [[illegible]]
pages.editorial_notes: Main text continues on 07-012. The marginal remark’s ending is cramped and uncertain. Andrews is a tentative reading.

pages.family_text:
Brushy, Texas, January 22, 1863.
Dear Brother,
I am writing a few lines again, though I cannot promise anything very interesting. I have sent you four letters and have yet to receive a line from you. We have looked anxiously for letters all week, but none have come. Laura went to the post office this evening. I was sure we would receive one, but we were disappointed again. I partly blame the mail, because surely you are writing. Your latest letter that we have is the January 7 one to Mary Orr.

Jan. 22nd /1863
Dear Brother.

Letter No. 9, Tuesday night, February 10, 1863.
Dear George,
Your February 1 letter arrived this evening. The letter, map and everything were very interesting. Ellen was delighted with her letter and has asked us to read it to her at least ten times tonight. You must write her another. Getting a letter does her as much good as it does me. Your January 25 letter arrived a week ago today. I will answer both in this letter, adding entries on successive days.

I do not think we have told you the news of Aunt Rebecca Hymann’s family. As Jessie returned from Arkansas, he camped with a man who had just come from Mississippi. The man said Federal troops had overrun her neighborhood, destroyed her farm and taken her house for a hospital. Her boys were all in the army, or had been. Henry was home because he had been wounded at Fort Donaldson [the typed copy adds a question mark].

Mollie O., Sue, Laurer and I went to hear Parson Austin last Sunday. He spoke about the Millennium. I suppose it was a good talk, but I did not understand much of it. When we came home, we heard that Mr. Orr had received a letter from Henry. We ate a few bites and went to see it. Dated January 21 and 23, it said they had been at Pine Bluff only a few days. They had hurried out of the White River country, leaving cooking utensils scattered from Brownsville to Little Rock because their teams were too exhausted to pull them. We still do not know what happened to Fayett and Jim. Henry had spoken with several men who escaped, who told—

—him they had seen Fayett and Jim in the rifle pits late on the first day of fighting. They were all right then. That is the latest news we have.

Wednesday night, February 11. Henry also wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell, who escaped from Arkansas Post. Jack said he had been assigned to dig ditches. When he saw the Federal flag over the town, he left. He was heading for Little Rock and hoped to get home from there. Burdet Weatherford and John Porter are home. I never expect to become a newspaper correspondent. I do not have enough ideas to share with the public, even if I could find the language. Still, “can’t” should be in no one’s vocabulary. In future—

pages.title: Typed copy: criticism of military authority and a plea for peace
pages.text:
I will try to be more interesting.

You ask “what I think of such opinions” as are advanced by your leader, I answer to say the least, They are arbitrary, unjust and tyrannical. Let such minds as these go into ascendency and have controll and where is our liberty, our privilege as rational beings? I answer gone! and gone forever!
I am sorry you are under command of one, who has so little feeling, so little humanity, and has so much tyranny of opinion about him; if he really thinks what he says, if he does not, I detest his moral principal as a man, and think him unfit for the position which he occupies. If he was to see this, I suppose he would be more of the opinion than ever, THAT correspondence should be stopped between the “utencils” of war and their equally worthless friends at home; for my part about all the good I wish him is, that he may never rise to higher command but sink to the position of one of the lowest high privates and then let him tyrannize over whom he can.

As for peace, it is what we cannot hope for, as long as the North choose to prosecute their present undertaking and the South holds out with it’s stubborn resistance. Oh! that the ruling powers would stop! Stop and think for what this strife is for! for what this stream of blood continues to flow. But no, of this they do not think: the love of power is stronger than any other, and all must Subserve to this. We cannot stop it, we can only move along with this vast current and trust to providence to bring us safely through. May the time speedily come when peace shall again smile upon us is my prayer.

Saturday night, my usual time for writing to you, has again arrived. Sue, Laura, and myself all writing, Mother is knitting. Father and the Children in bed.

pages.title: Typed copy: sickness at home and uncertainty after a lighthouse fight
pages.text:
Brushy, May 7, 1863
Dear George,
Laura being sick it falls to me to write to you again this week. We were fixing to go to preaching last Sunday, when Laura was taken with sick stomach. She has been right sick ever since till this morning. She is able to sit up some, and thinks she will be able to write some this evening; the balance are all well except myself; I waked up this morning with swimming in my head [[a line of question marks in the typescript]] FURTHER sickness. I recieved yours of the 8 to 15 the day I mailed mine no. 12; Laura allso got yours of the 16 and 17 the same day; as Laura’s was written just the day before the light house fight, which we notice on account of in the Telagraph, we were anxious to recieve your next letter, to learn whether you and Joda were in the engagement or not; if you were I hope you were unhurt, as the paper gave no account of any wounded on our side. We are very much in hopes you have not been sent to La. I suppose troops will have to be kept at Sabine, and as you are there we think perhaps you will be kept there: though it is very uncertain, for it seems troops are ordered one direction to day, and tomorrow are turned right around and sent to an entirely different place. Stones Reg. was ordered to the frontier and travelled three or four days when the order was countermanded, and they were sent to La. We have heard when they got the orders to got to La. about four hundred refused to go, and there was about to be a burst up how much truth there is in this report I cannot tell. That regiment appears to be composed of not very sound matierial any how from all I can learn, it is doubtful whether the Confederacy is ever benefitted much by thir service.

Brushy, May 7, 1863.
Dear George,
Laura is sick, so it falls to me to write again this week. We were getting ready for church last Sunday when her stomach became upset. She was quite ill until this morning. Now she can sit up a little and hopes to write this evening. Everyone else is well except me: I woke dizzy this morning. [The typed copy has an unreadable or omitted passage marked with question marks, ending with “further sickness.”]

Your letter covering the 8th through the 15th arrived the day I posted my No. 12. Laura received your letter of the 16th and 17th that same day. Hers was written just before the lighthouse fight reported in the Telegraph, so we were anxious for your next letter to learn whether you and Joda took part. If so, I hope you were unharmed; the paper reported no wounded on our side.

We very much hope you have not been sent to Louisiana. Troops will presumably have to remain at Sabine, and since you are there, perhaps you will stay. But orders seem to send men one way today and somewhere entirely different tomorrow. Stone’s regiment had traveled toward the frontier for three or four days when the order was reversed and they were sent to Louisiana. We heard that about four hundred refused and a serious disturbance nearly followed. I cannot say how true that report is. From what I hear, that regiment seems unreliable, and I doubt the Confederacy benefits much from its service.
pages.family_note: The writer explicitly questions the report of four hundred men refusing orders. The typed copy’s existing gap is preserved; it has not been filled from context.

Sunday night Feb. 1st
Dear George:
It doesnt seem hardly natural for a letter to go off and nothing in it to you therefore I scribble down a few lines, though dont promise to be very interesting. Mother went to Sisters to day. Rob and Nancy were over to day; also Mr Orr aunt Cynthia [[Claray?]] and Laura. Jim, poor fellow had no person to talk to but Ellen and Jimmie I know he missed you. Nancy is fat and can laugh as loud as ever.
Mrs [[Swann?]] is in a great deal of trouble [[just?]]

Hope you will find time to write to little me.

Sunday night, February 1 [year not written; possibly 1863].
Dear George,
It hardly seems natural to send off a letter without including something for you, so I will scribble a few lines, though I cannot promise much of interest. Mother went to Sister’s today. pages.text:
Letter Number 9 / Tuesday night Feb. 10th 1863
Dear George:
I received your letter of Feb. 1st this evening, letter, map, and all very interesting. Ellen was delighted with her letter she has had us to read it for her at least ten times this evening; you must write her another, it does her so much good as it does me to get a letter. I received your letter of 25th Jan. a week ago to day, and by a continuation of dates will try to answer them both in the same letter.

Well I believe we have never written to you about hearing from Aunt Rebecca [[Hymanns?]] folks. As Jeffie was returning from Ark. he camped with a man just from Miss. who told him, the Federals had overrun aunt Rebeccas neighbourhood destroyed her farm, and had taken her house for a hospital; her boys were all in the army or had been. Henry was at home on account of his haveing [[deleted: been]] been wounded at Ft. [[Donelson?]]

Letter No. 9, Tuesday night, February 10, 1863.
Dear George,
I received your February 1 letter this evening. The letter, map and everything were very interesting. Ellen was delighted with hers and has asked us to read it to her at least ten times tonight. You must write her another. A letter does her as much good as it does me. Your January 25 letter arrived a week ago today. I will answer both by adding entries to this letter on successive days.

I do not think we have told you the news of Aunt Rebecca [[Hymann’s?]] family. When Jeffie was returning from Arkansas, he camped with a man just arrived from Mississippi. The man said Federal troops had overrun her neighborhood, destroyed her farm and taken her house for a hospital. Her boys were all in the army, or had been. Henry was home because he had been wounded at Fort [[Donelson?]].
pages.family_note: This is the manuscript reading. The earlier typed copy in the scan uses Jessie for the traveler; the manuscript appears to read Jeffie. News of Rebecca’s family remains a secondhand report.

pages.text:
Mollie O. Sue, Laurer and myself all went over to hear parson Austin last Sunday. He gave us his views of the Millenium made a pretty good talk I suppose; but I didn't understand much of it; came home and heard Mr Orr had received a letter from Henry so we ate a few bites and went down to see what he had written; his letter was dated 21st and 23rd Jan. they were at [[deleted: illegible place]] [[inserted: Pine]] Bluff had been there only a few days; they left the White river country in a hurry; he said their cooking utensils were strewn from Brownsville to Little Rock their teams having given out so they could not pull them.
We have not heard Fayette and Jims fate. Henry wrote he had talked with several who had made their escape, who told him they had seen Fayette and Jim late in the evening on the first day of the fight, in the rifle pits all right then; that is the last account we have of them.

Wednesday night 11th Henry also wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell he had made his escape from Ark. Post

pages.family_text:
Mollie O., Sue, Laura and I went to hear Parson Austin last Sunday. He explained his views of the Millennium. I suppose it was a good talk, but I did not understand much of it. At home we learned that Mr. Orr had a letter from Henry, so we ate a little and went down to hear it. It was dated January 21 and 23. They were at Pine Bluff and had been there only a few days. They had left the White River country in a hurry. Henry said their cooking utensils were scattered between Brownsville and Little Rock because the exhausted teams could no longer pull them.

We have not learned Fayette and Jim’s fate. Henry had spoken to several men who escaped. They said they saw Fayette and Jim in the rifle pits late on the first day of the fight, all right then. That is our latest news of them.

Wednesday night, February 11: Henry also wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell, who had escaped from Arkansas Post—

—He said he had been assigned to dig ditches. When he saw the Federal flag over the town, he left. He was heading toward Little Rock and hoped to get home from there. pages.title: Lizzie’s reply to the opinions of George’s commander
pages.text:
Saturday 14th Feb.
Your letter of the 6th inst. came to hand this morning: glad to hear you were enjoying good health. Well, I find I must try to lengthen my epistles, draw them out spin a longer thread; in other words, try to compose a little. As for my ever becoming a newspaper correspondent, it is something to which I will never hope to attain: my brain is not full enough of ideas to try to communicate them to the masses, even if I had language at my controll by which to do so: but can't is a word, which should be in no ones vocabulary, therefore in the future, I will try to be more interesting.
You ask, “what I think of such opinions” as are advanced by your “Leader”, I answer to say the least, They are arbitrary, unjust and Tyrannical: Let such minds as these get in ascendency and have controll, and where is our liberty? our privilege as rational beings? I answer gone! and gone forever!
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 07-027, followed by 07-029. The Leader is unnamed on this page; do not assign a specific officer without corroboration.

Saturday, February 14.
Your February 6 letter arrived this morning. I am glad you are healthy. I see that I must lengthen my letters—spin a longer thread, or try to compose a little. I cannot hope to become a newspaper correspondent. My mind is not full enough of ideas to communicate to the public, even if I had the words to do it. But “can’t” should be in no one’s vocabulary, so I will try to be more interesting.

You ask what I think of the opinions your “Leader” expresses. At the very least, they are arbitrary, unjust and tyrannical. If such minds gain power and control, where will our liberty and our rights as rational beings be? Gone—gone forever!

pages.title: An angry response to military censorship and a longing for peace
pages.text:
Page 5th
I am sorry you are under command of one, who has so little feeling, so little humanity, and who has so much tyranny [[inserted: of opinion]] about him; if he really thinks what he says if he does not, I detest his moral principle as a man, and think him unfit for the position which he occupies.
If he was to see this I suppose he would be more of the opinion than ever, that correspondence should be stoped between the “utencils” of war and their, equally worthless, friends at home: for my part about all the good I wish him is, that he may never rise to higher command but sink to the position of one of the lowest high privates and then let him Tyranize over whom he can.
As for peace, it is what we cannot hope for, as long as the North chose to prosecute their present undertaking, and the South holds out with its Stubborn resistence. Oh! that the ruling powers would Stop! Stop and think for what this Strife is for! for what

pages.text:
Brushy May 7th 1863.
Dear George:
Laura being sick, it falls to me to write to you again this week. pages.family_title: Laura is ill; the family waits for news of the lighthouse fight
pages.family_text:
Brushy, May 7, 1863.
Dear George,
Laura is ill, so it is my turn to write again this week. We were preparing to go to church last Sunday when she developed a sick stomach. She has been quite ill since then, but this morning she can sit up a little and thinks she may write this evening. Everyone else is well except me. I woke feeling dizzy. [[A line about her health is lost at a fold.]]

I received your letter of the 8th through the 15th on the day I mailed my No. 12. Laura received yours of the 16th and 17th that day too. Hers was written just before the lighthouse fight reported in the Telegraph, so we are anxious for your next letter to learn whether you and Joda took part. If you did, I hope you are unhurt. The newspaper mentioned no wounded on our side.

We hope very much you have not been sent to Louisiana. Troops will presumably have to stay at Sabine, and perhaps you will remain there. It is uncertain: soldiers are ordered in one direction today and sent somewhere entirely different tomorrow. Stone’s regiment marched toward the frontier for three or four days before its orders were reversed and it was sent to Louisiana. We have heard that about four hundred men refused to go and there was nearly a rupture, but I cannot say how true that report is. From what I hear, the regiment is made of unreliable material, and I doubt whether its services benefit the Confederacy much.

If Joda gets leave, we expect him home in about ten days. I wish I knew you were coming too, but I have no hope of it—otherwise I would not be writing. Take good care of yourself—
pages.family_note: The letter reports a lighthouse engagement; it does not establish that George or Joda participated. The troop-refusal story is expressly a rumor.

pages.title: Reported death of Robert Jetton; Lizzie’s political views
pages.text:
Mr Orr got a letter from Mr Dyer the other day. He writes that John says cousin Robert Jetton died in Miss. three of Uncle Louis's boys, he says, were taken prisoners at Ft. Donaldson but had been exchanged and were back in Tennessee when he left there. John Jetton from inability, had never been in the army. I think John Orr must be mistaken about three of uncle Louis's boys being taken prisoners, for I do not think there were but two at Ft. Donaldson. But all is now hid behind the “vail of futurity”; when that is raised the picture may be sickening to look upon: how many may then be dead whom we have known since childhood, time alone can tell. O that this awful war would cease, and let those who are yet alive return to their homes.
It appears to me, there has lives enough been sacrificed to gratify the ambition of any man that has any heart at all but I suppose Lincoln does not care if the lives of every man in the South are sacrificed if he gets his beloved colored [[deleted: citizens]] liberated, and he can rule this Southern land. It is for who shall rule and who shall not they are fighting for, and not for the love of the union; but I think I would be willing to live under the rule of the Czar of Russia to get peace. Most any thing would satisfy me, but the setting of the negroes free here among us, that would be more than human nature could stand: if (old Lincoln) intends to make us and the negroes equals I want the South to fight him till he gets out of the notion, and then take him and make him serve in the capacity of one the ballance of his days. It seems all hopes of foreign intervention has failed entirely; and it remains now to fight fight till one side gives it up, or the other is conquered. I hope it will not be the latter for I do not think a conquered people could be happy: just think of a standing army over us to keep down insurrection. Should we gain our independence would it be desirable or not, I mean would the independence gained be desirable, there would be a standing army to support, a conscription term to serve if our president could carry out the views advanced before the Miss. Legislature.

[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
I got a letter from aunt Jane the other day. She and the children were well she said she had got a letter from you a short time before

Mr. Orr recently received a letter from Mr. Dyer. Dyer writes that John says cousin Robert Jetton died in Mississippi. He says three of Uncle Louis’s boys were captured at Fort Donelson, exchanged, and back in Tennessee when he left. John Jetton had never entered the army because he was unable to serve. I think John Orr is mistaken about three of Uncle Louis’s boys being captured; I believe only two were at Fort Donelson. Everything is hidden behind the “veil of the future.” When it lifts, the picture may be sickening. Only time will tell how many people we have known since childhood will have died. Oh, if this terrible war would end and those still alive could go home.

I think enough lives have been sacrificed to satisfy the ambition of any man with a heart. But I suppose Lincoln does not care if every Southern man dies, provided he frees his beloved Black people and can rule the South. They are fighting over who will rule, not out of love for the Union. I think I would accept the rule of the Russian czar to obtain peace. Almost anything would satisfy me except freeing the Black people here among us; I think that would be more than human nature could bear. If Lincoln intends to make us equal, I want the South to fight him until he abandons the idea, then take him and force him to serve as an enslaved person for the rest of his life.

All hope of foreign intervention seems gone. We must fight until one side gives up or the other is conquered. I hope we are not conquered: I do not think a conquered people could be happy. Imagine a standing army over us to suppress rebellion. Even if we win independence, would that independence be desirable? We would have a standing army to support and a term of compulsory service if our president could carry out the views he expressed before the Mississippi legislature.

Margin: Aunt Jane wrote recently. She and the children were well, and she said she had received a letter from you shortly before.
pages.family_note: These are Lizzie’s views, including her opposition to emancipation and racial equality. Her accusations about Lincoln’s motives are opinions, not established facts. News of Robert Jetton and the prisoners is relayed through several people; she herself questions the reported number.

pages.text:
“Between two evils choose you the least:” but as I said before most any thing would be better than war.
I expect you will be tired of this letter before you get done reading it so I will write a few more items and quit. Well I'm going to tell you somebody is married; and who in the world is left to marry, these war times [[deleted: there]] you begin to think? It is no other than Mr George Clayton and Livinia Andrews, after being engaged Seven years they have at last made out to marry; But he still is not ready to take her home I hear, he has to go down to where his tanyard is and fix up a house and prepare two months the report is before he is ready to take her home. Don Weatherspoon says Lizzie Chapman dared her Father to bring his wife there so Old Grady has gone to live at his wifes house. The report is Ed and Lizzie have bought the home place from their father. With an other item of gossipp if you wish to call it that I will quit and that is [[deleted: that]] your aunt Bettie Goodloe has another daughter. I reckon y that is as much as you can bear this time, so I must go and hunt Laura some more dewberries so goodbye for the present. Affectionately.
Lizzie

[[separate block: different hand, note to Joda]]
Dear Joda. I am expecting you home by the 18th of May and consequently will not write you a long letter this week but for fear you dont come I will put a word in Lizzie's letter to you. Yours per George gave me great hopes of seeing you soon. My only fear is that you may ere this have been ordered to Alexandria and if so I wont look for you till the war is over for I know you would come if you could. My health continues very good though Emmie has been puny ever since she had that colic of which I wrote you. I suppose Lizzie has told every thing in the way of news and this will have to suffice this time. if I get a letter that you are not coming I will write immediately. Hoping to see you soon I remain your devoted wife.
Susanna Bell.

pages.family_text:
“Of two evils, choose the lesser.” But as I said, almost anything would be better than war.

You may be tired of this letter before you finish it, so I will add just a few items. Someone has married! You may wonder who is left to marry in wartime. It is George Clayton and Livinia Andrews. After a seven-year engagement, they have finally married, but I hear he is still not ready to take her home. He must go to his tanyard, prepare a house and spend another two months getting ready, according to the report. Surely seven years should have been enough? I think so.

Don Weatherspoon says Lizzie Chapman challenged her father to bring his wife there, so Old Grady has gone to live at his wife’s house. The report is that Ed and Lizzie bought the home place from their father. One last piece of gossip, if you call it that: Aunt Bettie Goodloe has another daughter. That is probably enough for you this time. I must find more dewberries for Laura. Goodbye for now.
Affectionately, Lizzie.

Dear Joda,
I expect you home by May 18, so I will not write a long letter this week. In case you do not come, I am adding a few words to Lizzie’s letter. Your letter through George gave me great hope of seeing you soon. My only fear is that you have already been ordered to Alexandria. If so, I will not expect you until the war ends, because I know you would come if you could. My health remains very good, although Emmie has been unwell ever since the colic I wrote about. Lizzie has probably given you all the news. If I receive a letter saying you are not coming, I will write immediately. Hoping to see you soon, I remain your devoted wife,
Susanna Bell.

pages.text:
Letter No. 9.
Brushy Texas April 2nd 1863.
Dear Brother:
It has now been near two weeks since we received a letter from you; and you may imagine how anxious we are to hear from you, your whereabouts & C. as your last letter stated you would leave Galveston in a few days.
I cannot tell, why it is, we have not got letters lately unless it is the fault of the mails, as there has been a great deal of high water lately. Last Saturday and Saturday night it rained very hard harder at some places than it did the other big rain on the 25th Feb. but not so hard on Brushy as then: but it disappointed a great many people, about going to the quarterly meeting. Uncle Joes folks had been fixing for it for three weeks and Prudence was also making grand preparations for the reception of company, and allmost every body was “fixing up” to go to the quarterly meeting; but on Saturday morning the clouds, which had been hanging Sullenly around for the past few days, began to let fall their “garnered fullness” which soon made many a face, I have no doubt, look as gloomy as they. The consequence of it all was, the “magnificent meeting” as Mrs [[Thos.?]] Hillin would have it, was a “Sublime failure”.
I would have [[deleted: went]] [[inserted: gone]] Sunday any how despite the mud and water if it had not been, the horses, on that particular morning took care to keep themselves, clear out of sight: none up but Jenny, our new nag and you know I could not go by myself. Mary Orr had been nearly all week making a new dress to wear, so she was highly disappointed. Ann Kelly had all of her ribbons in a box ready to start down here, so you may be sure there was a “tempest in the teapot;” there. The miss Bransons of [[four?]] mile got to uncle Joes before the rain commenced so y[[lost: edge]] see there were a few strangers there. The miss [[Farrars?]] of Chambers Creek were also up, also Mr Duate, who has re[[lost: end of word at edge]] his health, and intends returning to the army soon I must continue

pages.family_text:
Letter No. 9. Brushy, Texas, April 2, 1863.
Dear Brother,
It has been nearly two weeks since we received a letter. We are anxious to hear where you are, since your last letter said you would soon leave Galveston. Perhaps high water has delayed the mail.

Last Saturday and Saturday night it rained very hard—in some places harder than the great rain of February 25, though less heavily here on Brushy. Many people were disappointed about the quarterly church meeting. Uncle Joe’s family had prepared for three weeks. Prudence was making elaborate arrangements for visitors, and almost everyone was getting ready. Then the clouds that had hung gloomily over us emptied their stored rain, making many faces just as gloomy. The “magnificent meeting,” as Mrs. [[Thos.?]] Hillin called it, became a “sublime failure.”

I would have gone Sunday despite the mud and water, but the horses kept completely out of sight. Only Jenny, our new mare, was around, and you know I could not go alone. Mary Orr had spent almost a week making a new dress and was very disappointed. Ann Kelly had packed all her ribbons, ready to come down here, so there was certainly a “tempest in the teapot” there.

The Miss Bransons from [[Four?]] Mile reached Uncle Joe’s before the rain, so a few visitors attended. The Miss [[Farrars?]] from Chambers Creek were there too, as was Mr. Duate, whose health has [[word clipped]] and who intends to return to the army soon. I must continue—
pages.family_note: The source calls this Letter No. 9 despite using the same number for February 10. Names at the lower edge remain uncertain or clipped.

Ann Kelly had all of her ribbons in a box ready to start down here, so you may be sure there was a “tempest in the teapot;” there. The miss Bransons of [[four?]] mile got to uncle Joes before the rain commenced so y[[lost: edge]] see there were a few strangers there. The miss [[Farrars?]] of Chambers Creek were also up, also Mr Duate, who has re[[lost: end of word at edge]] his health, and intends returning to the army soon I must continue

pages.title: Warren’s brief visit and four long months of separation
pages.text:
We were highly gratified, on tuesday evening last, by the arrival of Warren and Beck. Warren has about recovered from his sickness though he has not entirely regained his strength. They cannot stay long with us, on account of Warrens wanting to start back to the army about the first of next week. They will have to start home on Sunday next. We are very sorry of this, as we thought they would stay at least three or four weeks when they did come. But “to arms! to arms!” is the cry, and every man that can drag one foot after another must go. We have no late news from any where, every thing [[deleted: seems to be]] is a stand still in this way of news, but the war keeps going on there is no stop to that; and whatever raised such a hope of peace by the “first of March” and the “first of June” and the “first of July”; is more than I can tell. I have got out of all hopes of peace, soon. If Old Lincoln had ever meditated peace, he would not be enrolling his men from twenty to forty; and the South is not going to give it up, as long as they [[deleted: can]] muster a thousand men in my opinion.
Three O Clock P.M. Not feeling very well to day I have been trying to “snooze” a little and as I feel somewhat refreshed I will try to write some more, although I feel like I can't write any thing that would interest you. The ballance of the family are well and the health of the neighbourhood I believe is generally good, with the exception of Mrs Payne, who is now very low: it is feared she will not recover. Some of us will have to go over there to sit up to night. Sis Bell staid with us last night, the first time she has visited us since you left; which by the by is just four months ago to day. Four long months it seems to me more like a year. Lizzie Bell and Jennie have neither been here on a visit since you left They say they can't get time to come but they manage to get time to go every where else

pages.family_text:
We were very happy when Warren and Beck arrived last Tuesday evening. Warren has nearly recovered, though he has not regained all his strength. They cannot stay long because he wants to return to the army early next week. They must leave for home on Sunday. We are sorry: we had expected a visit of at least three or four weeks. But the cry is “To arms!” and every man who can drag one foot after the other must go.

We have no recent news. News may stand still, but the war does not. I cannot imagine why people hoped for peace by March 1, June 1 or July 1. I have lost hope of an early peace. If Lincoln intended peace, he would not be enrolling men from twenty to forty; and I think the South will not give up while it can muster a thousand men.

Three in the afternoon. I have felt unwell and tried to nap. I am a little refreshed and will write more, though I fear it will not interest you. The rest of the family is well, and the neighborhood is generally healthy except for Mrs. Payne. She is very ill and may not recover. Some of us must go sit up with her tonight.

Sis Bell stayed last night, her first visit since you left—exactly four months ago today. Four long months: they feel more like a year. Neither Lizzie Bell nor Jennie has visited since you left. They say they cannot find time, though they find time to go everywhere else—

pages.title: A verbal map of the farm and spring wildlife
pages.text:
I will not quarrel with them about it, of course; for if they do not want to come I will not want them to: but it pains me to think, that people whom I have always considered as friends, to appear so distant: not so distant either when we meet, for the always appear friendly and ask nay, beg me to come to see them, but I cannot think people sincere when every thing is in word, and nothing in action.
But “with these few remarks” we will drop the subject and wander on, and perhaps we will strike something more interesting. Father finished planting his six acres of corn [[deleted: just]] last week, or rather [[deleted: he]] Walker did: and this fine rain on it, I think it will do well, if we can just get it worked. Perhaps you would like to hear how the ground is divided off. We will begin at the west end of the field. Mr Graves takes the ground worked last year by Penee Nave and Walker; then Mr Dawkins comes in he has fourteen acres which includes the dewberry patch then Uncle Alf takes a few acres I don't know the exact number about four or five though, I think: this brings us down to the wheat. Father has left some ground just west of your wheat where he intends sowing the hungarian grass, then comes the corn and from the corn to the house and from the house to the Graves ground is left uncultivated I think there is about ten acres left for the weeds.
This has been a beautifully clear day. The wind is from the South plenty warm this evening to have both doors open. The cotton wood trees have leafed out enough to give considerable shade. And just let me inform you the varmints are getting pretty thick. I went out to milk the other morning looked down in the bottom right south of the calf pen and saw some kind of an animal I could not tell whether a fox or wild cat and I did not follow it, to make out its particular title.

[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
Mother staid with Mrs Payne last night she is no better

pages.title: Deer, conscription and a bitter observation about slavery
pages.text:
Friday 3rd. I got so sick yesterday evening, I had to drop my pen and quit writing. I feel right smartly better this morning and I think I will be well now. I wasnt very sick at first, but the medicine I took made me very sick.
The ballance are all well. Ellen has just come up to me and says tell Uncle George “just one more letter”.
I commenced telling you about the game yesterday evening. The deer have become allmost gentle; as I was going to the office the other day, I saw three, they circled around me about fifty yards off, held up their heads and looked at me as saucy as you please, while they trotted gently along. The turkeys appear to be very scarce this Spring; I have only heard one or two gobble yet: I saw a gang of six over the creek the other day, the only ones I have seen; directly afterwards Rob and his brotherinlaw Parks passed on down the creek after them, a gun awakened the echoes that evening, the first sound that had aroused them, for many a day.
I am very glad indeed, that the conscript let Rob off; for I consider him a good man, and very useful to the neighbourhood, besides, he never had any thing to do, in bringing on the present troubles; but alas many a poor fellow as innocent as he has to bear the trials and hardships in common with those that brought it on. But it is no use to talk about who brought it on, and did not now, for we are all into it: but a person cant help thinking about things: here is Graves and all of his family at home, and you off fighting for his negroes, a person can deny it looks hard: but let me not be ungrateful to Mr Graves, for he is the only one that interested himself about tending our ground, I should not have said the only one either, for Rob would have taken some I expect if Mr Graves had not.
I reckon I had better not ask you any more questions, as you were taken so heavily on account of my questions before. I think they were all put to it for something to talk about, to go to joking you about that. I wish you could get a good joke on that Capt. You can tell him old Mrs Partington heaved a sigh when she read he carried all of his wounded men out of the fray him self, and thought, “no [[deleted: doubt]] wonder the poor little delicate man fell down in the water, when that [[counchie?]] shoulder exclaimed Oh! my Susters [[separate block: side margin, continuing quotation]] if you dont take us away from here we will all be killed!!”

[[separate block: inverted upper margin]]
You must excuse this letter if it partakes some of my sickness, for I do feel pretty bad this morning you need'nt tell Evans what Old Mrs Partington said unless you can run a good joke on him by it. With my love to you and Joda I remain Affectionately Lizzie
pages.editorial_notes: Final leaf of April 2–3 letter. In the sentence about Graves, “can deny” is retained as read although “cannot deny” might be expected. The joke uses a difficult phrase read tentatively as counchie shoulder; no exact meaning or corrected wording is supplied. The next sentence names Evans in connection with the joke. The quotation runs along the lower and side margins.

pages.family_title: Deer, conscription and a bitter observation about slavery
pages.family_text:
Friday, April 3. I became so sick yesterday evening that I had to stop writing. I feel much better this morning and think I will recover. I was not very sick at first, but the medicine made me much worse. Everyone else is well. Ellen has just asked me to tell Uncle George, “Just one more letter.”

I began telling you about the wildlife yesterday. The deer are almost tame. On my way to the post office, three circled me about fifty yards away, holding up their heads and looking at me boldly as they trotted along. Turkeys seem scarce. I have heard only one or two gobble and have seen just one group of six across the creek. Rob and his brother-in-law Parks followed them. A gun awakened the echoes that evening—the first such sound for many days.

I am very glad Rob was exempted from conscription. He is a good man, useful to the neighborhood, and had nothing to do with starting these troubles. Yet many equally innocent men suffer alongside those responsible. It is useless now to debate who caused the war, since we are all caught in it, but one cannot help thinking. Graves and his whole family are at home while you are away fighting for the people he enslaves. [[The next phrase reads “a person can deny it looks hard”; its intended sense is uncertain.]] Still, I must not be ungrateful: Mr. Graves took an interest in having our ground cultivated. I should not call him the only one, since Rob would probably have taken some if Graves had not.

Perhaps I should stop asking questions, since you were teased so much about my earlier ones. They must have been short of conversation to joke about that. I wish you could play a good joke on the captain. Tell him old Mrs. Partington sighed when she read that he carried all his wounded men out of the fight himself, and thought, “No wonder the poor little delicate man fell into the water when that ‘[[counchie?]] shoulder’ cried, ‘Oh, my sisters, if you don’t take us away from here we will all be killed!’”

Excuse this letter if it shares some of my sickness; I still feel rather bad. Do not tell Evans what Mrs. Partington said unless it makes a good joke at his expense. With love to you and Joda, affectionately,
Lizzie.
pages.family_note: The passage about Graves criticizes the unequal burdens of the war and explicitly connects George’s service to slavery. It does not establish that Lizzie opposed slavery; her May letter expresses opposition to emancipation. The closing joke includes comic, nonstandard wording whose precise reference remains uncertain.

pages.text:
In Little Room Jan 28th 1863
Dear Brothers Warren & George
I received your letter of the 18th yesterday at noon we ar so anxious to hear from you all some of us go to the Office Twice a week & ar most all ways there the day your letters come as they arive most invariable on Tuesday or Friday, rain or shine some one is there. It has been very rainy for the last 3 weeks it rained all day for 2 Sundays Then in the middle of the week besides. Though it has not affected the well at all I think the old well is beyond cure. Every body else's wells ar full. The creek is runing briskly. Wheat looks tolerable well considering the dry fall, the ground is very soft since so much rain & the little Snow. We had more rain than we have had since last Spring the hog-wallows are all full it looks as if the drouth was over. if it is I look for better times for War & famine go together, now if the famine is over wont the war be soon Oh! I hope so.
I heard to day Lincoln has been killed Shot while in his carriage. now I cant give credit to this but Then it may be so. I wish it may be if it would in any way bring the war to a close probable if another were in power Thing would take a turn for the better. better or worse I suppose we must put up with it. We have no late news from Ark. All well last account. [[Darnells?]] Reg. has started east of this River to Vicksburg whether they get across or not is uncertain the River being full of gunboats. Nashville is not retaken. Memphis is. [[Hamman?]] [[Brinn?]] & Loyd were killed in that fight several more wounded I have not learned their names. Thus falls one by one of our acquaintances. [[3?]] of the Lancaster Co. have been killed several others died, will half get back.
I got a letter from Beck the other day of the 10th they were all well getting finely she had not got any letters relative to the fight up to that time. Mr Evins has not been down yet after the corn [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-042]]

pages.family_text:
In the little room, January 28, 1863.
Dear brothers Warren and George,
Your letter of the 18th arrived yesterday at noon. We are so anxious for news that someone goes to the post office twice a week. We are almost always there on the day your letters arrive, usually Tuesday or Friday, rain or shine.

It has rained heavily for three weeks—through two entire Sundays and during the weeks as well. Yet our well has not improved; I think it is beyond cure. Everyone else’s wells are full. The creek runs briskly and the wheat looks fairly good after the dry autumn. Rain and a little snow have softened the ground. We have had more rain than at any time since last spring, and all the hog wallows are full. The drought seems over. If so, perhaps better times are coming. War and famine go together; if famine ends, will the war end soon? I hope so.

Today I heard that Lincoln had been shot and killed in his carriage. I cannot believe it, although it might be true. I wish it were if that would end the war. Perhaps another person in power would improve matters. Better or worse, we must endure it.

There is no recent news from Arkansas; all were well at last report. [[Darnell’s?]] regiment has started east of this river toward Vicksburg. Whether they can cross is uncertain because the river is full of gunboats. Nashville has not been retaken; Memphis has, according to the news here. [[Hamman?]], [[Brinn?]] and Loyd were killed in that fight, and several others wounded whose names I do not know. Our acquaintances fall one by one. [[Three?]] from the Lancaster company have been killed and several others have died. Will half return?

Beck’s letter of the 10th said everyone was well and doing well. She had received no letters about the fight. Mr. Evins has not yet come for the corn—
pages.family_note: This reproduces Laura’s uncertain wartime reports. The story of Lincoln’s death is a false rumor dated January 1863. Her claims about military movements and captured towns have not been independently verified here. The final paragraph continues in the overlapping scan at 07-042.

pages.title: Laura’s pony, neighborhood parties and fears about conscription
pages.text:
some better allso I am independent about rideing now a Pony at my [[deleted: command]] [[inserted: command]] at any time convenience to consult but my own he is regularly drilled Cavalry Service. Poney know how to jump ditches & goles Right left wheel Charge & c & c
There has been several tow life Partys lately one at George [[Hoatters?]] one at Hursts. [[Magg?]] Lemmon attended (against her Mothers will) danced both places. Hursts was last Friday night next day they heard of Hammans death. The old man was in Lancaster when the news came he got drunk cursed & swore a round right [[deleted: swear]] afterward. how strange man will put no restraint on their passions even some girls ([[inserted: it is said]] [[Lemley?]]) got drunk that night at [[Hoatters?]] Party.
Jim Jeffries has returned from the Salt Works he could not get on big enough scale to keep him out the Army he took sick & had to come home I dont know what he intends doing. They have enrolled Dallas conscripts To forty all that would be enrolled. I dont know what will be done about those that would not be Nave & Bill [[B. Hill?]] ar the only ones I know of though I heard there was several others. nothing has been done or said as yet about them. Ellis is not being enrolled nor do I know when is enrolling day. [[deleted: There]] There is I understand a call session & the Represintive from here say he is going to urge the conscript Law To Sixty instead of forty. We are in a glorious place ant we. Let them extend to sixty then what who will attend to things at home. The prospects are gloomy there is now scarcely men enough to provide for Things what is the army to do. I am afraid There is suffering in the future. There is scarcely enough provisions in this part of the country to last till harvest Some of what is here has been [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-044]]

pages.family_title: Laura’s pony, neighborhood parties and fears about conscription
pages.family_text:
—somewhat better too. I am independent about riding now, with a pony at my command and only my own convenience to consider. He is regularly drilled for cavalry service and knows how to jump ditches and gullies, wheel right and left, and charge.

There have been several disreputable parties lately, one at George [[Hoatter’s?]] and one at Hurst’s. [[Magg?]] Lemmon attended against her mother’s wishes and danced at both. Hurst’s party was last Friday. The next day they heard of Hamman’s death. The old man was in Lancaster when the news came; he got drunk, cursed and swore afterward. It is strange how people fail to restrain their passions. Some girls, reportedly [[Lemley?]], got drunk at [[Hoatter’s?]] party too.

Jim Jeffries has returned from the saltworks. He could not operate on a large enough scale to keep him out of the army, became sick and had to come home. I do not know his plans. Dallas has enrolled men up to forty who would agree to enrollment. I do not know what will happen to those who refused. Nave and Bill [[B. Hill?]] are the only ones I know, although I hear there are others. Nothing has yet been done or said about them. Ellis is not enrolling men yet, and I do not know when it will.

I understand there is a special legislative session. Our representative says he will press to extend the conscription limit from forty to sixty. What a glorious situation we are in! If they extend it to sixty, who will manage things at home? Prospects are gloomy. There are already scarcely enough men to provide supplies. What will the army do? I fear suffering ahead. This district barely has provisions to last until harvest. Some supplies here have been—

Both write as often as convenient for [[deleted: Nothing]] Nothing gives us more satisfaction than letters from you. affectionately your sister
Laura Douglas

I have not yet got any envelops I have to turn or make them I hope I will get some when [[Carrol?]] goes To Cedar Hill
[[L. D.?]]

[[separate block: note signed Sue]]
Dear George
Take good care of yourself and and go to hear preaching if it is not exactly the substantial gospel perhaps there is some good even in the fine spun discourses which you have to listen to. When you get home I know you wont have to go to meeting if you are not inclined to do so.
Go down on the Beach and gather me some sea shells if you get time You can put a few in Warrens trunk for safe keeping.
Your Sister Sue.

[[separate block: note continued on 07-048]]

Both of you, write whenever you can. Nothing gives us greater pleasure than your letters.
Affectionately, your sister Laura Douglas.

I still have no envelopes, so I must turn old ones inside out or make my own. I hope to get some when [[Carrol?]] goes to Cedar Hill. [[L. D.?]]

Sue’s note:
Dear George,
Take care of yourself and go hear the preaching. Even if it is not exactly substantial gospel, perhaps there is good in those elaborate sermons. Once you are home, I know you will not have to attend if you do not want to. If you have time, gather some seashells for me on the beach and put a few in Warren’s trunk for safekeeping.
Your sister Sue.

Lizzie’s note:
Well, George, I stayed overnight with Phony last night, my first visit since going to Johnson. Spinning keeps me so busy that I hardly go anywhere. Phrony now says she does not want anyone else to go to war because Granville has gone. You know she used to think everyone ought to go because he was away. Gran writes hopefully. He thinks the war will end within six months and sees brighter prospects—

—around as grandly as ever. She is delighted that Cynthia gave her Jim, and can talk about old Branson until you would be sick of it. I have not seen the Red Oak girls lately, but, as Tom Roberson says, there is a strong likelihood that Ellen Petty and Higgins G. will marry. No more for now. Yours, Lizzie. No. 4.

pages.title: Joda sends cloth home despite scarce food and limited money
pages.text:
Dear Sue, I have been at work all day [[obscured: verb]] Cotton — consequently am very tired and feel but little like writing to night. I have been so buisy lately that I have neglected to write as often as I ought. I get Letters from you Tolerabley regular the last I got come in four days. I received a letter from Lizzie the other day She says she is well pleased with her new home She invites up to see her & to get something good to eat. If I can get off I will except the invitation if I cant get a leave of absence to go up and see her I will call on them as I go home. We are getting on about as usual plenty to do and but little to eat. it is hard to have to live as we do when we are in sight of such a bountiful supply of Flour Bacon and every [[inserted: thing]] & c. So it is I hope such a state of things will not last always.
I & George send by Dr. Lawrence two bolts calico [[54?]] yds in each bolt. I bought it at auction and owing to its being slightly damaged I got it at 26½ cts per yd; I think the stain will wash out if she ready if it dont an you have to tear it off it will be a good deal
pages.editorial_notes: First leaf of Joda’s note, signed on 07-051, accompanying George’s January 26, 1863 letter. The cotton-work verb is faded. Yardage is read tentatively as 54 per bolt; compare George’s statement of over 100 yards of each material at 07-053. The sentence concerning washing out the stain is awkward and retained rather than repaired in the direct transcript.

pages.family_text:
Dear Sue,
I have worked all day [[unclear verb]] cotton and am too tired to feel much like writing. I have been so busy that I have not written as often as I should. Your letters arrive fairly regularly; the last took four days.

Lizzie wrote that she is pleased with her new home. She invites us to visit and eat something good. I will accept if I can get leave; otherwise I will visit on my way home. Things here are much the same: plenty to do and little to eat. It is hard to live like this within sight of abundant flour, bacon and other supplies. I hope it will not last forever.

George and I are sending two bolts of calico with Dr. Lawrence, each containing [[54?]] yards. I bought them at auction for 26½ cents per yard because they were slightly damaged. I think the stain will wash out [[the following phrase is unclear]]. Even if you must tear off the damaged part, it will still be much—

pages.title: Cloth prices and Joda’s instructions for dividing the purchase
pages.text:
Cheaper than any I could have got by the retail; for Callico of that width is selling at 50 cts. we also send 2 bolts domestic upwards of Sixty yds. we paid for the wide 45 cts the narrow 35 it is of an inferior quality but is the best we could get at the prices. in fact nearly all the goods in market are of an inferior quality. I have saw one good lot of domestics [[inserted: sold]] them at 45 cts by the large lot. but little now in market. Me & George are equal Shares in the Stock the half of each piece is yours however you all can divide or [[deleted: illegible]] [[inserted: distribute]] to suit your [[deleted: illegible]] [[inserted: fancy]] the dark will make nice dresses I think. I would have sent you some thread if I had the money but it took all we could raise to get what we did if I have good luck I will soon be in funds again and if I can get off home I will try to get some more goods. I will write again soon So for the present good night
Joda

pages.family_title: Cloth prices and Joda’s instructions for dividing the purchase
pages.family_text:
—cheaper than buying at retail, where calico that wide sells for fifty cents a yard. We are also sending two bolts of domestic cotton cloth, described here as “upwards of sixty yards.” The wide cloth cost forty-five cents and the narrow thirty-five. It is inferior quality, but the best we could obtain at those prices. Nearly everything in the market is poor quality. I have seen one good lot of domestic cloth sold at forty-five cents in bulk, but little remains in the market.

George and I have equal shares. Half of each piece is yours, though you can divide or distribute it as you prefer. I think the dark cloth will make nice dresses. I would have sent thread too, but we spent all we could raise on this purchase. With luck, I will have money again soon; if I can get leave to come home, I will try to obtain more goods.

I will write again soon. Goodnight for now,
Joda.

I would have sent you some thread if I had the money but it took all we could raise to get what we did if I have good luck I will soon be in funds again and if I can get off home I will try to get some more goods. I will write again soon So for the present good night
Joda

pages.family_title: George writes from Houston about cold weather and short rations
pages.family_text:
Houston, January 26, 1863.
Replying to your letter of the 14th, I must hurry. It is sundown; I cannot write after dark, and I want this posted for tomorrow’s mail. We have had unusually cold weather for this latitude for several days, and it continues, although no rain or sleet has troubled us this time. We have enjoyed our stove and the frequent company of friends.

Rations are about usual for this season: plenty of meal, not quite enough beef, and nothing else. Soap, sugar, molasses, vinegar and similar things have run out. We still have some of “that,” but when it is gone we must fall back on “No. one” for supplies.

This evening Chas. G. went to [[Fox’s?]] soap factory to buy soap. The man asked whether we were soldiers and what—

pages.text:
Brushy Creek Apr. 2nd 64
Dear George
I got home on last Sunday Evening. I found all well I tell you I was glad to see them all. I took them on surprise for they had just got my letter of Mar. 15 telling them not to look for me, so my appearance was very unexpected. I found but little change in the looks of the home folks none of them appeared to look much older. I was glad to find them all looking so well. Ellen & Emmie have grown smartly. Little Mary is an interesting child & I think very pretty.
I must tell you something about my homeward trip. I was eleven days on the way I had to lay over one day at [[Bren.?]] & one at Houston at Beaumont I heard that our Batt was ordered to La. & that [[illegible: name or word]] were to go [[deleted: illegible]] Sabine P. to relieve

Brushy Creek, April 2, 1864.
Dear George,
I reached home last Sunday evening and found everyone well. I was so glad to see them. They were surprised, having just received my March 15 letter telling them not to expect me. The family looks much the same; no one seems much older. I was glad to see everyone looking so well. Ellen and Emmie have grown considerably. Little Mary is an engaging child and, I think, very pretty.

My journey home took eleven days, including a day’s delay at [[Bren.?]] and another at Houston. At Beaumont I heard our battalion had been ordered to Louisiana and that [[unclear name or unit]] were to go to Sabine Pass to relieve—

1863

Sunday morning: the wind is in the north it got there yesterday morning so I suppose by this time it has reached you. It is quite cloudy, but I do not think we will have rain to day. This is Fathers birth day: he is sixty two years old and enjoys better health than he has for years past, I suppose, on account of exercise. I will quit as I might run this into a “sister Jane of thousand words”. Affectionately Lizzie

George you must excuse me for finishing my letter to Joda on your paper but as we presume that each of you see the others letters we think it dont make much difference. Our paper and envelops are getting quite scarce as Warrall failed to go to Cedar hill to get us more at the stated time so we have to do the best we can. Lizzie has written so much that I dont know what else to offer. I think you are pretty severe in your criticism of her letters, but perhaps it will be an advantage to her in the end as it may serve to spur her mental capacities which would otherwise have remained dormant. Take good care of yourself keep company with the intelligent and [[separate block: right margin, continuing sentence]] well disposed kiss little white Lily for me and don't forget [[deleted: illegible]] your Emmie and little Ted. Yours Sue

[Corner annotation: 1863.]
Sunday morning. The wind shifted north yesterday morning, so it has probably reached you by now. It is cloudy, but I do not expect rain today. This is Father’s birthday. He is sixty-two and healthier than he has been for years—because of exercise, I suppose. I will stop before this becomes a “sister Jane of a thousand words.”
Affectionately, Lizzie.

George, excuse my finishing my letter to Joda on your paper. We assume you read each other’s letters, so it makes little difference. Paper and envelopes are scarce because Warrall did not go to Cedar Hill for more at the expected time. We must do the best we can.

Lizzie has written so much that I hardly know what to add. You criticize her letters rather severely, but perhaps it will help by stimulating abilities that might otherwise stay dormant. Take care of yourself and keep company with intelligent, well-disposed people. Kiss little White Lily for me, and do not forget your Emmie and little Ted.
Yours, Sue.

pages.title: George questions hopes for peace and describes wartime controls
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie
Sabine March [[30th?]] /64. No 64
As the month is almost out I thought I had as well finish it off by writing a day or two sooner than usual, not that there is any thing interesting going on but to pass off time. Bad colds were [[illegible]] in this [[illegible]] for I have quite a [[severe?]] bad cold. Somehow go [[ill?]] with me in this latitude than they did in Ellis, the only reason I can assign for the difference is, the cold in this section is damper.
Don't yell too fast on the Peace question, everybody is perfectly cool in this country; don't look for peace until one side or the other is completely exhausted, and it will take some time to do that. Report came here yesterday to the effect that the Yankees had taken Sabine Town and a battery with equipment at that place. (cant vouch for the truth of it, though I think it is generally credited). Sabinetown is 125 miles above here on the Sabine river, and about 100 miles due West from Alex. Taylors Cavalry have been ordered to La and have gone. All is quiet here and the Weather very good; We did have a cool norther but that has blown over.
Four men deserted from Bickleys Co night before last and went to the blockade. Somehow some of the rebs still have hankering for Sea life. This last act continuing in the service for the war in their present organizations all between the ages of 18 & 45 is an “eye opener” and rather gives the lie to the universal reenlistment of the troops on the other side. Well every thing has been done that can be done and that is some satisfaction. Firstly. Every able bodied white male citizen of the Confederacy between the ages of 17–50 is hereby declared to be in the Military Service of the Confed. for the War! & c
Secondly. Persons owning 15 able bodied field hands on the 1st Jany 1864 are hereby exempt, provided such persons sell all surplus provisions raised Year to Year to the Govt at fixed prices, & bind themselves to furnish [[100?]] lbs Meat [[illegible]] hand
pages.editorial_notes: Letter No. 64, continued on 07-063. The autograph date appears to be March 30, while later slip 07-061 says March 20; the reading remains tentative. The opening cold-related sentences are faded. Military reports and the digest of Confederate measures are George’s account, not independently verified legal text. The phrase field hands refers here to enslaved laborers counted for an owner’s exemption. The final quantity and wording are uncertain.

pages.family_title: George questions hopes for peace and describes wartime controls
pages.family_text:
Sister Lizzie,
Sabine, March [[30?]], 1864. Letter No. 64.
The month is almost over, so I thought I would finish it with a letter a day or two earlier than usual. There is nothing especially interesting happening; I am passing the time. [[Some words about colds are faded.]] I have quite a [[severe?]] cold. Colds seem to affect me worse here than in Ellis, perhaps because the cold weather here is damper.

Do not celebrate peace too soon. People here are cautious. I expect no peace until one side is completely exhausted, and that will take time. Yesterday a report arrived that the Federals had taken Sabine Town and its artillery battery and equipment. I cannot vouch for it, although it seems generally believed. Sabine Town is 125 miles upriver and about 100 miles west of Alexandria. Taylor’s cavalry has been ordered to Louisiana and has gone. It is quiet here and the weather is good; a cold norther has passed.

Four men deserted from Bickley’s company the night before last and went to the blockading ships. Some Confederates still seem drawn to life at sea. The latest act, keeping those aged eighteen to forty-five in their present units for the duration of the war, is an “eye-opener.” It rather contradicts claims that all troops on the other side voluntarily reenlisted.

Everything that can be done has been done; there is some satisfaction in that. First, every able-bodied white male Confederate citizen aged seventeen to fifty is declared in military service for the war. Second, owners of fifteen able-bodied enslaved field workers as of January 1, 1864 are exempt, provided they sell all surplus provisions annually to the government at fixed prices and undertake to furnish [[100?]] pounds of meat [[remaining wording unclear]].
pages.family_note: George is describing measures as he understood them; this is not a certified copy of the law. His report of Sabine Town’s capture is explicitly unverified. The date differs from the later identifying slip, and the exemption’s final quantity remains uncertain.

paragraphs.text:
Sister Lizzie
Sabine March [[30th?]] /64. No 64
As the month is almost out I thought I had as well finish it off by writing a day or two sooner than usual, not that there is any thing interesting going on but to pass off time. Bad colds were [[illegible]] in this [[illegible]] for I have quite a [[severe?]] bad cold. Somehow go [[ill?]] with me in this latitude than they did in Ellis, the only reason I can assign for the difference is, the cold in this section is damper.
Don't yell too fast on the Peace question, everybody is perfectly cool in this country; don't look for peace until one side or the other is completely exhausted, and it will take some time to do that. Report came here yesterday to the effect that the Yankees had taken Sabine Town and a battery with equipment at that place. (cant vouch for the truth of it, though I think it is generally credited). Sabinetown is 125 miles above here on the Sabine river, and about 100 miles due West from Alex. Taylors Cavalry have been ordered to La and have gone. All is quiet here and the Weather very good; We did have a cool norther but that has blown over.
Four men deserted from Bickleys Co night before last and went to the blockade. Somehow some of the rebs still have hankering for Sea life. This last act continuing in the service for the war in their present organizations all between the ages of 18 & 45 is an “eye opener” and rather gives the lie to the universal reenlistment of the troops on the other side. Well every thing has been done that can be done and that is some satisfaction. Firstly. Every able bodied white male citizen of the Confederacy between the ages of 17–50 is hereby declared to be in the Military Service of the Confed. for the War! & c
Secondly. Persons owning 15 able bodied field hands on the 1st Jany 1864 are hereby exempt, provided such persons sell all surplus provisions raised Year to Year to the Govt at fixed prices, & bind themselves to furnish [[100?]] lbs Meat [[illegible]] hand

pages.title: Civil liberties, prisoners and blockade-running news
pages.text:
Thirdly. Impressing officers will take whatever is necessary for the use of the Army wherever found at Govt prices, provided it is not all a fellow has and give some kind of paper pay for it, (no matter what, is the spirit).
Fourthly. All Confederate money West of the Miss will be taxed [[33⅓?]] per cent after the first of July (Now [[illegible phrase]])
Fifthly. The Writ of Habeas Corpus is hereby suspended in certain cases.
So at last all is gone step by step little by little of our public liberty to [[illegible word]] personal affairs, all is in the hands of the Govt.
This is something like [[illegible]] might have been anticipated from the beginning. The way things commenced and the way they have ended are in splendid keeping. The fuss was made about nothing, consequently had to or has to end in something. Wind blows higher from South, pretty apt to blow up a war shortly.
Griffin has gone to Galveston, don't know what for, to be absent Six days. Only two Howards have to wear the large balls, instead of three as before stated. Jackson & Doggett are only under guard for 90 days.
I would write to W. J. C. again if I knew where to direct to, tis reported here that they are ordered to La. tis a very hard matter to catch a cavalry man with a letter when he is always on a march or Scout. I directed to him always according to his instructions couldn't do any better of course. Ask Hefner what rank he held on Howells staff. The Steamer [[deleted: Isabel]] Isabella ran the blockade at Galveston, brought in a large quantity of ammunition arms & c, a few boxes wine for old Mag, also several Schooners have run in there recently. Confederate money [[illegible: remaining bottom line]]

Third, impressment officers will take whatever the army needs at government prices, wherever they find it, provided it is not everything a person owns. They give some kind of paper payment; the spirit seems to be that the kind does not matter.

Griffin has gone to Galveston for six days; I do not know why. Only two Howards must wear the large balls, rather than three as I said before. Jackson and Doggett are under guard for ninety days only.

I would write to W. J. C. again if I knew where to address him. They are reportedly ordered to Louisiana. It is hard to reach a cavalryman by letter while he is always marching or scouting. I have followed his addressing instructions and can do no better. Ask Hefner his rank on Howell’s staff.
