pages.title: George to his sisters: cold weather and desertion, January 11, 1864
pages.text:
No 51
Dear Sisters, Sabine Jany 11th 64
Another week has passed quite disagreably, considerable sleet fell the other night, the ground froze tolerably hard, the wind damp and chilly and all together disagreable. Today is cloudy and threatening rain, mud is abundant. It is all a joke about this Latitude being warm in the winter time it is not as cold as it is in Ellis but then the cold is damp thus making it more disagreable than it would be if it was dry. After all things considered we are faring very well for soldiers and should not complain. It is much more pleasant to be quartered in houses than it is to lie out without tents as they have to do out about Lavaca. Of beef and bread we get enough to live on tolerably well, fare we [[illegible]] a great deal better than some others.

Late advices from the east are discouraging, the yankees are jubilant and the rebels downcast, everything looks dark for the Confederacy, our armies are in bad condition and the enemy Vice Versa, our men all want to go home, the yankees say they intend to reenlist (See Tel, 8th Jany). The militia are very home sick and intend going home as soon as their six months is out, go where it leads. 50 desertions have occurred from our batt since the last big scout in Dec, it is reported that some of them have been taken but I am inclined to disbelieve the report, it came in rather a crooked way. The Davis Guards have continued to desert some eight or ten having gone to the yankees. As a Co they were moved by harsh treatment, for some slight offence one of them has been balled and chained and they say Magruder promised them that they should never be punished in so degrading a manner. They petitioned him to remit the sentence of this man, and he [[illegible: faded bottom line]]

pages.family_title: George to his sisters: cold weather and desertion, January 11, 1864
pages.family_text:
No. 51. Sabine, January 11, 1864. Dear sisters,
Another unpleasant week has passed. Sleet fell, the ground froze fairly hard, and the wind has been damp and chilly. Today is cloudy, rain threatens, and mud is everywhere. The claim that this latitude is warm in winter is a joke. It is less cold than Ellis County, but the damp makes it more uncomfortable than dry cold. All things considered, we are doing well for soldiers and should not complain. Living in houses is much better than sleeping outdoors without tents, as the men around Lavaca must. We have enough beef and bread to live reasonably well—[[illegible wording]]—much better than some others.

The latest news from the east is discouraging. The Yankees are jubilant and the Confederates downcast. Everything looks dark for the Confederacy. Our armies are in bad condition, while the enemy’s are the opposite. Our men all want to go home; the Yankees say they will reenlist. See the Telegraph of January 8. The militia are very homesick and intend to go home when their six months end, whatever happens. Fifty men have deserted our battalion since the big scouting expedition in December. Some are reportedly captured, but I doubt it: the report came indirectly. Eight or ten Davis Guards have also deserted to the Yankees. The company resents harsh treatment. One man was put in a ball and chain for a minor offense. They say Magruder had promised never to punish them in such a degrading way. They petitioned him to cancel the sentence, and he [[illegible: final line faded]].

pages.title: Resistance to punishment in Griffin’s battalion
pages.text:
Since the first, one or three more have been balled and chained and they threaten if they are not treated better they will give up the fort to the yankees the next time they come along. So much for so much, what the foregoing is worth remains to be seen, if the “Paddies” carry out their threat it will be a serious affair.

Great dissatisfaction exists in the Batt which threatens serious results, and if somebody dont back out some one will get hurt. About three months ago two men (not in Co C) missed roll call. The roll was called some fifteen minutes earlier than usual and before the drum beat. The orderly sergeant ordered them to carry some guns as a punishment for their absence, this they refused to do because the roll was called before the proper time. They were arrested and tried for disobedience of orders and sentenced to wear a barrel shirt [[20 Dy?]] [[inserted: twenty two hours each day]] and then ten days solitary confinement on bread and water alone. On the barrels was marked their names and the words “disobedience of orders and fatigue duty”. Yesterday the attempt was made to put the barrels on them when some of their Co came out with their guns to resist the enforcement of the order. The barrels proved to be too small and larger ones were procured by this morning. In the mean time however Col Griffin ordered the mutineers to be put in the guardhouse, this they resisted and a great many of the Batt promised to sustain them. This morning they left camps and went out in the country, thus abandoning their arms and cause. Col Griffin made a speech to the Batt and told them that if they resisted the decree of the court martial he would arrest all concerned for mutiny, and if he could not do it with what men were here he would report the fact to Magruder who would use every means in his power to arrest and punish them to the extent of the law. [[Shriver?]] as it would be mutiny to resist the order
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 07-065; sentence continues on 07-067. The first phrase appears to read “one or three”; it is not regularized to “two or three.” Duration of the barrel punishment and the final word/name are uncertain. “Paddies” is the writer’s derogatory term for Irish soldiers. All incidents are narrated from his perspective.

pages.family_title: Resistance to punishment in Griffin’s battalion
pages.family_text:
Since the first case, another one or three men have been put in a ball and chain. They threaten to surrender the fort to the Yankees next time unless they receive better treatment. We will see how much truth there is in this. If the Irish soldiers carry out their threat, it will be serious.

There is great discontent in the battalion. Unless someone backs down, someone will be hurt. About three months ago, two men outside Company C missed roll call. The roll had been called fifteen minutes early, before the drum sounded. Their orderly sergeant ordered them to carry guns as punishment. They refused because roll call had been held too early. They were arrested and tried for disobeying orders, then sentenced to wear a barrel “shirt” for [[twenty days?]], twenty-two hours a day, followed by ten days of solitary confinement on bread and water. The barrels bore their names and the words “disobedience of orders and fatigue duty.” Yesterday, when officers tried to put the barrels on them, some men in their company came out armed to resist. The barrels were too small, and larger ones arrived this morning. Meanwhile Colonel Griffin ordered the resisters into the guardhouse. They refused, and many in the battalion promised to support them. This morning they left camp for the countryside, abandoning their weapons and their cause. Griffin told the battalion that resistance to the court-martial’s decree was mutiny. He would arrest everyone involved; if he lacked enough men here, he would report it to Magruder, who would use every means to arrest and punish them to the full extent of the law. [[Uncertain word or name: Shriver?]] Since resisting the order would be mutiny—

pages.title: George criticizes discipline and doubts the Confederacy’s future
pages.text:
and the original parties having [[carried?]] it all quietly knocked under and allowed them to wear the barrels. Co C showed more disposition to mutiny than any of the others. Of the others or the men that came out with their guns to resist the order yesterday the Col declared it his intention to arrest if possible and punish. I suppose however they have abandoned the post a thing I would do if I were in similar circumstances, but I hope the time may never come when I will have to mutiny. Such rigorous punishments for such slight offences is having a very demoralizing effect on the army, it has caused directly near twenty desertions and it will cause a great many more. Griffin stands at least forty degrees below zero in the estimation of his command, he is despised for being so precise and military in his conduct, he governs men by the force of military law and not by anything like mildness: he treats them pretty much in the same manner an overseer treats his negroes, never has any thing to say to them only when he wants something done, this is the character of the man and I suppose he cant help it; but one thing I have learned never to get in a regt again commanded by a military man. All has quietly flowed over and it is to be hoped we will have peace in the command for the future.

I received your letter of Dec 19 the other day, and in answer to your query about Warren I can only say he is as big a fool as ever, he is like an old hard shell Baptist you cant convince [[inserted: him]] of any thing he dont want to be convinced of. Nearly everybody else is disgusted, and in my opinion the Confederacy cant last much longer unless some great change takes somewhere, something must [[deleted: turn out]] turn up that will change the whole aspect of affairs and that shortly or its “up” or “out”. Besides what I have already said I believe there is nothing new or interesting.

The comparison with an overseer explicitly invokes slavery. “Hard shell Baptist” is the writer’s religious comparison; no denominational identity is inferred for Warren.

—and the men originally involved [[unclear opening wording]], the others quietly gave in and allowed them to wear the barrels. Company C showed more willingness to mutiny than the others. The colonel declared that he intended to arrest and punish the armed men who resisted yesterday. I suppose they have now left the post. Everything has settled down, and I hope there will now be peace within the command.

pages.title: Impressment, defeat, and a faint hope of peace
pages.text:
From the reading of late official documents I learn that the impressment act is not working up to their expectations, apparently more dissatisfaction is expressed than was expected. Maybe Congress will repeal it, it would be a good plan I expect for taking things from private individuals by main force is a bad plan, if the people are not willing to support a government it is bound to fall inspite of all efforts made by a few to the contrary. If the people dont think enough of the country to save it themselves the policy is a poor one to try to force them to it.

The defeat at Chattanooga you will see will turn out pretty much as I predicted, it will cost the Confederacy Thirty Thousand men, and three fourths of them will be lost by prestige; look at the admissions made by the Houston Tel. Abe’s last proclamation is a [[tall news?]] document. As fast as the yankees get possession of the country the people will take the oath as prescribed by the proclamation. ’Tis a tempting bait to have security of persons and property guaranteed simply by taking an oath, which can be broke in two minutes after an opportunity is offered.

Morgans escape was a pretty “cute” thing and no doubt John will trouble the yankees a sight now yet. Dont you think that “[[View-au-Sie?]]” colors his pieces pretty highly, Somehow or other sensation pieces dont rate as high as they used to. &c &c.

With the slightest imaginable hope for peace this summer I remain affectionately George.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of January 11, 1864 letter, 07-065–068. Criticism of impressment, military losses, oaths, and newspaper reporting are George’s opinions. The name or pseudonym near the end and the phrase describing the proclamation remain uncertain. The letter does not establish the predicted casualty total as historical fact.

pages.family_title: Impressment, defeat, and a faint hope of peace
pages.family_text:
Recent official documents suggest that the impressment law—the government’s compulsory taking of supplies—is not working as expected. It seems to have caused more dissatisfaction than anticipated. Perhaps Congress will repeal it. Taking private people’s belongings by force is a bad policy. If people will not support a government willingly, it must fall despite the efforts of a few. If they do not value the country enough to save it themselves, forcing them to do so is a poor policy.

You will see that the defeat at Chattanooga turns out much as I predicted. I think it will cost the Confederacy thirty thousand men, with three-quarters lost through the loss of prestige. Look at the Houston Telegraph’s admissions. Abe’s latest proclamation is a [[description uncertain]] document. As the Yankees occupy the country, people will take the prescribed oath. Guaranteed safety for themselves and their property is tempting, especially when an oath can be broken in two minutes once an opportunity arises.

Morgan’s escape was clever, and no doubt John will give the Yankees plenty of trouble yet. Do you not think [[uncertain name or pen name: View-au-Sie?]] exaggerates his pieces? Sensational writing somehow does not count for as much as it once did.

With the slightest imaginable hope of peace this summer, I remain affectionately, George.

pages.title: George describes the march toward the gunboats, May 10, 1864
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie, Manhassett May 10th 64 [[illegible: letter number]]
The time since our last writing has been [[replete?]] with events of interest, and I suppose that before this reaches you you will have obtained the outlines of the news, so I will fill at once with the details. Last Wednesday night we got marching orders for Calcasieu, at sundown we struck and went as far as town, there we were supplied with three days rations of Crackers and bacon, each ones outfit then consisted of one blanket canteen three days rations musket and sixty rounds of ammunition. We were then ordered to go to sleep and in the long reeds [[illegible: several words crossed by show-through]] and commenced cursing the [[illegible]]. At daylight all arose and took up the line of march.

The first six miles lay across a bog marsh over which [[scores?]] of Stock had passed when wet and the walking was rendered more difficult by the rank grass. Here a great blunder was made by marching too far and fast without rest, several gave out to lie down in the first six miles. Our road now lay along a sandy ridge through a thin settlement where refreshment &c water could be obtained in abundance. At the end of the point 20 miles we stopped for the artillery to come up. pages.family_title: George describes the march toward the gunboats, May 10, 1864
pages.family_text:
Manhassett, May 10, 1864. Sister Lizzie,
Much has happened since I last wrote. You will probably have heard the outline before this arrives, so I will give the details. Last Wednesday night we received orders to march to Calcasieu. At sundown we broke camp and went to town, where we received three days’ rations of crackers and bacon. Each man carried a blanket, canteen, musket, sixty rounds of ammunition, and his food. We were ordered to sleep. [[Part of the description of the uncomfortable sleeping place is obscured.]] At daylight we rose and began the march.

The first six miles crossed a boggy marsh, trampled by livestock when wet and made harder to walk through by tall grass. We made a serious mistake by marching too far and too fast without rest. Several men were exhausted and had to lie down within those first six miles. We then followed a sandy ridge through a sparsely settled area where refreshments and water were plentiful. At the end of the point, twenty miles along, we stopped for the artillery. At four o’clock we resumed. About half an hour before sunset we passed the last house on the peninsula, with roughly eighteen miles still to go. [[Some remarks about the sergeants, captain, and next six miles are unclear.]] Around midnight we reached [[Oyster Bay?]], which led to [[illegible]]. We slept for an hour while the sappers and [[illegible]] built a bridge. The gunboats were still six miles away, and water three miles away. Every canteen was empty. [[Part of the description of thirst and grumbling is unclear.]] At the well we found nothing with which to draw water, so we had to march on without any prospect—

About midnight we reached [[Oyster?]] Bay which led to the [[illegible]], we snatched an hours sleep while the Sappers and [[illegible]] built the bridge. pages.title: The advance under fire
pages.text:
of getting any until the fight was over. This was rather a dry reflection in case of being wounded, on we went however and at daylight were in half mile of the boat. The force consisted of about three hundred of all kinds including [[Creuzbaur’s?]] artillery, the battery was planted and we moved off at double quick to the charge. The Infantry had been divided in to two divisions, three companies of [[Spaight’s?]] Batt with Co [[F?]] of Griffins under command of Capt OBrien were to attack the upper or lefthand boat. Co’s [[A?]], C, D, & E Griffins Batt were to attack the lower or righthand boat under command of Major McReynolds. Moving at double quick the four Co’s soon got mixed up together and rushed forward more like a drove of beeves than disciplined men. We had advanced about 200 yards when the batteries opened fire.

Seeing the confused state of the men the officers tried to get them in line, but no sooner had the command “Guide Right” been given than all [[deleted: illegible]] crowded over against the right guide and were getting directly between the battery and boat (the boat had not yet opened fire, we afterward learned the first intimation they had of our approach was the battery playing on them). The officers then commanded “Guide left” the crowd surged off to the left in a bunch. Seeing every man was pretty much his own commander, and every one had lost his place in ranks I concluded I would be my own general, I let the crowd go but continued forward in ranging from behind and before, for I knew the crowd would draw the grape and the shot and shell passed a few feet over me. I kept my eyes on the muzzles of the cannon in front and whenever one flashed I would fall a little quicker than I had ever performed the maneuver before. I kept on this way

—of getting water until the fighting ended. That was a grim prospect if we were wounded. Still, we continued and reached a point half a mile from the boat at daylight. Our whole force numbered about three hundred, including [[Creuzbaur’s?]] artillery. The battery took position, and we advanced at a run. The infantry had two divisions: three companies of [[Spaight’s?]] battalion and Company [[F?]] of Griffin’s, under Captain O’Brien, would attack the upper, left-hand boat. Companies [[A?]], C, D, and E of Griffin’s, under Major McReynolds, would attack the lower, right-hand boat. The four companies soon became mixed together, rushing forward more like a herd of cattle than disciplined soldiers. After we had gone about two hundred yards, the batteries opened fire.

The officers tried to restore the line. At “Guide right,” everyone crowded toward the right guide and began moving directly between our battery and the boat. The boat had not yet fired; we later learned that our artillery fire first alerted its crew to our approach. At “Guide left,” the crowd surged left together. Since everyone seemed to be commanding himself and had lost his place, I decided to be my own general. I let the crowd go and kept moving forward, sometimes behind and sometimes ahead. I knew the crowd would draw grapeshot. Shot and shell passed a few feet above me. I watched the cannon muzzles in front, dropping faster than I ever had before whenever one flashed. I continued in this way—

pages.title: Thirst, exposed positions, and breakfast under fire
pages.text:
until I was near the boat then I was in danger both of falling shells and minny balls, and as the grape began to go low and plentiful I [[obliqued?]] to the left and got out of range though in [[the?]] range. We were all in a hundred and fifty yards of the boat though not directly in range, the grape whistled pretty close. At last our fire was poured in from port holes from the minies and rifles until along the sides the feds could scarcely man their guns they kept up no steam and could not move the boat, the pilot wheel was so exposed no man could [[deleted: illegible]] live at it a minute, and the minnie balls went through the sheet iron around the port holes. Such was the condition of affairs half an hour after the fight commenced. I was so dry I could scarcely swallow and with dozens of others I lay down on the ground almost exhausted and rested. After I was some what rested we were ordered to save our ammunition and not shoot unless we saw some one whenever any one in the boat showed himself and the most quiet place.

In the position I was there was more danger from behind than from before for they were scattered some distance back in the grass and weeds firing. I had a great curiosity to see how things were going but this could not overpower the sense of danger. I had been in this place about an hour when the boat swung round broad side to us and we were ordered to fall back out of range. I kept close to the boat and [[illegible: route or movement described]] between the boat and battery and got out of range below her [[illegible]]. Feeling very hungry I called to Henry Collins who was close to come up and take a snack with me. We pitched in to a haversack of bacon and crackers in full view of the gunboats and made a pretty hearty breakfast. While eating a cannon ball cut down a weed

All well, affectionately your brother George.

pages.title: Food, gardens, and artillery drill, July 10, 1864
pages.text:
Dear Sister, Manhassett July 10th/64 — No [[77?]]
Your letter of June 26th came to hand last friday; and found us all hearty. Times are dry though we had a good rain the other day. We contrive to live pretty well for the times, had roasting ears and tomato soup for dinner dont you think that will do very well for a Reb? especially when it is obtained twice or thrice a week, we could live a good deal better if somebody would run in a load of garden seeds from some foreign port. Vegetables degenerate so rapidly here that in the course of two or three years they run out. I have been told beets will not go to seed here, and cabbage will only head the first year. There is no kind of vegetable here that is the same to be the natural production of the soil. Melons and grapes grow finely, I have seen tolerably good corn cotton and tobacco, potatoes sweet and Irish grow finely. Irish are about extinct, the people depended on getting seed from the north but the blockade shut down on that dependence and left them without. If I owned a place here I would have a vineyard. I think the soil here is well adapted to the growth of all kinds of grapes, mustang grapes grow spontaneously, the “French” grow pretty well in gardens. This is a fine country barring the musquitoes.

For the last three or four weeks we have loafed around camps and done nothing but this week a few more lessons will have to be taken at the big guns. Artillery drill is easier learned than infantry, but I dont like the way they rattle in a fight, they are what draw the balls bombs and Shrapnel. The latter is a spherical case filled with musket balls one side of the case is very thick the other quite thin, the thick side is put in the gun next the powder, the thin as a matter of course goes in front. When they explode the entire charge of balls is thrown forward scattering like an old blunderbuss and properly directed will kill and cripple all the men at a gun. [[illegible: concluding phrase; words “our cannon and” and “at Calcasieu” visible]]

Manhassett, July 10, 1864. No. [[77?]]. Dear sister,
Your June 26 letter arrived last Friday and found us all well. Things are dull, though we had a good rain recently. We manage to eat fairly well for these times: today we had fresh corn and tomato soup. That is good fare for a Confederate soldier, especially two or three times a week. We could eat much better if someone brought in garden seeds from abroad. Vegetables deteriorate so quickly here that their stock runs out within two or three years. I am told beets do not produce seed here and cabbages form heads only in the first year. [[The next sentence about locally grown vegetables is unclear.]] Melons and grapes do well, and I have seen fairly good corn, cotton, and tobacco. Sweet and Irish potatoes grow well, but Irish potatoes have nearly disappeared because people depended on northern seed supplies and the blockade cut them off. If I owned land here, I would plant a vineyard. The soil seems suited to all kinds of grapes. Mustang grapes grow wild, and “French” grapes do fairly well in gardens. This is a fine country except for the mosquitoes.

We have done little around camp for three or four weeks, but this week we will have more lessons on the big guns. Artillery drill is easier to learn than infantry drill, but I dislike being around the guns in battle: they attract shot, bombs, and shrapnel. Shrapnel is a spherical shell filled with musket balls, with one thick side and one thin side. The thick side goes toward the powder; the thin side faces forward. When it bursts, the balls fly forward like a blunderbuss and can kill or disable everyone serving a gun. [[The final phrase, referring to our cannon and Calcasieu, is illegible.]]

pages.title: Compulsory service and an unpopular inspection
pages.text:
For [[lawing?]] for angry Rebs [[Morrow?]] received some compensation but to what extent, according to the nature of the cases, I do not know. Almost every kind of cases came before him as to him another, some Lo Co [[gians?]] had themselves proved legally dead to avoid conscription. Everything between this and desertion came into his line of business. If men did not have to stay into and come into the service but very few would be in the ranks now. I confidently believe that if every man were discharged that would come in, in two months the yankees would be in every hamlet and village of the South. It is strange how men can be made do anything but they can be driven about by the leaders just like an ox driver drives his team about. News from Va is to the effect that Grant has been checked in his onward movements and that he has gone to fortifying and that he will have to take Richmond by siege. Nothing but from [[Johnson?]] and Sherman.

The other day we were inspected by an officer of Magruders staff a Capt with more conceit than brains and sense of both. There was so much grease on the guns he got his hands dirty which no doubt caused him a good deal of trouble, he presented quite a Dirty appearance and after inspection was over the boys began discussing his merits loud enough for him to hear. Some said he was [[illegible]] others Dutch others something else finally deciding however that he was Dutch and did not understand his business. He wanted to know of Evans if he allowed his men to talk that way. Evans who had not been paying attention to what was being said replied “yes he generally allowed them to say what they pleased”. He replied that would have to report us well armed and drilled and presenting a fine military appearance but in a very bad state of discipline. That chap wont want to inspect this Comp again shortly. A great many inspecting officers come around to see what we have on hand in the way of clothing &c and make reports to Hd Qrs but I never could see as it ever done us any good. Fayette is inclined to poke fun at me in the “Belle Lettres” department, However I think I keep ahead of “Websters Unabridged”. Affectionately George.

pages.family_text:
[[Morrow?]] received some payment for [[handling legal cases?]] for angry Confederate men, but I do not know how much; it depended on the case. Nearly every kind of case came before him. Some [[unclear designation]] had themselves declared legally dead to avoid conscription. His work covered everything between that and desertion. If men were not forced to enter and remain in service, very few would still be in the ranks. I believe that if every unwilling man were discharged, Yankees would occupy every southern village within two months. It is strange what men can be made to do. Leaders drive them around as an ox driver drives his team. News from Virginia says Grant’s advance has been checked, that he is building fortifications, and that he will have to besiege Richmond. [[The short report concerning Johnson and Sherman is unclear.]]

Recently a captain from Magruder’s staff inspected us. He had more conceit than brains or sense. Grease on our guns dirtied his hands, which plainly troubled him. Afterward the men discussed him loudly enough for him to hear. Some called him [[illegible]], others Dutch, finally deciding that he was Dutch and did not know his business. He asked Evans whether he allowed his men to talk like that. Evans, who had not listened to what they were saying, replied that he generally let them say what they pleased. The captain said he would report us as well armed, well drilled, and smart in appearance, but very badly disciplined. He will not want to inspect this company again soon. Inspectors often check our clothing and other supplies and report to headquarters, but I have never seen it do us any good. Fayette likes to tease me about my literary style, though I think I keep ahead of “Webster’s Unabridged.” Affectionately, George.

paragraphs.text: For [[lawing?]] for angry Rebs [[Morrow?]] received some compensation but to what extent, according to the nature of the cases, I do not know. Almost every kind of cases came before him as to him another, some Lo Co [[gians?]] had themselves proved legally dead to avoid conscription. Everything between this and desertion came into his line of business. If men did not have to stay into and come into the service but very few would be in the ranks now. I confidently believe that if every man were discharged that would come in, in two months the yankees would be in every hamlet and village of the South. It is strange how men can be made do anything but they can be driven about by the leaders just like an ox driver drives his team about. News from Va is to the effect that Grant has been checked in his onward movements and that he has gone to fortifying and that he will have to take Richmond by siege. Nothing but from [[Johnson?]] and Sherman.

The other day we were inspected by an officer of Magruders staff a Capt with more conceit than brains and sense of both. There was so much grease on the guns he got his hands dirty which no doubt caused him a good deal of trouble, he presented quite a Dirty appearance and after inspection was over the boys began discussing his merits loud enough for him to hear. Some said he was [[illegible]] others Dutch others something else finally deciding however that he was Dutch and did not understand his business. He wanted to know of Evans if he allowed his men to talk that way. Evans who had not been paying attention to what was being said replied “yes he generally allowed them to say what they pleased”. He replied that would have to report us well armed and drilled and presenting a fine military appearance but in a very bad state of discipline. That chap wont want to inspect this Comp again shortly. A great many inspecting officers come around to see what we have on hand in the way of clothing &c and make reports to Hd Qrs but I never could see as it ever done us any good. Fayette is inclined to poke fun at me in the “Belle Lettres” department, However I think I keep ahead of “Websters Unabridged”. Affectionately George.

pages.title: Bell asks Sue for clothing and describes unpaid wages
pages.text:
Sabine Pass Aug 31.
My Dear Sue,
Mr [[Erwin?]] will start home this Evening on a thirty days detail he lives at [[Steele?]] and will pass right by our house he has promised if I would write he would call and leave the Letter he says he will bring us any clothes you may have for me and George. I would like to have a pair of drawers for I need them very bad if you have any [[Linen?]] make me a pr if not you cant spare [[illegible]] as you will not have time to make the cloth he is home now [[Mr Saddler?]] and if you have time I would like for you to knit me a pair of mittens or gloves. Get one of [[lost: paper missing]] you made me last winter and if the other [[illegible]] I started back. I dislike very much to be put to the necessity of troubling you again for Something to wear for I know You have enough to do to clothe yourself and the children. It looks like the Gov ought to Supply the Soldiers with Something to wear it is too bad to furnish every thing we wear & fight for nothing for our wages are worse than nothing. To day we are due 12 months wages. I am about out of money I wish I had time to send you [[illegible]] you could put it to use it is worthless down here.

Every thing is going on about as usual down here the weather continues very hot Musquetoes very bad

pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, August 31. My dear Sue,
Mr. [[Erwin?]] will go home this evening on a thirty-day assignment. He lives at [[Steele?]] and will pass our house. He has promised to deliver this letter and bring back any clothes you have for George and me. I badly need a pair of drawers. If you have [[linen?]], please make a pair; [[part of the passage about available cloth, timing, and a saddler is unclear]]. If you have time, please knit me mittens or gloves. [[The next lines about an item you made last winter are damaged and partly missing.]] I hate to trouble you again for clothing when you already have enough to do for yourself and the children. The government ought to clothe its soldiers. It is too much to supply everything we wear and fight for nothing, since our wages are worse than nothing. Today we are owed twelve months’ pay. I am nearly out of money. I wish I had time to send you [[illegible]], which you could use; it is worthless here.

Things are much as usual. The weather is still very hot, and the mosquitoes are terrible—

pages.text:
day before yesterday we hear heavy firing In the direction of Calcasieu I do not yet learned what was the cause. The two vessels that were captured there have been disarmed and I learn one of them is Loaded with cotton and will try to run out. The Sachem is still lying here awaiting a chance to run out it will be almost sure to be captured as the Blockade is kept very strong now sometimes as high as six vessels are lying at anchor off this place.

I have heard nothing further of Col Griffins charges. I suppose nothing will be done with him until Gen Walker is here. he has become very Lenient since the charges have prefered he has made the guard duty less & he now speaks to men when he meets them in the street a thing he never was known to do before. there is now fewer men in the guard house than has been for a year. I havnt got a letter now for a long time the last was Aug 6 it came in georges what is the matter have you quit writing or not. I think it must be the fault of our mails. I hope I will get a letter tomorrow morning. George says all he wants is a pair of drawers. you must excuse this Scroll for I have had but a few minutes to fix it up in the Boat is now about ready to Start & I must close. I will write again in a few days [[illegible]] my love to all. Your true & devoted Husband J M Bell.

pages.family_text:
—and the day before yesterday we heard heavy firing toward Calcasieu. I have not learned the cause. The two captured vessels there have been disarmed; I hear one is loaded with cotton and will try to run the blockade. The Sachem is still here, waiting for a chance to escape. It will almost certainly be captured because the blockade is so strong: sometimes six vessels are anchored offshore.

I have heard nothing more about the charges against Colonel Griffin. I suppose nothing will happen until General Walker arrives. Griffin has become much more lenient since the charges were brought. He has reduced guard duty and now speaks to men in the street, something he never used to do. There are fewer men in the guardhouse than at any time in a year. I have had no letter for a long time. The last, dated August 6, came with George’s. Have you stopped writing? I think the mail must be at fault and hope for a letter tomorrow. George says he needs only a pair of drawers. Excuse this hurried scrawl: I had only minutes to write, and the boat is nearly ready to leave. I will write again soon. [[Unclear words.]] My love to everyone. Your true and devoted husband, J. M. Bell.

pages.text:
Saturday July 23 ’64
Dear Brother George
I recieved your welcome letter to day. Glorious news too! That [[reception?]]! Did not their hearts bound in acknowledgement of those suppressed expressions of sympathy? And does not my heart bound! And is the day far distant when a bounding of despondent hearts will be general. I hope not I almost believe not. But near or distant it will come! My faith in the overruling providence of God is that out of this great affliction he will bring peace; a calm, humble, thankful peace. This great nation the most arrogant and quarrelsome on the face of the earth has sinned grievously, and grievously

Saturday, July 23, 1864. Dear brother George,
I received your welcome letter today. Such glorious news! That [[reception?]]—did their hearts not leap in response to those long-suppressed expressions of sympathy? Mine does! Will it be long before all despondent hearts leap with joy? I hope not, and almost believe it will be soon. But sooner or later, it will come. I trust that God’s providence will bring peace out of this great suffering: a calm, humble, thankful peace. This great nation, the most arrogant and quarrelsome on earth, has sinned grievously and grievously—

pages.title: Rebecca hopes for reunion and an end to war
pages.text:
has it suffered for it.
If we suffer experience to teach us lessons of wisdom we may yet [[deleted: illegible]] and again be great united and happy. If rash and wicked counsels prevail we too well know that the bitter end is destruction. I do sincerely hope that the angry power of passion will cease and the voice of reason an reflection be heard and listened to and that this year will wind up with the things of the past this most unnatural war.

We are all well at present and thanks to our Heavenly Father Norvell is not in the war yet and with the blessing of God he never will be.

pages.title: Children, a journey to Eagle Pass, and crops
pages.text:
Mary and Elbert are going to school. Alice is nearly large enough. [[Fanny?]] is getting hearty though [[she?]] is very backward and “Sweet Henry” is fat and fine. My own health is very good I am fleshier than you ever saw me. Norvell’s health is tolerably good but he is very lean He is on his way now to Eagle pass. Roberson Rocket is driving one team “Any thing” Rob says “to keep me out of this war”. I will expect them back by the first of November if nothing happens.

Crops are indeed very fine as a general thing I will account for it in two ways In the first place large droves of negroes were run in here from Arkansas and Louisiana

At home, May 12, 1863. Brother George,
Yesterday I received your kind letter of April 20. I was glad to hear from you; I feared my own letter had not reached you. I am proud of your principles, George. Noble-minded people will respect you for them. When the clouds of war and the dark passions poisoning the air have passed, those principles will be a halo of glory around your head—or, better still, peace around your heart. They will never make you sigh with regret or blush with shame. If you die, they will be our only comfort. If you live, they will assure us that the hopes now gathering around you—

pages.title: Marriages, harvest, and concern for prisoners
pages.text: Well George Old Johnny Chapman is married to the widow Hogue and Jo Porter to the widow Strong and George Clayton to [[deleted: the]] Lavinia Andrews Gurlys reg. is dismounted and ordered east Stone’s men are nearly all at home fixing for harvest Wheat will be ripe next week. Corn is rather backward. Wheat is better than usual. As for war news we hear but little and nothing reliable. The Arkansas Post prisoners have never wrote back a word to this neighborhood it is said six hundred have died but I hope not so bad as that. I have nothing more that would interest you. Take good care of yourself you will be needed after a while to take care of the old folks and maybe some young ones Be a good boy. Goodbye. Rebecca.

Sunday Sept 4th ’64
Brother george I recieved yours of the 14th Aug some days ago Your opinions about the duration of the war and the causes likely to affect it are very reasonable or seem so from your stand point I will not argue the case but simply give you a detailed account of my visit two weeks ago to Mullicans neighborhood.
Well then I went down for the second time since they moved and took all the children. They were all well Martha and Matilda are nearly grown and very good looking modest girls Henry and John had grown out of my knowledge George and Orlando are dead. Thomas and Monroe are in the service
We saw Thomas wife and [[Coz?]] Mullican looks well. Mrs. Mullican looks badly. Mrs Vaughn and Josh Vaughn and Ruth and the children look very bad

pages.family_title: Rebecca visits the Mullican neighborhood, September 4, 1864
pages.family_text:
Sunday, September 4, 1864. Brother George,
Your letter of August 14 arrived a few days ago. Your ideas about how long the war will last and what may affect it seem reasonable from your position. I will not debate them, but instead describe my visit to the Mullicans’ neighborhood two weeks ago.
It was my second visit since they moved, and I took all the children. They were all well. Martha and Matilda are almost grown: attractive, modest girls. Henry and John had grown so much I hardly knew them. George and Orlando have died. Thomas and Monroe are in military service. We saw Thomas’s wife. [[Coz?]] Mullican looks well, but Mrs. Mullican looks unwell. Mrs. Vaughn, Josh Vaughn, Ruth, and the children look very unwell.

pages.title: A preacher interprets Revelation in wartime
pages.text:
Williams children look well
There was preaching at Mullicans house saturday night and at the school house on sunday; a brother Robinson preached. I saw Jimmy Myers and wife. Jimmy looks the same his wife is a large good looking woman. We met a one armed man going down and another stayed at Mullicans that night. The preacher seemed very zealous and appeared to understand the Scriptures very well
In a conversation at Mullicans on Revelations he took the position that the two Witnesses spoken of in the eleventh chapter are the old and new Testaments. That the days of their prophesying commenced at the time of the rise of the Roman Catholic church and that the period (1260 years) was out at the commencement of this war

William’s children look well. Brother Robinson preached at the Mullicans’ house on Saturday night and at the schoolhouse on Sunday. I saw Jimmy Myers and his wife. Jimmy looks the same; his wife is a large, attractive woman. On the way down we met a man with one arm, and another one-armed man stayed at the Mullicans’ that night. The preacher was enthusiastic and seemed to know the Bible well.
During a conversation about Revelation, he argued that the two witnesses in chapter 11 represent the Old and New Testaments. He believed their prophesying began with the rise of the Roman Catholic Church, and that its 1,260-year period ended when this war began.

He said the three and a half years during which their bodies would lie in the street are almost over. Then God’s spirit will enter them and they will be taken into heaven—meaning, he believed, that the Testaments will regain their proper place in the church and in Christians’ minds.
He interpreted the earthquake as the fall of a government, and the fall of a tenth of the city as the loss of the Church of Rome’s power. He connected this with conscription, claiming it interfered with the Pope’s authority because the Pope opposed Catholics’ participation in the war. He predicted that the Pope’s political power would end in 1866. A period of changes would follow, the most important of which—

pages.title: Rebecca considers moving to the Nueces, December 11, 1864
pages.text:
Sunday Dec. 11th ’64
Brother George
I suppose you have become domiciled again in camps by this time and perhaps the monotony of some lonely hours may be relieved by a line from me. We are all tolerably well my own health is not very good but now that winter has set in I hope to improve.
It has been pretty cold here since last wednesday and people are busy killing hogs as it happens though my chance for hog meat is pretty slim owing doubtless to the absence of the only one who was competent to take care of them.
My mind has been occupied lately with an idea of moving I think if I can possibly make the eddy I will leave here in the spring and go down on the Nueces

Sunday, December 11, 1864. Brother George,
I imagine you are settled in camp again, and perhaps a letter from me will relieve some lonely hours. We are all reasonably well, though my own health is poor. I hope winter will bring improvement.
It has been cold since Wednesday, and people are busy slaughtering hogs. My own prospects for pork are slim, probably because the only person who could look after the hogs is away.
Lately I have been thinking of moving. If I can manage it, I will leave in the spring and go down to the Nueces—

pages.title: Cotton hauling, cattle, and a proposed home near Fort Ewel
pages.text:
Norvell has wrote for me to come and bring the cattle if I can. I think that is a pretty large undertaking at this time as they are scattered every where and hands will be hard to get
Norvell aims to haul forty bales in the spring and as long as he must be absent from home he had as well try to make it pay. He has four teams now on the road or I suppose at Brownsville now hauling thirty bales at nine cents per lb from San Antonio
He will go into winter quarters about christmas. I expect to locate somewhere near Ft. Ewel so that he can call as he is passing and get a drink of buttermilk. He has a dutchman and two boys hired besides Rob and another man he bought two waggons and twelve yoke of oxen a horse and six shooters and Mexican blankets for $800

pages.title: Rebecca asks whether the war can continue
pages.text:
I have not been at Father’s since Henry left, I saw Laura the other day They were all tolerably well They were looking for Warren last night I expected to go over to day but was afraid to turnout in the cold
Well I dont know what to write about the girls as you didnt get acquainted with my pets All I can say is you must get acquainted when you come again by all means
Well George what about the war by this time, will it ever end and how, will the army stay there four years longer or can they? What remains for the South now but submission or extermination after all their boasts, and how long will it be before it will be every mans duty to think and act for himself? As for those bigots who would have our men killed our country wasted and our women and children brought to starvation it is time for them to hush
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 07-103. These are Rebecca’s contemporary opinions and questions, not an editor’s account of military prospects.

pages.family_title: Rebecca asks whether the war can continue
pages.family_text:
I have not visited Father since Henry left, though I saw Laura the other day. Everyone was reasonably well. They expected Warren last night. I meant to visit today but was afraid to go out in the cold.
I do not know what to tell you about the girls, since you did not get to know my darlings. You must get to know them when you next come.
George, what about the war now? Will it ever end, and how? Will the army stay another four years—can it? After all the South’s boasts, what remains but surrender or destruction? How long before every man has a duty to think and act for himself? Those bigots willing to see our men killed, our country ruined, and our women and children starved should be quiet.

paragraphs.text:
I have not been at Father’s since Henry left, I saw Laura the other day They were all tolerably well They were looking for Warren last night I expected to go over to day but was afraid to turnout in the cold
Well I dont know what to write about the girls as you didnt get acquainted with my pets All I can say is you must get acquainted when you come again by all means
Well George what about the war by this time, will it ever end and how, will the army stay there four years longer or can they? What remains for the South now but submission or extermination after all their boasts, and how long will it be before it will be every mans duty to think and act for himself? As for those bigots who would have our men killed our country wasted and our women and children brought to starvation it is time for them to hush

pages.title: Fear of requisitions, drought, and a hoped-for adobe house
pages.text:
Prices army has been beat back to Texas to winter I hear that for eighty miles this side Red River they are clearing up the country taking horses from two years old and mares and mules and oxen and of course all the beeves There is talk of them [[inserted: some]] coming in here for bread and I expect by next summer this country will feel all the horrors of war. It will make little difference whether we are invaded or not we will be stripped of everything unless peace is made. There is no use talking now we are fighting

It still continues very dry. We have had enough rain to bring up wheat but not enough to fill up the holes in the creek nor start our little well
You must write occasionally and when we get our adobe house built come and see us. Rebecca.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 07-102–104. Reports of Price’s army and requisitions are attributed to what Rebecca hears. Her invitation concerns an anticipated adobe house; the letter does not establish that it was built.

pages.family_title: Fear of requisitions, drought, and a hoped-for adobe house
pages.family_text:
Price’s army has been driven back to Texas for the winter. I hear that for eighty miles south of the Red River they are taking horses two years old and older, mares, mules, oxen, and all the beef cattle. Some may come here for food. By next summer, I expect this area to feel all the horrors of war. Whether an enemy invades may hardly matter: unless peace comes, we will be stripped of everything. There is no use talking now; we are fighting.

It is still very dry. We have had enough rain to sprout the wheat, but not enough to fill the pools in the creek or replenish our little well. Write occasionally, and when we have built our adobe house, come and visit. Rebecca.

pages.title: Winniford’s hauling work at Navassota, April 14, 1863
pages.text:
Navassota April the 14th 63
Mr George Douglas
Dear Sir I will devote a few leisure moments this morning in writing you a few lines by so doing I shall expect to hear from you. I am well at present I have bin here & at Navassota since the first of February hauling corn for Jeff Davis & Co. thay dont pay [[illegible]] much for my labour however I have got out of that [[snarl?]] now by engaging to hall them a load of Cotton to Browns ville. the give me ten dollars per hundred 8 in Confederate & 2 in Specie I have two waggons with me one of which I can do as I pleas with that I will load for a private individual at eight dollars in Gold
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 07-108. Strong reversed show-through and dark areas obstruct some words. Original spelling retained. “Jeff Davis & Co.” is the writer’s colloquial reference; do not infer a private firm. Rates are per hundredweight as written, with Confederate money, specie and gold distinguished.

pages.family_title: Winniford’s hauling work at Navassota, April 14, 1863
pages.family_text:
Navassota, April 14, 1863. Mr. George Douglas,
Dear Sir, I am taking a few free moments this morning to write, and I hope you will reply. I am well. Since early February I have been here at Navassota hauling corn for “Jeff Davis & Co.” They pay [[partly unreadable phrase]] for my labor. I have escaped that [[snarl?]] by agreeing to haul a load of cotton to Brownsville. They will pay $10 per hundredweight: $8 in Confederate money and $2 in coin. I have two wagons. I can use one as I choose, so I will load it for a private individual at $8 in gold.

pages.title: Request to buy Collins’s oxen before the Brownsville trip
pages.text:
I received a letter from home yesterday morning dated March 24th all wear well at that time no news of importance I Shall stay here tweleve or ten days yet before I Start to Brownsville. J. H. Collins has a yoke of oxen runing on Danville I want you to see him and know if he will sell them and lets me know his price and if it is not to mutch I will send you the money to by them for me
Give my best respects to J. M. Bell & Warren Also to Collins write to me
I am
[[N. B.?]] Winniford
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 07-107. Signature initials remain tentative. “Tweleve or ten” is retained in its original order. Danville is the visible place name; no location beyond the letter is inferred.

pages.family_title: Request to buy Collins’s oxen before the Brownsville trip
pages.family_text:
Yesterday morning I received a letter from home dated March 24. Everyone was well, and there was no important news. I will stay another ten or twelve days before leaving for Brownsville. J. H. Collins has a pair of oxen on the range at Danville. Please ask whether he will sell them and tell me his price. If it is reasonable, I will send you the money to buy them.
Give my regards to J. M. Bell, Warren, and Collins. Write to me. Yours, [[N. B.?]] Winniford.

pages.family_title: Furloughs, desertions, and recruiting at Dallas, March 5, 1864
pages.family_text:
Brushy, March 5, 1864. No. 5. Brother George,
Your letter of February 21 and another of the same date arrived [[details obscured]]. We were glad and surprised to hear that the socks arrived quickly and safely. We are also glad that some [[leave appears to be discussed, but text is damaged]] may finally be granted. A remark about “a burning” and what prompted headquarters to consider the men’s happiness is partly unreadable.
[[First name obscured]] Walker is home on leave. He says the brigade numbered 1,500 in November and now has 700. Men are being granted leave; a partly obscured remark connects this with desertion and headquarters.
Father visited [[name obscured]], who is home on short leave and hopes to be assigned to making shoes at Dallas. If he cannot obtain that assignment and must return to service, he wants to join your company with you, Joda, and Warren. Father asks you to consult Warren, find out whether the company is full, and write promptly. Send the names and locations of recruiting officers who are home.
The brigade is now scouting—or, as the writer puts it, helping friends “into the service.” The state has been divided into four districts; Dallas is headquarters for one. [[Name obscured]] feels fortunate to live nearby, but the writer doubts he will remain safe from recruitment. Coggins’s company, including Frank Farrer and Hal [[surname obscured]], is home on ten days’ leave. [[Further details obscured.]] Harper Goodloe is home. I have not seen him, but people say he has grown a great deal. He had room to grow, did he not?
[[Marginal writing cannot be read securely.]]
pages.family_note: Much of this page is physically obscured. The readable version retains gaps rather than supplying names or completing damaged arguments.

pages.family_title: Accusations of horse theft and hopes that cotton trade would end the war
pages.family_text:
It seems that at least some of Parsons’s men have taken to stealing. One of [[name obscured]] Branch’s or Beack’s sons [[name syntax unclear]], and a son of old [[name unreadable]], have been convicted. The punishment described is conscription into the infantry. One of [[Mr.?]] Hull’s sons was involved but escaped; his whereabouts are obscured.
Our fashionable friend James Hancock was involved in the same business, but the horse he took had [[partly obscured, apparently a “C. S.” brand]], which saved him. People say taking horses from “Feds”—meaning Unionist civilians—is [[qualification obscured]], but the men sometimes take our own people’s horses. The writer reports an argument in Coggins’s company: if the Yankees held Dallas, Confederate soldiers could take horses between [[places obscured]] to keep them from the enemy. Much of the argument is lost. The writer condemns the men’s conduct and fears that by the war’s end it will be a disgrace to be called one of Parsons’s men.
Laura received a letter from Squire today, dated [[obscured]], so the report that he deserted is mistaken. The writer distinguishes Coggins’s company’s connection to Parsons’s regiment or brigade, but part of the explanation is lost. A Saturday-night addition mentions a severe cold and Mother’s plans [[obscured]].

Mother is busy making candles. The closing passage sends her reassurance: she believes the scouts moving through the country are connected with cotton for “old Jeff” and sales to the Yankees, and that completing this will end the war and bring the men home. [[Important parts of the explanation are obscured.]] Keep your spirits up and do not become [[obscured]]. Henry Morris told Father about cotton from the Texas coast and men being allowed [[obscured]] without conscription trouble. Harper Goodloe reports [[obscured]] from the mouth of the Red River; the last lines mention gunboats but cannot be read as a complete statement.
pages.family_note: The page contains accusations and wartime rumors. Extensive damage prevents a complete reading; none of the accusations has been independently verified in this transcription.

pages.family_text:
185[[4?]]: Received from James Bass of Rutherford County, Tennessee, a fifty-dollar bill issued by the Union Bank of Tennessee. I also received a twenty-dollar bill on that bank from Peyton Smith for Bass. The money is to pay taxes and charges due on Bass’s Texas land:

4,428 acres in “McClellan” County, between Turtle Bayou and Tahuacany Creek, granted to Reuben Woods as assignee of Wm. H. Steel.
1,280 acres in Dallas County on the Trinity River, granted to James Tally.
4,605 acres on Bois D’ark, or Red Oak Creek, in Ellis County, granted to Wm. Allen.

Taxes paid in full, according to the assessor’s receipt:
1851: $7.38.
1852: $9.53.
1853: $12.56.
1854: $20.72.
1855: $25.19.
1856: $10.00.

This uses the full amount of the deposits left with me. April 17, 1857. N. L. Douglas.

Separate entry: Mr. R. P. Ransom deposited $20 on June 12, 1851, and $13.21 remained to pay taxes for 1855, making $33.21 in all.

pages.family_title: State and Confederate tax receipts, 1861–1864
pages.family_text:
The upper receipt records $9.82 received from Mr. N. L. Douglass for 1861 state and county taxes. It is dated May 9, 186[[last digit clipped]]. The property line includes $150 in coin, but the remaining abbreviations and part of the collector’s name are unreadable.

War tax receipt, May 9, 1862: Received from N. L. Douglass 45 cents in specie and sixteen dollars in Confederate Treasury notes, totaling $16.45, as full payment of his war tax for 1861. The collector’s name reads J. M. McCau[[ntt?]], district 41.

The third receipt records $3.12 paid by N. L. Douglas for [[principal’s name uncertain]] for state, special, and county tax in Ellis County. The tax year is 186[[unreadable]]. The payment date ends in 1864; the collector’s signature and the rest of the date are too faint to read.

Confederate receipt No. 192, May 5, 1864: Payment in Confederate Treasury notes for 1863 tax “on his Stock,” in the name [[N. L. ... Douglas?]]. The banner appears to give $22.59, while the written amount appears to be twenty-one dollars and 59 cents. Both readings are retained. The collector’s signature is unclear; the district is 51. A separate handwritten figure above the heading reads 27.56.
pages.family_note: A tax receipt records a payment. It does not by itself establish military service, political beliefs, or what the word “stock” included.

pages.family_title: Sarah E. Barr writes about marriage and childhood friendship, May 25
pages.family_text:
Lewis County, Tennessee, May 25, [[1854?]].
Miss [[S.?]] Douglass,
I take up my pen to let you know that I am well, and I hope you will be well when this reaches you. A few days ago I received your letter dated April 23. I was pleased to hear that you were well.

I am not married yet and do not know when I will be. There is more prospect of it now than when I last wrote, but I can tell you it will still be about three years. I have promised myself to someone in [[Raugherford—probably Rutherford?]], and I expect to wait for him. His letter reached me on the same day as yours.

When you are going to marry, send me word—and hurry up and get married! But do not stop writing to me as you have before. I love you as much as if you were here with me, because we grew up together as beloved children. We are a long way apart now, but I hope we will not forget each other until death takes us away.
pages.family_note: This is a reading of Sarah’s words, not proof of a particular marriage or of the addressee’s identity. The date, initial and place reading remain provisional.

pages.family_title: Sarah E. Barr: grandmother’s advice and news from home
pages.family_text:
Grandmother sends her love. She says she remembers you and advises you to marry, but not to pick up just any “snip” who comes along. She does not believe you would, though; she is giving you a little advice.

A letter from home last week said that everyone was well except Frank, who had the chills. [[D. C. Annatts?]] is going to marry and, for all I know, may be married by now. Sis Smith is married. Harriet Waddkins has married a man named Hayes. The next clause reads “and Harriets by the name of Farmer”; whose marriage this describes is unclear.

I want to go home, but I cannot get there until Pa comes for me. I expect him around September, though I cannot say when.

Do not forget to write. Write soon, and direct your letter to the same post office as before. Give my love to your father, mother, sisters and brothers. I have written all I have to say, so farewell for a while. Write as soon as you receive this.
Very respectfully,
Sarah E. Barr.

pages.title: A land warrant sold and news of cholera, June 5, 1854
pages.text:
Murfreesboro Rutherford County Tenn June 5th 1854
Mr N. L. Douglass my old and tried friend your letter dated April the 25th [[inserted: came to hand on the 27th of May]] enclosing an eighty acre land warrant regularly transferred, with the request that I would dispose of it to the best advantage and pay the proceeds to Mr G. A. Sublett, which request was attended to with as much punctuality as the nature of the case would admit of. which you will learn from his receipt which you will find herein enclosed. I sent the warrant to Nashville, and ninety dollars is the highest price that can be commanded in that market, the speculators commanding ninety three in New York. I have reserved a copy of the receipt to guard against miscarriage or other accidents

By the by our old friend Sublett continues in bad health I think his constitution is perfectly prostrate and that he never will regain any thing like general health again. I would here remark that the Cholera made its debut upon the City of Nashville on or about the 26th of last month, and also at several places in this County, more especially the west end of this County adjoining Davidson. There have been fifteen or twenty died in Nashville in two or three days when it first broke out, and also about the same number in this County, but it has some what abated (the weather having become more favorable to health) still there is a spirit of apprehension resting upon the bosom of the community

pages.family_title: A land warrant sold and news of cholera, June 5, 1854
pages.family_text:
Murfreesboro, Rutherford County, Tennessee, June 5, 1854.
Mr. N. L. Douglass, my old and trusted friend,
Your letter dated April 25 reached me on May 27. It enclosed a properly transferred warrant for eighty acres of land and asked me to sell it for the best price I could obtain and pay the proceeds to Mr. G. A. Sublett. I carried out your request as promptly as circumstances allowed. His receipt, enclosed here, will show you this.

I sent the warrant to Nashville. Ninety dollars is the highest price obtainable in that market, while speculators obtain ninety-three in New York. I have kept a copy of the receipt in case the original is lost in the mail or another accident occurs.

Our old friend Sublett remains in poor health. I think his constitution is exhausted and that he will never regain anything like his former health.

Cholera appeared in Nashville around the twenty-sixth of last month and also in several places in this county, especially its western end adjoining Davidson County. Fifteen or twenty people died in Nashville in the first two or three days of the outbreak, and about the same number died in this county. It has eased somewhat as the weather has become more favorable to health, but the community remains afraid.
pages.family_note: The warrant concerns eighty acres; $90 is its reported sale-market value. The letter’s disease explanation and mortality estimates are preserved as historical testimony, not modern medical findings.

pages.family_text:
Anderson Ott has sold his small farm near town and bought about 150 acres ten miles southeast of town on the Manchester turnpike. He and his family are well. Nat Ott runs a shop, but his health is very delicate. A year ago last spring he had a dangerous hemorrhage from his lungs, and it returned slightly this spring. In my opinion he is bleeding internally while working at his trade. His family is well at present.

Old Mr. John Ott died near the end of January or the beginning of February. At the children’s request, Nat is administering the estate. A suit is pending in Chancery Court between the heirs over the division of enslaved people and their children whom John Ott had set aside for the heirs some years earlier, to be divided at his death. The writer says that “Abate,” who already held a share when John died, refuses to surrender them for division. The wording around this name is difficult.

Mr. [[Wm Harrison?]] and his family are well and doing as well as anyone could wish.

Many of our longtime citizens have died since you left the county, including Major Gannaway, Jack Ransom, R. Halliburten and many others.

You have no doubt heard about Colonel Sam Richardson’s killing of Dr. W. Smith. I regard it as an extremely cold-blooded murder. At his first trial he was sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary, but he obtained a new trial, which has not yet taken place.

pages.title: Hicks reports on Murfreesboro and sends regards
pages.text:
He then is lying in jail. Your Kind folks on the river and Mr Nance below this from my best information are all well. I saw Lewis Jetton and Lady in Town a week or ten days since they were well. Murfreesboro has improved much both in appearance and population since you left here besides the Male College we now have two fine female colleges. The Methodist female college is considered one of the finest buildings in the west cost about twenty thousand dollars. This the second Session will close with about 160 Scholars.

My family have enjoyed general good health since you left this community. Should it be in my power to serve you in this country at any time draw upon my Services with confidence. Nothing further at present but Gods blessing upon you and yours. My love to your Lady and family
[[Wm D. Hicks?]]

He is now in jail. As far as I know, your kinfolk on the river and Mr. Nance below here are all well. I saw Lewis Jetton and his wife in town a week or ten days ago, and they were well.

Murfreesboro has grown considerably in appearance and population since you left. Besides the male college, we now have two fine female colleges. The Methodist female college is considered one of the finest buildings in the West and cost about $20,000. Its second session will end with about 160 students.

My family has generally enjoyed good health since you left this community. If I can do anything for you in this part of the country, call on me with confidence. I have nothing more to add, except to ask God’s blessing on you and yours. My love to your wife and family.
[[Wm D. Hicks?]]

pages.family_text:
Readyville, October 16, 1849.
Dear Sir,
I have delayed writing because others were writing to you and I did not want to repeat their news. My family has been sick all summer and fall with the flux, except [[damaged wording]] our son Robert. By heaven’s blessing, we are all up and about again. Rebeca’s health is now reasonably good, and she is as well filled out as ever. Our baby, who is being raised by hand, has grown very well.

The rest of our friends are well. Newton’s family has been with us since June and will leave for home in a few days. I answered your last letter, but I gather from yours that you had not [[received it?]].

My wife wrote a long letter in answer to Rebeca’s message, describing the death of our beloved daughters and her suffering at that time. Christian fortitude was all that saved her own life. My own heart was almost broken, but I hid it from my wife and tried to reason with and comfort her: we had others to live for, and we must let the Lord’s will be done. Yet even mentioning the beloved name Mary still makes the tears flow freely. May we all remember that a similar fate awaits us too.
pages.family_note: “Flux” is the source’s term for the illness. “Raised by hand” is retained as historical wording for infant care. The damaged passage, identities and exact circumstances of the deaths remain unresolved.

pages.family_title: Plans for Texas, a reported killing, and family news
pages.family_text:
Sam has written from Alabama. Before leaving for home, he had a dispute with Parson Drew, struck him with a piece of fence paling, and killed him. Sam says he acted in self-defense. I saw a newspaper report saying Drew was the aggressor. Sam is considering returning, surrendering to the authorities, and standing trial; otherwise he will go to California. He remained there for two weeks without being arrested and has now been home for four weeks without hearing from there. Fletcher is to write shortly, and then Sam will know what to do. Sam believes his actions were entirely justified.

[[J. Orr?]] still wants to go to Texas, but cannot go this fall because Cynthia gave birth to a son a few days ago—unless he travels by water. Theodosia Nance is expecting a child any day, so that household will not move this fall either.

Mrs. Gresham and Betsy are getting along badly and are quite unhappy. Hostility still exists between Julia and Orr. I long for peace.

The land was sold on the tenth of this month for $6.50 an acre, amounting to about $831 in all, with payment on one- and two-year credit. There has not yet been [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The fragment preceding Mrs. Gresham is unclear. No identities or family connections are added beyond the letter. The report of a killing and the statements about fault remain the writer’s account.

[[Continuing the land-sale account: no arrangement has yet been]] made for a division. Whenever there is one, I will act for you and myself.

Look out in December for Wm. Geasling and John Pace. They left on the tenth for your neighborhood. McCracken sent some dogs to do your barking. A following remark about Geasling, “Rough Coat” and “a Sharp face” cannot be read well enough to interpret reliably.

Malcom Smith leaves a week from Monday and says he intends to eat Christmas dinner with you. Oaks has failed to sell his land and will not leave this fall. Others are waiting to see how you get along after emigrating. The blacksmith Wm. Boyce has started for Cherokee County with two of the Mr. McKnights. Orr thinks he may travel by water in the spring.

You have heard how near cholera came to us. There were 119 deaths in Lebanon. The writer then gives a total of thirty people who died in [[Rutherford?]], including people you know: [[Gann?]] Mathews, old [[Mrs.?]] Wade, and Peter Holton. There was no case in Murfreesboro, according to the letter.

My son Granville has been in college all year. He says he will go to Texas as soon as he is free; in fact, all the children say they will go. Corn is good, there is hardly any wheat, and the cotton crop is fairly good.

I must close. Write soon and give us the details. Following Rebeca’s directions, my wife mailed her letter to her at our post office. My respects to all the [[ending cropped]].

pages.family_title: A long silence and plans to visit Texas, January 26, 1854
pages.family_text:
Readyville, January 26, 1854.
Dear Sir,
I appear before you again in the form of a letter. First, I want to know why you have been silent so long. I had almost concluded that you had died or taken offense. The other day I saw two letters from your neighborhood, from Sam and cousin John L., and was very grateful. I did not find your name in either one.

The old lady received a letter from Orlea saying she is no longer enjoying single blessedness. From what she says, she has plenty of room and little timber crowding the place where she lives.

I showed Sam’s letter to Major J. H. Wood, and he has been in a greater fever about Texas ever since. He wants me to go with him. He says he wants a thousand-acre field and wants to take four “jacks” in a two-horse wagon, as well as ride in it himself. He wants Chs. Lowe to come with us. Joe and I together would make quite a load in a wagon—at least five hundred pounds. So you will certainly see us when we reach your house.
pages.family_note: The writer uses humor about the size of the travelers and the wagon. “Jacks” is probably male donkeys but is kept in quotation marks. No departure or arrival is established by this statement of plans.

pages.family_text:
I want you to see that our boys look for business while they are young. They are qualified and only need to make a start. Once they have started, business will come to them.

I must tell you about Rebeca. She seems to gain weight daily and has reached the point where she no longer makes fun of me. Her figure is much like cousin [[Lucy Pay?]]’s; I think she weighs about 160 pounds. The rest of the family is well.

Tell the boys that John has gone back to college to get his diploma. Granville has gone to eastern Tennessee, near North Carolina, to work for young D. McFerrin. White is arranging to go to Statesville to teach school.

I have given you no news, knowing Sam would tell you all the particulars. I have sent nothing but foolishness, so you must excuse me.

The purpose of this letter is to tell you about your business. We met and settled the account. We find $315 due to you, against $290 that you owed for Sublett’s cattle.
pages.family_note: The family reading clarifies “sheepskin” as a diploma and preserves the humor and all names. The uncertain cousin’s name is not entered as a confirmed family relationship.

pages.text:

pages.family_title: An aging correspondent mourns Granville, July 29, 1868
pages.family_text:
Readyville, July 29, 1868.
Brother N. L. D.,
Dear Sir,
I have neglected writing to you for a long time, although I have often wanted to. For at least two-thirds of my time I cannot write. Now I am at a loss to know what would interest you, as words and ideas grow scarcer as I grow older. I am sure your own experience will allow you to accept my apologies.

My misfortunes over the last few years have been very great. I had hoped, and was greatly encouraged to believe, that Granville was about to make a start in the world. I denied myself things and sent him money to help him along. Alas, how soon the news came that he was gone.

So we are taught not to rely on the perishable things of this world. We are reminded and warned that we too must pass away and be forgotten. All we can do is fulfill our moral and religious duties to one another while we live here as pilgrims.

I learn from J. Orr and others that Granville’s widow and children cannot get along without substantial help, and that the rents [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The date and named people are retained. The greeting “Brother” does not establish a blood relationship. This page does not give Granville’s death date or cause.

pages.family_title: Whether Fanny and the children should return to Tennessee
pages.family_text:
The farm’s rent will not be enough to bring up the children, and Fanny cannot keep house and raise them alone. The family therefore thinks it would be best for them to return to Tennessee so I can help.

I am willing to do what is best. I do not want to put undue pressure on Fannie. I want her to use her own judgment so she will never regret the decision. At the same time, I want to act in a way that will leave no cause for criticism of me later.

Given present circumstances and the changes in the times, I cannot promise comfort and luxury. Everyone who is able to work must do so; otherwise, we will all “perish in a pile.”

I want to know what the tract of land is worth now and what it would rent for each year. I understand the debt is about $60, but I do not know the estate’s value. I have written much the same thing to Orr in reply to his letter.

I would like you, J. Orr, Francis and Charles to consult together about what would be best for the family. I will be grateful to all of you for whatever you do in this matter.
pages.family_note: The letter documents concern for Fanny’s own decision as well as financial constraints. It does not establish the eventual move, sale price or estate value.
