pages.family_title: Lewis Jetton visits old friends and sends family news
pages.family_text:
[[A faint line continuing the previous page is unreadable.]]
Two weeks ago, Rebeca and I took a trip through [[Lincoln?]] County for our health. We spent a pleasant week, including a day or two in Winchester. Your old friend J. Huggins lives there. I visited him one evening and found him stacking hay. He is quite a jolly old man. He has married an Irish woman and they have two little children—[[“half Irish, of course,” possibly a joke about the children]]. He has plenty and lives well. Last week I learned that he and his wife had joined the Christian Church at Winchester.

Aunt Polly Wright looks older than her mother ever did. E. H. Jones is in the mountains of Warren hunting deer. The poor old fellow can hardly walk; I expect he will die with a gun on his shoulder and a dog by his side.

The wife of my son [[J. L.?]], whom he married last winter, had a premature baby who lived four days and died. My son John’s health is still very poor, though he travels about. As far as I know, the rest of our friends are well. Our own little family is reasonably well. I hope these lines find you, your family and your friends all well.
To N. L. Douglass,
Lewis Jetton.
pages.family_note: The visit, marriage and infant’s death are reported by Jetton. Uncertain initials prevent a firm identification of the baby’s parents.

We have just finished threshing wheat. Only about half a crop was made across the country. It is worth $1.70 to $1.80. Old corn is worth 80 cents, and bacon sides 18 cents. [[The page does not specify the units.]]

We had a very severe drought and things looked alarming, but rain began twelve days ago. The corn has recovered wonderfully, and I think we will have plenty. The cotton looks fine. My “convalescents” have thirty acres planted. I cannot think of anything more.
N. L. D.

pages.family_text:
Readyville, April 28, 1851.
Dear Sir,
Your friend Lewis Jetton has been unwell for some time, so I am writing to send the money requested in your last letter, which arrived safely. Enclosed is a twenty-dollar bill, part of your wife’s money that has now been collected. Another $7.40 remains in his hands. As soon as he is well enough to write himself, you may expect another five-dollar bill by mail. He will keep the balance until he makes another collection for you, sometime around next November.

As far as I know, your friends and acquaintances here are presently well, with few exceptions. Jetton’s family is in good health except for him and Rob, a Black boy described as belonging to his household and apparently enslaved. After feeling unwell for a week or two, Jetton took to his bed two weeks ago yesterday with a fever, perhaps what was called congestive fever. Doctors [[Crenshaw?]] and Dickens have treated him since then. They now consider him to be recovering, and from his appearance we hope he will be [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The fever terminology is historical, not a modern diagnosis. The letter calls the money his wife’s but does not explain its source.

pages.family_title: Rising land prices and the search for an affordable home
pages.family_text:
[[Money is scarce because of]] poor harvests, which have left less surplus to sell than usual. Cotton has sold locally for 8 to 12¼ cents a pound. Bacon is now worth 7½ cents a pound, and corn $2.50 to $3 a barrel. Fodder, oats and hay are scarce and expensive. People are planting large crops this year, especially cotton, and are nearly finished. The outlook for small grains is reasonably good so far.

Transport improvements in this part of the state are advancing rapidly. Trains on the Nashville and Chattanooga railroad are expected to reach Murfreesboro by July 4. Another railroad will probably be built from Nashville to Louisville, Kentucky. The Murfreesboro and Woodbury turnpike, through Readyville, is progressing rapidly and is contracted to be finished by Christmas. Another such road is being discussed from Murfreesboro to Liberty, by way of Halls Hill or Browns Mill. Its main obstacle is reconciling the competing interests along the different routes. Sooner or later it will be built.

Land is rising in value here and, as far as I can judge, will continue to do so. That makes it increasingly necessary for people without a secure foothold here to move to a suitable place where good homes are easier to obtain.

As for me, my path for some years has been uneven and sometimes very rough. If I have tasted life’s sweetest nectar, I have also drunk its bitterest dregs. I have tried to bear the destruction of all my [[continues]].

early hopes of happiness—with as much calmness as my nature will allow me—I have been at Readyville engaged with my friend Mr Peay in selling goods untill recently—I am now winding up our books—which show a good proffit—some of it slow however—Mrs Peay is confined with fever of some kind—but is likely to recover—I attended the burial of the wife of J D [[Alexander?]] Esq who was Mary Baird before she was married—on yesterday evening—doubtless you remember her—Her disease was Hemorrige of the lungs—Your old neighbour Mr Bass lost his youngest child about the first of February Mrs Crocker died also about the same time.

pages.family_title: A hoped-for visit to Texas, “that far famed Eden”
pages.family_text:
[[I have tried to bear the destruction of all my]] early hopes of happiness as calmly as my nature allows. Until recently, I worked with my friend Mr. Peay in Readyville selling goods. I am now closing our books, which show a good profit, although some payments are slow. Mrs. Peay is in bed with a fever but is likely to recover.

Yesterday evening I attended the burial of J. D. [[Alexander?]]’s wife, formerly Mary Baird. You doubtless remember her. She died of bleeding from the lungs. Your old neighbor Mr. Bass lost his youngest child around the beginning of February. Mrs. Crocker died at about the same time.

I expect to visit some of my friends in Texas next October and, while there, take a bird’s-eye view of “that far famed Eden.”

Please accept my respects and my kindest wishes for your family’s health and happiness. Remember me to any other friends there who ask about me. I would be glad to hear from you at any time. Tell Uncle Henry and Hiram that I would like them to give me some of their time by writing, too.
Very truly your friend,
[[James H. C. McKinny?]], M.D.

P.S. As soon as you receive the money, please let us know [[at once?]], because he will be anxious. [[The exact final wording is uncertain.]]

pages.text:
[[separate block: top note]] Red Oak

Murfreesboro June 21st 1866
N L Douglass Esqr
Dear Sir

pages.family_title: A letter about Stones River and the losses of old neighbors, June 1866
pages.family_text:
Murfreesboro, June 21, 1866. [[A separate note says “Red Oak.”]]
To N. L. Douglass,
Dear Sir,
Yesterday I saw Esquire Jetton, who showed me your letter of May 24. Among other questions, you asked where the Battle of Stones River was fought and which of our citizens had been killed. I will explain as well as I can, although I have never been over the battlefield.

The right wing of the Union army rested on the Franklin Road near McCulloch’s old residence. Its line extended down the river to a short distance below Uncle Billy Mitchell’s place. The center rested on the turnpike a little beyond [[Cavin’s?]] residence. The monument to the Union dead stands about two or three hundred yards west of [[Cavin’s?]] cotton gin, which used to stand to the right of the turnpike, nearly opposite his residence. A little farther down, on the old [[Menife?]] place, is the National Cemetery between the railroad and turnpike.

You also asked which people from town or the county had been killed. I recall only a few names: Fred James, Allen James’s eldest son; a son of Madison Smith; Samuel Marley, who grew up near Middleton; and Albert [[Abernathy?]], Mrs. Clementine Hall’s grandson. Those are all I presently remember who died in the battle here.

Many others died on other battlefields: a son of John N. Black at Shiloh; Walter Wendel, D. D. Wendel’s son, at Perryville, Kentucky; Samuel Ransom, John’s son; Richard Sublett, E. A. Sublett’s son, at Petersburg; John Wrather, son of our printer John Wrather at [[Murfreesboro?]]; and George Lee Parker, Isaac’s son, killed at [[continues]].

[[Clipped marginal postscript:]] “… son is living.” Mr. Mosby asks me to say that Mr. Nance visited a few days ago with his baby girl. [[Some words are clipped.]] “… and wife all well.” Initials: [[D. W. S.?]].
pages.family_note: “Yanky” is rendered Union for readability. This is a contemporary correspondent’s incomplete report, not an independently verified casualty roll or battlefield map. Cropped statements are not reconstructed.

our town & County have been greatly damaged by the two Armies, they destroied all the timber for miles around burnt all the rails for 3 or 4 miles in all directions burnt & pulled down at least 50 houses in town & of this number was the Old Presbyterian Church, destroied the fence around the grave, broke tombstones & desecrated the grave Yard generally, Sent Some of the Citizens through their lines & took possession of their houses & Stole, & Sent off, their beding, & furniture—in short they were a Set of Vandals—Esqr Jetton wishes me to Say to you that he will Send you a Check in a few days for one hundred dollars—John D Alexander is in town, rd. your letter, & request me to Send you his best respects & Say he will write to you Very Soon—and Wm Brick has promised to write to you Soon—and Robt S Burney, is editor of the Murfreesboro Monitor promised to Send you a Copy of his paper Soon—I encouraged him to do so as I thought you would take it as a Special favour—you will please write to me, whenever you feel like writing & tell me all about your part of Texas how you are getting along & of the products & all else you can think of, which will interest your old friend

pages.family_title: War deaths, destruction and the wish to hear about Texas
pages.family_text:
[[George Lee Parker was killed at]] Chickamauga. Colonel John Butler, Thomas O. Butler’s son, was killed at Perryville, Kentucky, as was a young man named Wharton who came here from Virginia after you left. My second son, Robert, was killed at Marietta, Georgia. Those are all the war deaths from this town and area that I can presently recall.

Here are older citizens who have died in recent years from natural causes: Henry D. Jamison; Burrill Gannaway; Elisha Williams; Love and Moses Reeves; William Snell; William F. Lytle; W. D. Cannon; Thomas O. Butler; Silas Tucker; Lewis Tucker; Reverend William Eagleton; William Brick; William M. Fadden; Henry Hall; Benjamin Clayton; and Benjamin Rucker. Our fellow townsman Reuben Ballis was killed three or four weeks ago while trying to pull down a cabin he had bought and intended to move.

The two armies badly damaged our town and county. They destroyed the timber for miles around and burned all the fence rails for three or four miles in every direction. They burned or pulled down at least fifty houses in town, including the old Presbyterian Church. They destroyed the graveyard fence, broke tombstones and desecrated the cemetery. They sent some citizens through their lines, occupied their houses, and stole and sent away their bedding and furniture. In short, they were a set of vandals.

Esquire Jetton asks me to say that he will send you a check for one hundred dollars in a few days. John D. Alexander is in town, has read your letter, and sends his best regards. He says he will write very soon. William Brick has also promised to write soon. Robert S. Burney, editor of the Murfreesboro Monitor, has promised to send you a copy of his paper. I encouraged him because I thought you would appreciate it.

Please write whenever you feel like it. Tell me about your part of Texas, how you are getting along, what you grow, and anything else you can think of that would interest your old friend.
pages.family_note: All losses and destruction are reported by the correspondent. The apparent contradiction concerning William Brick is retained. This letter offers research leads, but its names and casualty details need corroboration.

pages.family_text:
Readyville, February 10, 1853.
Dear Sir,
As promised, I send a few hasty lines. We and our friends are generally well, except for my son Granville’s wife, who is very ill with consumption. Twelve months ago she was one of the strongest women in the area. Rebeca is somewhat better this week, although still not very strong.

Regarding your business, I received a power authorizing me to act for you and Polly. I also received an order bearing only your signature. You said in your last letter that you had given a promissory note for the same amount. Mr. Sublett was very eager to collect the cash on the order. He says you never gave a note, unless you meant a short letter or request that you wrote just before he left. You were very ill at the time. He says perhaps Washie could provide the document. [[The personal name is uncertain.]] I have that paper. There was also some difficulty concerning [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The letter reports disagreement over financial documents. It does not establish wrongdoing by either party. “Consumption” is preserved as the historical description of illness.

pages.family_title: Why both N. L. Douglas and Polly must sign the receipt
pages.family_text:
[[There was difficulty with the]] matter, so I spent two or three days accommodating Major Sublett, knowing he was your friend. I obtained the money from J. M. Alexander and paid the order, with ten percent added. I took a repayment bond from Major Ledbetter to protect me in case a promissory note should also turn up, together with a form of receipt in the same document. Since the order was payable to Ledbetter, I handled the transaction jointly with him and Sublett.

You know that Tennessee’s laws have changed greatly in favor of women, so an order signed by you alone would not serve as a valid voucher. I was about to send it back to you when Colonel Kibbler told me to keep it until you and Polly sent a joint acknowledgment that you had received the amount from me as your attorney in the matter.

The amount paid to Sublett, including interest up to that time, was $263.72. Mr. Alexander charged ten percent on the money, bringing the total to $290.09.
pages.family_note: “Attorney” here is the agent acting under the power described in the letter. The edition does not independently verify the legal rule or identify the exact women’s-property statute.

pages.family_title: Cattle purchased with proceeds from land and the sale of enslaved people
pages.family_text:
Mr. Alexander should therefore receive a credit for $290.09 on his note, on your account. You and Polly can send a joint receipt for that amount. You may think I have been overly particular, but we are far apart and life is uncertain. I have no doubt that you want to do everything correctly.

Your cattle are paid for. I am glad you bought them and think they are a good investment. Please tell me from time to time how the herd increases; I would be very interested.

We sold the land for $1,822 and the enslaved people for $1,075. Polly is entitled to one-thirteenth plus one-third of another thirteenth of the land proceeds, and one-twelfth of the proceeds from the sale of the enslaved people. After paying for the cows, about twenty or twenty-five dollars remains in her favor. There may be a little expense, but it should be very small.
pages.family_note: The historical record directly connects this financial distribution and cattle purchase with proceeds from selling enslaved people. Their names, number and relationships are not supplied here. The fractions are retained as written, and no unsupported estate identification is added.

pages.family_title: Freezing ink, Hannah and Julia, and a hoped-for visit
pages.family_text:
It is very cold, my fingers are cold, and the ink is freezing. I have missed some words, which you will have to supply. You may already have heard that Hannah and Julia are living with me. Hannah is much more difficult to care for than before. Her mental abilities have declined greatly, and her health is considerably impaired.

Please answer as soon as possible and attend to the business promptly so everything can be put right. Give my regards to our friends and the children, and a due share to yourself and Polly.
Lewis Jetton.
To N. L. Douglass.

P.S. Major Wood, Charley [[Sowel?]] and I are talking about visiting you this fall. Do not think badly of it: the visit would come from pure friendship.

[[Marginal note: Tennessee, Rutherford County?]]

pages.family_text:
Readyville, January 1868.
Brother N. L. Douglass,
Dear Sir,
After a long silence on both our parts—though not an intentional one on mine—I will dispense with apologies and say that our family and friends are well. We are doing as well as circumstances allow.

Our family is beginning to scatter. They all seem ready to “paddle their own boat” and “make their own landing.” We old folks need not complain, since that is probably natural in every generation. Our youngest son Albert married last winter. They have a baby and will move into their own home in a week or so. John L. married Miss Joanna Goodloe about two weeks ago. They were a little too closely related, but I did not make a fuss. They will probably move this spring or summer.

Our household will then be small: only my wife and me, our son William, and our daughter Sarah. [[Charles F.?]] went on a wild-goose chase and has ended up in your neighborhood. The poor fellow has had [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The letter names Jetton’s children and John L.’s wife but gives no exact degree of kinship between the newlyweds. The son’s initials at the end remain provisional.

pages.title: A difficult start after army service, and Jetton’s view of Reconstruction
pages.text: a bad chance to start in this world he was put in the army when he ought to have been at school I was opposed to him going to Texas—he was doing verry well here but thought he could do better in your country so he put out so if he does well and becomes satisfied with the country I will endeaver to help him start in lifes rugged road—now we are wandering about in the dark of this political Chang of our government we cant surmise or even guess what the future may be—& its even hard to tell the past in fact I cant I just know that I past through greate trouble Just immagine the greate Chang that is made to see the negroes march out Election days to vote Congressmen Legislators and all officers & all the white men stay at home how degrading though I have the right to vote hardly ever do so because the ballance of my race is deprived of this priviledg—now you know that we are both geting old its not expected that we can labor & make a support I am now warned of the fact while writing this epistle my eyes refuse to see almost still I am trying to carry on my farm it cost me one half of the proceeds to do so—then time the stealing comes their is but little left for me so a support is all I can expect

pages.family_title: A difficult start after army service, and Jetton’s view of Reconstruction
pages.family_text:
[[He has had]] a poor start in life. He was put into the army when he should have been at school. I opposed his going to Texas. He was doing very well here but thought he could do better where you are, so he left. If he does well and is happy there, I will try to help him start along life’s rough road.

We are wandering in the dark amid the political changes in our government. We cannot even guess what the future holds. It is hard to describe the past, too; I can only say that I have been through great trouble. Imagine the change, seeing Black men going out on election day to vote for congressmen, legislators and other officers, while the white men stay home. I find that degrading. Although I have the right to vote, I hardly ever do, because the rest of my race is deprived of the privilege. [[These are Jetton’s racist views and his own sweeping description of voting rights.]]

You know we are both growing old and cannot be expected to earn our support by hard labor. Even writing this letter reminds me of that: my eyes almost refuse to see. Still, I try to keep my farm going. It costs half the proceeds to operate it, and after the stealing there is little left for me. Enough to live on is all I can expect.
pages.family_note: The family edition preserves the political passage and its prejudice rather than presenting the writer’s assertions as objective history. His allegations of theft are not independently established.

paragraphs.text: a bad chance to start in this world he was put in the army when he ought to have been at school I was opposed to him going to Texas—he was doing verry well here but thought he could do better in your country so he put out so if he does well and becomes satisfied with the country I will endeaver to help him start in lifes rugged road—now we are wandering about in the dark of this political Chang of our government we cant surmise or even guess what the future may be—& its even hard to tell the past in fact I cant I just know that I past through greate trouble Just immagine the greate Chang that is made to see the negroes march out Election days to vote Congressmen Legislators and all officers & all the white men stay at home how degrading though I have the right to vote hardly ever do so because the ballance of my race is deprived of this priviledg—now you know that we are both geting old its not expected that we can labor & make a support I am now warned of the fact while writing this epistle my eyes refuse to see almost still I am trying to carry on my farm it cost me one half of the proceeds to do so—then time the stealing comes their is but little left for me so a support is all I can expect

times is growing remarkably hard money is scarce trade is [[flatter?]] than we knew it before the negroes more trifling more roguish & more impudent than ever has been known in any country free or not free

I regret verry much that a difficulty or misunderstanding should have taken place between you & Mr Nance I made a trip last May to West Tennessee I called on Mr Nance he told me that he [[inserted: had]] written a letter to you rather snubish I told him I was sorry to hear it he said it was no worse than the one he received previous—I knowing you well and [[inserted: &]] your temperament that you did not intend to ruffle any bodys feeling N L you know we have been on the best of Terms ever since we were Brotherlaws I always had the highest regard for you and all Confidence that one man could have another—I still believe thier is no misunderstanding—if the thing is understood I know you & Mr Nance would not do a wrong if you knew it I am certain of it (excitement is always excepted in all cases)

pages.family_title: A dispute with Mr. Nance—and an explicit brother-in-law relationship
pages.family_text:
Times are becoming very hard. Money is scarce and trade is [[flatter?]] than we have ever known. Jetton then makes a racist generalization, describing Black people as more “trifling,” dishonest and insolent than people in any other country, whether free or enslaved.

I deeply regret that a dispute or misunderstanding arose between you and Mr. Nance. Last May I traveled to western Tennessee and visited him. He said he had written you a rather curt letter. I told him I was sorry to hear it. He replied that it was no worse than the letter he had received earlier. Knowing you and your temperament, I do not think you intended to hurt anyone’s feelings.

N. L., you know that we have been on the best of terms ever since we became brothers-in-law. I have always held you in the highest regard and had as much confidence in you as one man can have in another. I still believe that, once the matter is understood, there need be no misunderstanding. I am certain neither you nor Mr. Nance would knowingly do wrong—apart, of course, from what anyone might do when upset.
pages.family_note: Jetton explicitly calls them brothers-in-law. This is a useful family-history clue but does not identify which marriage created the relationship. The opening racial allegation is attributed to him and not endorsed.

If the dispute with Mr. Nance still exists, I offer my help. With your consent, I am willing to mediate. I presume that only [[property or money?—the word is uncertain]] remains to be settled.

I propose a compromise. I would prefer to keep the lawyers from growing rich and the client poor. I searched diligently for the papers but could never find any of them. A number of similar suits have been lost completely, without a cent recovered.

pages.title: News of Julia’s death and a request to administer her estate

Readyville Sept 1st [[1860?]]
Dear Sir I take the present opportunity to drop you few lines believing that you have never received a letter that was addressed to you some time ago in relation to Julia Lows Death if you had—you certainly would have answered it so I take it for granted that you have not received it—Julia Died suddenly on the 23d of June she was attacked at [[illegible: line at dark fold]] in 24 h she could never speake so as to be understood—we gave the particulars in a former letter to you & to Granville we recd a letter from Granville since he never said a word about his aunt he may have never got his—yours and his were mail together—I again state to you that it is nesesary for some person to administer upon her estate I have written to all the legatees they have all answered me agreeing for me to administer—so I am waiting to hear from the relations in Texas—if I have any thing to do with the matter I wish it to be agreeable with all I went to Murfreesboro on yesterday to see Capt Sam Davis I had a conversation with him in relation to Julias lands in Texas he knows all about it he says he saw it and inquired about it for Julias satisfaction at her request the day that Davis got home from Texas she died—Mr J L [[Dyer?]] who Julia employed to get up the case would never give her any satisfaction about the matter

June 23 is clear, but the year is uncertain. The letter explicitly calls Julia Granville’s aunt without specifying the exact line of kinship. Reading the entire letter, including the reference to Bell and Everett on 08-130 and the continuing enslavement of a boy on 08-129, supports 1860 for the uncertain year; the date remains marked pending further checking.

pages.family_title: News of Julia’s death and a request to administer her estate
pages.family_text:
Readyville, September 1, [[1860?]].
Dear Sir,
I am writing because I believe you never received an earlier letter about Julia [[Low’s?]] death. If you had, you would surely have answered. Julia died suddenly on June 23. She suffered an attack [[the description is obscured by a fold]], and within the period described as twenty-four hours she could not speak intelligibly. We gave the details in the earlier letters to you and Granville. We have since heard from Granville, but he said nothing about his aunt. Perhaps his letter never reached him either; the two were mailed together.

Someone must administer Julia’s estate. I have written to all the people named to inherit, and all have agreed that I should do it. I am now waiting to hear from the relatives in Texas. If I undertake the work, I want everyone to agree.

Yesterday I went to Murfreesboro to see Captain Sam Davis about Julia’s Texas land. He says he knows all about it, saw it, and investigated it at her request. She died the very day he returned from Texas. Mr. J. L. [[Dyer?]], whom Julia had hired to prepare the case, had never given her a satisfactory account of it.
pages.family_note: The family reading does not invent the obscured cause or precise sequence of Julia’s final illness. The year and surname require further checking. Statements about the land and the earlier attorney are the correspondent’s reports.

pages.title: A proposal to recover, occupy and eventually sell Julia’s Texas land
pages.text: Tharefore she lost confidence in him for that reason she got Mr Davis to examin into the whole matter—So Mr Davis Reports to me that the land is worth some $3[[obscured: digit]]00—that it is improved and has one hundred acres under fence and that it ought to be taken possession of imediately by Consent or a writ of possession to be run against those that have it in possession he further states that thair is about five hundred Dollars expens attach to it Lawyers fees &c now I propose to [[obscured: word at fold]] the land into Market Sell it pay Expences & all Attorneys fees and let the residue be divided amongst the heirs—I think Alfred might go down & see it if you should not be able—I guess you are like my self not always able to go about—Alfred could live a year upon it before it would be advisable to sell it probable—as I understand that the abolition and the drouth has reduced the price of Texas lands verry much perhaps it would be best to delay the sale of the lands till the excitement pass off—I shall write to the ballance of the legatees for them to write to you to use thier names in a petition to Court for a Decree to sell [[inserted: the]] land—when ever you and Texas kin think it advisable—Capt Sam Davis sets out for Texas this day he will call on you—you can advise with him about the lands—he attending business of that [[inserted: kind]] an Attorney I think he is a Gentleman and a reliable man [[lost: bottom continuation]]
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 08-127. A blot obscures part of the reported valuation: $3?00, not a confidently read $3,000. Abolition and drought are the writer’s explanation of lower land prices. Legal proposals are not evidence of completed court proceedings or sale. “Abolition” is the writer’s word and is not modernized as completed emancipation; the letter’s likely date is 1860.

pages.family_title: A proposal to recover, occupy and eventually sell Julia’s Texas land
pages.family_text:
Julia therefore lost confidence in him and asked Mr. Davis to investigate the whole matter. Davis reports that the land is worth about $3[[obscured digit]]00, is improved, and has one hundred acres fenced. He says possession should be recovered immediately, either by agreement or through a writ against the people occupying it. He also reports about $500 in expenses, including lawyers’ fees.

I propose putting the land on the market, selling it, paying expenses and attorneys’ fees, and dividing the balance among the heirs. If you cannot go, perhaps Alfred could inspect it. I suspect you are like me, not always able to travel. Alfred could perhaps live there for a year before a sale became advisable. I understand that “abolition” and drought have greatly reduced Texas land prices. It may be best to wait until the excitement subsides.

I will ask the remaining beneficiaries to write authorizing you to use their names in a court petition for a decree permitting sale, whenever you and the Texas relatives think it advisable. Captain Sam Davis leaves for Texas today and will call on you. You can consult him about the land. He handles that kind of business as an attorney, and I think him a gentleman and a reliable man. [[The last line is clipped.]]
pages.family_note: The valuation contains an obscured digit and must not be used as an exact amount. Proposed possession, Alfred’s possible residence and a future sale are plans only. The explanation of falling prices is attributed to the letter writer.

pages.text:
you and the kin will take interest in the matter and look into the case Mr [[Horril?]] was the Attorney in the case he lives in Palestine he should be consulted and perhaps continued you must be the Judge of the matter if none of you will act I [[obscured: word]] no chance for an agent unless we get Mr Davis to attend to it—I will have to administer at the 1st monday in Oct as that is Court day as longer delay will be injurious to the [[obscured: word]] the property here consist in a negro boy worth some $1200—she has some beds & beding—some three or four hundred Dollars in notes—she owes some money I do not know how much—my wife thinks she ought in Justice to have the house stuff for taking care of Julia—her and the kin for that—I am fearful Mr [[Dyer?]] will try to press his claim upon the Estate here for [[inserted: his]] services in the Texas matter—when I know he was to take it [[inserted: out]] of the lands—he may have the advantage in absence of a contract the boy is hired out and has been for the last seven years I cant get possession of him till Christmas of course I cant sell him till that time

I have wrote a rough [[word?]] if you can understand me—I would have yesterday wrote by Mr Davis—but it was a big day Murfreesboro—& I am so nervous at times particular when warm I cant write so you see I have to take advantage of my nervous system when I write while they [[inserted: are]] quiet—(I am a Sober man too

The page treats an unnamed enslaved boy as estate property and records seven years of hiring him out; those statements are preserved without endorsing them. The first attorney’s surname is uncertain.

pages.family_title: Julia’s estate, an unnamed enslaved boy, and disputed fees
pages.family_text:
You and the relatives should take an interest in the matter and investigate it. Mr. [[Horril?]], the attorney in the case, lives in Palestine. He should be consulted and perhaps retained. You must judge the matter. If none of you will act, I see no possibility of an agent unless we ask Mr. Davis to attend to it.

I will have to take up administration on the first Monday in October, which is court day; a longer delay will be harmful. [[Part of the sentence is obscured.]] The property here is described as an unnamed enslaved boy, valued by the writer at about $1,200, some beds and bedding, and $300 or $400 in promissory notes. Julia also owed money, though I do not know how much. My wife thinks it would be just for her to have the household goods for caring for Julia, with the relatives’ agreement. [[The clause about the relatives is awkward and uncertain.]]

I fear Mr. [[Dyer?]] will try to claim payment from the Tennessee estate for his work on the Texas matter, although I understand that his payment was to come from the land. Without a contract, he may have the advantage. The boy has been hired out for seven years. The writer says he cannot regain custody of him until Christmas and therefore cannot sell him before then.

This has been a rough letter, but I hope you can understand me. I would have written yesterday to send it with Mr. Davis, but it was a busy day in Murfreesboro. At times I am so nervous, especially in warm weather, that I cannot write. I have to write when my nerves are quiet. I am a sober man, too.

pages.title: Crop failure, an Arkansas journey and Uncle Jake at eighty-two
pages.text:
this letter leaves us all well Rebeca health is much better than usual she spent some five weeks at the [[Christal?]] Springs July and part of aug which improve her great deal uncle Jake is down & confined to his bed I fear never to get up again he is verry old & feeble 82 years—like a child knows nothing hardly—politic verry high Bell & everet will carry the state beyond a doubt Mr Davis will tell you all about it you have heard of our short Crop the like was never been known in Tenn before we are sending our hogs to Illinois & indiana to be fatten several thousand already gone by Rail Road—and others will go—we will make from two to three barrels of corn pr acre some places hardly any they are asking five Dollars from the heap—which is mighty hard for Tennesseans—my son White & [[Hotell?]] starts for Arkansas in a few days if they like the Country they will locate—or return—tell Granville that John wont make one barrel of corn to the acre this year—I will make two on an average you will Show this letter to all that are concerned I would write to all separately—it is uneasary and I have so much of it to do—excuse me if you please tell Alfred to write if pleases—for he never will git a letter from Tenn till he writes—answer this imediately we send our love & respects to all of the kin
N L Douglass

pages.editorial_notes: Concludes 08-127–129. The political reference to Bell and Everett helps assess the uncertain date as 1860. Resort name and companion’s surname are uncertain. Crop yields and political prediction are reported by Jetton. Uncle Jake’s age is stated as 82; no surname or exact birth date is supplied.

pages.family_title: Crop failure, an Arkansas journey and Uncle Jake at eighty-two
pages.family_text:
We are all well as this letter leaves. Rebeca’s health is much better than usual. She spent about five weeks at [[Christal?]] Springs during July and part of August, which helped her greatly. Uncle Jake is confined to bed, and I fear he will never get up again. He is very old and frail, eighty-two years old, and the writer describes him as childlike and hardly aware of things.

Political excitement is intense. I believe Bell and Everett will certainly carry the state; Mr. Davis will tell you about it. You have heard of our poor crop. Nothing like it has been known in Tennessee. We are sending hogs to Illinois and Indiana to be fattened. Several thousand have already gone by railroad, and more will follow. We will harvest only two or three barrels of corn an acre, and some places almost none. They are asking five dollars for corn from the heap, which is very hard on Tennesseans.

My son White and [[Hotell?]] leave for Arkansas in a few days. If they like it, they will settle; otherwise, they will return. Tell Granville that John will not get even one barrel of corn an acre this year. I expect an average of two.

Please show this letter to everyone concerned. I would write separately, but that is unnecessary, and I already have so much writing to do. Please excuse me. Tell Alfred to write if he wishes: he will receive no letter from Tennessee until he does! Answer promptly. We send love and respects to all the relatives.
To N. L. Douglass,
Lewis Jetton.
pages.family_note: The poor harvest and plans to move are the writer’s report. Uncle Jake cannot be identified from this page alone. The quoted corn price lacks an explicit unit in that sentence.

pages.text:
Readyville March 7th 1854
Dear Sir after longer delay than I expected in consequence of failing to make collection I enclose you a twenty Dollar Bill = in my next I will enclose a five on the reception of the last you will please to forward a receipt for the whole you polly both sign it = we are all well at present = the spring verry unfavorable for farming—but little news some little excitement about provisions for the turky & Rucia war but [[inserted: small]] a advance in prices as yet—you will please write to me & let me kno how the boys are doing and their prospects and say something about your self
I remain most obedient friend
N L Douglass
Lewis Jetton
pages.editorial_notes: Single-page letter. The war names are retained as the writer spelled them in the direct transcript. Twenty dollars is enclosed and five promised; they are not conflated as money already received.

pages.family_title: A twenty-dollar remittance and news of prices, March 1854
pages.family_text:
Readyville, March 7, 1854.
Dear Sir,
After a longer delay than expected because I could not make the collection, I enclose a twenty-dollar bill. In my next letter I will send five dollars more. Once that last payment arrives, please send a receipt for the whole amount signed by both you and Polly.

We are all well. The spring has been very unfavorable for farming. There is little news, apart from some excitement about provisions for the war between Turkey and Russia, but prices have risen only slightly so far.

Please write and let me know how the boys are doing and what their prospects are. Tell me something about yourself, too.
I remain your most obedient friend,
Lewis Jetton.
To N. L. Douglass.
pages.family_note: The reference to foreign war is retained as part of the letter’s account of local commodity prices.

pages.text:
Readyville Jan 4th 1859
Brother N L Douglass
Dear Sir after a long silence I have taken my seat with two candles and my [[deleted: and]] glasses on—to drop you a few lines to let you kno that we are still in the land of the living and enjoying the blessings of health hopeing these lines will finde you & family enjoying the like blessing—it has been so long since I have written to you I hardly [[lost: word at tear]] what will interest you to give you a history of your old acquaintance would be a repetition of that I heretofore written to you—for all that I will say there is but few of the old settlers alive thats living about here Esq Martin & lady is no more—several more has past away Esq Ready & uncle Jake are almost gone they are in thier dotage in a maner kno nothing—so old men are growing scarce—so they the people call me one of the old men [[inserted: the]] of neighborhood—our country has undergone a greate Chang since you left the country old man Ready and myself are the only men that resides in the same place from Woodbury to Murfreesboro—this is remarkable

Readyville, January 4, 1859.
Brother N. L. Douglass,
Dear Sir,
After a long silence, I have sat down with two candles and my glasses on to send a few lines. We are still in the land of the living and enjoying good health. I hope you and your family are equally well.

It has been so long since I wrote that I hardly [[know?—the page is damaged]] what will interest you. An account of your old acquaintances would repeat what I have written before. I will only say that few of the old settlers are still alive here. Esquire Martin and his wife have died, as have several others. Esquire Ready and Uncle Jake are near the end of life and, in the writer’s description, barely aware of things. Old men are becoming scarce, and people now call me one of the neighborhood’s old men.

This area has changed greatly since you left. Old Mr. Ready and I are the only men between Woodbury and Murfreesboro who still live in the same places. That is remarkable.
pages.family_note: The claim about the remaining residents is Jetton’s recollection, not a census-based finding. The missing word is supplied only tentatively in the readable edition.

Readyville Jan 4th 1859
Brother N L Douglass
Dear Sir after a long silence I have taken my seat with two candles and my [[deleted: and]] glasses on—to drop you a few lines to let you kno that we are still in the land of the living and enjoying the blessings of health hopeing these lines will finde you & family enjoying the like blessing—it has been so long since I have written to you I hardly [[lost: word at tear]] what will interest you to give you a history of your old acquaintance would be a repetition of that I heretofore written to you—for all that I will say there is but few of the old settlers alive thats living about here Esq Martin & lady is no more—several more has past away Esq Ready & uncle Jake are almost gone they are in thier dotage in a maner kno nothing—so old men are growing scarce—so they the people call me one of the old men [[inserted: the]] of neighborhood—our country has undergone a greate Chang since you left the country old man Ready and myself are the only men that resides in the same place from Woodbury to Murfreesboro—this is remarkable

pages.family_title: Henry travels to marry in Kentucky; Granville heads toward Texas
pages.family_text:
The whole family and I were happy that Henry cared enough about us to spend the time and money to visit. We were delighted to have his company again and sorry he could not stay longer. We excused his departure only because he had an appointment to be married. I therefore thought I should send White with him to Kentucky. They left in the buggy with all our good wishes. White returned fifteen days later, having seen something of the world. [[One word is obscured.]] We will always be grateful for Henry’s visit. I wish we could all see one another again in person.

Granville and his father-in-law set out with their families for Arkansas on September 13 and reached Washington County. We have received only one letter from him. His sister-in-law wrote to her cousin, and I learned from that letter that his father-in-law had bought land and settled. Granville did not like the area and is on his way to your part of the country. The letter says he left Washington County on December 16. I suppose he will go to your house or to Henry’s. If he comes to your house, I would regard it as a great favor if you would show [[continues]].
pages.family_note: The letter supports a visit by Henry and travel toward a Kentucky marriage, but gives no bride’s name or ceremony date on this page. Granville’s movements are partly secondhand.

pages.family_title: Help Granville choose a home; news of Alfred, Betsy and Julia
pages.family_text:
[[Please show]] Granville the country and help him choose a home, since he is unfamiliar with your soils and area. I expect his travel will use up most of his money before he reaches you. He still has about $800 here, which I am to send once he finds a home he likes. Otherwise, he will come back for it. Granville is a very industrious man.

We have not heard a line from Robert Fletcher near Austin in I do not know how long. [[A damaged clause appears to say a letter arrived]] from Mr. Nance today; they are all well.

Alfred will move to my Mitchell farm this week, leaving Short Mountain. He will grow a crop in the [[Suite?]] settlement this year and talks of moving west in the fall. He has two children, both daughters. Betsy lives with him and has become almost helpless. Her hip worsens as she grows older. Her financial resources have been greatly reduced through Dudley Gresham, but the poor man is now dead. [[The letter does not explain what happened to the money.]]

Julia is still alive, sends her regards, and wants the girls to write to her.
pages.family_note: These are separate people’s circumstances; Alfred’s proposed westward move is not treated as a completed migration. The financial reference to Dudley Gresham is not expanded into an allegation unsupported by the page.

pages.family_title: Deaths and messages to the extended family
pages.family_text:
Mr. Barr’s family are all well. Mary Goodloe remains in her distressing circumstances. Cousin John Stephens has visited us and says we are related. He is quite an unusual-looking man.

Some time ago I received a letter saying that James Stephens died on November 22, leaving five children in poor circumstances. John said Uncle Aquilla Goodloe of Virginia had died, the last of the old [[stock?]]. George Stephens is dead. Old Jerry Stephens is still alive in Missouri. Your old friend Jefro Thompson died two weeks ago.

There might be many other things new to you if I could remember them. It is now bedtime, and I am being reminded to finish. We all send love to you, Polly, all the children and relatives, Mr. Orr, Cynthia and their children. Tell James D. and Harper that I have never received so much as a pen scratch from them. Please write soon and often.
To N. L. Douglass,
Lewis Jetton.
pages.family_note: James’s death is reported as November 22 of the preceding year, apparently 1858. The edition preserves the names but does not assume that each named person is a Douglas ancestor.

Sec 33. Where the wife dies, her husband surviving, administration [[inserted: is unnecessary]] except as to any separate estate which may have belonged to her. The husband continues to have the same power of disposition over the community property which he possessed during the continuance of marriage. pages.family_title: Historical notes on managing community property after a spouse’s death
pages.family_text:
Section 33. When a wife dies and her husband survives, formal estate administration is unnecessary except for any separate property she owned. The husband keeps the authority over community property that he held during the marriage. He must nevertheless submit an inventory and valuation of it and file a bond, with one or more guarantors, approved by and payable to the county’s district clerk. The bond must equal the whole value of the community property. It guarantees that he will manage the property faithfully and, after paying debts properly chargeable against it, turn over half the remaining surplus to the people entitled to it.

Section 34. The husband may be required to account for his management at any time after one year from the bond’s date.

Section 35. The bond may be sued upon and recovered on in the same way as an administrator’s bond, and is otherwise treated the same.

Section 36. A surviving wife may keep sole management and control of the couple’s community property under the same conditions, rights and rules described in the preceding three sections until she remarries. On remarriage she loses [[continues]].

pages.title: A. B. Norton asks Douglas to pay a state order, March 1869
pages.text:
Dallas, Texas, Mch. 26. 1869
Friend Douglass—
Dear Sir;
By J. T. Conner Esq deputy Sheriff of Dallas county I send an order from Geo. C. Rives, Actg. Comptroller for the sum of Five Hundred and eighty three 34/100 dollars payable to my order, which you will much oblige me by paying to him.

I go to Cleburne on Monday to hold Court there two weeks—I will write to you occasionally—I trust that your health is restored by a few days rest—
Truly thy friend
A B Norton
N. L. Douglass Esqr
Red oak Ellis Co.
Texas.
pages.editorial_notes: The amount is $583.34 and the messenger is J. T. Conner, deputy sheriff of Dallas County. Read alongside the payment memorandum 08-145 and endorsement 08-150; those cross-references do not turn the request into separate proof of payment.

pages.family_text:
Dallas, Texas, March 26, 1869.
Friend Douglass,
Dear Sir,
I am sending an order through J. T. Conner, deputy sheriff of Dallas County. It is from George C. Rives, acting comptroller, for $583.34, payable to my order. I would be much obliged if you would pay it to Conner.

I go to Cleburne on Monday to hold court for two weeks. I will write occasionally. I trust that a few days’ rest have restored your health.
Truly your friend,
A. B. Norton.
To N. L. Douglass, Red Oak, Ellis County, Texas.
pages.family_note: The letter is a payment request and an expression of concern for Douglas’s health. The precise illness is not stated.

pages.title: Joseph Spence reassures Douglas about a draft, April 1869
pages.text:
Austin Texas April 10/69
N L Douglass Esq
Waco Texas
Sir
The Draft was received by the Comptroller this morning. It came yesterday but when we called for it the mail had not been distributed, hence we did not get it. I have endorsed the draft in accordance with the authority you gave me and the draft will be sent to Houston for collection. As soon as we hear from it I will send you the Comptrollers receipt for the amount. You need not give yourself any uneasiness about it. I will attend to it and you shall be troubled no further. With the best wishes for your safe return to your home & family I remain
Your Friend
Joseph Spence

I will write to you at Red oak in a few days
Spence
pages.editorial_notes: Date is written April 10/69. The draft amount is not repeated here, so it is not assumed to be the Norton payment or any particular deposit without further evidence.

pages.family_title: Joseph Spence reassures Douglas about a draft, April 1869
pages.family_text:
Austin, Texas, April 10, 1869.
To N. L. Douglass, Waco, Texas.
Sir,
The comptroller received the draft this morning. It arrived yesterday, but when we called, the mail had not yet been sorted, so we could not collect it. I have endorsed the draft under the authority you gave me. It will be sent to Houston for collection. As soon as we hear back, I will send you the comptroller’s receipt for the amount.

Do not worry about it. I will attend to the matter, and you will have no further trouble. With best wishes for your safe return to your home and family, I remain your friend,
Joseph Spence.

I will write to you at Red Oak in a few days.
Spence.
pages.family_note: The letter documents an agent handling a draft for Douglas, but gives neither its amount nor the underlying tax or transaction.

General Land Office
Austin Texas Apl 20/69
N L. Douglas Esq
Red Oak Ellis County.
Sir
I herein enclose the Deposit Warrants from the Treasury department for $1817.25 amount of [[Ennis?]] & Goodwins draft, upon which the money has been paid. One Warrant No 163 is for $1591.60 paid towards the Convention Tax. The other is No 315 for 225.65 paid on State Revenue, making the above sum of 1817.25 dollars. I trust these warrants may reach you [[inserted: promptly]] by due Course of mail. I wrote you the day after you left that the Draft had come to hand which I suppose reached you at Waco. I trust you were able to arrive at home safely and that being free now from the annoyances and anxiety incident to your Office you may speedily regain strength & health.
Your Friend
Joseph Spence

pages.family_title: Joseph Spence sends treasury warrants, April 20, 1869
pages.family_text:
General Land Office, Austin, Texas, April 20, 1869.
To N. L. Douglas, Red Oak, Ellis County.
Sir,
I enclose the treasury deposit warrants for $1,817.25, the amount paid on the draft from [[Ennis?]] & Goodwin. Warrant No. 163 is for $1,591.60 toward the convention tax. Warrant No. 315 is for $225.65 toward state revenue. Together they make $1,817.25.

I hope these warrants reach you promptly by mail. The day after you left, I wrote that the draft had arrived; I suppose that letter reached you at Waco. I hope you arrived home safely. Now that you are free of the troubles and anxiety of your office, I hope you soon regain your strength and health.
Your friend,
Joseph Spence.
pages.family_note: The writer connects Douglas’s official duties with anxiety and poor health. This is his contemporary observation, not a medical diagnosis.

pages.title: Nance asks whether Douglas helped free Sam, June 1867
pages.text:
Quincy Tenn
June 5th 67
N. L. Douglass — Sir — I recd your verry Short epistle, accompanied by a Recept a Short time Since — In this I would ask you a Single question — Did you In any way assist In freeing the Negro Sam? I write this to know the certainty, you know, and you will please answer the question — if you answer In the affirmative I will forward to you your recept. If not, I will take grate pains to forward your money — I am verry good for the amt Claimed —

Now Sir, You & I are getting old, and Soon our earthly Interests will [[deleted: have]] be at an end, Consequently I dont want to do wrong — Now all I mean in this is, If you assisted In taking my property from me, you can get your money by ligal process — If not, I will take pleasure If forwarding It to you —
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 08-165. The final If may be a slip for in; direct wording is retained. The letter’s claim of ownership and accusation are the writer’s, not editorial findings.
pages.review: initial AI visual reading of supplied scan
pages.family_title: Nance asks whether Douglas helped free Sam, June 1867
pages.family_text:
Quincy, Tennessee, June 5, 1867.
N. L. Douglass—Sir,
A short time ago, I received your very short letter with a receipt. I have one question: Did you help in any way to free Sam, the enslaved man? I want to know for certain. You know the answer, and please tell me. If your answer is yes, I will send your receipt back. If not, I will make every effort to send your money. I am quite able to pay the amount claimed.

You and I are getting old, and our earthly interests will soon end, so I do not want to do wrong. What I mean is this: if you helped take what I regarded as my property from me, you can get your money through legal proceedings. If not, I will gladly send it to you.
pages.family_note: Nance speaks of Sam as property and makes repayment conditional on Douglas’s role in his freedom. This letter names Sam but does not give his surname, tell how he became free, or establish whether Douglas assisted him. No answer is present on this page.

pages.title: N. L. Douglas’s oath of allegiance and office
pages.text:
Oath of Office.
I N L Douglas do solemnly swear that I have never voluntarily borne arms against the United States since I have been a citizen thereof; that I have voluntarily given no aid countenance council or encouragement to persons engaged in armed hostility thereto; that I have neither sought nor accepted nor attempted to exercise the functions of any office whatever under [[deleted: the]] any authority or pretended authority in hostility to the United States; that I have not yielded a voluntary support to any pretended government authority power or constitution within the United States hostile or inimical thereto; And I do further swear that to the best of my knowledge and ability I will support and defend the constitution of the United States against all enemies foreign and domestic, that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same, that I take this obligation freely without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter So help me God.
pages.editorial_notes: The reverse is labelled January 1868 (08-166). The oath names N. L. Douglas in its opening, but this scan shows no separate signature, witness, attestation or specific office. It cannot by itself prove that an official administered or accepted the oath. Original council retained.

pages.family_title: N. L. Douglas’s oath of allegiance and office
pages.family_text:
Oath of Office.
I, N. L. Douglas, solemnly swear that since becoming a United States citizen, I have never voluntarily taken up arms against the United States. I have voluntarily given no help, approval, advice or encouragement to people fighting it. I have neither sought nor accepted an office, nor tried to perform the duties of any office, under an authority claiming power in opposition to the United States. I have not voluntarily supported any claimed government, authority, power or constitution within the United States that was hostile to it.

I further swear that, to the best of my knowledge and ability, I will support and defend the United States Constitution against all foreign and domestic enemies. I will remain faithful and loyal to it. I take this obligation freely, without hidden reservations or intent to evade it, and will faithfully perform the duties of the office I am about to enter. So help me God.
pages.family_note: The reverse dates this paper to January 1868. This is the wording of an oath in Douglas’s name; the scan does not show a witness, certification or separate signature. It is evidence of the declaration he recorded, not independent proof of every claim in it.

Rutherford Co Tennessee April 18th 1852
Dear dauhter I received your Letter with Rebeccas dated October 18 1851 it come to hand in due time I would have answered it but I thought I would get another as soon as Mr Andrews got there—and I have bin waiting all this time and has got none
You wish me to [[deleted: illegible]] write often as I know by myself how glad I am to get one yes I am glad from my very hart to hear from you all—I am glad to hear that Susana wes Baptized I hope she will do good that she be rich in good works ready to distribute willing to Communicate laying up in store for herself a good foundation against the time to Come that she may lay hold [[deleted: illegible]] on eternal life
My sister Betsey is no more she died the 26 of january she suffered greatly she was [[tapt?]] 7 times she Lived 9 days on a little snow and snow water it was all she wanted she was very willing to die there [[inserted: fe]] ll a big snow on the 18 of january I visited her all I could while she was sick I was there by her when she died—I heard from you all by john Cock he said you was all well but Mr Douglass I am sorry to hear of his affliction I wish he could take care of himself and get well—I do not know how you can do there where every thing is so scearce and so dear—I [[deleted: illegible]] would like to hear whether the few things I sent you by Mr Andrews was damaged or not in cashing if the peafowl feathers went safe

Biblical passage and marginal reference are retained; it echoes 1 Timothy 6:18–19. “Cashing” is the source’s spelling, context uncertain.

pages.family_title: Rebecca Goodloe to her daughter Mary, April 18, 1852
pages.family_text:
Rutherford County, Tennessee, April 18, 1852. Dear daughter,
Your letter and Rebecca’s, dated October 18, 1851, arrived in good time. I would have answered, but expected another once Mr. Andrews reached you. I have waited all this time without receiving one.
You ask me to write often. I know how glad I am to receive a letter, and it warms my heart to hear from you all. I am glad Susanna was baptized. I hope she will do good, be generous and ready to share, building a foundation for eternal life, as the passage in Timothy says.
My sister Betsey died on January 26. She suffered greatly and was [[“tapt” seven times?—word uncertain]]. For nine days she lived on a little snow and melted snow; it was all she wanted. She was ready to die. Heavy snow fell on January 18. I visited whenever I could and was with her when she died.
John Cock told me that everyone was well except Mr. Douglass. I am sorry he is ill and hope he can care for himself and recover. I do not know how you manage where everything is so scarce and expensive. Please tell me whether the things I sent with Mr. Andrews were damaged during [[“cashing,” meaning uncertain]], and whether the peafowl feathers arrived safely.

pages.family_title: Weaving, gardening, household work, and neighborhood news
pages.family_text:
Give my sincere regards to Mr. and Mrs. Andrew for their kindness and generosity. I hope they like their new country, prosper in this life, and find happiness in the next. Rebecca asks what became of all the girls who married after she left. I cannot tell her everything; I think some would have been better off single. Isabella Hill moved to the western district. She had a daughter, Rhoda Louisa, and I heard her health was poor when she left.
Now for my own affairs. Thank God, I am reasonably healthy. I can get about and manage business, knit, sew, card wool or cotton, and do some spinning on the little wheel. I bought a loom, and Mary has woven [[number unclear: “2” followed by another figure]] lengths of cloth this winter. That is better than having my weaving done elsewhere. I have been gardening: peas are up and supported; Irish potatoes and onions are growing; beans and okra are planted; and beets, cucumbers, peppers, and cabbage plants are growing. We have planted some corn and will plant cotton this week. Mary tends the crop and garden with Sam.
Judy has a baby boy named Jim, said to be three months old. She does the cooking and washing. Amanda is at Betsey Graham’s; I do not know whether I can spare her from the crop. Alfred arranged for William Arbuckil to take Tom for the year in return for food and clothing and to teach him to work efficiently. Bill is here, carrying water and watching the children. Enough about that.

pages.family_title: Family marriages and moves; signed Mother Rebecca Goodloe
pages.family_text:
Cousin Betsey Adams, Billy Adams’s widow, has moved here and rented the [[Gonnatya?]] house from Mr. Hall. I let her boys farm some land. Her son Billy works at the sawmill and gristmill. Brother Jacob bought the mills from Ned Adam and is doing good business. He is busy as a bee, building a bridge. Everyone at home is well; Rebecca and Anda Alexander are well too.
Granville Jetton married Miss Elizabeth [[Conn?]]. Dick Jones married his third wife, Miss Mary, Elder McHenry’s daughter. Mary Waight has married Sam Rucker. Mary Goodloe remains helpless and was worse when I last heard. William Goodloe moved to Trenton, Gibson County, in the western district. Henry Goodloe’s daughters Altamira and Emily went along to spend the summer with relatives. James Goodloe married Miss Ann Neal of Gibson County and lives in Trenton.
Rebecca asked about Ned Adams and Cousin Betsey. They are well and doing better, although their little girl, one of the twins, has died. I cannot remember half the news Rebecca wants. Cousin Livve Posey and everyone in my family are well except Hannah, who is frail and has severe spells of illness. Betsey bought a house and lot in Woodbury with her own money and has the deed in her name.
Polly, just here Alfred arrived with your long-awaited letter. I read it with great satisfaction. I began this letter on Sunday, added to it yesterday, and now it is Tuesday. I was nearly finished when Alfred came. Julie is staying with Betsey in Woodbury. Your loving mother, Rebecca Goodloe. To Mary Douglass.

pages.title: Rebecca Goodloe to her granddaughter Susannah, April 21, 1852
pages.text:
Wednesday 21
Dear Susannah I was nearly done writeing when your grateful letter came to hand I read it with pleasure and I do [[deleted: illegible]] assure you it was a grate consolation to me I thank you my dear grand daughter for your gratitude and I hope you will always Remember me as your grandmother it is a very good letter I did not think you could write so good—I am very sorry for your Father I would allmost persuade him to try the water practice it might cure him if he know how to apply it he must be the best judge of himself
for the cramp colick hot [[inserted: watter]] dip a blanket in it and ring it out and wrap the person in as warm as posible put on warm blankets or a big feather bed put warm rocks or boiled corn to the feet and shoulders so as to sweat them quick I write this for the benefit of your mother as she use to be subject to the colick—dear susannah you must write again and tell me what you are all doing give my love to Rebeca & tell her to rite to me as soon as [[deleted: illegible]] this comes tell the boys to rite to me I send my love to all the Family I expect I will try to write again The rest of this Family must write for them selves
this is all I can do now no more from your affectionate grandmother
Rebecca Goodloe
Susannah Douglass
Hannah was mighty glad to hear from you all
pages.editorial_notes: The date reads Wednesday 21, following the April 18 letter. Descriptions of “water practice” and treatment for colic are historical remedies, transcribed as evidence, not recommended medical instructions.

pages.family_title: Rebecca Goodloe to her granddaughter Susannah, April 21, 1852
pages.family_text:
Wednesday, April 21. Dear Susannah,
I was nearly done writing when your grateful letter arrived. It gave me great pleasure and comfort. Thank you, dear granddaughter. I hope you will always remember me as your grandmother. Your letter was very good; I did not know you could write so well. I am sorry your father is ill. I would almost urge him to try a water treatment if he knew how to use it, though he must judge for himself.
The remedy I describe for cramping colic is a blanket dipped in hot water and wrung out, wrapped around the person with more warm blankets or a featherbed, and heated rocks or boiled corn at the feet and shoulders to bring on sweating. I mention this for your mother, who used to suffer from colic.
Write again and tell me what everyone is doing. Give Rebecca my love and ask her to write as soon as this arrives. Tell the boys to write too. My love to all the family. I will try to write again; the others here must write for themselves. That is all I can do now. Your affectionate grandmother, Rebecca Goodloe. To Susannah Douglass.
Hannah was very glad to hear from you all.
pages.family_note: The water and heat treatments are reproduced solely as historical content, not present-day medical advice.

pages.title: S. J. Goodloe reports his mother’s death, June 18, 1852
pages.text:
Woodbury Cannon County Tenn
June 18th 1852.
Mr N L Douglas.
Dear Sir, I understand that Lewis Jetton wrote to you concerning the Death of Mother, though he did not state to you the particular incidents connected with that solemn unexpected and lamentable event, My dear Mother is no more; She departed this life on the 6th of May last; After having lived to the age of nearly Three Score and Ten years, and passing through the trials and vissicitudes of life with that patience, exercise and Christian deportment that characterize and distinguish her to a hight that many do not reach, in the paths of rectitude Morality and religion, She at last goes down in peace and quietude to the silent Tomb of the grave ready and prepared to take her Flight to the Mansions of Heaven in the Eternal Kingdom of God on the Morning of the resurrection.
pages.editorial_notes: Letter continues on 09-007–009, signed S. J. Goodloe and addressed to N. L. Douglas. Wrapper 09-010 expands the writer to Sam J. Goodloe and explicitly identifies the deceased mother as Rebecca Goodloe. “Nearly three score and ten” means nearly seventy.

pages.family_title: S. J. Goodloe reports his mother’s death, June 18, 1852
pages.family_text:
Woodbury, Cannon County, Tennessee, June 18, 1852. Mr. N. L. Douglas,
Dear Sir, I understand Lewis Jetton wrote about Mother’s death, but did not describe the circumstances of that sudden and sorrowful event. My dear mother is gone. She died on May 6, nearly seventy years old. She faced life’s hardships with patience and Christian conduct, reaching a standard of integrity, morality, and faith that few attain. At last she rests peacefully in the grave, ready, in our faith, to rise to heaven in God’s eternal kingdom on the morning of resurrection.

pages.title: The sudden collapse on May 6
pages.text: She arose from her bed on the Morning of the 6th of May last apparently well as usual and Seemed to administer her domestic affairs with ordinary diligence and ease, until late in the Evening while Sewing upon a pair of pantaloons, She fell Suddenly from her Chair, as if Having received a general Shock of paralysis, [[Jena?]] a negro girl being the only person in the Room ran to her assistance and aided her to the bed, Mother called Julia at the time She fell from her chair, though Julia did not go thinking nothing Serious the matter and being engaged at Something in another Room of the House, however Julia got to her about the time She reached the Bed, and on interrogating her Mother observed that She was very Sick and Seemed to be very Stupid, and from every Symptom She Seemed to have had a Stroke of the Apolexy, However She immediately appeared to feel better, [[deleted: illegible]] though manifesting by her expressions a loss of Memory at times. I being

pages.family_title: The sudden collapse on May 6
pages.family_text: On the morning of May 6, she got up apparently as well as usual and managed household business normally. Late that evening, while sewing trousers, she suddenly fell from her chair, as though paralyzed. [[Jena?]], a Black girl and the only other person in the room, helped her to bed. Mother called Julia when she fell, but Julia was occupied in another room and did not initially think it serious. Julia arrived about the time Mother reached the bed. When asked how she felt, Mother said she was very ill and seemed dazed. Her symptoms suggested what the writer called apoplexy. She soon seemed better, although at times her words showed lapses of memory. I had been—

pages.family_title: Her final half-hour and those present
pages.family_text:
—away all day. I returned just before sunset, and Julia told me Mother was sick. At her bedside I asked what was wrong. She said her stomach was upset and her eyes and head hurt, though she felt better. I left the room; about ten minutes later Julia called that Mother was dying. I hurried back and saw that she was close to death. About half an hour later she was gone. She scarcely struggled and clasped my hand as though saying goodbye. She had not spoken since telling me she felt better.
The writer lists [[Jena?]], Hannah, and himself as those of the family present; some nearby neighbors were also there. Hannah grieves deeply and is in poor health. Julia, Hannah, and Alfred will stay on the farm—

pages.text:
October the 6th 1851
Dear Polly I hope this will find you all well with the Blessing of god I am as well as usual Hannah is still complaining she can walk about and smoke the pipe & that all she doe
I have just heard from the [[deleted: illegible]] western District Mr Nance has the fever and Lucy and four of the children has the chills and fever Cynthia an all her family has bin sick Your Brother Sam is in Lebanon going to the Law school we have not heard from Mobile since last spring my sister Betsey woods is very sick & low with the Dropsy she was tapt last thursday & 4 gallons of water was taken from her which relieved her misery some I have no hopes of her ever recovering Mr Andrews family will give you all the news
Well Polly I send you some cloth by Mr Andrews for you to dispose of as you think best I [[inserted: wish]] Mr Douglas and Warren to have Coats if they chose—there is 22 yards of jeans in trunk I allowed the green for George Cote and breaches I could not get them all dyed the weaver Martha ann [[goad?]] Adams was in a hurry to get the cloth out of the loome as John wanted to move to Arkansas you must have some walnut bark and a little coppres and dye his breaches black as the last end is not all of a coler there is 13 yards of dark brown and 5 pale brown I send some [[deleted: illegible]] summer cloth for Jessee and [[deleted: illegible]] Warren pantaloons and eight and a half yards of plad for the little girls winter dreses I send a pair of yarn socks for Mr Douglass and a pair of Cotton Stockins for yourself and a pair for Laura a pair for Mary little blue ones & some yarn to nit the

pages.family_title: Rebecca sends cloth and clothing to Polly, October 6, 1851
pages.family_text:
October 6, 1851. Dear Polly,
I hope everyone is well. Thank God, I am as well as usual. Hannah is still unwell; walking about and smoking her pipe are all she does.
News from the western district: Mr. Nance has a fever, while Lucy and four children have chills and fever. Cynthia and her whole family have been sick. Your brother Sam is attending law school in Lebanon. We have heard nothing from Mobile since last spring. My sister Betsey Woods is very ill with dropsy. Last Thursday four gallons of fluid were drained from her, relieving her suffering somewhat, but I do not expect her to recover. The Andrews family will bring you all the news.
I am sending cloth with Mr. Andrews for you to use as you think best. I hope Mr. Douglas and Warren will have coats if they wish. There are twenty-two yards of jeans fabric in the trunk. I intended the green for George’s coat and trousers. I could not get it all dyed. The weaver, Martha Ann [[goad?]] Adams, hurried to finish because John wanted to move to Arkansas. I suggest walnut bark and a little copperas to dye George’s trousers black, since the last piece is uneven in color. There are thirteen yards of dark brown and five of pale brown. I am also sending summer cloth for Jesse’s and Warren’s trousers, and eight and a half yards of plaid for the little girls’ winter dresses. There are yarn socks for Mr. Douglass, cotton stockings for you and Laura, little blue ones for Mary, and yarn to knit—

pages.family_title: Seeds, quills, baptisms, and a marriage rumor
pages.family_text:
—stockings for the other children. I am sending Rebecca eight yards of calico. If that is not enough for her dress, she should give it to Susanna. I am sending cotton dresses for Susanna and Laura, and three and a half yards of blue checked calico for little Mary. If that will not make a dress, use it for something else. There are peafowl feathers, goose quills, sage, garden comfrey seed I grew myself, and a little starch.
I am sorry to burden Mr. Andrew, but he willingly does what he can for Mr. Douglass, whom he calls a great friend. Give my love to Jesse, Henry, and everyone else, and accept the same yourself. Your mother, Rebecca Goodloe.
We had a four- or five-day meeting at Riplecreek Meetinghouse. Brothers Trot and Corlee preached, as did [[Sanda?]] Jones. Fourteen were baptized; the list includes John Smith, [[Eveart and Houghs?]], two of Nathan Hale’s daughters, and [[Polenna?]] Jones. Emily Goodloe and Altamira had been baptized earlier. I cannot write any more now. Write as often as possible, and ask Rebecca and Susanna to write whenever they can send mail. I nearly forgot: I heard Sarah Barr is going to marry.
To Mary Douglass. The braid is to trim Susanna’s green sack jacket; put two rows around it.

pages.title: The Pleasures of Memory: an unsigned essay
pages.text:
The Pleasures of Memory.

How often our minds revert [[inserted: pleasures]] to by gone days. Pleasures that were impressed upon our minds before we knew the cares of this world, never to be effaced by the corrosive hand of Time.
It is true, our minds are often burdened with the cares and perplexities of life, and we feel there is nothing bright to look upon; when all at once some familiar sound, a silvery voice, breaks the stillness of our hearts, and calls us back to some cherished scene of the past.
We think of the dear ones at home, whose loving hands were ever ministering to our wants, and whose guardian influence [[deleted: was]] ever directing our footsteps through the uneven scenes of life.

The Pleasures of Memory
How often our thoughts return to the pleasures of earlier days, formed before we knew the cares of the world—memories that time cannot erase.
Life’s worries often weigh on us until we see nothing bright. Then a familiar sound or a clear, musical voice suddenly stirs our hearts and returns us to a treasured scene.
We remember loved ones at home, whose hands cared for us and whose guidance led us through life’s uneven paths.

pages.title: Memories of home, prairie flowers, and streams
pages.text:
We think of Home, that sacred spot where have been passed the happiest hours of life.
It matters not how drear the spot
How proud or poor the home
Love still retains some deathless chains
That bind the heart to home.

We think of the surroundings of this home; the many happy hours spent in roaming over the broad prairies gathering the many colored flowers which was then the hith of our ambition. And again how much delight we would take in wandering along the mosscovered banks of the beautiful streams which were nearest us forgetful of Times rapid flight.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-013. The four verse lines are set apart in the manuscript. “Hith” is retained as written, evidently meaning height in context.

pages.family_title: Memories of home, prairie flowers, and streams
pages.family_text:
We remember home, that sacred place where we spent our happiest hours:
No matter how bleak the place,
How grand or humble the home,
Love keeps bonds that never die
And ties our hearts to home.

We remember its surroundings and the hours spent wandering the broad prairies gathering colorful flowers. That was then the height of our ambitions. We delighted in following the moss-covered banks of nearby streams, forgetting how quickly time passed.
