pages.title: Sunday-school memories and the comfort of remembrance
pages.text:
Let us think for a moment of the pleasures realized in after time, when we are old enough to attend Sunday school; how happy is each heart on entering the school room, as they crowd round their teacher in eagerness to learn sacred lessons from the holy Scriptures.
With what implicit confidence they look into their teachers face, and how indellibly his instructions are impressed upon their minds,
These scenes are permanently impressed upon my mind and I can imagine after our earthly race is almost run, we can truly say
There are moments in life [[inserted: that]] we never forget,
Which brighten and brighten, as time steals away;
They give a new charm to the happiest lot,
And shine on the gloom of the lonliest day.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of the unsigned essay 09-013–014. Quoted or verse-form concluding lines retained as part of the manuscript; no external authorship attribution has been imposed.

pages.family_title: Sunday-school memories and the comfort of remembrance
pages.family_text:
Think of the later pleasure of being old enough for Sunday school: the happiness of entering the room, gathering eagerly around the teacher, and learning from the Bible.
Children look into the teacher’s face with complete trust, and the lessons leave a lasting impression. Those scenes remain in my memory. I imagine that near the end of life we can still say:
There are moments in life we never forget,
Growing brighter as time slips away;
They add new delight to our happiest days,
And bring light to our loneliest day.

pages.family_title: Patriotic Song, bearing Emily Douglas’s name
pages.family_text:
Patriotic Song
Of all the lands in east or west,
I love my native country best.
It overflows with God’s good gifts.
Though neither gold nor gems are found,
People with noble hearts abound,
And eyes shine brightly with joy. [Repeat.]

Of all the tongues in east or west,
I love my native language best.
It may not be so smoothly spoken,
Or woven with Italian skill,
But when heart speaks to heart,
Its word is never broken. [Repeat.]

Of all the peoples east or west,
I love my countrymen the best,
A people of a noble spirit.
A sober mind, a generous heart,
Taught goodness, free from artifice,
They inherit [[from?]] their ancestors. [Repeat.]

I offer my hand to all the world,
But give my heart to my native land,
Seeking its good and glory.
I honor every nation’s name,
Respect its fortune and its fame,
But love the land that bore me. [Repeat.]

Emily Douglas.

pages.title: Miriam Stevenson reconnects with Polly from Columbus, October 24, 1855
pages.text:
Columbus Oct. 24. 1855
Mrs Douglas
My Dear old friend
This evening I have determined to do what I have long wished to do, but not knowing your address (untill recently), I hope you will excuse me. I have just returned from Tennessee our old native place, There I learned your whereabouts. While there I saw Mrs Sam Davis who delivered a message sent by her husband I was more than happy to hear of your wellfare and future prospects, May you live long and be happy is the wish of my heart, and believe me my dear friend, there is none that feels more deeply interested for you and yours, than your humble servant. Well Polly (for so I am wont to speak) we both have had many troubles and trials to contend with since we parted, but it is all for our good if we love the Lord, I have long since learned that all things earthly are transitory and that this is not my abiding place, but look for a city whose maker and builder is God, My heart and Treasure is There, I have no cause to murmur, My health is fine, weigh 144. When I was in Tennessee I saw your sisters Mrs Jones and Mrs Nance, Doca was on a visit looks very thin, so does Julia, I did not see

pages.family_text:
Columbus, October 24, 1855. Mrs. Douglas, my dear old friend,
This evening I am finally doing what I have long wished: writing to you. Until recently I did not know your address. I have just returned from Tennessee, our old home, where I learned where you live. Mrs. Sam Davis passed along a message from her husband. I was delighted to hear that you are doing well and have good prospects. I wish you a long, happy life; no one cares more deeply about you and your family.
Polly—as I am used to calling you—we have both faced many troubles since we parted. I believe they work for our good if we love the Lord. I have learned that earthly things pass away. This is not my permanent home; I look toward the city built by God. My heart and treasure are there, and I have no reason to complain. I am healthy and weigh 144.
In Tennessee I saw your sisters, Mrs. Jones and Mrs. Nance. Doca was visiting and looks very thin, as does Julia. I did not see—

pages.title: Changes in Tennessee and Miriam’s life after her husband’s death
pages.text:
Rebecca nor Betsey, as it was not convenient for me to visit them. I heard that they were well, saw a great many of our old neighbors, and some new ones that I never saw before. Mary Weather[[s?]] for instance, has seven daughters. just to think but no, I must stop, The very country appears strange I saw few persons or things that looked natural,
Rebecca Alexander looks very well, Andy looks badly, Uncle Jacob and Aunt Polly are very much broken, though as anxious about the things of this world as ever, There are so many changes that I can not speak of them all, I received a letter from sister Louisa this morning stating that Virginia McKnight, (Johnson that was) is dead, went to her mothers on Sunday and was taken that night, died on Thursday, Sister Lou lives very comfortably, makes plenty of every thing to supply on I stoped a few minutes in Murfreesboro, saw Aunt Brown Amanda Mosby Dora Brown, and Dora Nance all together, could not stay long enough to learn any thing particular
Now I must tell you something of myself I am still teaching and trying to make my self useful. I kept house two and a half years the happiest time of my life, After I lost my husband I kept house no more. He had 4 children, his relations took 3, I kept one, a sweet little girl now nearly ten years old her name is Virginia

—Rebecca or Betsey, because I could not conveniently visit, though I heard they were well. I saw many old neighbors and new people too. Mary Weather[[s?]], for instance, has seven daughters! Even the countryside seems strange; few people or things looked familiar.
Rebecca Alexander looks well, but Andy looks unwell. Uncle Jacob and Aunt Polly look much aged, although they worry as much as ever about worldly affairs. There are too many changes to recount. Sister Louisa wrote this morning that Virginia McKnight, formerly Johnson, died. She visited her mother on Sunday, became ill that night, and died on Thursday. Sister Lou lives comfortably and produces plenty for her needs. During a short stop in Murfreesboro, I saw Aunt Brown, Amanda Mosby, Dora Brown, and Dora Nance together, but could not stay to hear much news.
As for me, I still teach and try to be useful. I kept house for two and a half years—the happiest period of my life. After my husband died, I stopped keeping my own household. He had four children. His relatives took three, and I kept one: a sweet girl named Virginia, now almost ten.

pages.title: Teaching, raising Virginia, and maintaining old friendships
pages.text:
The only care of my life is to raise and educate this child, She is pretty well advanced for her age. I am happy to tell you that my means are sufficient, without my labor to support us, but I prefer employment, I know it is conducive to health and happiness, I have been boarding at the hotel for several years, consequently have not much to do but go to school and Church. We have a very nice house of worship meet every Lords day and worship according to Bible. Mr Darnall Elizabeth an Eveline have all had the chills lately, They are living near by and doing very well. Thomas Sherrill is also living here and is one of the best Artists [[obscured]] I will send you a specimen of his work for a remembrance in my next, if this should be so fortunate as to reach you, I hope you will favor me with a long letter very soon. Remember me to all the family who have any recollection of me, Mr Douglass has not forgotten me no never, say to him I would be delighted to rec. a letter from him, Ann [[illegible]]
Farewell my kind farewell
Yours sincerely Miriam Stevenson

pages.family_title: Teaching, raising Virginia, and maintaining old friendships
pages.family_text:
My chief concern is to raise and educate her. She is advanced for her age. I have enough money to support us without working, but I prefer employment because it is good for health and happiness. For several years I have boarded at a hotel, so I have little to do besides attend school and church. We have a pleasant church building and meet every Sunday to worship according to the Bible.
Mr. Darnall, Elizabeth, and Eveline have recently had chills, but they live nearby and are doing well. Thomas Sherrill also lives here and is one of the best artists [[words obscured]]. If this letter reaches you, I will send an example of his work as a keepsake with my next letter. Please write a long reply soon. Remember me to anyone in the family who recalls me. Surely Mr. Douglass has not forgotten me; tell him I would be delighted to receive a letter. [[Unclear fragment.]]
A fond farewell. Yours sincerely, Miriam Stevenson.

pages.title: Miriam sends her portrait, March 29, 1856
pages.text:
Columbus March 29th. 1856
Dearest Mrs Douglass
After so long a delay It is with much pleasure that I acknowledge the receipt of your truly welcome letter. We have had a very cold and disagreeable winter, consequently great irregularity in our mails. but now the weather is pleasant I will venture to send my type, not because I thought it of much importance to any one, but I wish to live in your memory, and may be so you have forgotten my exact contour. If so, it will recall by gone days. yes this is me in my 48th year, weighing 145 and as youthful as when 19 (that is in my feelings and disposition
My health is fine except a slight touch of that fashionable disease, Neuralgia which knots me up a little at times. I am still teaching but think now that this is my last session, I am getting tired of confinement, I should like very much to travel if I were not a coward, but I must confess that water and steam affect my nerves so as to produce very unpleasant feelings.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-022. “Type” refers to the likeness being sent; the specific photographic process is not stated. Age and weight are retained as written. This letter describes a portrait but does not prove that the image survives among the supplied scans.

pages.family_title: Miriam sends her portrait, March 29, 1856
pages.family_text:
Columbus, March 29, 1856. Dearest Mrs. Douglass,
After a long delay I gladly acknowledge your welcome letter. The cold, unpleasant winter made the mail irregular. Now that the weather is better, I will venture to send my portrait. I do not think it important to anyone, but I want to remain in your memory. Perhaps you have forgotten exactly how I look; if so, it will recall earlier days. Here I am in my forty-eighth year, weighing 145 and feeling as young as nineteen.
I am healthy except for occasional neuralgia, that fashionable complaint, which ties me in knots. I still teach, but think this may be my last term. I am tired of being confined. I would love to travel if I were braver, but water and steam make me very nervous.

pages.title: An enduring friendship and news from Sister Lou
pages.text:
I am truly rejoiced to learn of [[inserted: your]] wellfare and also of your childrens, they are all dear to me, because they are yours. & I would be happy to see you all but cannot now promise my self the pleasure of ever doing so But time nor absence can ever efface from memory the pleasant recollections of youthful days. No they are as green spots in my recollection that time nor distance will ever obliterate.
I received a letter from Sister Lou not long since, she says that your Cousin Tompson Wright was married to Miss [[Bowen?]] and that Virginia McKnight, (Williams wife) was dead. My friends here are all well, and desire to be remembered to your family. Say to Mr. D. I appreciate his good wishes, and kind regards and return them four fold.
My love to my dear Cousins James and Cynthie I do remember [[inserted: them]] fondly, and desire to be remembered by them. Please let me hear from you soon. My best wishes attend all that relates to you and yours, now farewell my dear kind friend farewell. May the Lord bless and protect you through life comfort you in death, and receive you in Heaven is the prayer of your friend. Miriam Stevenson.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-021. Bride’s surname tentative. “Your Cousin Tompson Wright” is an explicit relationship statement, but degree of cousinship is not supplied. Virginia McKnight is identified as William’s wife here.

pages.family_title: An enduring friendship and news from Sister Lou
pages.family_text:
I am delighted that you and your children are well. They are dear to me because they are yours. I would love to see everyone, though I cannot promise I ever will. Neither time nor absence can erase the happy memories of our youth; they remain fresh places in my memory that distance cannot destroy.
Sister Lou wrote recently that your cousin Tompson Wright married Miss [[Bowen?]], and that Virginia McKnight, William’s wife, died. Everyone here is well and sends greetings. Tell Mr. Douglass I value his kindness and return his good wishes fourfold.
My love to my dear cousins James and Cynthie. I remember them fondly and hope they remember me. Write soon. My best wishes go with you and your family. Farewell, dear friend. May the Lord protect you through life, comfort you in death, and receive you in heaven. Your friend, Miriam Stevenson.

paragraphs.text:
I am truly rejoiced to learn of [[inserted: your]] wellfare and also of your childrens, they are all dear to me, because they are yours. & I would be happy to see you all but cannot now promise my self the pleasure of ever doing so But time nor absence can ever efface from memory the pleasant recollections of youthful days. No they are as green spots in my recollection that time nor distance will ever obliterate.
I received a letter from Sister Lou not long since, she says that your Cousin Tompson Wright was married to Miss [[Bowen?]] and that Virginia McKnight, (Williams wife) was dead. My friends here are all well, and desire to be remembered to your family. Say to Mr. D. I appreciate his good wishes, and kind regards and return them four fold.
My love to my dear Cousins James and Cynthie I do remember [[inserted: them]] fondly, and desire to be remembered by them. Please let me hear from you soon. My best wishes attend all that relates to you and yours, now farewell my dear kind friend farewell. May the Lord bless and protect you through life comfort you in death, and receive you in Heaven is the prayer of your friend. Miriam Stevenson.

pages.title: Miriam describes the portrait’s dress and hairstyle, July 6, 1856
pages.text:
Columbus July 6th 1856
My Dear kind friend Mrs Douglas
Your favor of May the 26 came safe to hand and found a warm reception, I was amused at the idea of your thinking that there had been a mistake perhaps in the picture. I do assure you that it is my own dear self, I had a head dress on of mohair with 3 curls on each side, My dress is of rich brocade, blue and brown, but the colors did not Take, I rejoice to learn of your [[deleted: illegible]] health and prospects. I pray that your life may be long useful and happy and that I may be permitted to see your face again in the flesh, O how pleasant the thought, but we must [[inserted: not]] presume upon the future, the present only is ours. When I call to mind the many pleasant hours we have spent together it spreads a gloom over my feelings to know that [[inserted: they]] can never be recalled. But we must not permit the recollections of the past cast a shadow upon the future.
My health is pretty good, I shall leave for the country soon and remain 2 months, the warm season is not pleasant here
pages.editorial_notes: Continues through 09-027. The writer explicitly identifies the picture as herself and describes mohair headwear, curls, and blue-and-brown brocade. “The colors did not Take” describes the result in the image; do not infer a particular photographic process.

pages.family_text:
Columbus, July 6, 1856. My dear friend Mrs. Douglas,
Your letter of May 26 arrived safely and was warmly welcomed. I was amused that you thought there might have been a mistake with the picture. I assure you it is me! I wore a mohair headdress with three curls on each side. My dress was rich blue-and-brown brocade, but the colors did not show in the picture.
I am glad to hear of your health and prospects. I pray you have a long, useful, happy life, and that I may see you again. What a pleasant thought! But we must not presume upon the future; only the present is ours. Remembering our happy hours together saddens me because they cannot return. Still, we should not let memories of the past darken the future.
I am fairly well and will soon spend two months in the country. The hot season is unpleasant here—

pages.title: Country air and religious fellowship
pages.text:
It is very pleasant to get out and breathe the pure country atmosphere O I long to be off. I have been closely confined for 10 months but now I am free once more.
Well, having just returned from Church I will finish my letter. We had no preaching to day as our preacher is sick, but it is our practice to attend to the ordinances of the Lords house preacher or not, this we never neglect, and Oh that all could see and Appreciate their liberties as they ought, Then we should [[inserted: see]] Christians meeting together to sing, praise, and give thanks, rejoicing in the commandments of our Lord and Saviour. My dear friend this to me is the greatest pleasure of my life, I feel under many obligations to my Heavenly Father for his goodness to me particularly since I have been living in the South, circumstances have been peculiarly favourable to Christianity. You know that I was persecuted and shuned and sneered at on account of my faith and practice in my early career, but I always did and do now rejoice that I am counted worthy to be made partaker of his sufferings, who suffered so much for me.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-024. Statements about past persecution and the South’s religious climate are Miriam’s personal testimony. No specific denomination or persecutor is named here.

—and it will be lovely to breathe the country air. I long to go. After ten months of being closely confined, I am free again.
I have just returned from church and will finish the letter. Our preacher was sick, so there was no sermon, but we observe our worship practices whether a preacher is present or not. We never neglect that. If everyone valued their religious freedom, Christians would gather to sing, praise, and give thanks, rejoicing in the Lord’s commands.
For me, this is life’s greatest pleasure. I owe much to God for his kindness, especially since I moved south, where circumstances have favored my Christian life. You know that earlier I was persecuted, shunned, and mocked for my beliefs and practices. Yet I have always rejoiced—and still do—that I may share in the suffering of the one who suffered so much for me.

pages.title: Miriam responds to Mary’s discouragement
pages.text: My dear friend you speak despondingly in your last. I fear that you attach too much importance to earthly matters, You say few and evil has been the days of my pilgrimage Now dear friend do not let such thoughts [[inserted: intrude]] themselves, Surely you have one of the kindest of husbands (at least I think so) and a circle of children that have never disgraced you, Think again my dear, and you will find ten thousand things to give thanks for instead of repining, I fear that you have never submitted wholly and solely to the government of High Heaven. If not you must not expect peace, There is no peace to the wicked, You must [[not?]] infer from this that I consider you a great sinner no, no, but I mean that you must be a member of his body, or else you are none of his, Look to it my friend and make your title good to mansions in the skies. I hope to hear from you soon again for indeed it is a source of great pleasure to me. I intend to send you a present if an opportunity offers. Do present my [[double breasted?]] affection to Mr Douglass, he shares largely in my respect and esteem, also to your children those of them who remember me
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-025. A possibly omitted or faint “not” before “infer” is marked rather than silently inserted; the following “no, no” supports the intended sense. Unusual phrase modifying “affection” remains tentative. The theological advice expresses the correspondent’s beliefs.

pages.family_title: Miriam responds to Mary’s discouragement
pages.family_text:
You sounded discouraged in your last letter. I fear you give too much weight to worldly troubles. You wrote that the days of your pilgrimage had been few and unhappy. Do not let such thoughts intrude. You have, I believe, a very kind husband and children who have never disgraced you. Reflect again, and you will find countless reasons for gratitude instead of complaint.
I fear you may not have surrendered fully to God’s guidance. Without that, I believe, you cannot expect peace. Do not take this to mean I consider you a great sinner—no! I mean you must belong to Christ’s body. Attend to that, my friend, and secure your place in heaven.
Please write again; your letters give me great pleasure. I hope to send you a present when the opportunity comes. Give Mr. Douglass my affection [[the original modifier is uncertain]], respect, and esteem, and remember me to the children who recall me.

pages.title: W. Douglas to his sister Rebecca, June 3, 1856
pages.text:
Wardville June 3d 1856
Dear Sister
I have recd. and read with much pleasure your kind favor of the 20th Ult.
I was surprised a little at first, but upon a thought I was surprised that I was surprised at all. For what is more to be expected than that we should often think of & write to each other. It is surprising that we never have before. As for me to forget you or to love you less, with the lapse of Time, & the change of circumstances the thing is simply impossible! for all my recollections of the past are inseperably connected with you.
Back to the extreme limit to which my memory stretches; you were the constant and almost only playmate of my early childhood and still onward through boyhood and youth and up to full Maturity you were my companion how then can or could we cease to cherish a warm and steady affection for each other
No, other ties may be formed—other friendships decay—but ours is part and parcel of our very lives, an affection [[inserted: that]] [[roots not low?]] in the clay.
I am well, and that is about all that I have to write about myself for nothing occurs to me that would interest you
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-029–030, where the writer signs W. Douglas and names the recipient Rebecca Winnifrid. Metaphorical phrase near the bottom remains tentative. The initial is not expanded to a forename.

pages.family_title: W. Douglas to his sister Rebecca, June 3, 1856
pages.family_text:
Wardville, June 3, 1856. Dear Sister,
I was delighted to receive your letter of May 20. At first I was a little surprised—then surprised at my own surprise. What could be more natural than for us to think of one another and write often? It is surprising we have not done so before. I could never forget you or love you less as time and circumstances change. Every memory of my past is inseparably connected with you.
As far back as I can remember, you were my constant and almost only childhood playmate. Through boyhood, youth, and adulthood, you remained my companion. How could we ever lose our warm, lasting affection?
Other relationships may form and other friendships fade, but ours is woven into our lives—an affection [[the following image about roots and clay is uncertain]].
I am well. There is little else to report about myself, since nothing happens that would interest you—

pages.title: Why he wants to leave Texas for California
pages.text:
these hard times. We had a greatdeal of wet weather this spring but it has been quite dry for some 3 weeks and rain is much needed.
The prospect for corn is pretty good wheat is nowhere in this country
I have recd. a letter from Henry by the same Mail that brought yours, he was well but times are dull with him too, & like me I think he is a little unsettled in his mind about his future course.
You seem a little horrified at the idea of my going to California; you need not be I think—for men, & better than yours, are & are going there. Every man of intelligence that I have ever conversed with who has seen California speaks highly of it as a Country. Many advise me to go & some are going the second time, with their families
I find it impossible to rise above a mere hand-to-mouth living in Texas, without the practice of the most stringent dealings & economy. Things that find place neither in my nature, nor my philosophy. Why then should I be so closely bound to Texas when I am already separated effectually, and hopelessly from you and all others, who love me.
If there is a better place why not find it Why not enjoy the best of a little world like this, when even that best, is bad enough
I do not think of any sudden acquirement

pages.family_text:
—in these hard times. Spring was very wet, but now we have had three dry weeks and badly need rain. The corn looks fairly promising; wheat is doing poorly here.
Henry’s letter came with yours. He was well, but business is slow for him too. Like me, he seems uncertain about his future.
You sound horrified by my idea of going to California. I do not think you need to be. Other men—better men than your brother—are there or going there. Every intelligent person I have spoken to who has seen California speaks highly of it. Many urge me to go; some are returning with their families.
I cannot get beyond a hand-to-mouth existence in Texas without being extremely strict in business and spending. Neither suits my nature or my outlook. Why should I feel so tied to Texas when I am already effectively and hopelessly separated from you and everyone else who loves me?
If there is a better place, why not find it? Why not enjoy the best this little world offers, when even its best is poor enough? I do not expect sudden—

pages.text:
of wealth by the move, but I think I can do better there than here, at any rate I have had it in my head for a long time, and it is worth my while going there if even it is only to correct the mistake if it should turn out a mistake.—You may put it up as pretty Certain, that I will go to Cal. in the spring if life is Spared me; for to that end I have already begun to make my arrangements
District Court begins here on monday and I have to attend as a witness in a land case, If nothing happens I will come down immediately after, but it is uncertain as I do not know what business may come up for me. Indeed I can think of nothing more, at present, Uncle Lewis &c were well last accounts. My Respects to Norvell & all enquiring friends. I Remain Truly
Your Brother
W. Douglas
Rebecca Winnifrid

Write often, your letters will always afford me new pleasure
W. D.

pages.title: Condolences on George’s father’s death, July 9, probably 1874
pages.text:
Corinth Miss July 9 [[1874?]]
[[deleted: illegible]] Cousin George
I have just Rec your letter of June 23d Bringing the sad news of the death of your Father we were Sorry indeed to hear it. tho acording to the natural corse of things we could expect nothing else for he lived to a good old age. we are all well and doing very well those of us that is living Sister Marthah died last August [[Ma?]] has had better health this year than She has had for several years—
as far the [[illegible]] is concerned I never intended that any of you should Sufer any uneasiness about them I thought that I had written to that effect several times so you can give the amount to Aunt Polly and cousin Lizzie & if that do not settle it you can write to me again we have a good crop and I have been hoeing cotton to day so feel very little like writing so that will account for short letter and bad writing
I would like you to write me a long letter and give me a history of the country the changes how the Rail Roads Runs and the price of Land &c Give my love to all. Yours &c
E. M. Hyneman

The financial subject after “as far the” is faint; no amount is given. “Cousin,” “Aunt Polly,” and “Sister Marthah” are the writer’s relationship terms, without a stated degree of cousinship.

pages.family_title: Condolences on George’s father’s death, July 9, probably 1874
pages.family_text:
Corinth, Mississippi, July 9, [[1874?]]. Cousin George,
I have received your June 23 letter with the sad news of your father’s death. We were very sorry, though at his advanced age it was to be expected in the natural course of life. Those of us still living are well and doing well. Sister Marthah died last August. [[Ma?]] has been healthier this year than for several years.
About the [[unclear financial matter]], I never meant any of you to worry. I thought I had written that several times. Give the amount to Aunt Polly and Cousin Lizzie; if that does not settle matters, write again. We have a good crop. I have been hoeing cotton today and feel little like writing, which explains this short letter and poor handwriting.
Please write a long letter describing the country, its changes, the railroad routes, and land prices. Love to everyone. Yours, E. M. Hyneman.

pages.family_text:
Corinth, Mississippi, September [[16?]], [[1869?]]. My very dear cousin,
After a long delay, I have decided to answer my darling cousin’s letter. Do not think my affection has diminished; I have been busy. If I did not know how forgiving you are, I would have long ago concluded that you thought me inconsiderate. It is a great pleasure to answer your letters.
The family is well. [[Some wording is unclear.]] Cholera is all around us, and almost everyone who catches it dies very quickly. I hope we escape it. Corinth is rather dull. We have excellent crops and [[unclear wording]] wonderful watermelons, but they are almost gone now. I do not know what I will do; there is no fruit in the country. I suppose it is for the best.
How is my Texan [[name or description unreadable]]? All right, I hope.
There will be a grand tournament here on the fifteenth of next month. I expect it to be enjoyable. It is time we had something to break the town’s monotony, since we have had—[[continuation not present on this page]].

Murfreesboro, Tennessee, October 28, 1859. [[Opening damaged.]] Uncle,
After neglecting to write for a long time, I am sitting down to let you know I have not forgotten you. I wrote earlier; I suppose the letter never arrived, or you would have answered.
My family is well. It is a large family: I have five girls and one boy with Jane. [[Damaged words.]] The older one turns twenty-one on December 27, and the other is nineteen. Both attend [[damaged word, apparently college]] in Murfreesboro. William finishes at the beginning of December. Both belong to the college literary society and rank highly as speakers. William was chosen twice in the past year to give an address in the town church before a large audience; he does himself credit.
Samuel has been unfortunate. He has lost the use of one leg through what is called scrofulous hip disease and must always use a crutch. He is a good scholar, has taught a school, and was well liked. I hope he will do well.
Besides William and Samuel at college, I have had four girls in school this year. It is expensive. We have had one of the worst droughts I have ever seen. For the first time since I began farming, I must buy [[missing commodity]] and pork. Money will be tight at Christmas. I bought Father’s land at the sale, and the—

—payment is now due. I hope I can meet it. My family is so [[damaged]] that living costs a great deal. Every year is harder. This fall I must work harder than ever. Since William went to college, my only help is [[Tillis?]], a boy of about thirteen, and a girl of about ten. My little girls help pick cotton.
I have 180 acres, about 100 cleared. I will rent out about forty acres next year. I also have a [[damaged description]] and lot in town, rented for $100 a year. That and the farm provide all my income. I hope the boys will cost me no more [[damaged word]] after this year. They can now [[damaged wording about supporting themselves]]. Both are very [[damaged adjective]] and attentive to business.
Brother Nathaniel is on a farm. His health failed after bleeding from the lungs, but he is doing well now. Sister Cate lives on his farm and manages well. Sister Brandon lives in Kentucky. Brandon practices medicine and was doing well at the last report.

pages.text:
Quincy Tenn Dec the 16th 1860
My Dear niece
I received your letter in due time but neglected to answer it I hope you will pardon me for my negligence we were very glad to hear from all the family through you. we were very sorry to hear of the death of Georges wife through Henry Orr. Henry wished to know in his letter why we never mentioned Adaline in our letters. She is no more. pages.family_title: Theodosia Nance to Lizzy and Mary, December 16, 1860
pages.family_text:
Quincy, Tennessee, December 16, 1860. My dear niece,
Your letter arrived on time, but I neglected to answer. Please forgive me. We were glad to hear about the family through you and very sorry to learn through Henry Orr that George’s wife had died.
Henry asked why our letters never mentioned Adaline. She has died. Mr. Nance wrote to your father soon afterward. She died of typhus fever on August 29, 1856, in her seventeenth year. She was a kind, affectionate child and a devoted Christian.
White and Robert Jetton have gone to Arkansas and bought land. On the way, they spent a day and night with us. They are intelligent, handsome young men. White resembles his mother and Robert his father. We regret that Henry did not visit when he was in Kentucky; we would have loved to see him and his wife.
Love to the whole family. Tell them to write. My affection and best wishes for your future happiness. Write soon. T. B. Nance, to Lizzy Douglas.
My dear sister,
God has blessed us with health, food, and clothing, for which we are thankful. My health has improved somewhat since my last letter. I am very grateful—

—to you and Sister Cynthia for inviting me to visit. Sadly, I cannot. I would love to see everyone again and talk face to face.
I traveled about 200 miles by train to Alabama to see Brother Newton. I left Thursday and arrived the next day, October 6. Everyone was well and about to move to Mobile. Newton is healthy and has aged little. Sister Margaret’s health is poor, but better than usual this year.
Their family is delightful. Columbia is exceptionally kind, well educated, and capable at all kinds of work. Lula and Mary are very nice girls. Newton has six children—three sons and three daughters. The youngest, Robert Newton, is five. French is a handsome man, well suited to business; Thomas is a lively boy. Martha Fletcher wrote that Newton and his family arrived safely and liked their new home.
Sister Betsey lives with Sister Nancy and says she is happy there. I have invited her to stay with me. Mr. Fletcher has an interest in two steamboats. Newton works as a clerk on one for $200 a month. Brother Robert is doing well in Mobile and has seven children. Lewis Jetton wrote recently; everyone there was well. Uncle Isaac Waight has died. He died—

—on December 4, of dropsy.
Sister Julia’s enslaved boy Sam is to be sold on January 6. Lewis thinks the price will be low because of political unrest and scarce money. E. H. Jones has married for the third time, to the widow Hancock.
Sister, when did you last hear from Brother Samuel’s widow? Can her relatives support her? Have you met her children? Tell me everything about her. Ask Sister Cynthia to write. I will write to her and Henry soon. Love to all our relatives. Mr. Nance joins me in sending love to you, Mr. Douglas, and the children. Write soon. Your affectionate sister, Theodosia B. Nance, to Mary Douglas.

I will add a few lines in the space Theo left. There is little special news. As you know, slavery is causing considerable agitation in our state. No one knows where it will end. I seriously fear that the Union is nearing its end. Our country neighborhood is quiet, but there is great unrest in towns and villages.
This has been one of the healthiest years since we moved to this end of the state. Despite a severe drought, we produced plenty to support ourselves. Prices: corn, 350 cents; wheat, 120 cents; pork, [[6–7?]] cents. [[The original does not state the units.]]

pages.title: Cageville church and letters awaiting forwarding
pages.text:
Old br Cosby & Hall are yet living, and enjoying pretty good healths of their age—Our place of worship is at Cageville a village about 4 ms off we meet every lords day here brother D. Hall lives, when I moved to this Country, I found Some 18 members assembling in his house to worship, we Continued to meet there for some months, untill we could a house where we have been meeting up to the present. We have great Cause to thank god and take Courage, for the success the gospel has had and still having around Cageville, our numbers have gradually Increased till we now number 250 [[members?]] and I would further Inform you that near 100 of our [[number?]] Came from our old County (Rutherford) So you will See we have a host of old acquaintances in our region of Tenn—We had a relative, Wm Goodloe a preacher on last [[illegible]] last year held a meeting for us which resulted in Some 30 [[illegible]] additions. he is quite a very Smart man, he now lives in Ala. If you read the American Christian Review, you have noticed his name—
I have 2 or 3 letters that were Sent from Some of your family I suppose To Henry Douglass, to my Care, I forwarded one to Henry in Ky I then recd notice from him not to Send any others to him untill I heard from him. So I waited & waited and have not heard from him Since and Still have them. I will forward them to your address Soon. Give my love to all the friends. I would like to hear from you all more frequent So write often Farewell
W. W. N.

pages.family_title: Cageville church and letters awaiting forwarding
pages.family_text:
Old Brothers Cosby and Hall are still alive and reasonably healthy for their age. We worship at Cageville, a village about four miles away, every Sunday. Brother D. Hall lives there. When I moved here, about eighteen members worshiped in his house. We continued there for several months until we could [[missing verb]] a meetinghouse, where we still gather.
We have much reason for gratitude and encouragement. The congregation has grown to about 250 members, nearly 100 of whom came from our old county, Rutherford. We therefore have many old acquaintances here in Tennessee. Our relative William Goodloe, a preacher, held a meeting last year that brought about thirty [[unclear wording]] additions. He is a very capable man and now lives in Alabama. You may have seen his name in the American Christian Review.
I still hold two or three letters, apparently from your family, sent to Henry Douglass in my care. I forwarded one to him in Kentucky. He then asked me to send no more until I heard from him. I have waited without further word, so I still have the others. I will forward them to your address soon.
Love to all our friends. I would like to hear more often, so please write. Farewell, W. W. N.

pages.title: W. W. Nance on the war and a sick son, April 20, probably 1862
pages.text:
[[obscured: county name]] Co, Tenn
20th Apl [[1862?]]
Mr [[J.?]] D Orr
Dear Sir
Your very welcome letter of 28d March Came to hand yesterday,—found all in usual health. wife rather feeble, health generally good. We were very sorry to hear of James Sickness and hope he has before this time, So far recovered as to be able to come home,—We know Something of parents anxiety for a Sick Son away from home, and can truly Simpathize with you—
I am much pleased with the Spirit of your letter, and have in It expressed my Sentiments in refference to this unholy war waged against people who have never wronged a Yankey in no matter whatever while they cannot Say the Same of us. So Im In for everlastingly Separating from Such people. we now only [[obscured]] them to return to their homes and let us alone, thats all, and If they fail to do so many of their vile bodies will find a Southern home & by & by—Altho we have met with several disasters on the waters yet I feel encouraged, all seem to be satisfied that when they leave the waters we will make them bite the dust—
The roar of heavy ordinance is so common now as to attract but little attention, altho thers been none nearer than the Mis river. The enemy have possession of that river as far down as to Fort Pillow. that fortifycation is at Randolph opposite Covington the County cite of Tipton Co. I am told Its a strong place, but I dont know whether we will be able to hold It or not but I recon they will have a pretty lively time passing that point with their Gun boats I hear very heavy guns in that direction ever few [[obscured]] but cant learn any results [[obscured]] to get news as

pages.family_title: W. W. Nance on the war and a sick son, April 20, probably 1862
pages.family_text:
[[County name obscured]], Tennessee, April 20, [[1862?]]. Mr. [[J.?]] D. Orr,
Your welcome letter of March 28 arrived yesterday. We are in our usual health; my wife is rather frail, but health generally is good. We were sorry James was ill and hope he has recovered enough to return home. We know a parent’s anxiety over a sick son far away and sympathize deeply.
Your letter expresses my own feelings about what I consider this unholy war. I believe we have not wronged the Yankees, though they have wronged us, and I favor permanent separation. We want them to go home and leave us alone. Otherwise, many will be buried in the South. Despite our setbacks on the rivers, I remain encouraged and believe we can defeat them on land.
Heavy artillery is now heard so often that it draws little notice, though none has been closer than the Mississippi River. The enemy controls the river down to Fort Pillow. I describe that fortification as being at Randolph, opposite Covington, the Tipton County seat. I am told it is strong. Whether we can hold it, I do not know, but their gunboats will have a lively time passing. I hear heavy guns in that direction every few [[obscured words]], but cannot learn the results. [[Unclear words about obtaining news; continues.]]
pages.family_note: The political views and military information are Nance’s contemporary perspective. His geographic descriptions and expectations have not been silently corrected.

pages.title: Reports from Shiloh and news of wounded relatives
pages.text:
[[lost: left edge]] re not permitted [[obscured]] Camp. On 6th & 7th (Sunday and Monday one week ago) [[obscured]] before this reaches you. There was [[obscured]] splendid battle [[obscured]] Shiloh, (a church house), near Corinth Miss, [[lost: left edge]] our boys done Some [[obscured]] fighting on those days. William went through both days without receiving a Scratch, but, 2 of his Company fell, and Several wounded, one of our near neighbour boys was killed and another wounded, the wounded one came home, I met him on [[inserted: my]] way to Corinth, I was not allowed to proceed, and came back.
The great wonder is that our whole Regiment was not nearly all killed, for they made 7 charges and took a battery every charge. Strange to tell they lost only 25 or 30 men out of their Regiment.
We live about 80 ms from Corinth or Shilo, quite a number of our wounded have come into this region of country. among them one of my Sisters Sons (Shelton) who was Shot through the breast, he is not thought to be dangerously wounded. I had no knowledge of his being in the army untill day before yesterday evening, when I went to Gadsden Station on the M. & oh RR, at which place I understood that he was in that neighbourhood, I went to him Immediately, and Saw him. Charly, he enlisted at or near Nashville. The yankies have possession of Union City (at the crossing of the Mobile & oh & North Western RR, in Obion county) They have Pensacola—You may not be Surprised to hear a Stampede of yankies from Tenn. Price & Van dorn are at Memphis, encamped there with their commands. this has been reported for several days but I have not been Satisfied of the fact untill Since I commenced writing this letter—
You write that Its probable that your boys may come to Tenn, and [[obscured]] may be they are at Memphis with Price. If So, and I learn the fact I will hunt them out, when permitted

Battle account is secondhand: the writer explicitly says he was refused permission to proceed to Corinth. Seven charges and casualty counts are his reports, not independently verified figures. “One week ago” is retained despite possible tension with the heading’s date. Charly appears after the reference to his sister’s son Shelton; the syntax associates them but does not provide a complete formal name.

pages.family_title: Reports from Shiloh and news of wounded relatives
pages.family_text:
—[[we are not permitted into the camp; wording damaged]]. On the sixth and seventh, Sunday and Monday, “one week ago,” [[damaged words]] there was a great battle at Shiloh, a church near Corinth, Mississippi. Our boys fought [[unclear adjective]] on those days.
William came through both days unscratched, but two men in his company died and several were wounded. A nearby neighbor’s boy was killed and another wounded. The wounded one came home; I met him while heading toward Corinth. I was not allowed to proceed and returned.
I am amazed the regiment was not almost wiped out. They reportedly made seven charges and captured a battery each time, yet lost only twenty-five or thirty men.
We live about eighty miles from Corinth or Shiloh. Many wounded men have come here, including my sister’s son Shelton, shot through the chest. His wound is not thought dangerous. I had not known he was in the army until the evening before yesterday. At Gadsden station on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, I learned he was nearby and immediately visited him. Charly enlisted at or near Nashville.
The Yankees hold Union City, at the railroad crossing in Obion County, and Pensacola. You may soon hear of them fleeing Tennessee. Reports say Price and Van Dorn are encamped at Memphis; I have only become convinced of this since beginning my letter.
You say your boys may come to Tennessee. Perhaps they are already at Memphis with Price. If so, I will find them when I am allowed—
pages.family_note: These are wartime reports and expectations, not an independently checked military history. The writer’s own visit to the wounded relative is distinguished from reports about the battle.

pages.text:
to visit the encampment—[[obscured]] especially the [[obscured]] generally, dont like yankies [[obscured]] to do with them [[lost: left edge]] as possible, and are as Sullen as a [[obscured]] It has been [[obscured]] circulated for the last few days [[obscured]] Nashville has been recaptured, but I dont Credit the report. All I wish is that It may be true and that every yankey handled without Gloves—
We have a great many men among us, who, I believe would make Splendid tories If they had the Chance, Such men I had rather Shoot than a regularly built Yankey. there are none who dare, at this time to Show their hand, but, If in case the enemy Should get among us we may look out— I have not heard from our friends In Middle Tenn in Some time, the last I heard, they were all well. I must close, I of late have So much [[lost: left edge]] to writing, It is quite an uphill business for me to Sit down to address a friend, as much as I like to correspond. I will however, answer all the letters written to me from you or any of the friends; Say to them write to us. You will please write on the reception of this—Wife joins me in love to you family and all the Connexion, let them all hear from us—

pages.family_title: Wartime rumors and Nance’s farewell
pages.family_text:
—to visit the camp. [[Damaged passage about dislike of Yankees.]] A rumor has circulated that Nashville has been recaptured, but I do not believe it. I wish it were true, and wish every Yankee would be treated harshly.
I think many men here would become “Tories” if given the chance. I would rather shoot such men than a regular Yankee. None dares reveal himself now, but if the enemy arrives, we must beware.
I have not heard from our friends in Middle Tennessee lately; at last word they were well. I suppose the boys are at Corinth. If I can visit the camp, I will find them.
I must finish. [[A word describing his feelings about writing is lost.]] Writing a letter has become difficult, much as I enjoy correspondence. Still, I will answer every letter from you or our friends. Tell them to write, and reply when this reaches you. My wife joins me in sending love to your family and all our relations. Share our news with everyone.
Farewell for now, W. W. Nance.

pages.family_title: Theodosia’s worry for four sons in the army
pages.family_text:
[[Opening damaged.]] Sister, since Mr. Nance did not fill the page, I will add a few lines. We have nothing here but trouble and agitation. I know you have your own troubles, with four sons in the army who have left home to defend their homes, country, and liberties. May they return to the family circle to enjoy peace and happiness. [[Closing words of the wish are unclear.]]
When we last heard, Sister Rebecca’s sons had been ordered to Fort Donaldson. The widow Elery had four sons in the same company; two were killed there. We cannot now get letters from Middle Tennessee. I worry deeply about Sister’s boys and do not know whether they fought in the battle.
Cousin William [[Godden?]] and his family went to Rutherford last fall and returned a few weeks ago. If I could see them, I could learn more. After a very wet winter and spring, the water is [[damaged wording]] high. Once I can cross the river, I will go to Trenton to see them.
Daniel Hall [[an unclear reference also mentions old Daniel Hall]] died at Belmont, leaving a wife and one child. The South considers Shiloh a great victory, but I think it was dearly bought: we lost so many promising young men. Ned Smith, son of Captain Smith formerly of Rutherford, was killed. Colonel Battle and two sons from Rutherford were also reportedly killed. The Yankees are going through Tennessee arresting sick and wounded soldiers.
Tell Lizzy Douglas I will write soon. I would have written earlier, but was told letters could not pass from here to Texas. Love to all our relations; tell them I would like to hear from—[[end of page]].
pages.family_note: These are the writer’s reports and fears. The named deaths and battlefield claims require independent corroboration. The four sons belong to the sister being addressed; that sister is not securely named on this page.

pages.family_title: R. C. Orr describes a repulsed charge, May 17, 1864
pages.family_text:
Bayou Deglaize, Louisiana, May 17, 1864. Dear Father,
I have an opportunity to write a few lines, though I hardly know how to begin. These are eventful times. As you already know, we have fought almost every day since April 12.
Yesterday was the fiercest day we have experienced. The battle began in the morning with heavy cannon fire until about one o’clock. We were then ordered to charge their breastworks. We did, but were driven back with many killed and wounded. John Morgan was—[[the next page continues “killed”]].

[[Swan?]] lake ark
Sept 23rd 64
Dear Father & Mother
Having an opportunity of Sending A letter to Texas I get down beside an old rotten Brush to write you a few lines although I have nothing of interest to write we are camped three miles below the goodloe place on the Arkansas River [[inserted: having fine times]] and no Prospect of A fight. Co D is Detached from the Regt we are camping for Forage [[illegible]] right Smart hard Riding &c I have just Returned from Monticello I was detailed to guard Some cotton Smuglers up there. the health of the command is very good at this time there has been Some chills though not many. As my health is [[illegible]] very good.
Old Cider gave out on the way and I traded him for A Mule Made A very good Swop.
I was glad that Henry got the detail to get clothing But I wish it was I as Mr B M got loss if [[illegible]]
Father you must excuse this Scribbling as I am in a great hurry [[illegible]] But do write to me.
Nothing More at Present, Your Son Bob

pages.family_title: Bob’s camp on the Arkansas River, September 23, 1864
pages.family_text:
[[Swan?]] Lake, Arkansas, September 23, 1864. Dear Father and Mother,
With an opportunity to send a letter to Texas, I am sitting beside an old rotten bush to write. There is little news. We are camped three miles below the Goodloe place on the Arkansas River, enjoying ourselves with no battle in prospect. Company D is detached from the regiment. We are camped for forage [[unclear wording]] and doing a good deal of hard riding.
I have just returned from Monticello, where I was detailed to guard some cotton smugglers. The command is healthy, with a few cases of chills. My own health is very good.
Old Cider gave out on the journey, so I traded him for a mule—a very good exchange.
I was glad Henry received the assignment to collect clothing, though I wish it had been me. [[The following reference to Mr. B. M. is unclear.]]
Please forgive this scribble; I am in a great hurry. Do write. Nothing more for now. Your son, Bob.

pages.title: R. C. Orr at Camp Pisgah, October 15, 1863
pages.text:
Camp Pisgah La
Oct 15th 1863
Dear Father and Mother
After A long Silence I once more take up my pen to write you A few lines Although I have nothing of Interest to communicate I received your letter to Henry last Monday, and was very glad to hear from home and that you was all well. but was very Sorry to hear of your misfortune. this leaves me in good health I have had A few chills lately but have got clear of them. Henry has gone out with Lieut Cox to [[buy beeves?]] has been gone About two weeks I expect he will return Soon he was in good health when he left.
The health of the command is improving but there is A great deal of Sickness in it yet mostly chills and fever.
Jack [[Levins?]] Jim Lancaster gran Alexander and [[Pickering?]] Started for Texas this Morning on furlough They furlough four from the company every Sixty days my time will come After awhile.
I would have wrote to you Yesterday and sent it by Jack but didnt know that he was going to Start until nearly night. we are looking for old Jef every day with our clothing In hopes he will come Soon as I am getting tired of camp and want to get out on A scout. Wait until after Drill
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-058. Purpose of Henry’s trip with Lieutenant Cox is tentative. Two names in the furlough list are uncertain. The parents’ “misfortune” is not explained in this letter.

pages.family_title: R. C. Orr at Camp Pisgah, October 15, 1863
pages.family_text:
Camp Pisgah, Louisiana, October 15, 1863. Dear Father and Mother,
After a long silence, I am writing a few lines, though there is little news. I received your letter to Henry last Monday and was glad everyone at home was well, but sorry about your misfortune. I am healthy now. I had a few chills recently but have recovered. Henry went out with Lieutenant Cox [[to buy cattle?]] about two weeks ago. He was well when he left and should return soon.
The command’s health is improving, although many still have chills and fever.
Jack [[Levins?]], Jim Lancaster, Gran Alexander, and [[Pickering?]] left for Texas on leave this morning. Four men from the company get leave every sixty days; my turn will come eventually.
I would have written yesterday and sent this with Jack, but I did not learn he was leaving until nearly night. We expect old Jeff any day with our clothing. I hope he comes soon: I am tired of camp and want to go out scouting. I must stop until after drill.

pages.title: Mock battle, winter clothing, and better food
pages.text:
Drill is over and I resume my pen. we had general review and inspection yesterday morning and Big Drill in the evening with our Regt and capt Pratt Battery the Boys would charge the Battery and they would fire blank cartridges At them it went like A fight sure enough. Col Burford Pitched About like A hog in high rye with [[Hayberg?]] after him—There was A great many Spectators and old Persons tried to show off to an advantage fortunately I was not in the Drill.
Our Regiment drew A fine lot of clothing the other day Henry was lucky enough to get A fine overcoat which he was very much in need of. I drew A pair of Pants and A Shirt we have drawn A Plenty we are living better in the way of eatables at this camp than we ever have Since we have been in the Service. col Burford Says he thinks we will Stay here all winter.
You must excuse this Short letter and bad writing as my pen is very bad Tell Mary to write me and give All the news and Maybe I will answer Nothing More At Present only I Remain Your Obedient Son
R C Orr
P S Gran Jetton and all of your friends are well [[R.C.O.?]]
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-057. “Persons” is retained as written, possibly referring to Parsons; no silent correction. Name following Burford’s mock-battle antics is uncertain.

pages.family_title: Mock battle, winter clothing, and better food
pages.family_text:
Drill is over, so I can continue. Yesterday morning we had a general review and inspection. That evening our regiment drilled with Captain Pratt’s battery. The men charged the guns, which fired blank cartridges at them—it sounded like a real battle. Colonel Burford bounded about “like a hog in high rye,” with [[Hayberg?]] following him. There were many spectators, and old Persons tried to make a good impression. Fortunately, I was not taking part.
Our regiment received good clothing recently. Henry was lucky enough to get a fine overcoat, which he badly needed. I received trousers and a shirt. We have had plenty of clothing, and the food here is better than anywhere else during our service. Colonel Burford thinks we will stay here all winter.
Excuse the short letter and poor writing; my pen is bad. Tell Mary to write with all the news, and perhaps I will answer. Nothing more for now. Your obedient son, R. C. Orr.
P.S. Gran Jetton and all your friends are well.

pages.title: George urges his sister not to impoverish the family, July 22, 1862
pages.text:
Sabine Pass, July 22/62
Sister Lizzy
To day I am able to knock about [[illegible]] though I am still very weak. I recd your letter of 20th this morning you must have forgot to put in a few [[illegible]] by the way you numbered the pages.
It is cloudy and rainy to day the musquitoes are so bad I have to stay in the porch all the time. I am writing on my lap which is all in a [[illegible]]. I recd Fathers and [[illegible]] letters the other day and got Warren to answer them for me as at the time I was not able to write.
If I remember rightly I only said [[illegible: amount or wording at line break]] for a Substitute, this you are all willing to give and more but do not give so much as to impoverish the estate, and render you entirely dependent upon me though I am willing to do all that I can for you in any way, but it might be, after getting one that the time would be extended to [[55?]] and they would take me again and leave you flat. I dont [[illegible]] on a substitute for fear of accident. I know you would like to have me at home and I would like to be at home but at the same time I dont want you to impoverish yourselves for my benefit.
There is no telling the war may soon end or yet it may be a long time first. If it should end soon there might be a large sum of money lost by paying high for a substitute. My advice is not to get one unless you can pay for him without
pages.editorial_notes: Letter continues through 09-062, signed George and addressed here to “Sister Lizzy.” The proposed substitute’s price and a possible age limit are too uncertain for a firm historical or financial inference. “Estate” is the writer’s word for property here; it does not establish that his father was deceased. This discusses a proposal, not a completed substitute arrangement.

pages.family_title: George urges his sister not to impoverish the family, July 22, 1862
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, July 22, 1862. Sister Lizzy,
Today I can move about [[unclear words]], though I am still very weak. Your letter of the 20th arrived this morning. From the numbering, it seems you forgot to include [[some pages; the exact wording is unclear]].
It is cloudy and rainy. The mosquitoes are so bad that I must stay on the porch. I am writing on my lap [[unclear description]]. Father’s letter and another letter arrived recently. Warren answered them for me because I could not write then.
If I remember correctly, I only suggested [[an unclear amount or condition]] for a substitute. You are all willing to give that much and more, but do not pay so much that you impoverish the property and become entirely dependent on me. I am willing to do everything I can for you. But after we found a substitute, the service requirement might be extended [[a possible age limit is unclear]], and they might take me again, leaving you with nothing. [[The next phrase about the substitute is unclear.]]
I know you want me home, and I want to be there. But I do not want you to impoverish yourselves for my benefit. The war might end soon or continue a long time. If it ends soon, paying a high price for a substitute could waste a large sum. My advice is not to obtain one unless you can pay without—

Sabine Pass, July 22/62
Sister Lizzy
To day I am able to knock about [[illegible]] though I am still very weak. I recd your letter of 20th this morning you must have forgot to put in a few [[illegible]] by the way you numbered the pages.
It is cloudy and rainy to day the musquitoes are so bad I have to stay in the porch all the time. I am writing on my lap which is all in a [[illegible]]. I recd Fathers and [[illegible]] letters the other day and got Warren to answer them for me as at the time I was not able to write.
If I remember rightly I only said [[illegible: amount or wording at line break]] for a Substitute, this you are all willing to give and more but do not give so much as to impoverish the estate, and render you entirely dependent upon me though I am willing to do all that I can for you in any way, but it might be, after getting one that the time would be extended to [[55?]] and they would take me again and leave you flat. I dont [[illegible]] on a substitute for fear of accident. I know you would like to have me at home and I would like to be at home but at the same time I dont want you to impoverish yourselves for my benefit.
There is no telling the war may soon end or yet it may be a long time first. If it should end soon there might be a large sum of money lost by paying high for a substitute. My advice is not to get one unless you can pay for him without

pages.title: George contrasts strict camp rules with guard duty at Galveston
pages.text:
The entire batt. is prejudiced against him from the manner in which he has treated them, in enforcing the regulations so strictly. He has issued an order for every man in the Batt to have an uniform the men did not like to take them but were forced to. He is out in another order for every man to wear a uniform cap. And there has to be a dress parade every evening. He wont allow the guard to sit down while on guard he has to walk his post continually and not let his gun out of his hands.
Now this looks well enough on paper but it is mighty hard to practice. When the guard is relieved instead of marching direct to the guard house he has to go around with the relief untill all are relieved.
We never done this way before while at Galveston (and we were looking to be attacked every day about the 1st of Jany) when relieved we always went directly to the guard house and went to sleep. While on post we set down lay down and walked as we pleased if we got tired of our gun we would set it down by the side of a house and wrap up in our blanket about two or three times the relief while the Corporal was relieving the first sentinel, would go on ahead and relieve the balance of the Guard before the Corp—could catch up. All this was known to the head officers at Galveston and they never grumbled nary time.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-059–060. “batt.” expanded as battalion in family reading. The clause beginning “about two or three times the relief” concerns the relief party going ahead of its corporal; it is not a claim that George fell asleep while on post.

pages.family_title: George contrasts strict camp rules with guard duty at Galveston
pages.family_text:
The whole battalion dislikes him because he enforces the regulations so strictly. He ordered every man to have a uniform. The men did not want them but were forced to take them. Now he has ordered everyone to wear a uniform cap, with dress parade every evening. A guard may not sit down: he must keep walking his post and hold his gun the whole time.
That looks reasonable on paper but is very hard in practice. When a guard is relieved, he must accompany the relief party until every guard has been replaced, instead of going straight to the guardhouse.
We never did this at Galveston, even when we expected an attack daily around January 1. After being relieved, we went directly to the guardhouse and slept. On duty we sat, lay down, or walked as we pleased. If our guns became tiring, we leaned them against a house and wrapped ourselves in blankets. Two or three times, while the corporal was replacing the first sentry, the relief party went ahead and replaced everyone else before he could catch up. The senior officers at Galveston knew all this and never complained.

pages.title: Letter 31: criticism of government cotton dealings, August 8, 1863
pages.text:
Saturday Aug. 8th 1863.
Letter 31
To All at Home.
Writing time has come again but [[illegible]] nothing from home the fault is in the [[illegible]] gap between Beaumont and [[illegible]] every day almost they run off the track or some [[illegible]] they would let us go [[illegible]] any but to waste time.
We have no late intelligence from abroad the [[Pony express?]] came into Beaumont night before last but brought no news. Capt [[Odlum?]] has been absent several days at Beaumont, and returned at night on the [[Dime?]] says he is a little lower in the mouth than any one I have heard express himself yet. Every thing seems to have gone wrong at general headquarters and he has found it out.
This grand scheme of Rio Grand speculation is leaked out and been established fully by circumstantial evidence and there is no longer disguising the facts. Only twenty five bales of Gov. cotton has ever reached Brownsville and no body but Gov. friends have had the control of the transportation. The Mexican breakers were employed by the [[illegible]] of superior officers to take Gov cotton to the Rio and are there yet. It is plain who has made a pile and this is what has disheartened our Capt. It is enough to dishearten any man that has a honest feeling for the Gov.
A man by the name of [[Chisham?]] belonging to our Batt has been wagoning to the Rio grande since we left Galveston he is now with us, says that when [[Magruder?]] was at Brownsville he sent three of his staff to Havanna, yet gave it as his opinion that [[Magruder?]] was acting himself as a private citizen.
Such men have gone to speculating who will [[lost: bottom edge]]

pages.family_title: Letter 31: criticism of government cotton dealings, August 8, 1863
pages.family_text:
Saturday, August 8, 1863. Letter 31. To everyone at home,
It is time to write again, but I have heard nothing from home. [[Some wording about the transport link through Beaumont is unclear.]] Almost every day there is a derailment or another problem. [[The rest of this opening complaint is unclear.]]
There is no recent news from elsewhere. The [[Pony Express?]] reached Beaumont the night before last but brought nothing new. Captain [[Odlum?]] returned from several days in Beaumont, aboard the [[Dime?]]. He is more downhearted than anyone I have heard. Everything seems to have gone wrong at headquarters, and he has found out about it.
The great Rio Grande speculation scheme has leaked out. I think circumstantial evidence establishes it and the facts can no longer be hidden. Only twenty-five bales of government cotton have reached Brownsville, although only the government’s friends have controlled the transport. Mexican “breakers” were employed [[unclear phrase concerning senior officers]] to take government cotton to the Rio Grande and remain there. It seems plain who has made a fortune. This has discouraged our captain, as it would anyone with an honest concern for the government.
A man in our battalion named [[Chisham?]], who has been hauling goods to the Rio Grande since we left Galveston, is now with us. He says that when [[Magruder?]] was in Brownsville, he sent three staff members to Havana. Yet the man thought he was acting privately. Such men have gone into speculation—[[the ending is clipped]].
pages.family_note: This preserves George’s strong accusations and the reports he repeats. The letter alone does not establish misconduct or the accuracy of the cotton total.

pages.text:
I do not know but what I would as soon go to Galveston as to stay here, yet we are not as apt to get as good quarters there again as we did have, but we can see more hear more and have a livelier time generally, if they dont put us to digging dirt and such like [[illegible]]. Some say that Cooks artillery are to take our place, but to make this place defensible it will require both artillery and pickets and plenty of them.
That [[illegible]] how my [[train?]] of ideas is getting shorter than a sheet of paper here lately as I find it difficult to manufacture something without material. To day is my guard day somehow I get my share of the Sunday for guard in this little difficulty of ours. I am to go down the river to night to keep watch in that direction, we have watched in that direction for a long time never to have discovered any thing dangerous. We go after dark and come away before it is light enough to be seen by the enemy.
There is seven prisoners in the guard house now for petty offences, it is quite an easy place so [[illegible]] it and some had rather be in than out there ought to be a lock up for these little petty officers who have not self respect enough to keep themselves out of such places, and put better innocent men by imprisoning them.
Rogers who done the stealing at Dallas and was guarded by us to Houston and there left in charge of the Provost Marshal and there tried and sentenced to work on the fortifications three months was returned the other day to his company for duty, and in about three days was put in the guard house for getting drunk [[illegible]] on guard.

pages.family_title: Guard duty and a proposed return to Galveston
pages.family_text:
I might as soon return to Galveston as stay here, though we probably would not get quarters as good as before. We would see and hear more and have a livelier time, unless they set us to digging. Some say Cook’s artillery will replace us. Defending this place will require both artillery and plenty of pickets.
[[A partly unclear transition complains about running out of ideas.]] Lately my thoughts do not fill a sheet: it is hard to make something out of nothing. Today is my turn on guard, and somehow I get my share of Sundays on duty. Tonight I must go downriver to watch. We have watched that direction a long time without discovering anything dangerous. We leave after dark and return before the enemy could see us.
Seven prisoners are in the guardhouse for petty offenses. It is an easy place, and some prefer being inside to being outside. I think there should be a lockup for petty officers who lack self-respect and imprison better, innocent men. [[Part of the original wording is unclear.]]
Rogers—the man accused of stealing at Dallas, whom we guarded to Houston and handed over to the provost marshal—was tried there and sentenced to three months’ work on fortifications. He recently returned to his company. Within about three days he was in the guardhouse again for drunkenness [[unclear words]] on guard.

pages.title: Letter 32: unpaid troops and reports of mutiny, August 15
pages.text:
Sabine City Aug 15th
Letter 32
Sister Lizzie
I received yours of July Monday evening I received yours of July 19th to day and Lauras of Jun 27th. They had all taken a resting spell somewhere on the road I do not know where. Lieut Baily returned from Houston yesterday bringing orders for us to go to Gal. as soon as two companies of Elmores regt one company of [[Goulds?]] regt and [[deleted: illegible]] Capt Jones artillery should come to relieve us, it will be some ten days before we get off if that soon: we are to report to Col De Bray for duty. Lieut Baily says that Sorrells regt are in a state of mutiny and that the troops at Ft Point have turned the cannon on the city, and demand better rations.
It is rather a bad state of affairs if they cant feed men well enough to keep them from mutinying in this confederate gov. but I will learn more about this when I get there. There was a case of insubordination here the other day, Capt [[Odlums?]] Co. or rather the principal part of them refused to drill one morning, giving as a reason for so doing that they had not any soap to wash with and had not had for a long time and that they were out of money and wanted the pay that was due them five months pay is now due. After trying the guard house a few hours they concluded to return to duty.
The spirit of insubordination is abroad and despondency with it, about one half of this Batt. is whipped and ready to give it up as a bad job.
Since Vicksburg has fallen the men look gloomily to the future all communication being cut off with the east, and no reliable cheering news of late

Reports of Sorrell’s regiment and Fort Point are explicitly Lieutenant Baily’s reports. The regiment name before Captain Jones and the captain’s surname remain tentative.

pages.family_title: Letter 32: unpaid troops and reports of mutiny, August 15
pages.family_text:
Sabine City, August 15 [[1863 from context]]. Letter 32. Sister Lizzie,
Your July letter arrived Monday evening. Today I received your July 19 letter and Laura’s of June 27. They had all rested somewhere along the way.
Lieutenant Baily returned from Houston yesterday with orders for us to move to Galveston once two companies from Elmore’s regiment, one from [[Gould’s?]], and Captain Jones’s artillery relieve us. It will be at least ten days before we leave. We must report to Colonel De Bray. Baily says Sorrell’s regiment is mutinous and the troops at Fort Point have turned their guns on the city, demanding better rations.
It is a bad state of affairs if this Confederate government cannot feed men well enough to prevent mutiny. I will learn more when I get there. Here, most of Captain [[Odlum’s?]] company recently refused morning drill. They said they had long been without soap, had no money, and wanted their unpaid wages. Five months’ pay is overdue. After a few hours in the guardhouse, they agreed to return to duty.
Insubordination and discouragement are widespread. About half our battalion feels beaten and ready to give up. Since Vicksburg fell, the men have looked gloomily ahead. Communication with the east is cut off, and there has been no reliable good news lately—

pages.family_title: Letter 32: damaged discussion of military news
pages.family_text:
[[Most lines on this page lose their endings at the right edge, so a continuous translation would be misleading.]]
The surviving text discusses the effect of bad news on the men, fighting near Jackson involving Grant and “Johnson,” Banks’s movements, and the future of the war on either side of the Mississippi. George hopes they will be left alone. He questions extravagant reports about Lee at Williamsport, saying there is little truth in such big stories. [[A number beginning “90,” is incomplete.]]

[[The left side of most lines is missing.]] George reports no serious illness that he knows of, then discusses changes in artillery positions. Two brass howitzers are mentioned, along with a railroad bridge roughly nine or ten miles up the lake. The men assigned there will face mosquitoes without shelter. [[Gun sizes and parts of the place names are missing.]]
At last the mosquito nets have arrived, making nights more comfortable. George distinguishes four kinds of mosquitoes: a familiar kind, a smaller striped kind, a charcoal-black fuzzy kind, and the largest kind. He proposes sending a specimen if it survives being crushed in the mail. The largest now seems the most common, swarming in the evenings, at night, and in the mornings. The men must hand over their nets to their replacements when they leave.
[[The final incomplete lines compare this year’s mosquitoes with earlier conditions, then mention a man, sharks, nighttime activity, and calves. Their exact meaning remains unresolved.]]
