pages.title: Letter 32: summer heat, food, and canceled transfer orders
pages.text:
The weather is getting hot down here sure enough, I dont think I ever saw it so hot in Ellis as it is here, there is scarce ever any breeze stirring, hot cloudy and calm. An abundance of watermelons have been brought here from Sabine Bayou in two little lighters and [[schooners?]] which they sell at tolerably fair prices, they are very good as are our water pumpkins can be had tolerably cheap and are pretty good with bread and beef a change, anyhow.
The Zehorlda brought a couple of Co's to relieve us last night. But the order for us to go to Galveston had been previously countermanded so we will stay here for an indefinite length of time yet. I prefer this place to Gal. until the yellow fever season is over, for here we have a chance to skedaddle while at Gal. we would not have. If there is any yellow fever at Houston I have never heard of it I guess it is all a mistake, such reports are apt to get out at this time of year anywhere. I have heard that a great many men are going home from La on short furloughs, but most generally “they have left their certificates of disability behind.” We are all in good health at present, [[Jeems?]] has been complaining for a few days but there is not much the matter with him. I suppose that there is no healthy man here for we are all well so far as I know. Tell [[Essie?]] that I will write to her yet awhile, but I never was born a poet and shall never be as well. I believe I have told all the news
My love to all Your Brother George
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-065–067, signed George. Vessel name read “Zehorlda,” possibly the same name written elsewhere as “Zehorla”; retained without normalization. Phrase “no healthy man here” is retained as read despite the following statement that all are well. Recipient name in the last request is tentative. Yellow-fever reports and furlough claims are described as things heard, not verified by George.

pages.family_title: Letter 32: summer heat, food, and canceled transfer orders
pages.family_text:
It is becoming truly hot here. I do not think I ever saw Ellis County this hot. There is scarcely a breeze: just heat, clouds, and still air. Two small lighters and [[schooners?]] have brought plenty of good watermelons from Sabine Bayou, sold at fair prices. Our water is good too. Pumpkins are fairly cheap and make a welcome change with bread and beef.
The Zehorlda brought two companies to relieve us last night. But the orders to move to Galveston had already been canceled, so we will remain here indefinitely. I prefer this place until yellow-fever season ends: here we could escape, whereas in Galveston we could not. I have heard nothing of yellow fever in Houston and suspect the report is mistaken. Such stories often circulate at this season.
I hear many men are going home from Louisiana on short leave, generally having “left their certificates of disability behind.” Everyone here is in good health. [[Jeems?]] has felt unwell for a few days, but little seems wrong. [[An unclear or inconsistent phrase follows; George then repeats that everyone is well as far as he knows.]]
Tell [[Essie?]] I will write to her after a while. I was not born a poet and never shall be one. I think that is all the news. Love to everyone. Your brother, George.

Sabine Pass, May 14, 1863. Letter 21. Sister Lizzie,
Yesterday I received your letters of April 29 and 30. They were mailed May 2 and took only eleven days. I do not know why mine fail to reach you; I have written every week.
Since my last letter, the men have had a merry night. I did not join in. The staff are very fond of liquor and leave no stone unturned to obtain it. First they took a demijohn from a boatman, then a barrel of whiskey found in the countryside, then half a barrel of rum from a Frenchman. They reported it destroyed to keep soldiers from getting drunk—but were “destroying” it slowly themselves.
The men finally grew tired of this and decided to finish the whiskey. One night after the tattoo drum signal, the cavalry went to headquarters, rolled out the barrels, and called everyone to come drink for free. They carried the barrels onto the prairie. Everyone brought cups, canteens, coffeepots, and buckets; nearly everyone became drunk.
The staff tried to save the liquor but could not assemble a guard in time. Company C had been organizing its own party to seize it when the cavalry and boat hands arrived. As soon as the commotion began, the long roll sounded. Lanier ordered any man who did not answer his name sent to the—

guard house. Some of the boys came up and told the Capt about it, and asked him if they must fall into line. he told to fall in or not just as they pleased and that none of his men should go in the guardhouse. Since then the Staff has been quite dry, no doubt, but maybe it will learn them not to take whisky that dont belong to them. pages.title: Letter 28: the lighthouse expedition, July 22, 1863
pages.text:
Wednesday Evening, July 22
Letter, Number, 28th, 1863
Sister Lizzie,
I have delayed writing longer this time than usual on account of a three days residence at the lighthouse. Col Griffin set a trap to catch some Yankees at the lighthouse. Some body imagined that they saw one or two Yankees there, so last Wednesday night a detachment of 60 or 70 men under Bickley [[invested?]] and took possession of the place without opposition. Warren with a squad of 20 men were left to take in such yankees as might come along. Saturday night they were relieved by Lieut Deen and 20 men, of the latter I was one. We went down as near the L H as we could get in a boat. We got the boat in about thirty feet of the shore, the interval was knee deep mud. One man took a sack of provisions and started ashore he got about half way and stuck fast, Warren and his squad soon arrived with some plank which was laid down to walk on and the rest of us got safe ashore without sticking. Then commenced the battle in real earnest—but not with the mosquitoes instead of Yankees
pages.editorial_notes: Reading order of this letter is 09-074, 09-076 (marked Page 2nd), 09-075 (marked page 3rd), 09-077. A possibly superfluous “not” before “with the mosquitoes” is retained as written; sense is clear from the continuation. The opening force appears “60 or 70,” and the two smaller detachments each number 20.

pages.family_title: Letter 28: the lighthouse expedition, July 22, 1863
pages.family_text:
Wednesday evening, July 22, 1863. Letter 28. Sister Lizzie,
My letter is later than usual because I spent three days at the lighthouse. Colonel Griffin set a trap for Yankees there after someone thought he saw one or two. Last Wednesday night, sixty or seventy men under Bickley took possession without resistance. Warren and twenty men remained to capture any Yankees who appeared.
On Saturday night, Lieutenant Deen and twenty men relieved them. I was one of those twenty. Our boat came within about thirty feet of shore, with knee-deep mud between us and land. One man tried to carry a sack of provisions across but became stuck halfway. Warren’s party soon brought planks to walk on, and the rest of us reached shore safely. Then the real battle began—with mosquitoes instead of Yankees.

Sister Lizzie,

Some body imagined that they saw one or two Yankees there, so last Wednesday night a detachment of 60 or 70 men under Bickley [[invested?]] and took possession of the place without opposition. Warren with a squad of 20 men were left to take in such yankees as might come along. Saturday night they were relieved by Lieut Deen and 20 men, of the latter I was one. We went down as near the L H as we could get in a boat. We got the boat in about thirty feet of the shore, the interval was knee deep mud. One man took a sack of provisions and started ashore he got about half way and stuck fast, Warren and his squad soon arrived with some plank which was laid down to walk on and the rest of us got safe ashore without sticking. Then commenced the battle in real earnest—but not with the mosquitoes instead of Yankees

pages.text:
Page 2nd
We fought them manfully until day light when we brought a battery of smoke to bear on them and succeeded to drive them pretty effectually from one room. After waiting & watching for neds last night we came back having caught nothing. No one is there now.

Thursday, 23rd
The boat came in late yesterday evening but brought no letter to me, I have not received later dates from home than Lauras of the 24th and 25th of June, what is the reason of this I cannot have any idea for letters have come from Tarrant Co as late as July 6th. pages.title: Letter 28: inspection, fort construction, and fading hopes of peace
pages.text:
Well as the steamer leaves this evening I will close. Lieut Col Mc Neil inspected us this morning in grand style, he first reviewed us and then had us to pass in review before him, he then inspected our arms in regular military style, next we had to manœuvre in Batt drill till he got tired of that, and then company drill awhile, then the manual of arms and then we quit, after having been on the parade ground from half past eight until eleven.
So much for so much we were glad to get rid of his presence I assure you, Men like to show their authority “mighty well” in this latitude. Capt Evans has been released from arrest and I think from all that I can learn Major Hammer has been also. Col Griffin assured him so that his resignation would be accepted he has a certificate of disability from the Drs, and this will insure its acceptance. We are glad to get rid of him on any terms, and hope next time we will get a better one.
The Fort is progressing slowly. More darkies have been sent for to work on it when it will be finished it is impossible to say. It is estimated that it will cost the Government $100,000. I wish you would write to me who all were drafted in our county for I have a curiosity to know how many will be or are left.
All hope of a speedy end of the war is abandoned in this part of the country, pretty much everybody believes that Vicksburg has fallen, and the pet notion of foreign intervention has died.
The weather still continues rainy though the last few days have been tolerably pleasant. My paper is about full, so for the present
Goodbye, George
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of the letter beginning 09-074; reading order 074, 076, 075, 077. Source uses a racial term for the Black people sought for fort construction. Their legal status and whether/how they were compelled are not specified in this passage. Cost is a reported estimate, not an audited expenditure. The name Evans here supplies the captain’s name absent from the arrest statement on 09-076.

The steamer leaves this evening, so I must close. Lieutenant Colonel McNeil inspected us grandly this morning: review, marching past him, weapons inspection, battalion drill, company drill, then the manual of arms. We were on the parade ground from 8:30 until 11. We were glad to see him leave. Men here certainly enjoy displaying authority.
Captain Evans has been released from arrest; from what I hear, Major Hammer has too. Griffin has assured Hammer his resignation will be accepted. A doctor’s certificate of disability should ensure it. We will be glad to lose him on any terms and hope for a better replacement.
Work on the fort is slow. More Black workers have been requested. No one can say when it will be finished. The estimated cost to the government is $100,000. Please tell me who has been drafted in our county; I want to know how many men remain.
People here have abandoned hope of an early end to the war. Almost everyone believes Vicksburg has fallen, and the cherished idea of foreign intervention has died.
It is still rainy, though the past few days have been fairly pleasant. My paper is nearly full. Goodbye for now, George.

pages.title: Letter 23: food and soap at Sabine Pass, May 28, 1863
pages.text:
Number 23
Sabine Pass May 28th 63
As I said I got yours of 7 the other day and now I will answer the more in full. I was sorry to hear that Samm was sick, for sickness is such a disagreeable thing anyhow. I have been quite puny for some time but am about well again. Sabine beef and bread is dog living compared to what I have seen it is true we get a few other articles but no vegetables except what we buy and it has been so dry here this spring that the people made but little more than they have use for, as they live by gardening mostly anyhow they have no farms and all they have to eat is vegetables and beef, besides what they buy. Most of them have large stocks of cattle, but some how this year they failed to make much milk & butter for sale. Some wont sell anything to us but give, all such as these men will go to for anything, others that do sell are soon bought out entirely, and so they have nothing to sell.
It is almost impossible to get washing done at present, the Government dont furnish soap enough to wash socks, and the citizens are out generally. The country for 3 or 4 miles around has been ransacked, to get washing done but the universal cry is “no soap!”
I am very thankful for the socks you sent me, but would much rather had woolen ones. The pills also came to hand by warren and the fine comb, the latter I am happy say I have not needed since I left home and hope I shall not [[lost: bottom line partly cut off in the source image]]

No medical use is inferred for the pills. pages.family_title: Letter 23: food and soap at Sabine Pass, May 28, 1863
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, May 28, 1863. Letter 23.
As I mentioned, your letter of the 7th arrived the other day. I will answer it more fully now. I was sorry Sam was sick; illness is so unpleasant. I have been rather unwell myself, but am nearly recovered.
Living on Sabine beef and bread is miserable compared with what I have known. We get a few other things, but must buy any vegetables. This spring has been so dry that local people have grown little more than they need. They mostly keep gardens, with no farms, and live on vegetables, beef, and whatever they buy. Most own many cattle, but this year have produced little milk or butter to sell. Some will only give us things, never sell them, so the men keep going to those people. Those who do sell are soon bought out.
It is almost impossible to get clothes washed. The government does not supply enough soap even for socks, and the townspeople are generally out. Men have searched three or four miles around for washing, but everywhere the answer is “no soap!”
Thank you for the socks, though I would have preferred woolen ones. Warren also brought the pills and fine comb. Happily, I have not needed the comb since leaving home and hope I will not [[the rest of the line is cut off]].

pages.title: Letter 23: delayed mail and cancelled furloughs, May 28–31, 1863
pages.text:
It takes a letter longer [[deleted: than]] to go from here home than from Gal by half it seems I seldom get one under twenty days. One did get through in eleven from the time it was mailed. The Sunflower is due this evening and I think a letter or two besides. Capt Evans and Corp Long started home the other day Sammy had allowed the same old rates of furlow. They had been gone one day when the order was again countermanded whether they will go on home without getting [[deleted: getting]] [[inserted: Sammy]] angered or not I do not know. The furlough order had only been in force thirty six hours when it was revoked Something bad must have turned up somewhere to cause its sudden revoke.
I have seen [[Marl?]] papers of the 20th, and they stated that a big fight was about to come off at Grand Gulf Some forty or fifty miles below Vicksburg probably we have been defeated at this place But it is useless for me to quote papers to you as you have as good a chance at them as I do. Let me know when the Telegraph will stop and I will try to [[inserted: send]] the news to you for a while as the Tel has doubled its rates your subscription must be nearly out.
A very pleasant shower has fallen this evening the first for about a month, the worst of it was it didnt rain half enough as water is getting scarce in the cisterns.
Sunday May 31st
No boat has yet arrived though the Sunflower is confidently looked for to day. The cause of her long delay lies in the fact that she has been carrying troops to Nibletts bluff for several days past. how many are being sent across I have no idea There must be some danger in that direction of late.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-080. pages.family_title: Letter 23: delayed mail and cancelled furloughs, May 28–31, 1863
pages.family_text:
Letters seem to take half as long again between here and home as they did from Galveston. I seldom receive one in fewer than twenty days, though one arrived eleven days after posting. The Sunflower is due this evening; perhaps a letter or two will come too.
Captain Evans and Corporal Long started home after Sammy restored the old furlough arrangements. One day after they left, the order was cancelled again. I do not know whether they can continue home without angering Sammy. The order lasted only thirty-six hours; something bad must have happened to cause such a sudden reversal.
Newspapers dated the 20th said a major battle was expected at Grand Gulf, forty or fifty miles below Vicksburg. Perhaps we have been defeated there. But you have as much access to newspapers as I do. Tell me when your Telegraph subscription ends, and I will try to send news for a while. Its rates have doubled, so yours must be nearly finished.
We had a pleasant shower this evening, the first in about a month, but far too little. Water is growing scarce in the cisterns.
Sunday, May 31. No boat has arrived yet, though the Sunflower is confidently expected today. She has been carrying troops to Niblett’s Bluff for several days. I have no idea how many are crossing; there must lately have been some danger in that direction.

pages.title: Galveston under shellfire: letter dated January 22, uncertain year
pages.text:
Galveston Jan [[22th?]] [[1862?]]
Dear Sister
Time passes off in quite a monotonous manner. Galveston is a much prettier place than Houston. there is less mud and the streets can be better drained. The shell for paving purposes are more convenient than at Houston and I think it is a much healthier place. The monotony was somewhat relieved yesterday by the Federals shelling the town and ft point which is about two miles east from here
They commenced about three oclock I reckon and fired 107 shots which did no further damage than the wounding of four men at Ft Point one of whom has since died. A good many of the citizens had returned to their homes these fled to the west of town with their families; some negroes who were at work at the east end of town went through to the west at quick time, some mischevous soldiers threw a barrel head among them and hollered “Theres a bomb” the affrighted blacks fell flat of their faces on the hard pavement.
During most of the engagement I was on top of our quarters in a lookout and [[inserted: could]] see every shot that was fired or rather the smoke from the guns and I could hear the report also.
The most of the firing was done from the Sciota a gunboat whether ironclad or not I do not know it came up in about a mile of what is called the south battery and fired at the town and surrounding country in order I suppose to find out if there was any batteries about, the Brooklyn fired at ft point all the

pages.family_title: Galveston under shellfire: letter dated January 22, uncertain year
pages.family_text:
Galveston, January [[22?]], [[1862?; year uncertain]]. Dear Sister,
Life here is monotonous. Galveston is much prettier than Houston, with less mud, better drainage, and easier access to shells for paving. I think it is much healthier too.
Yesterday the Federals interrupted the monotony by shelling the town and Fort Point, about two miles east of us. They began around three o’clock and fired 107 shots. The damage I know of was four men wounded at Fort Point, one of whom has since died.
Many residents had returned home; they now fled west with their families. Black workers at the east end hurried west too. Some soldiers threw a barrel head among them and shouted, “There’s a bomb!” The frightened people fell face down on the hard pavement.
I spent most of the bombardment in a lookout above our quarters, where I could see the smoke from every shot and hear the guns.
Most of the firing came from the gunboat Sciota. I do not know whether she is ironclad. She came within about a mile of the south battery and fired at the town and surrounding ground, presumably to discover any batteries. The Brooklyn fired at Fort Point throughout—

A good many of the citizens had returned to their homes these fled to the west of town with their families; some negroes who were at work at the east end of town went through to the west at quick time, some mischevous soldiers threw a barrel head among them and hollered “Theres a bomb” the affrighted blacks fell flat of their faces on the hard pavement.

The most of the firing was done from the Sciota a gunboat whether ironclad or not I do not know it came up in about a mile of what is called the south battery and fired at the town and surrounding country in order I suppose to find out if there was any batteries about, the Brooklyn fired at ft point all the

[[The opening discussion of religion is too faint for a continuous reading.]]
I cannot see how anyone can, in good conscience, pray for an army’s success in a battle where wholesale murder reigns. Both sides kneel to the same God and pray for opposite results. Early in March, the roads were hard enough to bear a man’s weight. [[The remaining weather remark and part of the statement that no letter has come from home are faint.]]
Goodbye, George.

I am only sorry that so much money tax was not levied sufficient to carry on govt & war & thus depreciated its

pages.family_title: September 22, 1864: surveying office, military service, and taxation
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, September 22, 1864. Dear Brother,
Your bundle of letters has arrived, including our sister’s and your note of August 20 [[place unclear]].
I appreciate your concern and your acceptance of the surveyor’s office with my interests in mind. But I doubt the plan can help me, under my understanding of the law. Being a surveyor can keep a man out of military service, but cannot release one already serving. Chief justices, sheriffs and county clerks can be released because Confederate law requires those offices; surveyors do not have the same standing.
I sympathize with your financial troubles and fully share your hatred of oppression, tyranny and misuse of public funds. I do not go quite as far in opposing the taxes, excessive and poorly based though they are. Such a war inevitably burdens us heavily; a new government cannot be blamed simply for high taxation. I am sorry sufficient money taxes were not raised to pay for government and war [[the wording about depreciation and its continuation is awkward]].

I never to be sure did nor understand how to Calculate Latitude & departure which are the base & perpendicular of a triangle of which the distance is the hypothenuse and degree for angle of departure known. In practice the degree being known either line of the triangle may be measured & the table gives the other two. All irregularities in surveys can & must be reduced to triangles in calculating area The base & perpendicular multiplied together & product divided by 2 gives the area.

pages.family_text:
—dividers, and sometimes the protractor, which I think I left at home. A traverse table is indispensable for irregularly shaped surveys. [[The next sentence’s wording is awkward.]] Latitude and departure form the base and perpendicular of a triangle whose measured distance is the hypotenuse. With the direction known, a measured side and the table give the other two sides. Irregular surveys must be divided into triangles to calculate their area. Multiply the base by the perpendicular and divide by two.
When a survey rests against another, treat the older lines as the base. The divergence from their direction is the departure, and the last lines are the latitude, regardless of the compass points. Field notes must balance. The traverse table is the easiest way to correct or determine unknown lengths in irregular surveys.
In practice, measurements may fail to close by a chain or two on [[uneven?]] ground. Leave the most favorable side to be measured last. Manhassett, July 17, 1864. Sister Laura,
Once again I am trying to write with nothing amusing or interesting to say. Life is dull and quiet. [[A phrase about peace is incomplete.]] For the first time in a long while, our company has had preaching. The preacher [[name damaged]] is a Baptist, though I do not remember which branch. Today’s mail brought your July letter with a brief account of the meeting in progress [[details damaged]].
[[Several damaged lines discuss ornaments.]] I have some idea how fond people are of adornment, from a [[shell?]] ring to a breastpin—anything to attract attention and make a display. Every kind of taste is enlisted for that purpose, whether it succeeds or not.
Men confined to one place will do almost anything to pass the time. Following that general human tendency, Company D had gathered tools and begun making combs, shoes and other useful articles. The inspecting officer reported to headquarters that they were making more money than [[the comparison is damaged]]. Headquarters ordered their tools taken away and prohibited manufacturing, whether for sale or otherwise. Their time is now doubly monotonous.
Manufacturing still proceeds at a moderate pace here. The “head fiddler” is away on furlough, so trade is not thriving. Many hours are idle, though nearly a quarter of our company now sit in chairs of their own.

pages.family_title: George to Lizzie: rain, coastal war news, and a change of command, August 20, 1864
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, August 20, 1864. Sister Lizzie,
Your letter of the 5th is before me. I scarcely remember whether I have answered it. Life has been dull for the past week because heavy rain has made getting around town difficult. There is plenty of deep mud, but the sun is drying it. A few rainless days should make things pleasant again. The rain lasted three days.
[[Some coastal news is damaged.]] Fort Gaines has surrendered, and a Yankee fleet is in the bay. Fort Morgan still holds out, though it may be taken. The last two newspapers offered no further news, and people are anxious about both Mobile and Atlanta.
A private report says Johnson was called from Georgia to command an expedition to [[Maryland?]], over Breckinridge, Early and others. I would not rely much on this report, though it might be true.
Magruder has left for Arkansas, to the troops’ general delight. No man has been given up with less regret. General Hébert is temporarily in command until Walker arrives. We hope Walker will do better, especially about furloughs. [[The final damaged lines continue discussing Magruder’s lack of popularity.]]

pages.family_title: Peach cobbler and the difficulty of writing a long letter
pages.family_text:
I went into the country this morning and bought a bucket of peaches for five dollars. I expect peach cobbler for supper. Would you like to join me? The peach crop has been heavy, considering how few orchards there are. [[Part of the discussion of orchards is damaged.]] This climate suits peaches, oranges, figs, pomegranates, lemons, quinces, bananas and other tropical produce. Orange trees are loaded; if we remain until winter, we may eat more of their fine fruit.
[[A damaged passage discusses the paper he is using and reassures Lizzie that she may write freely without concern about its cost.]]
You wanted a long letter, but I must disappoint you: nothing exciting is happening in camp or elsewhere that I know of. Little short of a fight could stir me to a long letter, and I have grown used to receiving short ones from home. If a fight or something unusually interesting happens, I will tell you in as few words as possible.
[[Part of his explanation is damaged.]] I cannot keep up the excitement needed to write four or six pages every time. If we traveled, perhaps something worth writing about would turn up.
[[The letter ends with teasing about an unnamed person, followed by a comic list including red hair, freckles, crooked teeth, a wide mouth, long nose, stooped shoulders, thin legs, knock knees, club feet and a “raw boned specimen of humanity.” Some linking words are lost.]]

pages.title: May 31: a flag of truce and a Northern newspaper
pages.text:
May 31st
The boat is just in sight some ten or fifteen miles off so I will try to finish by the time it [[deleted: got]] gets here. pages.family_title: May 31: a flag of truce and a Northern newspaper
pages.family_text:
May 31, probably 1863. The boat is in sight, ten or fifteen miles away, so I will try to finish before it arrives. Boats are welcome as our link with the outside world.
A flag-of-truce boat recently went out to the blockading ships to learn what had happened to a man named Taylor. Ill treatment by secessionists had driven him to the Yankees, and he was wounded in the lighthouse fight. His wife, who lives about twenty-five miles upriver, requested the inquiry. If his fate was learned, it has not been announced.
The boat brought recent Northern newspapers. I read the New York Times yesterday. It firmly supports the Union as it was and the Constitution as it is, offers the rebels no peace, and calls on patriotic men to keep fighting until the rebellion is suppressed. If two more years will not finish it, the next administration may pursue it with renewed vigor.
Its account of the recent Hooker–Lee battle gives a Union loss figure that is now damaged, and Confederate losses of roughly 20,000–25,000 [[part of the range is damaged]]. It claims 2,500 prisoners and seventeen artillery pieces. It says a sudden rise in the Rappahannock cut rail communication with the rear for twelve [[unit lost]], and that Confederate troops did not interfere with the retreat. It also prints Commodore Porter’s report on the capture of Grand Gulf [[date damaged]].

pages.title: George’s response to Laura: “I write every thing about myself”
pages.text:
Porter says he has the door to vicksburg. He said in his dispatches that if the fortifications had been complete he never could have taken the place as it is a stronger natural defense than vicksburg. The paper says that a great many of the prisoners nearly one half will take the oath of allegiance. It also contained an account of Gen Stonemans raid in Virginia with his cavalry. They claim to have passed in the rear of Lees army destroying his railroad communication with Richmond also destroying all the bridges [[deleted: of]] over the Chickahominy, and went within two miles of Richmond and captured one aid on Gen Winders staff. It also gives a secure & northern account [[lost: left edge]] troops are in high spirits and sanguine of final success. Report says that Stonewall Jackson died from the effects of his wound also that Gen Van Dorn has been killed in a private quarrel.
The boat brought me Lauras letter of 15–16th Laura complains of my reserve in writing about myself. I dont think I am reserved at all, I write every thing about myself, or every thing I do. The temptations of camp life I had supposed you were familiar with, so there is my particular writing. Nothing to do is the greatest drawback aside from the regular form of military life so there is no [[lost: left edge]] for grumbling and discontent there. If anything dont go to my notion it is none of my fault. I have not the management of things there is no use of getting mad about it. If I dont [[deleted: of]] like it I think very contemptibly to myself and dont trouble any body with it. I have not the control of things nothing turns [[lost: left edge]] to vex and disquiet me, no responsibility rests on me beyond the regular routine of soldiering and it is but little difficulty to act a part I have got used to it.
Affectionately George

pages.family_title: George’s response to Laura: “I write every thing about myself”
pages.family_text:
Porter says he has the gateway to Vicksburg. In his dispatch, he says the natural defenses at Grand Gulf are stronger than Vicksburg’s and that completed fortifications would have made the place impossible for him to take. The newspaper says nearly half the prisoners will take the oath of allegiance.
It also describes General Stoneman’s cavalry raid behind Lee’s army, claiming destruction of rail connections to Richmond and bridges over the Chickahominy, an approach within two miles of Richmond, and the capture of an aide on General Winder’s staff. It describes Northern troops as confident of eventual success. Reports also say Stonewall Jackson has died of his wound and General Van Dorn has been killed in a private quarrel.
The boat brought Laura’s letter of the 15th–16th. She says I am reserved about myself. I do not think so: I tell you everything about myself, or everything I do. I assumed you already knew the temptations of camp life. [[A short phrase about writing is unclear.]]
Having nothing to do is the worst drawback, apart from military routine itself. [[A few words before the reference to grumbling and discontent are missing.]] If something does not suit me, it is not my fault; I do not manage things, so getting angry does no good. When I dislike something, I think contemptuous thoughts privately without troubling anyone else.
Because I have no control, I have little to fret over. My only responsibility is the ordinary routine of soldiering, and playing my part is not difficult now that I am used to it.
Affectionately, George.

pages.title: George in Houston: uncertainty about orders, March 19, 1865
pages.text:
Houston March 19th/65
Sister Lizzie
Again I will write you from this place with but little idea how long we will be permitted to remain. Nothing have we heard yet in a reliable shape connected with our future movements though tis the general opinion that we will go east of the Miss sometime this Spring. But very few have any inclination to travel in that direction I assure you, though if ordered twill be very few who will refuse to go. I have heard no late news of any importance lately. A few days ago a rumor was afloat that a battle had occurred between Sherman & Beauregard in which the former was routed and the latter killed. The papers however say nothing about it. Last authentic accounts from there said Sherman and Hardee were racing for Charlotte and Sherman was about to get there first.
Evidently there will be active times there this spring and if some Yankees dont come this way Somebody from this Dept will have to go East of the Mississippi sure. One of two things is evident. Either an attack is feared at Galveston or the troops on the Coast are to be relieved and sent to the field. All the old troops from La & Ark are coming this way
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-102. March 19, 1865 is written in the heading. Reports of troop movements and the supposed death of Beauregard are the writer’s contemporary information; he explicitly says the newspapers do not confirm the rumor. “Miss” expands to Mississippi in the family reading.

pages.family_text:
Houston, March 19, 1865. Sister Lizzie,
I am writing again from here with little idea how long we may remain. We have no reliable information about our next movements, though most think we will go east of the Mississippi this spring. Few want to go, I assure you, but few would refuse if ordered.
There is little important news. A rumor a few days ago said Sherman had been defeated in battle and Beauregard killed. The newspapers say nothing about it. The last reliable reports said Sherman and Hardee were racing for Charlotte, with Sherman likely to arrive first.
There will clearly be active campaigning there this spring. Unless Yankees come this way, someone from this department will surely have to go east of the Mississippi. Either an attack on Galveston is feared, or coastal troops will be relieved and sent into the field. The old troops from Louisiana and Arkansas are all coming this way.

pages.title: Troop movements, coffee, and a sermon without politics
pages.text:
I got a letter from Henry Orr dated 13th inst in which he [[deleted: said]] said he expected they would move to the Brazos Country in a few days as the forage was exhausted about Waverly, and said for me to answer him at Hempstead. De Brays Regt is at Hempstead now. Tom wrote from Tyler under date 10th and says his old Regt is on the march for Hempstead. Walkers old Division is ordered I understand also [[deleted: the]] Greens old Brigade. This I think is indicative of apprehensions of an attack on the coast or Starvation in La & Ark.
We still have good health and live pretty well all things considered. We joined funds the other day and bought a Sack of flour & thirty pounds of Coffee. So we have Coffee & Biscuit at our house. This makes about 45 pound Coffee which we have bought since we came here. Confed money has fallen to 27 again and not very current. Specie is also Scarcer than it was, goods generally a lower owing to the Scarcity of money. Blockade Running Still continues at Galveston by which means goods plentiful in the Market. Cotton Cards brought 1.60 per pair by the dozen pair at auction. Today I went to hear the old presbyterian, had an excellent Discourse in which no allusion was made to the present War any way, the Confed, Jeff, [[deleted: Abe]] Abe or any other political Dignitary.
As ever your brother Geo.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-101. “27” is recorded without a stated conversion basis; it should not be presented as a verified exchange rate to a specific currency. “Cotton Cards” are tools for preparing cotton fiber, not playing cards. Initial deletion before the repeated Abe is retained.

pages.family_title: Troop movements, coffee, and a sermon without politics
pages.family_text:
Henry Orr wrote on the 13th that they expected to move to the Brazos country in a few days: forage around Waverly was exhausted. He asked me to reply to Hempstead, where DeBray’s regiment already is. Tom wrote from Tyler on the 10th that his old regiment was marching to Hempstead. I understand Walker’s old division and Green’s old brigade have orders too. To me, this suggests fear of an attack on the coast, or starvation in Louisiana and Arkansas.
We are healthy and live fairly well. We pooled our money and bought a sack of flour and thirty pounds of coffee, so our household has coffee and biscuits. That brings our coffee purchases since arriving here to about forty-five pounds.
Confederate money has fallen to “27” again [[the basis is not stated]] and circulates poorly. Coin is scarcer too. Goods are generally cheaper because money is scarce. Blockade running continues at Galveston and keeps the market supplied. Cotton carding tools sold at auction for 1.60 a pair when bought by the dozen pairs.
Today I heard the old Presbyterian preacher give an excellent sermon without mentioning the war, the Confederacy, Jeff, Abe or any other political dignitary.
As ever, your brother, George.

pages.text:
March [[22nd?]]
Sister Lizzie
I will answer yours which came in Jodys, date 4th No 7. Received day before yesterday.
I can say that you are improving a good deal in letter writing and a few more severe criticisms would do you some good, but I dont intend to be hard on you. Merely Correct a few words occasionally Such as “[[horrizon?]]” “[[pos ble?]]”
To day is a very pleasant one. The sea breeze blows all the time now that winter has broke and spring come. If it was not for the warm atmosphere I could not tell that spring had opened, for roses have bloomed all winter and the numerous evergreens never change their appearance. The gardens look well as they have done all winter. There is no timber on the Isle

pages.title: George mourns his sister, March 10, 1865
pages.text:
To all at Home. Houston Texas March 10th/65
It was with the deepest Sorrow that I heard of the death of my Sister through Capt Evans who came down a few days ago. Little did I expect to hear of so sad an event, it came unexpectedly but ah! too true, and we can but weep over the departed with unavailing Sorrow, for they cannot be recalled, but the evidences of the Higher Hope of immortality which they have left, gives comfort to the sorrowing hearts that are left behind.
To me it is a greater Source of happiness to know that She died in [[full?]] hope of Heaven and everlasting bliss, than to have been crowned [[the?]] richest Queen of the Earth. and while we mourn her loss [[illegible: fold obscures part of line]] her gain. It looks hard for her to be called [[away?]] from her young family, but the ways of Providence are [[always?]] the best and tis but meet that we yield without a murmur to its decrees. Sad indeed it is to the children to be thus early deprived of their protector, deprived of her care and love [[such?]] as only a mother can bestow and thrown almost upon the World for awhile. Sympathy for them increases our sorrow for [[our?]] loss, but we must do all that lies in our power in their [[behalf?]], Seperated by fate or fortune from their only parent.
More than ever I feel that I am needed at home but less [[and?]] less the Chances appear to me for returning any time shortly, the future grows darker and darker as we advance and [[not one?]] ray of light appears ahead.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-109, signed Geo. Douglas. The deceased sister is not named on these two pages. Dark folds and a clipped left edge obscure several words; bracketed reconstructions are not certain readings. The phrase about the children’s “only parent” is preserved without inferring the other parent’s fate.

pages.family_text:
Houston, Texas, March 10, 1865. To everyone at home,
I was deeply saddened to hear of my sister’s death from Captain Evans, who arrived a few days ago. I never expected such sad news. It came unexpectedly, but was all too true. We can only weep for those who have died, though our sorrow cannot bring them back. The evidence they left of their hope of immortality comforts those left behind.
It gives me greater happiness to know that she died hoping for heaven and everlasting joy than if she had been crowned the richest queen on earth. We mourn her loss, but [[a damaged passage refers to her gain]]. It seems hard that she should be taken from her young family. Yet Providence’s ways are best, and we must submit without complaint.
It is terribly sad for the children to lose their protector so early, and the care and love only a mother can give, leaving them almost on their own in the world for a time. Sympathy for them deepens our sorrow. We must do everything we can for them, separated by fate or fortune from their only parent.
More than ever I feel needed at home, but my chances of returning soon seem smaller and smaller. As we go on, the future grows darker, with [[not one?]] ray of light ahead.

paragraphs.text:
To all at Home. Houston Texas March 10th/65
It was with the deepest Sorrow that I heard of the death of my Sister through Capt Evans who came down a few days ago. Little did I expect to hear of so sad an event, it came unexpectedly but ah! too true, and we can but weep over the departed with unavailing Sorrow, for they cannot be recalled, but the evidences of the Higher Hope of immortality which they have left, gives comfort to the sorrowing hearts that are left behind.
To me it is a greater Source of happiness to know that She died in [[full?]] hope of Heaven and everlasting bliss, than to have been crowned [[the?]] richest Queen of the Earth. and while we mourn her loss [[illegible: fold obscures part of line]] her gain. It looks hard for her to be called [[away?]] from her young family, but the ways of Providence are [[always?]] the best and tis but meet that we yield without a murmur to its decrees. Sad indeed it is to the children to be thus early deprived of their protector, deprived of her care and love [[such?]] as only a mother can bestow and thrown almost upon the World for awhile. Sympathy for them increases our sorrow for [[our?]] loss, but we must do all that lies in our power in their [[behalf?]], Seperated by fate or fortune from their only parent.
More than ever I feel that I am needed at home but less [[and?]] less the Chances appear to me for returning any time shortly, the future grows darker and darker as we advance and [[not one?]] ray of light appears ahead.

pages.title: “Any way almost would suit me now”: George longs for the war to end
pages.text:
Rumors are plentiful about being ordered across the Miss river and to La and I am pretty confident that that we will start Somewhere east by the first of next month. We may be sent east of the river and if so the Chances for a single individual to remain on this side are very Slim, for under Such circumstances no transfers would be given. The men are almost unanimously opposed to such a move but you all know what orders are. It is reported that Lee has ordered 30,000 troops east of the Miss and if this be true I look for the worst. However I will not trouble myself about it any more than I can help, only wish my term of service was out.
No news reaches us except what comes through the blockade. Sherman is occupying the coast cities almost [[without?]] opposition and [[Lee?]] is concentrating. Indicating I think a field Campaign this year almost altogether; Perhaps twill hasten the war to a close, by subjugation if no other way, any way almost would suit me now.
To day has been fast day and all has been quiet. I do not attend their war meetings and preachings.
The Country is ready to receive anything in the Shape of Govt now, will submit to anything, their Spirit is broken. It is late and cold so I will close.
With best love to all I remain as ever affectionately
Geo. Douglas.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-108, dated March 10, 1865. “Lee” and “without” are obscured by a dark fold. The asserted troop order is explicitly a report, and the statements about the country’s spirit are the writer’s opinions. “Fast day” refers to a day of fasting, not speed.

pages.title: George to Laura: dry weather and the stranded Clifton, March 11, 1864
pages.text:
Sabine Pass, March 11th/64 — No 60
Sister Laura
This weeks mail brought me your letter of the 21st ult, and found us all on the Square. I see you have had some cold weather as [[inserted: well]] as us, from what I have been able to learn the past winter has been tolerably severe in every place.
The weather still continues very dry and unless we have rain soon all the cistern water will be gone, and the well water is quite indifferent. In and around the precinct of Sabine Pass everything moves on in the usual way, but little arises to excite attention, and the general pleasantness of the weather tends to increase that disease commonly known as laziness, and which always prevails in a garrison to a considerable extent. There is two of our Co sick at this time, one at Beaumont and one here; both pneumonia one caused by the measles the other an ordinary attack, neither from what I can learn very dangerous.
The Clifton has not yet departed, made an unsuccessful attempt to go about two weeks ago, grounded on an oyster reef at high tide and lay out of plum a day and night which sprung a leak somewhere in the bottom though not bad enough to keep her in port, she will try again the first favorable time.
pages.editorial_notes: Letter No. 60. Continues on 09-112–114. “Ult” means the preceding month. “Out of plum” is retained as written; the family reading interprets it as lying out of upright alignment. Medical descriptions are the writer’s report, not a modern diagnosis.

pages.family_title: George to Laura: dry weather and the stranded Clifton, March 11, 1864
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, March 11, 1864. Letter 60. Sister Laura,
This week’s mail brought your letter of February 21. It found us all doing well. You have had cold weather too; from what I hear, the winter has been fairly severe everywhere.
It remains very dry. Without rain soon, our cistern water will run out, and the well water is poor. Life around Sabine Pass goes on as usual, with little to attract attention. The pleasant weather only increases the common garrison disease of laziness.
Two men in our company are ill, one at Beaumont and one here. Both have pneumonia, one following measles, the other an ordinary case. From what I can learn, neither is in much danger.
The Clifton has not left yet. She tried about two weeks ago but ran aground on an oyster reef at high tide. She lay tilted for a day and a night, opening a leak in her bottom. It is not bad enough to keep her in port, and she will try again when conditions are favorable.

pages.title: George questions newspaper victories and growing rumors
pages.text:
Our foreign news is quite meagre, merely what we get from the papers and of course we get the best side of the tale if it is not always to be relied on. Lying has got to be so fashionable that almost every source of intelligence is filled with it, somebody, or some people rather are getting so well up to, and used to it, that they can lie without knowing it, it seems. Twice has Sherman been badly whipt in Miss! The first time he ran pretty fast no doubt, but unfortunately for the South the Rebs walked in the lead. If his last Skedaddling was like the first, where now is Polk? The farther a tale travels the bigger it gets, this rule works everywhere and now Since the fall of Vicksburg tales have to come a roundabout way, consequently they assume large proportions. No reliance can now be placed in the details of affairs east of the Miss, only the general items can be credited and the general features of the case are rather dark.
Some Strange ideas have worked themselves into the upper country, I see by the tone of your letters. Yanks and Rebs are on better terms Westward than here if they allow Schooners to run in and out at will, only fire a few blanks at them, here they always Shoot to hurt. When no better amusement presents itself the Yankees Shell our Pickets on the beach.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-111. “Foreign news” here is the writer’s label for news beyond his immediate area, including east of the Mississippi. His claim that Sherman was twice defeated is ironic: the following sentences question the reports. The family reading keeps that irony explicit.

pages.family_title: George questions newspaper victories and growing rumors
pages.family_text:
Our news from outside is scanty: only what the newspapers supply. Naturally, they give us the favorable version, even when it is unreliable. Lying has become so fashionable that nearly every source of information is full of it. Some people seem so practiced and accustomed to it that they can lie without knowing it.
Sherman has supposedly been badly beaten in Mississippi twice! The first time, he certainly ran fast—but unfortunately for the South, the Rebels were ahead of him. If his latest retreat was like the first, where is Polk now?
The farther a story travels, the bigger it becomes. Since Vicksburg fell, news must come by a roundabout route and grows accordingly. We cannot trust details from east of the Mississippi, only the broad outline—and that looks rather dark.
Your letters suggest some strange ideas have reached the upper country. Yankees and Rebels must be on better terms farther west if schooners can pass in and out freely with only a few blank shots fired at them. Here they shoot to hurt. When nothing more entertaining offers itself, the Yankees shell our sentries on the beach.

pages.title: War weariness and teasing Laura about marriage
pages.text:
Several came ashore the other evening about dark but the cavalry failed to take them in, couldnt find them in the night. Evidently the people of your section are badly whipt, even worse than the Soldiers, or express themselves more freely. Maybe we are bold and maybe not, who knows.
Fewer remarks are made about military affairs now than formerly, all somehow seem to be careless about it any way. To brag about Confederates and run down Yankees is an old song worn out long ago, and tis scarcely ever hummed nowadays. No one pretends to say how the Women and children will live after the supply now on hand is gone nor do they seem to take any lively interest about it. However the present stillness may not last beyond a few weeks, and then, all may be storm and commotion again.
And still they marry! I was Surprised to hear of Mary [[Pattons?]] union for I Supposed She was too young to leave her mamma. Em Chapman I only know by character and hardly by that. She is cousin to Lizzie I believe, wonder if Lizzie will do likewise. White folks are very uncertain, so are the Women. Dont marry yourself off to Some gentleman of the “Bush” merely because you get a chance, better call back “[[Bowle?]]” first, though he is aged, and rather “red” headed,
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-111–112. Mary’s surname and the quoted nickname at the end remain uncertain. The statement that Em Chapman is Lizzie’s cousin is qualified by “I believe” in the source. “Gentleman of the Bush” is left as the writer’s phrase, without identifying a particular man.

pages.family_title: War weariness and teasing Laura about marriage
pages.family_text:
Several Yankees came ashore around dark the other evening. Our cavalry failed to capture them because they could not find them in the night. The people in your area seem thoroughly beaten down, even more than the soldiers—or perhaps they speak more freely. Maybe we are brave and maybe not; who knows?
There is less talk about military affairs now. Everyone seems indifferent. Boasting about Confederates and belittling Yankees is an old, worn-out song, scarcely hummed anymore. No one explains how women and children will live when their present supplies are gone, or seems greatly interested. Still, this quiet may last only a few weeks before everything becomes turmoil again.
And people still marry! I was surprised by Mary [[Patton’s?]] marriage, thinking her too young to leave her mother. I know Em Chapman only by reputation, and barely that. I believe she is Lizzie’s cousin; I wonder whether Lizzie will do the same. White people are unpredictable, and so are women.
Do not marry some gentleman of the “Bush” merely because the opportunity comes. Better call back “[[Bowle?]]” first, though he is old and rather redheaded.

pages.title: Jayhawkers, writing paper, and beef buried with military honors
pages.text:
A raid of Jayhawkers towards Nibletts from some of the La Swamps has excited some little attention. I understand Greens Brigade has been ordered to that region for their benefit. There is quite a a nest of them beyond Calcasieu lake from here and have been doing some mischief in that region. It is reported that they are sustained by Banks, but every species of rascality now days is attributed to Yankee credit.
I have a sufficiency of paper to last Six months so you need not trouble yourselves on my account. I am very much obliged to Sister for her present, but will not need it for some time to come. In the varying scenes of war I hope I may have a chance to be at home and get [[inserted: it]] by the time I have use for it. Tell her I will try to write to her during this month. I received Marys letter the other day, and will have to send her word that She is Still very modest; She had better outgrow that.
One of our co has been released from the guard house; Gilbert the man that left [[Millican?]] sick and went home last fall.
We still get plenty to eat such as it is, but the quality is rather poor. Some of the troops on Galveston Island have not had beef for a week. The last the got was so poor they buried it with the honors of War, and have refused to take any more because it was no better.
Affectionately, George
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of the March 11, 1864 letter, 09-111–114. Banks’s supposed support of Jayhawkers is explicitly reported hearsay; George questions the tendency to blame every offense on Yankees. The place/name after “left” is uncertain. The present from “Sister” is not identified beyond the surrounding discussion of paper.

pages.title: George travels down the Brazos, April 11, 1865
pages.text:
Sister Laura Houston April 11th 1865
I promised last week to write a larger letter this week so I suppose I will have to comply with Said promise. Wednesday morning I Started for Velasco, twas dry though cloudy, arrived at Columbia on the Brazos River at four oclock in the evening. Columbia is a Small place noted only for being the terminus of the [[H.T. & B.R.R.?]] The Country traversed by this road is low and flat, mostly prairie and very fertile. Tis thinly Settled, though a few rich planters live along the route. The Brazos is the prettiest river that I have Seen in this latitude, tis about one hundred yards wide and very deep, the banks are lined with Cottonwood and willow, and covered with quick Sand.
Left Columbia thursday morning on the Steamboat “Era No. 3” for Velasco distant about fifty miles by the river route. The weather still continued cloudy wind blowing [[lost: start of line]] and from the east. Eight miles below Columbia is Brazoria [[also?]] a Small place on the river bank in the woods. This [[is?]] the only town below Columbia. The boat Stopped [[frequently?]] along to take in men belonging to Bates Regt [[who?]] had been in the bottoms hunting and cutting poles to [[build?]] cook houses with at the mouth of the river.
[[lost: fragments of another line at bottom edge]]
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-116–118. Left edge and bottom of the reproduction clip parts of words and a following line. The railroad initials are tentative and have not been silently expanded. The boat name reads Era No. 3. This is the writer’s travel description; distances and assessments of settlement are his own.

pages.family_title: George travels down the Brazos, April 11, 1865
pages.family_text:
Houston, April 11, 1865. Sister Laura,
I promised a longer letter this week, so I must keep my promise. On Wednesday morning I started for Velasco. It was dry but cloudy. I reached Columbia on the Brazos River at four that afternoon.
Columbia is a small place, notable chiefly as the railway terminus [[the initials are uncertain]]. The railway crosses low, flat, fertile country, mostly prairie and sparsely settled, though a few wealthy planters live along it. The Brazos is the prettiest river I have seen in this part of the country. It is about a hundred yards wide and very deep, with cottonwoods, willows, and quicksand along its banks.
On Thursday morning I left Columbia aboard the steamboat Era No. 3 for Velasco, about fifty miles downriver. The sky remained cloudy, with wind from the east [[part of the description is lost]]. Eight miles below Columbia lies Brazoria, a small town in the riverside woods and the only town below Columbia. The boat stopped along the way to collect men of Bates’s regiment who had been hunting in the river bottoms and cutting poles for cookhouses at the river’s mouth. [[A further line is clipped.]]

pages.title: Delivering a prisoner and finding Dock at Velasco
pages.text:
Some four or five miles above Velasco the timber [[deleted: gave]] [[inserted: gives]] out and the river emerges into the open prairie. Like Sabine the Country is low and flat, the banks of the river Scarcely eighteen inches high. Near the lower edge of the timber was Some of Magruders ground hoggery in the Shape of a Small field fortification with two embrasures for guns. About two miles above the mouth is another earthwork mounting one gun. Arrived at Velasco at near three oclock, wind very hard from east and pretty cold, hunted up Hd Qrs [[G.C.M.?]] & turned over my prisoner according to orders and then began looking about for Dock. I Soon met with him but would not have known him, His beard has not heard of a razor for years and besides he is tolerably gray as much so as father. He was in good health but very sick of the war and anxious to hear from home as he had not heard Since the battle of Shiloh.
Velasco is on the east Side of the river and Quintana on the west. The principal portion of the troops are at Quintana Hd Qrs are at Quintana. Velasco Contains five or Six dwellings only, Quintana about twice that No. The two Cities are exactly opposite each other, the river between is about three hundred yards wide. There is no bay at the mouth. There is a fort on each side immediately on the beach, each commanding the Channel
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-115. “Dock” is not expanded to a formal name. The headquarters abbreviation is tentative. “Ground hoggery” is the writer’s mocking description of Magruder’s earthworks. The remark about Dock’s gray beard provides no age or exact relationship.

pages.family_title: Delivering a prisoner and finding Dock at Velasco
pages.family_text:
Four or five miles above Velasco, the woods end and the river emerges onto open prairie. Like Sabine, the land is low and flat, with riverbanks scarcely eighteen inches high. Near the edge of the woods stood some of what I call Magruder’s “ground hoggery”: a small field fort with two openings for guns. Another earthwork, holding one gun, stands about two miles above the mouth.
We arrived at Velasco around three o’clock, with a strong, cold east wind. I found headquarters [[the following abbreviation is uncertain]] and delivered my prisoner as ordered. Then I looked for Dock. I soon found him but would not have recognized him. His beard has not seen a razor for years, and he is about as gray as Father. He was healthy but very tired of the war and eager for news from home: he had heard none since the battle of Shiloh.
Velasco lies east of the river and Quintana west. Most troops and headquarters are at Quintana. Velasco has only five or six houses, and Quintana about twice as many. The two “cities” face each other across about three hundred yards of river. There is no bay at the mouth. A fort stands on each side, right on the beach, covering the channel.

pages.family_title: A schooner founders off Velasco
pages.family_text:
During the night there was considerable rain and a strong northeast wind. Two schooners were loaded to sail. One started out and struck the steamboat with her bow, damaging the [[bow?]] and a chimney. The schooner broke the main chain between her cutwater and bowsprit, but the crew did not notice until she reached the sea.
In deep water and heavy swells, she sprang a leak and had to return. The crew worked the pumps, but water entered so fast that she sank less than half a mile from shore, inside the outer bar on the sheltered side of the channel. The sea was too rough for the crew to leave before daylight, even though water washed over the decks.
At dawn, three men set out in the schooner’s only small boat. Four remained [[in the rigging?]], none able to swim. The boat soon capsized in the breakers. [[One?]] man let go and swam ashore; the other [[two?]] held onto the boat and drifted ashore four miles [[down?]] the beach.
The waves were so high that no boat could leave shore to help the men on the schooner, though they were less than half a mile away. Only a lifeboat could have survived in such a sea.

pages.title: Men stranded in the rigging; George returns to Houston
pages.text:
There was no life boat nearer than the wreck of the Acacia ten miles off on the beach to windward, and no boat could be launched on the open Sea in [[deleted: illegible]] Such a gale. Up to the time the boat left nothing had been done for the relief [[deleted: of]] of the poor fellows who were left clinging in the ropes and nothing could be done without a life boat and that was not obtainable. I never Saw so rough a Sea in my life before and hope never to see again when a vessel is in distress. There was no Chance to get the men off untill the Sea calmed. Saturday morning the wind was from the north and if they had not fallen from the rigging from exhaustion they were doubtless relieved. But two nights and a day was a long time to hang on to ropes and the Vessel rocking like a cradle in the Sand with every Swell of the Sea, and threatning to part.
Friday I returned to Columbia, it rained a good portion the day and was disagreeably cold it continued raining friday night & Saturday, Saturday I came on to Houston, arrived in the night and found the mud very deep & thin. Everything had been in an uproar on account of Whartons death but all was [[deleted: illegible]] quiet.
[[separate block: inverted writing above main text]]
All well here at present. We are not ordered away yet tis rumored that transportation has been ordered for 30,000 men — George [[Dou... ?]]

pages.family_title: Men stranded in the rigging; George returns to Houston
pages.family_text:
The nearest lifeboat was at the wreck of the Acacia, ten miles upwind along the beach. No boat could be launched into the open sea in such a gale. When our boat left, nothing had been done for the men clinging to the ropes. Without an available lifeboat, nothing could be done. I had never seen such rough seas and hope never to see them again with a vessel in distress.
They could not be taken off until the sea calmed. By Saturday morning the wind came from the north. If they had not fallen from exhaustion, they were probably rescued then. But two nights and a day was a long time to cling to ropes while the vessel rocked in the sand with every swell and threatened to break apart.
On Friday I returned to Columbia in rain and unpleasant cold. Rain continued through Friday night and Saturday. I reached Houston on Saturday night and found deep, thin mud. Wharton’s death had caused an uproar, but everything was quiet again.
All are well here. We have no orders to leave yet. There is a rumor that transportation has been ordered for 30,000 men.
George [[surname partly clipped]].

pages.title: Sabine Pass, April 25: a burst cannon and uncertain battle reports
pages.text:
Sabine Pass Apr 25th
Number 18
I received yours of number 9 I wrote to you the other day, [[Lauras?]] at the Same time No 8. Yours was mailed the 4th of this month 21 days ago a long time for a letter to be on the way inside of the State. Henry [[Mundwell?]] got in day before yesterday, and says that Warren will not start for camps before the first of May.
I wrote all about the skirmish in my last; since that time there has been no hostile manoeuvres. Five feds come a Shore the other night, and run our cavalry picketts in to town, or rather the pickets they got scared and came of their own accord.
H R A serious [[deleted: accident]] accident has occurred here thursday. The cannon on the Bell a 64 pound rifle gun burst while they were practicing with it, killing two men and wounding two. It was a mate to the one that burst on the Bayou City the morning of the Gal fight.
The defeat of Sibley at new Iberia is confirmed by report but as yet I have seen no published acct of it. It is said that he lost 250 killed, and is now himself under arrest for being drunk on the day of the fight.
There is also another report current the Yankees have Taken Alexandria, La,

Standalone “H R” and a printed H at the right edge are not expanded as personal names.

pages.family_title: Sabine Pass, April 25: a burst cannon and uncertain battle reports
pages.family_text:
Sabine Pass, April 25, year unstated. Letter 18.
I received your number 9, and [[Laura’s?]] number 8 at the same time. I wrote to you the other day. Your letter was mailed on the 4th—twenty-one days ago, a long time for a letter within the state. Henry [[Mundwell?]] arrived two days ago. He says Warren will not leave for camp before May 1.
I described the skirmish in my last letter. There has been no hostile movement since. Five Federals came ashore the other night and drove our cavalry sentries into town—or rather, the sentries became frightened and came in of their own accord.
A serious accident occurred on Thursday. The Bell’s 64-pound rifled cannon burst during practice, killing two men and wounding two. It matched the gun that burst on the Bayou City on the morning of the Galveston fight.
Reports continue to say Sibley was defeated at New Iberia, though I have seen no published account. They claim 250 were killed and that he is under arrest for being drunk during the battle. Another rumor says the Yankees have taken Alexandria, Louisiana—

pages.title: George returns to Galveston, May 4, 1865
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie. Galveston May 4th 1865
Since I last wrote you we have changed base to this city. We came down yesterday on a Special train, quitted our old quarters after breakfast and got into our new ones time enough to get Supper. The weather was fine and altogether twas the most pleasant move we ever made. On the Second we were reviewed by Col Spaight, marched about over the principal part of Houston in column of platoons, owing to the absence of O Briens Co our position was on the left wing of the regt (“the tail” as tis called) and had to pad along behind a Co of Creoles who could neither keep a line or time or distance. In Consequence we Showed only at a moderate advantage. Several of the Ladies were out to to See us though no excitement at all was displayed. Scarcely ever a kerchief waved and “never a yell.” One little “[[Husky?]]” in her teens looked So much like She wanted to do Something I lifted my hat to her and She acknowledged the Same by a polite bow, I did not excite further notice afterwards.
Many were the regrets [[deleted: that]] of the Citizens at our departure, Some of the most prominent did their best to persuade Magruder to let us remain but he would not hear to them. They (the citizens) gave the regt a box of Tobacco and 620 pounds of Coffee on the morning of our leaving, and Some Said they would be willing to pay “C” Co $10.00 per month Specie per man to let us Stay. That Shows how we Stand in Houston after a residence of five months. Our being moved is explained in few words. Magruder wants Ashbel Smith to command Galveston island [[El... ?]]

His description of the other company and local opinion is retained as his perspective. “Specie” means coin.

pages.family_title: George returns to Galveston, May 4, 1865
pages.family_text:
Galveston, May 4, 1865. Sister Lizzie,
We have moved here since I last wrote. Yesterday we left our old quarters after breakfast, traveled by special train, and settled into the new quarters in time for supper. In fine weather, it was our most pleasant move yet.
On May 2, Colonel Spaight reviewed us, and we marched through central Houston in platoon columns. O’Brien’s company was absent, so we were at the regiment’s left, or “tail,” following a Creole company that could not keep its line, step, or distance. This did little for our appearance. Several women came out, but there was little enthusiasm: scarcely a waved handkerchief and no cheers. One teenage girl looked eager to do something. I raised my hat and she bowed politely. I attracted no more notice.
Many citizens regretted our departure. Prominent people tried to persuade Magruder to let us stay, but he refused. On the morning we left, the citizens gave the regiment a box of tobacco and 620 pounds of coffee. Some even said they would pay each man in Company C ten dollars a month in coin to keep us there. That shows our standing after five months in Houston.
The reason for the move is simple. Magruder wants Ashbel Smith to command Galveston Island—[[the final name is partly clipped; the next page explains]].

pages.title: Schoolhouse quarters, a sea bath, and reports of surrender
pages.text:
on the island but Elmore was Senior Col to Smith and must be removed and Spaight was the only junior Col in the Sub district to Smith, so we came for Smiths accommodation.
We are quartered in the Robb Schoolhouse, room plenty for the Co and no other with us quartered with us and none nearer than a block distant. The location is pleasant, in the Southern part of the city a little over half mile from the South battery and about a half from our old quarters on Strand Street. On the east Side of the Street running from Smiths garden to the Custom house and Market, three blocks if I am not mistaken from the custom house, Jody will know the location.
To day I luxuriated in a “roll in the brine” and “Shipped” a little Sea water in the operation. A blockader was off, not very far, I could See the men walking about the decks and the black ports frowned darkly, but they did not interrupt us; [[deleted: uncertain number]] [[inserted: Twelve]] vessels in the fleet. They had a flag of truce to day, have not heard from it yet. The “Wren” came in night before last loaded with cannon and ammunition brought N. Y. dates to 22d ult, they report that Johnson and Beauregard Surrendered on the Same terms as Lee. There must be Something of it as the blockade fired a Salute the other day. I heard to day that Some news had come in which the authorities [[deleted: were]] would not allow published. I got a letter from [[Doc H?]] this evening, he was not well, he wrote on the [[28th?]] ult. When we get a little better settled I will write again. Supper is about ready so I will quit. Excuse Haste
Affectionately George

—but Elmore outranked Smith as colonel and had to be moved. Spaight was the only colonel in the subdistrict junior to Smith, so we came to accommodate Smith.
Our company has plenty of room in the Robb Schoolhouse, with no other company sharing it and none closer than a block away. It is a pleasant spot in the southern part of the city, a little over half a mile from the South Battery and about half a mile from our former quarters on Strand Street. It is on the east side of the street from Smith’s garden to the customs house and market, about three blocks from the customs house. Jody will know it.
Today I enjoyed a roll in the salt water and swallowed a little in the process. A blockading ship lay close enough for me to see men on deck and its dark gunports, but they left us alone. There are twelve vessels in the fleet. There was a flag of truce today; I have heard no result yet.
The Wren arrived the night before last with cannon, ammunition, and New York news through April 22. The reports say Johnson and Beauregard surrendered on the same terms as Lee. There must be something to it, since the blockading fleet fired a salute recently. Today I heard that news had arrived which the authorities would not allow to be published.
I received a letter this evening from [[Doc H?]], dated April [[28?]]. He was unwell. I will write again once we are better settled. Supper is almost ready, so I must stop. Excuse the haste.
Affectionately, George. All are well in camp.

pages.title: A damaged and deserted Galveston, May 7, 1865
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie, Galveston Texas May 7th 1865
Yours of 22d ult came to hand last evening, one must evidently be lost as there Seems to be a lack of connection. As to what I promised to tell you when I got back from Velasco I can Say I believe I forgot it, however twas only Jody going home which was then only prospective. The Capt says tell Jody to not hurry back, get what he went for if possible, no one has come in Consequently cant give an extension of time, Jody will not be looked for before the 1st of June nohow and not a great deal then unless transportation can be had conveniently.
Galveston is badly Shattered by hard treatment, marks of abuse are everywhere visible, tis not near as pretty a city as it was two years ago, though tis ahead of Houston yet in beauty. Business has Stagnated, nothing is doing, the city looks deserted. Most of the wealthier Classes have gone, the poor are still here but there is no employment for them and how the get along is more than I can tell, no money in circulation that I have yet observed, all the business is done at Houston and Galveston is neglected and forgotten.
There are Several regts here I do not know how many. They are quartered in every part of the city, and everywhere They have been they have Succeeded in ruining the houses. The Tremont house and Island City hotel are worthless. Every fence and old house has been burned for wood that any pretext could be found to commence on. Magruder has ditched and dug this end of the island full of holes thus ruining the landscape. An unbroken breastwork extends from the South Battery to Ft [[Scurry?]] and I dont know how much further. All the Sand hills between the S Battery and Ft S. have been leveled by order of Bankhead Lt Col, but under the influence of the wind they are rapidly reforming. [[illegible: clipped final line, includes “Street back near the Court house”]]

pages.family_title: A damaged and deserted Galveston, May 7, 1865
pages.family_text:
Galveston, Texas, May 7, 1865. Sister Lizzie,
Your letter of April 22 arrived last evening. One letter must be missing, since the correspondence does not quite connect. I think I forgot what I promised to tell you after returning from Velasco. It was only that Jody might go home; at that point it was still a prospect.
The captain says to tell Jody not to hurry back and to get what he went for, if possible. No one has come in, so he cannot give an extension of time. Jody will not be expected before June 1, and not especially then unless transportation is convenient.
Galveston has suffered badly. Signs of rough treatment are everywhere. It is much less attractive than two years ago, though still prettier than Houston. Business has stopped and the city looks deserted. Most wealthier residents have left. Poor people remain without employment; I cannot tell how they survive. I have seen no money circulating. Business is in Houston, while Galveston is neglected and forgotten.
Several regiments are quartered all over the city. Wherever they have stayed, they have ruined the houses. The Tremont House and Island City Hotel are worthless. Fences and old houses have been burned for fuel wherever an excuse could be found. Magruder has filled this end of the island with ditches and holes, ruining the landscape. An uninterrupted breastwork runs from the South Battery to Fort [[Scurry?]] and farther than I know. Lieutenant Colonel Bankhead ordered the sandhills between the battery and fort leveled, but the wind is rapidly rebuilding them. [[The last line is clipped; it refers to a street near the courthouse.]]
