There are Several regts here I do not know how many. They are quartered in every part of the city, and everywhere They have been they have Succeeded in ruining the houses. The Tremont house and Island City hotel are worthless. Every fence and old house has been burned for wood that any pretext could be found to commence on. Magruder has ditched and dug this end of the island full of holes thus ruining the landscape. An unbroken breastwork extends from the South Battery to Ft [[Scurry?]] and I dont know how much further. All the Sand hills between the S Battery and Ft S. have been leveled by order of Bankhead Lt Col, but under the influence of the wind they are rapidly reforming. [[illegible: clipped final line, includes “Street back near the Court house”]]

pages.title: Rumors that the war is over—and George’s explicit caution
pages.text:
Well now for News! Great and multiform are the rumors afloat but from them all this much can be deduced without peeping behind the Scenes. Johnston has either Surrendered or in Such a fair way too that he cant avoid it, but of the details you can [[know?]] as much as I. Now for behind the curtain. It has been rumored for Sometime that there was Some unpublished news on hand in fact this was definitely known, Flake of the Bulletin said as much. Of this news I have got an inkling. Col Wilkes has just arrived from New O. paroled, and Says Sherman and Johnston have come to the agreement that Johnston Surrender the Confederate Army everywhere, turn over all the arms [[deleted: illegible]] to the several State arsenals, disband the troops and Send them home. The Several State governments to continue in their present organizations, only renounce the Confed and renew their allegiance to the U.S. local laws and officers to continue as they are and all return to the Union. And an armistice of forty days agreed on to consult the Washington Cabinet. The Cabinet rejected the propositions as they recognized State Govts. Grant says he will sustain Shermans course with his army as it is a Military Surrender; made with the approval of Breckenridge and Davis. So matters stand if my inkling is correct.
Warren is my informant and he is not likely to jump at a conclusion of this kind, he thinks the war over and that this news is only Suppressed untill it come officially for this Dept to give up and go home, and let the Change be effected as quietly as possible. If this is not premature a couple of months will wind up the Drama. Very likely a good deal of it is ahead of the hounds, yet the air of mystery around the published accounts warrant some surmises.
Stoneman has made a raid in rear of Johnson and destroyed an immense amount of Supplies, Railroads and R.R. bridges, this is unpublished news, came by Wilkes. The foregoing you can take for what tis worth I cant vouch [[for its correctness?]] [[lost: rest of final line]]
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-123. No clear signature survives at the clipped bottom. This is a chain of reported information through Wilkes and Warren, expressly qualified by George. The described terms and claimed forty-day armistice have not been presented as verified historical facts. Johnston/Johnson spellings are retained as they occur.

pages.family_title: Rumors that the war is over—and George’s explicit caution
pages.family_text:
Now for the news. Rumors are numerous and varied. At least this seems clear: Johnston has surrendered, or is so close that he cannot avoid it. You may know as much of the details as I do.
Behind the scenes, there have been rumors of unpublished news. Flake of the Bulletin admitted as much. I have heard a little: Colonel Wilkes has arrived on parole from New Orleans. According to him, Sherman and Johnston agreed that Johnston would surrender Confederate forces everywhere, place their weapons in state arsenals, disband the troops, and send them home. State governments, laws, and officers would remain, but renounce the Confederacy, renew allegiance to the United States, and return to the Union. He says a forty-day armistice was arranged to consult the Washington cabinet, which rejected the proposal because it recognized state governments. He also reports that Grant would support Sherman with his army, treating the agreement as a military surrender approved by Breckenridge and Davis. That is the story, if my information is correct.
Warren told me this, and he is not one to jump to such a conclusion. He believes the war is over and the news is being withheld until official orders tell this department to give up and go home, allowing the change to happen quietly. If this is not premature, a couple of months will finish the drama. Much may be getting ahead of the facts, but the mystery around the published accounts encourages speculation.
Wilkes also brings unpublished news that Stoneman raided Johnson’s rear and destroyed immense quantities of supplies, railroads, and bridges. Take all this for what it is worth: I cannot vouch [[for its correctness; the last line is partly lost]].

pages.title: February 26, 1865: sore eyes, spring weather, and Confederate money
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie Houston Feby 26th 1865
Your last of 11th inst came to hand a day or two ago. Glad to hear that you were well of the Sore eyes [[for?]] the little experience which I have had with them has abundantly proved to me that they are unpleasant in the highest degree, fortunately however I have been but very little bothered with them so far.
The past week has been very fair and very foul, Some days it rained and [[some?]] it never though all in all quite a quantity has [[fallen?]] during the past week. Friday and friday night it rained [[very?]] hard. Though Saturday was a pretty day and to day the [[mud?]] has dried very fast. Spring has opened I think [[in?]] this latitude, Some few cold days will come yet but [[none?]] to do any harm I predict.
Prices current this [[week?]] a little higher than last. Confederate Money has [[risen?]] to 25, and not a great deal in circulation. There Seems to be a determination to reduce the circulation [[of?]] it Somehow though Something extraordinary will be [[accomplished?]] if it ever becomes good again, and I think [[nothing?]] will ever make it good but an uncompromising [[tyranny?]] carried on under the immediate Supervision of [[the?]] Military, and plenty of that will be Served up during [[the?]] ensuing year in all kinds of Style to Suit Vendors,
pages.editorial_notes: Continues on 09-126–128. The supplied reproduction clips many line beginnings; reconstructed words are bracketed. The currency figure “25” has no explicit exchange basis. No modern medical diagnosis is assigned to “Sore eyes.”

pages.family_title: February 26, 1865: sore eyes, spring weather, and Confederate money
pages.family_text:
Houston, February 26, 1865. Sister Lizzie,
Your letter of the 11th arrived a day or two ago. I am glad your sore eyes have recovered. My own limited experience shows how unpleasant they are, though fortunately they have troubled me little so far.
The past week brought both fair and foul weather, with considerable rain overall. Friday and Friday night were very wet, but Saturday was fine and the mud is drying quickly today. I think spring has begun here. There may be a few cold days yet, but I expect none severe enough to cause harm.
Prices are slightly higher than last week. Confederate money has risen to “25” [[the exchange basis is unstated]], with little circulating. There seems to be an effort to reduce its circulation. Restoring its value would be an extraordinary achievement. I think only uncompromising [[tyranny?]] under military supervision could make it good again—and we will get plenty of that in the coming year, in every form to suit those providing it.

pages.title: George mocks appeals to “military necessity” and unlimited sacrifice
pages.text:
War news this week is very meagre. No fighting going on which has amounted to anything of importance reported, Since peace prospects were broken off. But very little truth ever escapes these latter days I opine owing to the precarious condition of Confed affairs east of the Mississippi. There is a good deal of “Freedom of Conscience” and “Speech” and “Press” I presume [[under?]] the present regime of Military [[Despotism?]], I presume [[it?]] is under and a long ways under, So far under that it will never get out. “So mote it be.” There is always a way to patch up broken places and tis really amusing to see the manner in which States rights are patched, & all other Strongholds [[of?]] Liberty. All are justified under the plea of “Military Necessity” and he is not a “patriot” who growls at anything done by the Government when the ultimate object is Laudable.
All means are expedient just and proper and even Laudable [[when?]] one iota of good can be accomplished. It is nothing [[more?]] than the part of a “Good Patriot” to Surrender all he [[has?]] in property produce and Personal Liberty to the Govt [[for?]] “the time being” to accomplish the “Glorious End” of “[[Southern?]] Independence.” It is better to Sacrifice the “Last [[woman?]] & Child” on the “Altar of Liberty” than to Submit [[to?]] Yankee rule! Anihilation is preferable to “Such Slavery.” [[And?]] he is a coward and a knave who will not do all for his [[country?]]. Such is the Spirit of the Fire Eating press of to day
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-125. The left edge clips several words. This passage is sustained sarcasm criticizing the “Fire Eating press”; the extreme demands are not George’s recommendations. Tentative “Despotism” is partly overwritten. Quotation marks in the source are retained.

pages.family_title: George mocks appeals to “military necessity” and unlimited sacrifice
pages.family_text:
There is little war news this week. Since peace prospects collapsed, no important fighting has been reported. Very little truth gets out nowadays, probably because Confederate affairs east of the Mississippi are so precarious.
We supposedly have freedom of conscience, speech, and the press under military [[despotism?]]. They are certainly “under” it—buried so deeply that they may never get out. So be it! It is amusing to watch states’ rights and every other defense of liberty patched up and excused as “military necessity.” Anyone who complains about government action is called unpatriotic whenever its final purpose is said to be worthy.
By that reasoning, any means become proper, just, and even praiseworthy if they accomplish the smallest good. A “good patriot” must surrender property, produce, and personal freedom to the government “for the time being” to achieve the “glorious end” of Southern independence. The last [[woman?]] and child must be sacrificed on liberty’s altar rather than accept Yankee rule; annihilation is supposedly preferable to such “slavery.” Anyone who will not give everything is called a coward and a scoundrel. That is the spirit of today’s fire-eating press.
pages.family_note: George is criticizing these arguments through irony; the extreme language is not an instruction or endorsement.

pages.title: The loudest war advocates—and an unkind assessment of city fashions
pages.text:
Brave Editors behind desks, and brave legislators in Congress brave old men in chimney corners Smoking pipes and brave boys under the Conscript age can talk about what “Well do” with the Yankees how long “Well fight” and all this Sort of thing. Men who never smelled burnt powder and never will, will fight longer than any body else, and those who talks most of fighting are the very ones that never do any of it. Some of the Stump Speaking, fire eating, patriots, who at the beginning of this war Said that they would Spill the “last drop of blood” told an unconscious truth, they will be the last to Spill a drop of “blood.”
I went to the M. E. Church to day, house was full of Soldiers Citizens and Ladies. There Seems to me to be more ugly Women in this City than any place I was ever at. As long as I have been here I do not remember of having Seen a handsome one yet. They always Spoil their looks with Superfluous clothing Some fancy touch Somewhere or everywhere reveals a [[soft?]] place in the “Phrenological Regions.” There is [[too?]] much of the Spirit of Novelty among them to Suit me, [[Vanity?]] in other words, a morbid desire to display Something [[new?]] that will attract attention, reminding of Burns
“O wad Some power the giftie gie us”
“To See oursels as ithers See us”
“’Twad from many a blunder free us, An foolish notion”
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-125–126. Left edge clips a few words in the lower passage. The disparaging statements about women are preserved as the writer’s opinion. His quotation attributed to Burns is transcribed in the wording visible here, not corrected from an outside edition. “M. E.” is expanded as Methodist Episcopal in the family reading.

pages.family_title: The loudest war advocates—and an unkind assessment of city fashions
pages.family_text:
Brave editors behind desks, brave legislators in Congress, brave old men smoking by the fireplace, and brave boys too young for conscription can talk about what “we’ll do” to the Yankees and how long “we’ll fight.” Men who have never smelled gunpowder and never will are ready to fight longer than anyone else. Those who talk most about fighting do none of it. Some patriotic firebrands who promised to spill the “last drop of blood” unknowingly spoke the truth: they will be the last to spill any blood.
I went to the Methodist Episcopal church today. It was full of soldiers, civilians, and women. To me, this city seems to have more unattractive women than anywhere I have been. I cannot remember seeing a handsome one here. They spoil their appearance with excessive clothing and fashionable touches that suggest a [[soft?]] spot in the brain. Their love of novelty—or vanity—and desire to display something new and attract attention do not suit me. It reminds me of Burns: if some power gave us the gift of seeing ourselves as others see us, it would spare us many a blunder and foolish notion.

pages.title: Children playing bring George’s childhood to mind
pages.text:
6h P.M. This Evening I took a Stroll through the western part of the city which presented quite an interesting picture when compared with the business portion. Everything was quiet and in Sunday attire. Some were Strolling the Streets enjoying the balmy Spring air and pleasant Sunshine but by far the greater portion were grouped in their handsome parlors passing the time, apparently, pleasantly enough.
Pleasant Cottages and their homelike associations are pleasant to look at even if they cannot be [[deleted: illegible]] enjoyed at the present by me. Groups of merry children playing on sunny slopes and in grassy yards reminded me of days past but fondly recollected. Scenes which cannot recur but can always be held freshly in the Memory when types of them are presented to the view, and nothing can bring back to mind the Scenes of the past as quick as groups of gay children.
The Church bell is ringing and I will attend So will close this and mail as it will go up tomorrow. I do not remember Miss Luna or Kate [[Denny?]] but Miss Lizzie K. I do. Tell the girls to “go it while they are young” for when they get old may be they Cant. With Best love to all I am as ever your Brother George
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-125–128, February 26, 1865. The surname after Kate is tentative. “Gay” has its period sense of cheerful. No childhood location is identified in this recollection.

pages.family_title: Children playing bring George’s childhood to mind
pages.family_text:
6 p.m. This evening I walked through the western part of the city. Compared with the business district, it made an interesting picture. Everything was quiet, with people in their Sunday clothes. Some walked in the mild spring air and sunshine, but most sat together in their attractive parlors, apparently enjoying themselves.
Comfortable cottages and their associations with home are pleasant to see, even if I cannot enjoy them myself now. Merry children playing on sunny slopes and grassy lawns reminded me of fondly remembered days. Those scenes cannot return, but similar sights keep them fresh in memory. Nothing recalls the past as quickly as a group of happy children.
The church bell is ringing, and I intend to go. I will finish and mail this so it can leave tomorrow. I do not remember Miss Luna or Kate [[Denny?]], but I do remember Miss Lizzie K. Tell the girls to enjoy themselves while they are young; when they are old, perhaps they cannot.
With love to all, your brother, George.

pages.title: Houston, December 11, 1864: yellow fever and church music
pages.text:
Sister Lizzie Houston Dec 11th 1864
Your letter of 19th ult has been Recd. Found all present well in body and mind So far as I am capable of judging. During the past week we have had plenty of cool and Some cold weather. Sufficient I think unless the weather turns [[illegible: fold]] again to clear the city of yellow fever. There has been a good deal of it here lately but confined exclusively to citizens houses. No cases have occurred among those who have returned Since the freeze of 20th Nov except Such as occupied houses where it had been during the Summer. I feel no apprehensions of it breaking out among the troops as we are quartered in houses where none has been this Season.
I attended church this morning at the Methodist Church, Speaker and Sermon were neither extra and congregation Small for a city. Up in one corner was an Organ from which music was pumped for the occasion. A big Negro worked the handle, while a Lady fingered the keys Scientifically.
pages.editorial_notes: Letter continues through 09-134. Dark fold obscures words about a change in the weather. George’s belief that cold weather and prior house occupancy governed yellow fever risk is recorded as a historical belief, not a medical explanation. The organ attendant’s race is stated; his name and legal status are not.

pages.family_text:
Houston, December 11, 1864. Sister Lizzie,
Your letter of November 19 has arrived. It found everyone well in body and mind, as far as I can judge. We have had plenty of cool and some cold weather this week. I think it is enough to clear the city of yellow fever unless the weather changes again [[part of the phrase is obscured]].
There has been much fever lately, confined to civilians’ houses. Among people returning since the November 20 freeze, cases have occurred only in houses where it had been during summer. I am not afraid of an outbreak among the troops, since we occupy houses without cases this season.
This morning I attended the Methodist church. Neither preacher nor sermon was exceptional, and the congregation was small for a city. An organ stood in one corner. A large Black man worked its pumping handle while a woman skillfully played the keys.
pages.family_note: The account preserves George’s understanding of yellow fever at the time; it is not a modern explanation of transmission.

pages.title: George compares Methodist and Episcopal worship
pages.text:
Music is as much out of place in church as a dog in a parlor, I felt like I was at preaching untill the the organ began [[moaning?]] then I felt as though I was at a party. I dont See where people get the doctrine of Music in churches, tis not in the Testament as I can find, if it is it is in Some unnoticed corner where my perceptions has never reached.
Last Sunday I went to hear the Episcopal. They have quite a large brick church built on the Catholic plan of Gothic Architecture Superb and magnificent. The Parson came out of a closet in one corner with a robe on Catholic fashion, knelt by a desk a moment in Secret prayer where every body could See him; then began the Service. The Worship is read part by the preacher and members, he reading one verse aloud and all of them the next, in prayer he repeats a sentence and then the members all repeat it audibly after him. They Sing Psalms in stead of hymns which Sounded Very well, being diversified a little in the tune yet in perfect harmony. After Service followed the Catechism of the youthful members to See what progress they were making towards full membership; the repeating of the Creed &c, the Creed is identical with that of the presbyterians. [[illegible: words obscured by fold]] very good if they follow what they preach.
Each Child is baptized in infancy, and two persons Standing by act as “Sponsors” Pledging themselves, in case the childs parents die or any other accidents happen that will render them incapable of taking care of the child, to take and raise or See that the child is raised in a proper and religious Manner. There is a great deal of form and Ceremony about their Worship resembling the Catholics a good deal. Preaching is tolerably plain, but there is so much fashion and Show about it that I dont much like it.
I am pretty much the Same opinion as “Fanny Fern” on these matters; “True religion may go to Church in yellow gloves

Accounts of denominational practice are the writer’s understanding, not editorially verified doctrine. A quotation he attributes to Fanny Fern begins at the bottom and continues on the next scan.

pages.family_title: George compares Methodist and Episcopal worship
pages.family_text:
To me, instrumental music is as out of place in church as a dog in a parlor. I felt I was at a sermon until the organ began; then it seemed like a party. I cannot find support in the New Testament for music in churches—unless it hides in some corner I have overlooked.
Last Sunday I attended the Episcopal church. It is a large, magnificent brick building in Gothic style, which I associate with Catholic churches. The minister emerged from a side room in a robe, knelt for private prayer where everyone could see him, and began the service. Minister and congregation alternated reading verses aloud, and the congregation repeated his prayer sentences. They sang psalms instead of hymns. These sounded very good, with some variation in tune but perfect harmony.
Afterward the younger members were questioned on the catechism to assess their progress toward full membership, including reciting the creed. I consider the creed identical to the Presbyterians’ [[the next words are obscured]], and very good if they practice what they preach.
Infants are baptized with two sponsors who promise to raise them, or ensure they are properly and religiously raised, if their parents die or cannot care for them. There is much ceremony, resembling Catholic worship. The preaching is fairly plain, but I dislike the fashion and display around it.
I largely agree with Fanny Fern: “True religion may go to Church in yellow gloves—”

pages.title: Wealth, religious display, and George’s preference for modest dress
pages.text:
and embroidered handkerchiefs, worth five hundred dollars but I dont believe it!” Though I do not know as I have any right to so judge the people of Houston because they are wealthy.
I have noticed Several new Style Ladies Hats on the Street. The Kind I like best is high crowned narrow brimmed leghorn hats which does Some better I think than the old fashioned broad brims that used to [[deleted: illegible]] about So Conspicuously on the prairies. In my humble opinion however the old fashioned close Split bonnetts [[deleted: illegible]] the handsomest articles that ever a woman wore on her head. You may call that old fashioned and out of date in this day of Splash and dash when brilliants are all the [[rage?]], but it is modest, and that is the nicest quality which ever adorned a woman no matter what the world and the balance of mankind may Say to the contrary. above all things be modest.
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-130. Opening completes the quotation attributed by George to Fanny Fern; its wording is not corrected from an external text. “Close Split bonnetts” is retained as read, without silently substituting a fabric or garment name. The social judgments are the writer’s.

You may call that outdated in an age of showy display, when brilliance is all the [[rage?]]. But it is modest, and I consider modesty a woman’s finest quality, whatever the world says. Above all, be modest.

pages.title: Auctions, flour supplies, and Sherman’s move into Georgia
pages.text:
Sunday night 11th — 7 Oclock. By candle light I resume to give a few more ideas in my usual disconnected Style of composition and flit. The boys are going to preaching to the Methodist Church So I will be alone, too cold for me to go without they would let music alone and have preaching instead of fun.
There are auctions almost every day in town, dry goods of almost every description at very high prices though coming down a little, the figures are a little under what I wrote last. Flour is plenty in town by the wholesale or retail in lots to Suit purchasers. When asked where it all comes from the answer is invariably “Up the Country.” I have not heard of a great deal being Sold in that Country to Citizens, thought the Govt took all for the army &c &c.
The latest news is Some little Stirring. Sherman has made a bold move into Ga much to the astonishment of all thereby creating a great Stir in military Circles. For once he outgeneralled Hood and all his advisers, [[lost: final words clipped]]
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of the December 11, 1864 letter. Bottom of the source reproduction clips the last line. The writer contrasts flour for sale with his impression that the government had requisitioned it. This is not evidence of a specific theft or diversion.

pages.family_title: Auctions, flour supplies, and Sherman’s move into Georgia
pages.family_text:
Sunday, December 11, 7 p.m. I am writing by candlelight again, adding a few thoughts in my usual disconnected way. The boys are going to the Methodist church, leaving me alone. It is too cold for me to go unless they abandon the music and provide preaching instead of entertainment.
There are auctions almost daily, offering nearly every kind of dry goods at very high, though slightly falling, prices. Flour is plentiful wholesale and retail, in quantities to suit buyers. Asked where it comes from, people always say “up the country.” I have not heard of much being sold to civilians there; I thought the government took it all for the army.
The latest news is somewhat stirring. Sherman has made a bold move into Georgia, surprising everyone and causing excitement in military circles. For once, he has outmaneuvered Hood and all his advisers. [[The final words are clipped.]]

pages.title: Guarded soldiers’ opinions, private gossip, and expected emancipation
pages.text:
It is a mistake about Magruder being ordered back to Texas. It is Strange how men who ought to know Start and credit Such reports. Walker will still continue to Command here and furloughs will continue to jog along as usual. Spaight is doing his best to get all details ordered in, if all were present the Regt would number nearly one thousand. This is now about the largest Regt in the State.
There is Somewhere in the neighborhood of a dozen home on leave from this Co now. Only one has thought enough of the fair to marry so far. If accounts be true Eddings, and old “bach” married a widow in [[Stewart?]] a few days ago, he has not yet returned to Camps.
You were a little mistaken on Shialot on the war question, Soldiers generally profess more patriotism than they actually feel for they dont know what Kind of people they are dealing with, and always make sure to be on the Safe Side whether they are or not.
On the Subject of Matrimony I confess I was no little astonished, though I am in the habit of doing things by fits and starts, but this Start Stumped me. I was not aware that She had ever done any thing disreputable. True I learned Henry had denounced his intentions but I thought this was merely a lovers or Something of that Sort. What else I learned merely Settled an opinion I long ago had formed, Viz; Lack of moral Courage and Self resolution. I positively know now nothing more than I knew three years ago, of what may or may not have happened Since I left home or even in the Service rather, I am totally ignorant; nor can I Say I care to know. So here the Subject must drop. [[He?]] had better let marrying alone and go to Mexico and get out of troublous times. The negro is bound to be freed before this war ends, and Jeff Wont give it up as long as he can get a white man or negro to fight for him. “Mr Southern is Some by himself.”
pages.editorial_notes: Continuation of 09-132. “Shialot” is the literal place/name reading; no identification is certain. Location of Eddings’s marriage and a pronoun near the bottom are tentative. The private discussion does not name the woman and George expressly disclaims knowledge; no allegation is treated as established fact. His expectation of emancipation is a prediction written in December 1864.

pages.family_title: Guarded soldiers’ opinions, private gossip, and expected emancipation
pages.family_text:
The report that Magruder was ordered back to Texas is wrong. It is strange how people who should know better start and believe such rumors. Walker will remain in command, and furloughs will continue as usual. Spaight is trying to recall everyone on detached duty. With all present, the regiment would number nearly a thousand, making it about the largest in the state.
About a dozen men from our company are home on leave. Only one has married so far: according to reports, the old bachelor Eddings married a widow in [[Stewart?]] a few days ago. He has not returned.
You were somewhat mistaken at “Shialot” about the war question. Soldiers generally profess more patriotism than they feel because they do not know whom they are dealing with and prefer to be safe.
As for the marriage matter, I was very surprised. Although I often act by fits and starts, this one stumped me. I did not know that she had done anything disreputable. I heard Henry had renounced his intentions, but thought it was a lovers’ matter. What else I heard only confirmed an old opinion about a lack of moral courage and resolve. I know no more than I knew three years ago about what has happened since I left home or entered service, and I do not care to know. Let the subject drop. [[He?]] had better forget marriage and go to Mexico to escape these troubled times.
Black people are bound to be freed before the war ends, and Jeff will not give up while he can get a white or Black man to fight for him. “Mr. Southern is something by himself.”

pages.title: Blockade running, conscription, and a cold room
pages.text:
There is a Schooner at the landing on the bayou, just in from Tampico laden with merchandise. It belongs to [[Reichman?]] and Myers of this city.
Quite a number keep out of the Service along the coast by blockade running, though they do not run on them themselves. A few men are around gathering conscripts and forwarding them to the front, they had better be gathering up loose & useless officers and putting them where they belong instead of bothering honest men.
As it is late and cold having no fire in our room I will Close. I have to take this to the P.O tonight So it will get off in the morning to Millican.
With best love to all
I remain Your brother
Geo Douglas.
pages.editorial_notes: Conclusion of 09-129–133, dated December 11, 1864. First merchant’s name is tentative. Claims about avoiding military service are the writer’s opinion, not a verified finding concerning every merchant or shipowner named.

pages.family_title: Blockade running, conscription, and a cold room
pages.family_text:
A schooner has just reached the bayou landing from Tampico with merchandise. It belongs to [[Reichman?]] and Myers of this city.
Many people along the coast avoid service through blockade running, though they do not sail on the vessels themselves. A few men are gathering conscripts and sending them to the front. They should instead collect idle, useless officers and put them where they belong, rather than trouble honest men.
It is late and cold, and our room has no fire, so I will close. I must take this to the post office tonight so it can leave for Millican in the morning.
With love to all, your brother, George Douglas.

This two-page draft is too faint and heavily revised for a reliable continuous modern version.

pages.family_title: Verse on death, memory, and the generations that follow
pages.family_text:
The first manuscript page of this spread is largely unreadable. It mentions hills, wreaths of flowers, midnight, and thoughts of things that might have been.

The facing page is more readable. These scenes and thoughts awaken us, and we forget the Indigenous person’s grave and the white person’s tomb. They lived and loved, knew joys and follies, yet death broke the cherished bonds that held them to life. The draft then speaks of idle mourning over their revered remains and of desecrating tombs raised by affection to honor and guard the dead. Part of the revised wording remains unclear.

Soon we will pass away, leaving [[unreadable wording]] behind to tell what we were: a single trace. Like fragile spider silk carried by the wind, we will go, and no one may ever mark where we fall. pages.family_title: “We are growing old together Jim”
pages.family_text:
We are growing old together, Jim.
The years come swiftly on.
Our hair is growing gray and thin;
The days of our youth are gone.
Some thirty years have taken flight
Since you and I were born.
We have gathered flowers, fair and bright,
And felt the piercing thorn.
Where is our gentle [[Mary?]] now,
Who accepted our early [[pledge?]]?
What sorrows [[might she know?]]?
What cares may surround us both?
Perhaps beside a rippling stream,
Where murmuring waters flow,
They live a [[peaceful?]] life
That we may never know.
On the facing page:
[[The opening line is unclear.]]
With all our boyhood’s games,
The bat and ball—but never mind,
Their names are not forgotten.
The sunny scenes of long ago
Are hidden by clouds and gloom,
And many a winter’s icy [[blast?]]
Has nipped the summer’s bloom.
We cannot follow where they have gone;
Our paths have separated widely.
But in the Great Beyond
Nothing can divide us.
The final stanza recalls former companions and says that some have fallen and some sleep, but several words are too faint to read.
pages.family_note: This is a modern reading of an unsigned poem, retaining uncertain passages. It is not assumed to describe George’s own life or a relative named Jim. See 10-023 for the ending.

pages.family_title: A poem of bereavement beside property calculations
pages.family_text:
The poem recalls friends of the speaker’s youth, pale figures beckoning toward the shore of death, and a mound beneath a weeping willow. Its clearer closing lines say that the [[darling?]] of the speaker’s heart is sleeping there and call on the death angel to “gather me there to sleep as well.” The beginning and some connecting lines are unreadable.
The facing page contains property notes: [[wagons?]] 100, [[buggy?]] 35, and faint entries for [[a horse?]] and [[mules?]]. Figures include 51235, 148, 36435, 18217, 2275, [[175?]].
A lower list reads 300 horses, 74 hogs, 120 cattle, and 40 followed by unclear wording; further entries are faint. A calculation includes 510, 148, 362, and half of 362 shown as 181. Nearby figures include 142, 71, 120, 73, and [[58095?]].
pages.family_note: The poem expresses bereavement but does not identify the deceased. Inventory figures must not be treated as animal counts without further evidence. A clearer related version of Bachelor’s Lament is at 10-047. It helps explain the poem but is not an exact replacement for this draft.

pages.title: “Parody”: a rose offered in friendship, April 1868
pages.text:
154
Parody.

’Tis the first rose of Summer
Fresh blooming and fair
Which sheds its sweet fragrance
Upon the soft air;
Oh! how sweetly it blushes
Like a young maiden’s cheek
When emotions are burning
The lip cannot speak.

I’ll not leave thee, thou fair one
To bloom on the stem,
But will gather thee gently
The days sweetest gem;
While the dewdrop yet lingers
Upon thy bright leaves;
As the tear on the lashes
When th’heart fondly grieves.

And soon will I give thee
In Friendship’s true name
To one who will prize thee
Through life still the same;
True hearts ne’er are withered
Tho’ Youth’s bloom be gone
And that Love is immutable
Where Friendship first shone.

April 1868.

pages.family_text:
The first rose of summer,
fresh, blooming, and beautiful,
sends its sweet fragrance
into the gentle air.
How sweetly it blushes,
like a young woman’s cheek
when she feels emotions
her lips cannot express.

I will not leave you, beautiful rose,
to bloom on your stem.
I will gather you gently,
the day’s sweetest jewel,
while the dewdrop still rests
on your bright leaves,
like a tear on the eyelashes
when a loving heart grieves.

Soon I will give you
as a token of true friendship
to someone who will value you
with the same affection throughout life.
True hearts never wither,
even when youth’s beauty has gone;
love remains unchanged
where friendship first appeared.

April 1868.

pages.title: “To Emma,” of Zephyrus Bower
pages.text:
153
To Emma.
Of Zephyrus Bower,—By “Moore” the second.

Part First.
Awake my sweet Lyre
To Love I aspire
Pure as the desire
Of Angels above
Hopes which I cherish
Never let perish
And cast a dark gloom
O’er Fancy’s first bloom
But live forever
And flow as a river
A torrent of Love.
Then welcome the hour
It finds Emma’s bower
Where by thy sweet power
I’m carried along;
The Muses around
Enchant The fair ground
With Music’s sweet sound
A heavenly Song.
Then joy so complete
While at Emma’s feet
I softly repeat
And for each word vouch
That fondly I love her
By all that’s above her
And will till times over
My dear Emma Couch.

Part Second
Awake my sweet Lyre
Affections desire
A heavenly fire
Courses my veins
Oh! let thy sweet sound
Come floating around
With gentle rebound
In melodious strains;
For Emma divine
Will never be mine
Unless I can shine
By Poesy’s power.
For no other score
Will I go before
A second “Tom Moore”
To zephyrus bower,
But that me will raise
I fondly surmise
And in Emma’s eyes
Perhaps may succeed
Then Life will be bright
And joyous and light,
And in young Love’s sight
Elysium indeed.

Part Third.
Awake my sweet Lyre
You know my desire;
Oh! now go and fire
Another young heart
Thus you will prove
That you can wake Love
In Bower or Grove
Wherever you start.
Let Love’s sweetest Song
Thy cadence prolong
While moving along
That verdant bower
Whose perfumes shaken
Emma will waken
[[separate block: final two lines in the right margin]]
To live the peerless
Maid of thy bower.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 153, in two columns. Part Second runs from the bottom of the left column to the top of the right; Part Third ends in two rotated margin lines. “Moore” the second and “Tom Moore” are the poem’s own descriptions, not a verified attribution. “times over” is reproduced as written. The text names Emma Couch, but neither her identity nor a historical relationship is established here.

pages.family_title: “To Emma,” of Zephyrus Bower
pages.family_text:
To Emma, of Zephyrus Bower, by “Moore” the second.

Part One
Wake, my sweet lyre.
I long for love
as pure as the desires
of angels in heaven.
May the hopes I cherish
never die
and cast a dark shadow
over imagination’s first flowering.
May they live forever,
flowing like a river,
a torrent of love.
Welcome the hour
when it reaches Emma’s garden retreat,
where your sweet power
carries me along.
The Muses all around
enchant the beautiful place
with music’s sweet sound,
a heavenly song.
My happiness is complete
as, at Emma’s feet,
I softly say,
and swear to every word,
that I love her dearly—
by everything above her—
and will until time is over:
my dear Emma Couch.

Part Two
Wake, my sweet lyre.
Affection’s longing,
a heavenly fire,
runs through my veins.
Let your sweet sound
float all around,
echoing gently
in melodious music.
For wonderful Emma
will never be mine
unless I can shine
through poetry’s power.
For no other reason
will I present myself
as a second “Tom Moore”
at Zephyrus Bower.
But I fondly imagine
that poetry will raise me up,
and perhaps I may succeed
in Emma’s eyes.
Then life will be bright,
joyful and light;
and to young love
it will truly be paradise.

Part Three
Wake, my sweet lyre.
You know what I want.
Go now and kindle love
in another young heart.
Then you will prove
that you can awaken love
in a garden retreat or a grove,
wherever you begin.
Let love’s sweetest song
prolong your music
as it moves through
that leafy retreat.
Its stirred perfumes
will awaken Emma
to live as the unrivaled
maiden of your garden.
pages.family_note: “Lyre” is the poet’s instrument and a figure for poetry; “bower” is a leafy retreat; “Elysium” means a paradise. The romantic voice is not treated as proof of an actual courtship.

pages.title: “Bachelor’s Lament,” July 1875
pages.text:
Bachelor’s Lament.
July 1875

O! where is the hope of the vine covered cottage
The visions of Youth will so oft conjure up
Forever ’tis gone, and now gray in my dotage
I’ve drained to the dregs Life’s bitterest cup.
And where is the dear One I’ve loved with devotion
Thro’ life’s changeful scenes of unhallowed commotion
With ever the same constant and changeless emotion
Beloved at the first and beloved to the close.

No answer comes back from my voiceless surroundings
For silence and gloom are my comrades alway,
I’m sad as if sunk ’neath the Sea’s deepest Soundings
Where the [[deleted: uncoffined dead]] [[inserted: dead of the past]] lie mould’ring away,
O! when will this cease here, this dread desolation
Which binds my soul down in its deep tribulation
And is there no season of calm consolation
No morning unfolding again as the rose?

Alone now I wander on life’s rugged byways
The friends of my Youth I may never greet more
For many have fallen on far distant highways
And beckon me on to the Stygian shore;
And ’neath yon low mound where the willow stands weeping
My heart’s only darling forever is sleeping
O! may the Death Angel make haste with his reaping
And gather me there to a dreamless repose!

Forever shall cease then those ties that are breaking
And sweetly I’ll rest in the calm of the tomb.
No storms can assail ’till the morn of awaking
Shall beckon the dead back to joy or gloom—
Around me shall linger no omen of danger
Which compassed my way while a sad lonely ranger
To all save a Peace—deep and dreamless a Stranger
There calmly I’ll rest from my life’s gloomy woes.
pages.editorial_notes: A clearer version of passages also present in the faint notebook drafts at 10-021 and 10-026. The interlinear revision in stanza two is shown explicitly. No signature is visible. The poem’s references to aging, a lost beloved, and death are literary statements; they do not by themselves establish the author’s age, marital status, or a named person’s death.

pages.family_title: “Bachelor’s Lament,” July 1875
pages.family_text:
Oh, where is the hope of a vine-covered cottage,
the dream that youth so often calls to mind?
It has gone forever; now, gray and grown old,
I have drunk life’s bitterest cup to its last drop.
Where is the dear one I have loved devotedly
through life’s changing scenes of troubled turmoil,
with the same constant, unchanging feeling,
loved at the beginning and loved to the end?

No answer comes from my silent surroundings.
Silence and gloom are always my companions.
I am as sad as if I had sunk to the ocean’s greatest depths,
where the dead of the past lie decaying.
When will this dreadful desolation end,
this suffering that holds my soul down?
Will there be no time of peaceful comfort,
no morning opening again like a rose?

Now I wander alone along life’s rough paths.
I may never again greet the friends of my youth.
Many have fallen on faraway roads
and beckon me toward the shore of death.
Beneath that low mound, where the willow weeps,
my heart’s only darling sleeps forever.
May the Angel of Death hurry with his harvest
and gather me there to dreamless rest!

Then those breaking bonds will cease forever,
and I will rest sweetly in the grave’s calm.
No storms can reach me until the morning of resurrection
calls the dead back to joy or sorrow.
No sign of danger will linger around me,
as it did when I wandered sadly and alone.
A stranger to everything except deep, dreamless peace,
I will rest quietly from the sorrows of my life.
pages.family_note: The Stygian shore is a classical image of the world of the dead. This modern-language reading follows the revised wording in stanza two. Compare the earlier notebook drafts at 10-021 and 10-026; they are separate versions, not evidence that every faint word is now resolved.

pages.title: “To Victoria,” concluding stanzas, July 1875
pages.text:
75
Thus Inez to me was the dross in the gold
The Midnight’s dead shade o’er the hope of the soul
The glowworm’s cold light where poison vines weep
Their death dealing dews in the dark forest deep.

But back thro’ the lapse of the shadowy years
My Ida’s sweet smile ever changeless appears
Ere the tempter invaded my Eden of Bliss
And destroyed my sweet flower, leaving me this.

July 1875.

pages.title: “To Victoria”: welcome to Brushy
pages.text:
74
To Victoria.

Welcome Victoria! to Brushy’s green slopes
The Cradle and Grave of my Bachelor hopes
Here they opened and flourished and fell in decay
As flowers nipt by a frost in the genial May.

But why should I trouble you with Sorrows of Mine!
For thousands have felt them, and thousands repine
But may the kind Angel who is guarding thy way
Protect you from them wherever you Stray.

Thrice happy the hours since to Brushy you came
For enjoyments exist now which were only a name;
And sweeter than roses the converse we hold
And the swift flying moments are brighter than gold.

I speak not of Love, that fountain is dry
Deception and Falsehood have quenched its supply
Experience has taught me, the daughters of Eve
The fairest the brightest were born to deceive.

Sweet Ida was fickle, but still in my heart
Her image is graven and will never depart,
But Inez with falsehood has stained her young fame
And the curse of a Douglas now rests on her name.

Tell me why should the truthful one sympathy hold
For that glittering dross which alloys the gold
Or what what concord has night with the morn of the day
The glow worms cold glare with the sun’s gentle ray.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 74. Continued at 10-048 (manuscript page 75), where the poem is dated July 1875. The repeated “what what” is retained. “A Douglas” appears in the poem, but it is not an author’s signature. Brushy is not assigned to a specific modern location here. The accusations about Ida, Inez, and women generally are the speaker’s rhetoric, not independently verified statements.

pages.family_title: “To Victoria”: welcome to Brushy
pages.family_text:
Welcome, Victoria, to Brushy’s green slopes,
where my bachelor hopes were born and buried.
Here they opened, flourished, and decayed,
like flowers struck by frost in a pleasant May.

But why should I trouble you with my sorrows?
Thousands have felt them, and thousands complain.
May the kind angel watching over your path
protect you from them wherever you go.

The hours have been wonderfully happy since you came to Brushy.
Pleasures that once existed only in name are real now.
Our conversations are sweeter than roses,
and the swiftly passing moments are brighter than gold.

I am not speaking of love: that spring has dried up.
Deception and falsehood have stopped its flow.
Experience has taught me that the daughters of Eve,
even the fairest and brightest, were born to deceive.

Sweet Ida was fickle, yet her image
is carved in my heart and will never leave.
But Inez has stained her young reputation with falsehood,
and a Douglas’s curse now rests on her name.

Tell me why an honest person should feel sympathy
for the glittering impurity mixed into gold.
What harmony is there between night and morning,
or between a glowworm’s cold light and the sun’s gentle ray?
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-048. The poem expresses bitterness as well as welcome. The speaker’s allegations and broad claims about women are preserved as literary content, without endorsement or genealogical inference.

pages.title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: remembered childhood landscapes
pages.text:
13
On the Banks of Brushy.

Fair Brushy! again beside thy winding stream
I rove again as in my childhood’s days
And with ardor dream again each early dream
Which once beguiled my young artless ways;
O’er them still my Memory fondly strays
Sweet treasures of the Past forever fled
And doomed to rot in dark Oblivion’s maze
Where all that’s pure and bright is tending fast
To mingle with Earth’s common clay at last.

Here first I heard the sky-lark’s warbling notes
As it high ascended from its dewy nest:
And here from a thousand other funny throats
I heard the tones which swelled each tender breast
Rising to Heaven as though they blest
The great Creator’s name with guileless heart
Who had all things in such beauty drest
And given them here fair Freedom’s part
Unstained by Man, with his dark wily art.

Here too I culled the lovely flowers which grew
In rich profusion on each verdant lawn
Adding their charms of every varied hue
Which could not be restored when they were gone
Then with listless steps I wandered on
To seek for others still more sweet
Until the approach of evening’s dawn
Homeward turned my wandering feet
From many a pleasant flower adorned retreat.

But ere from each pleasant landscape I withdrew
I culled from many a lone mossy glen
The lovely violets which in rich profusion grew
In every woodland brake and tangled fen—
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 13, continuing at 10-051 (page 14). “Funny throats” and “evening’s dawn” are retained as written. The speaker’s childhood landscape is called Brushy, but the poem alone does not securely identify either its author or the geographical location. The complete identified reading order is 10-050, 10-051, 10-060, 10-061, 10-052, 10-053 (manuscript pages 13–18).

pages.family_title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: remembered childhood landscapes
pages.family_text:
Beautiful Brushy! Once again I wander beside your winding stream,
as I did in childhood.
Eagerly I dream again the early dreams
that once delighted my innocent younger self.
My memory still wanders fondly over them,
sweet treasures of a past that has gone forever,
doomed to decay in the darkness of forgetting,
where everything pure and bright is quickly heading,
to mingle at last with the earth’s ordinary clay.

Here I first heard the skylark singing
as it rose high above its dew-covered nest.
Here, from a thousand other comical little throats,
I heard the songs swelling each tender breast,
rising to heaven as though, with innocent hearts,
they blessed the great Creator’s name:
he who clothed everything in such beauty
and gave them freedom here,
untouched by humanity’s dark and cunning ways.

Here too I gathered the lovely flowers
that grew abundantly on each green lawn,
adding the charm of their many colors—
beauty that could not be restored once the flowers were gone.
Then I wandered on with aimless steps
to find others sweeter still,
until the coming of evening
turned my wandering feet toward home,
away from many a pleasant, flower-filled retreat.

But before leaving each lovely landscape,
I gathered from many a lonely, mossy valley
the beautiful violets growing so abundantly
in woodland thickets and tangled marshes—

pages.title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: flower battles and youthful ambition
pages.text:
14
And naming each for earth’s illustrious men
And counting signal numbers for each side,
Vigorously began the mock battle—and when
The flowery fight was done—and all but one had died
O’er that Last victor my heart thrilled in boyish pride

To think that I like it would triumph over all
Who were arrayed against me as my foes
That I would thus witness the last one fall
Whom my right of sway would ever dare oppose.
And of my life victory and peace would be the close
Was the emblem which I saw in that flower
And did not note how soon it died with those
It had o’erthrown in battle’s stormy hour
Yielding with them all unto a mightier power.

But as those lovely flowers withering died
Together in one fragrant floral heap
So perished those early joys which were allied
Unto the future where broad Fancy’s sweep
Grasped the immortal and bade me keep
An erect brow through swiftly coming years
And clamber up Fame’s long wished steep
Whose shaggy brow in the dim future rears
Aloft above the rabble’s taunting jeers.

But still those early scenes in freshness bloom
Those brighter fancies of my childhood’s time
Shine from afar, though intervening gloom
And the wide distance gives them doubly the sublime
Of Beauty, Glory, and Grandeur, which in their prime
They wore unto my young enraptured eyes,
As the measured feet of impassioned rhyme
Lends dignity unto the writings of the wise
Which Clothed in Poetry more majestically rise.

pages.family_title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: flower battles and youthful ambition
pages.family_text:
I named each flower after one of the world’s famous men,
counted out the designated numbers for each side,
and eagerly began a pretend battle.
When the battle of flowers ended and all but one had died,
my heart thrilled with a boy’s pride in the last victor.

I imagined that, like that flower, I would defeat
all who stood against me as enemies.
I would see the last opponent fall
who dared challenge my right to rule.
My life would end in victory and peace:
that was the symbol I saw in the flower.
I failed to notice how soon it died beside
those it had defeated in its stormy battle,
all of them yielding to a greater power.

But as those lovely flowers withered and died
together in one fragrant heap,
so those early joys died—joys linked
to a future in which my sweeping imagination
grasped at immortality and urged me
to hold my head high through the coming years
and climb the long-desired heights of fame,
whose rugged summit rose in the distant future
above the crowd’s mocking jeers.

Still, those early scenes remain fresh.
The brighter dreams of childhood
shine from far away, through the darkness between us.
Their distance makes them seem twice as sublime
in beauty, glory, and grandeur as they appeared
to my young, delighted eyes—
just as the measured rhythms of passionate verse
lend dignity to wise writing,
making it more majestic when clothed in poetry.
pages.family_note: Continues 10-050. The next manuscript page is displaced in the PDF: continue at 10-060, then 10-061, 10-052, and 10-053.

paragraphs.text:
14
And naming each for earth’s illustrious men
And counting signal numbers for each side,
Vigorously began the mock battle—and when
The flowery fight was done—and all but one had died
O’er that Last victor my heart thrilled in boyish pride

To think that I like it would triumph over all
Who were arrayed against me as my foes
That I would thus witness the last one fall
Whom my right of sway would ever dare oppose.
And of my life victory and peace would be the close
Was the emblem which I saw in that flower
And did not note how soon it died with those
It had o’erthrown in battle’s stormy hour
Yielding with them all unto a mightier power.

But as those lovely flowers withering died
Together in one fragrant floral heap
So perished those early joys which were allied
Unto the future where broad Fancy’s sweep
Grasped the immortal and bade me keep
An erect brow through swiftly coming years
And clamber up Fame’s long wished steep
Whose shaggy brow in the dim future rears
Aloft above the rabble’s taunting jeers.

But still those early scenes in freshness bloom
Those brighter fancies of my childhood’s time
Shine from afar, though intervening gloom
And the wide distance gives them doubly the sublime
Of Beauty, Glory, and Grandeur, which in their prime
They wore unto my young enraptured eyes,
As the measured feet of impassioned rhyme
Lends dignity unto the writings of the wise
Which Clothed in Poetry more majestically rise.

pages.title: Childhood morning, school, and play: “On the Banks of Brushy” sequence
pages.text:
17
But once more the sun is in the glowing east,
Once more the day has come beautiful and bright,
Once more from Sweet Slumber’s bond released
All Nature hails the grand return of Light.
Once more unto my eager ravished sight
The dew drops sparkle brightly on a thousand flowers
From the pure crimson to the spotless white
Which richly glow in Nature’s vernal bowers
Adding sweetest perfumes to the returning hours.

The lowing herds wandering forth to crop the grass
O’er mead and hill in boundless pastures free
The soft tinkling bells upon them as they pass
Ringing on the morning air so merrily,
And in a thousand brakes the song birds cheerily
Hymning on High their Sweet discordant notes
All forming [[deleted: the sweetest]] [[inserted: a Sweeter]] chorus [[deleted: which]] [[inserted: than]] ever we
Have heard from any choirs of well trained throats
As it through the Soft air, gently heavenward floats

But the hour for School has come, we must along
With Satchel and basket, and beneath the teachers eye
Con our lessons over with a hum-drum Song
With many a furtive glance at the bright blue sky
And longing from the close School-room to fly
To the cooling Stream or groves deep vernal shade
Or o’er the flowery plain to chase the butterfly
Where thro’ the long hours of morning it has Strayed
Sipping the sweet from the flowers where it has played.

Hail glorious playtime! for awhile set free
With wild shouts we hail thee in the open air
Happy as any class of mortals well can be
Having to pleasure now our odd hour to spare,

pages.family_title: Childhood morning, school, and play: “On the Banks of Brushy” sequence
pages.family_text:
Once again the sun is in the glowing east,
and the day has arrived, beautiful and bright.
Released once more from sweet sleep,
all nature welcomes the great return of light.
Once again, before my eager, delighted eyes,
dewdrops sparkle on a thousand flowers,
from pure crimson to spotless white,
glowing richly in nature’s springtime retreats
and adding their sweetest perfumes to the returning hours.

The lowing herds wander out to graze
freely across meadows and hills in wide pastures.
Their softly tinkling bells ring merrily
on the morning air as they pass.
In a thousand thickets, songbirds cheerfully
sing their sweet, contrasting notes to heaven,
forming a sweeter chorus than any
we have heard from well-trained choirs,
as it floats gently heavenward through the soft air.

But school time has come; we must go
with satchels and baskets, and under the teacher’s eye
study our lessons in a monotonous chant,
stealing many glances at the bright blue sky.
We long to escape the confined schoolroom
for the cool stream or the grove’s deep springtime shade,
or to chase a butterfly across the flowery plain,
where it has wandered all morning,
sipping sweetness from the flowers among which it played.

Welcome, wonderful playtime! Free for a while,
we greet you with wild shouts in the open air,
as happy as people can be,
with our spare hour now available for pleasure—

pages.title: Schoolboy friendship threatened by cruelty and slander
pages.text:
18
And laying aside every thought and care
Which jocund joy might possibly impede
And dividing into equal sides prepare
For boyish games; and firing to nought else heed
With laugh and shout the winged hours we speed.

Thrice happy time! with no foreboding cares opprest
The glowing hours in joy are winged away
And present Hopes with full fruition blest
Portend no shadows in Lifes evening day.
Alas! that those should ever o’er us stray
To blight young Friendship in the early bud
And drown their first purest blessed joy
Beneath dark Detractions turbid flood—
Whose boiling tide inundates all that’s good.

Oh! why should the Schoolboys path of flowers
Be lined with thorns at every step he treads?
Oh! why should his Life’s young gladsome bowers
Conceal that Serpent in their floral beds
Whose poisonous fangs obscured in hydra heads
Of hate, malice, Scorn, Contempt, and pride,
Strike with all their venom natively inbred
Until the nobler passions of the heart have died
Or with the baseness of Lucifer allied.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 18 continues the playtime stanza at 10-052. “Firing” appears in the line about paying no heed and is retained, although “giving” would be expected in context. The enlarged native scan resolves the end of the venom line as “natively inbred.” This page has no separate title, date, or signature. The complete identified reading order is 10-050, 10-051, 10-060, 10-061, 10-052, 10-053 (manuscript pages 13–18).

pages.family_title: Schoolboy friendship threatened by cruelty and slander
pages.family_text:
Putting aside every thought and worry
that might get in the way of cheerful pleasure,
we divide into equal sides and prepare
for boys’ games, paying attention to nothing else.
With laughter and shouts, we hurry the flying hours along.

How happy that time is! Unburdened by anxious forebodings,
the bright hours fly by in joy.
Our present hopes are fully satisfied
and suggest no shadows in life’s evening.
Sadly, those shadows do come over us,
blighting young friendship at its earliest stage
and drowning its first, purest, blessed happiness
beneath the dark, muddy flood of slander,
whose boiling tide overwhelms everything good.

Why must the schoolboy’s flowery path
be lined with thorns at every step?
Why must the happy gardens of his young life
hide a serpent among their flowers?
Its poisonous fangs, hidden in the many heads
of hatred, malice, scorn, contempt, and pride,
strike with all their innate venom,
until the heart’s nobler feelings have died
or joined themselves to Lucifer’s baseness.
pages.family_note: Continues 10-052. The meaning “paying attention to nothing else” is inferred from a grammatically awkward source line.

pages.title: “Things I Love,” written for Miss Ida
pages.text:
64
Things I Love
Written for Miss Ida;

I love to love all lovely things
From which the charm of Beauty [[springs?]]
To captivate the heart,
From lichens on the mountain crest
To lowly vales in sunlight drest
The high, the lowly part,
The Hero’s proud and pompous sway
The Senate’s stern command,
The Ploughman’s noteless little day,
The humblest in our land,
The grandly great, the low-[[illegible]]
Alike possess a charm
There’s Splendor there, And Beauty here
To keep the life blood warm,

The mutual pledge and mutual trust
Are joys which time can never rust
Nor lessen in degree
They spring from heart to kindred heart
And form of Life the sweeter part
Whose [[joys?]] never flee
Forms may decay, and friends grow strange
And lovely objects fly,
And Time’s mute step, with silent change
May bid the fairest die
But these will e’er remain to cheer
Tho’ all beside are gone
And Life be bright with roseate light,
With one perpetual dawn,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 64; continues on manuscript page 65 at 10-057, then page 66 at 10-056. That concluding page is dated February 1873. Faded words are marked; the line beginning “The grandly great” is not completed from the rhyme or expected meaning. Miss Ida is not identified beyond the dedication.

pages.family_title: “Things I Love,” written for Miss Ida
pages.family_text:
I love all lovely things
whose beauty [[arises?]]
to captivate the heart:
from lichens on a mountain summit
to low valleys clothed in sunlight,
the high places and the low;
the hero’s proud, grand authority,
the Senate’s stern commands,
the plowman’s small, unnoticed day,
the humblest people in our land,
the magnificently great and the lowly [[word unreadable]]—
all have their charm.
There is splendor in one and beauty in another,
keeping life’s blood warm.

Mutual promises and mutual trust
are joys that time can never corrode
or diminish.
They pass from one sympathetic heart to another
and make up life’s sweeter part,
whose [[joys?]] never disappear.
Bodies may decay, friends may become distant,
and beautiful things may vanish.
Time’s silent steps and quiet changes
may bring death to the fairest.
But these joys will always remain to comfort us,
even when everything else is gone,
and life will shine with rosy light,
as if dawn lasted forever.
pages.family_note: Read 10-054, 10-057, then 10-056 for the manuscript’s sequence. The poem is dedicated to Miss Ida, whose surname and relationship to the writer remain unestablished.

pages.title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”: concluding stanzas, June 1874
pages.text:
63
Soon shall we pass away, nor leave behind
To tell what we have been, a single trace
Like some frail gossamer wafted by the wind
We’ll go, and none may ever mark the place
Where we shall fall. Life’s eager busy race
Will have no time to pause. When we are gone
The young the gay will laugh around, the chase
Of Life’s vain [[phantoms?]], still will lead them on
Until they too with us, shall try the Great Beyond.

Flow on thou River, Still flow on. The Sea
Will welcome thee to its deep dark abyss,
Thy course is marked, and I can [[mark?]] in Thee
The type of Human Life. Nor can we miss
The doom awaiting us, The woe, the bliss
Of that last hour, to which we all must come
And there resign the pomp the fame of this
In the deep sleep of our last quiet [[illegible]]
Till called to swell the throng in yon eternal dome.

June 1874.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 63, a conclusion whose river imagery and gossamer stanza also appear in the faint drafts at 10-016–10-018. Several words are faded even in the native scan. The place and duration of the speaker’s life cannot be inferred from the general meditation on death. The opening is at 10-059 (page 61), followed by 10-058 (page 62) and this page (63).

pages.family_title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”: concluding stanzas, June 1874
pages.family_text:
Soon we will pass away, leaving
not a single trace to show what we were.
Like a fragile thread of spider silk blown by the wind,
we will go, and no one may ever mark
where we fall. Life’s eager, busy people
will have no time to pause. After we are gone,
the young and cheerful will laugh around us,
still led onward in pursuit of life’s empty [[illusions?]],
until they too join us in experiencing the Great Beyond.

Flow on, river; keep flowing. The sea
will welcome you into its deep, dark depths.
Your course is set, and in you I can [[see?]]
a likeness of human life. We too cannot escape
the fate awaiting us: the sorrow or happiness
of the last hour that must come to everyone.
There we give up this life’s splendor and fame
in the deep sleep of our final quiet [[word unreadable]],
until called to join the multitude in that eternal heavenly hall.

June 1874.
pages.family_note: A modern-language reading of the concluding page. Faded words remain marked; related notebook drafts are at 10-016–10-018. Read 10-059 and 10-058 before this conclusion.

pages.title: “Things I Love”: friendship and faith, February 1873
pages.text:
66
And too, I love the friendly flow,
The Social feelings’ ardent glow
The heart’s [[responsive?]] beat
The happy hours of Sunlit glee
With friends commingling frank and [[free?]]
The fireside’s fond retreat,
The mantling cheek and sparkling eye
Which speak of Souls Sincere
Of Hope and Aspiration high
Which youthful bosoms bear,
The mystic power, of Twilight’s hour
When stars begin to shine,
The soft repose of daylight’s close
Are joys I number mine.

But far above the grandest thing
Which Earth can yield or Genius bring
I prize the heirs of Heaven
Who bow beneath the hand of God
And smile thro’ tears and kiss the rod
Ere yet the blow is given,
Lone Pilgrims still, and strangers here
Amid a world of strife
With practice pure, and conscience clear
Their title deed to [[Life?]],
With living Faith that conquers death
A high and holy trust
They calmly wait, the last [[mandate?]]
“Thou Shalt return to dust”

Feby 1873

pages.family_title: “Things I Love”: friendship and faith, February 1873
pages.family_text:
I also love the easy flow of friendship,
the warm glow of sociable feelings,
the heart’s [[responding?]] beat;
happy, sunlit hours of delight,
spent openly and [[freely?]] with friends,
and the beloved retreat beside the fire;
the blushing cheek and sparkling eye
that speak of sincere souls,
of hopes and high ambitions
carried in young hearts;
the mysterious power of twilight
when the stars begin to shine;
and the gentle rest of day’s end—
these are joys I count as mine.

But more than the grandest things
the earth can offer or genius can create,
I value those who will inherit heaven:
those who bow beneath God’s hand,
smile through their tears, and kiss the rod
before its blow has even fallen.
Still lonely pilgrims and strangers here
in a world of conflict,
they live purely and keep clear consciences,
their claim to [[eternal life?]].
With a living faith that conquers death,
a lofty and holy trust,
they calmly await the final [[command?]]:
“You shall return to dust.”

February 1873.

pages.title: “Things I Love”: beauty in ordinary places
pages.text:
65
Who will not pause to note the bliss
That springs from raptured scenes [[ideal?]]
Is dead to all that’s dear,
In vain the seasons may return
The Poles may freeze and Tropics [[burn?]]
Alike to him the year,
The flowers which strew the prairies green
May make a mute appeal
The Choral grove,—the Sylvan Scene
All—cannot make him feel,
But still can I each rapture Spy,
That springs on plain or spray;
And love them still, with earnest will
The gentle and the gay.

However humble is the Scene,
I’m sure a raptured thrill [[has been?]]
Down there awhile to stay,
I’ll gather then the nameless sweet
From out each lone obscure [[retreat?]]
Half hidden from the day,
For still the mead and mountains brow
Their varied beauties [[yield?]],—
The Summer’s bloom, and Winter’s snow
Still give me joys annealed,
With eager grasp, each one I clasp,
With grateful throbbing heart
I love them all, the great and [[small?]]
The rapture giving part.

Faded ends of lines remain marked rather than filled solely from rhyme. “Annealed” is the visible source word. The difficult phrase following “raptured thrill” is a tentative reading, not a reconstructed line.

pages.family_title: “Things I Love”: beauty in ordinary places
pages.family_text:
Anyone who will not pause to notice the happiness
arising from delightful [[imagined?]] scenes
is dead to everything dear.
The seasons return for him in vain;
the poles may freeze and the tropics [[burn?]],
but the year is all the same to him.
Flowers scattered across the green prairies
may appeal silently,
yet neither a grove full of song nor a woodland scene
can make him feel anything.
I can still notice every delight
arising on a plain or a leafy branch,
and sincerely love them,
both the gentle and the cheerful.

However humble the scene,
I am sure a thrill of delight [[has been?]]
there for a while.
So I will gather the unnamed sweetness
from every lonely, obscure [[retreat?]],
half hidden from the daylight.
Meadows and mountain summits still
[[offer?]] their varied beauties.
Summer’s flowers and winter’s snow
still give me joys made enduring.
I eagerly embrace each one
with a grateful, beating heart.
I love them all, the great and the [[small?]],
for the delight they give.

pages.title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”: companionship and remembrance
pages.text:
62
And yield ourselves unto the gentle wile
That bids the cares of day so quick [[depart?]]
With all their load of human hate and guile
And leave untrammelled once our nobler part
Where reigns supreme the sweeter passions of the heart.

Delightful then it is at eve to stray
Along yon rocky mountains wooded brow
And while the pleasant sunny hours away
In Social converse—whose influence now
Is felt with all the charms of life I know,
Of [[illegible]] Life, [[deleted: that]] [[inserted: which]] shared by one dear friend
As [[illegible]] on that aged Live Oak bough
Esteem and confidence alike did blend
While Youth and Hope stood by, their mutual charm to lend.

Around, were spread thy own eternal hills
All garlanded with wreaths of fadeless green
Amid whose bowers the mock-birds’ gentle [[trills?]]
Awakened thoughts of things which “might have been,
Below, thy winding vallies fair were seen
Tilled by the sturdy ploughman’s ready hand,,
The rustic cot, there humbly crowned the scene,
The poor man’s home—his tender darling band
The dearest tie of all, in every patriots Land.

These scenes, these thoughts awake and we forget
The Indian’s grave, the white man’s Sepulchre,
They lived and loved and hoped and toiled—but yet
Death came and severed all those ties so dear
Which bound them unto life, And [[illegible]]
Idly listless, above their venerated dust
And desecrate the tombs Affections’ tear
Have reared to consecrate and guard the just
Against the tooth of Time, or dark Oblivion’s rust.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 62 continues page 61 at 10-059 and precedes page 63 at 10-055. Several pale phrases remain unresolved. The poem’s Indigenous imagery and generalized historical claims are preserved as literary content, not archaeological evidence or verified local history.

pages.family_title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”: companionship and remembrance
pages.family_text:
We surrender to the gentle charm
that quickly makes the day’s worries [[depart?]],
with all their burden of human hatred and deceit,
and frees the nobler part of ourselves,
where the heart’s sweeter feelings reign.

How delightful it is then to wander in the evening
along that rocky mountain’s wooded crest,
passing pleasant, sunny hours
in friendly conversation, whose influence
I still feel with all the charms of life I know.
Of [[words unreadable]] life, shared with one dear friend,
as [[words unreadable]] on that old live-oak bough,
mutual respect and confidence mingled,
while youth and hope added their shared charm.

Your eternal hills spread around us,
garlanded with unfading greenery.
In their leafy retreats the mockingbirds’ gentle [[songs?]]
awakened thoughts of what might have been.
Below lay your beautiful, winding valleys,
cultivated by the sturdy plowman.
The simple cottage humbly completed the scene:
a poor man’s home and his beloved household,
the dearest bond in every patriot’s country.

These scenes and thoughts awaken us, and we forget
the Indigenous person’s grave and the white person’s tomb.
They lived, loved, hoped, and worked; yet
death came and broke all the cherished bonds
that tied them to life. And [[words unreadable]]
idle and indifferent above their honored remains,
and violate the tombs that affection’s tears
raised to honor and protect the worthy dead
against time’s destruction and the decay of forgetting.

paragraphs.text:
62
And yield ourselves unto the gentle wile
That bids the cares of day so quick [[depart?]]
With all their load of human hate and guile
And leave untrammelled once our nobler part
Where reigns supreme the sweeter passions of the heart.

Delightful then it is at eve to stray
Along yon rocky mountains wooded brow
And while the pleasant sunny hours away
In Social converse—whose influence now
Is felt with all the charms of life I know,
Of [[illegible]] Life, [[deleted: that]] [[inserted: which]] shared by one dear friend
As [[illegible]] on that aged Live Oak bough
Esteem and confidence alike did blend
While Youth and Hope stood by, their mutual charm to lend.

Around, were spread thy own eternal hills
All garlanded with wreaths of fadeless green
Amid whose bowers the mock-birds’ gentle [[trills?]]
Awakened thoughts of things which “might have been,
Below, thy winding vallies fair were seen
Tilled by the sturdy ploughman’s ready hand,,
The rustic cot, there humbly crowned the scene,
The poor man’s home—his tender darling band
The dearest tie of all, in every patriots Land.

These scenes, these thoughts awake and we forget
The Indian’s grave, the white man’s Sepulchre,
They lived and loved and hoped and toiled—but yet
Death came and severed all those ties so dear
Which bound them unto life, And [[illegible]]
Idly listless, above their venerated dust
And desecrate the tombs Affections’ tear
Have reared to consecrate and guard the just
Against the tooth of Time, or dark Oblivion’s rust.

pages.title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”
pages.text:
61
Apostrophe To the Brazos.

Sweet Brazos! Still thy murmuring waters lave
Thy pebbly strand beneath yon Mountain height
Whose summit crowned by an ancient Indian [[inserted: grave]]
At once his nation’s pride and nation’s might,
Some hundred years have winged their weary flight
Since he was laid within the warriors tomb
O! what a change hath been! What withering blight
Has stamped the red man with an early doom—
And swept him from the earth, to give the pale face room.

But still thou flowest on as in days of yore
With the same old tones, within thy Rocky bed
The rugged cliffs still crown thy winding shore—
Perchance an aged tree still rears its head;
And saving these, all [[other?]] Scenes have fled,
The Warrior proud and strong—his dusky Bride
The stalwart Chief—and trusted Steed—are dead
The Wigwam gone—with all the Red Man’s pride
Swept with the flying years, [[illegible]] from their changeful tide.

Though these are gone, still hearts as fondly brave
And deeply true, still beat along thy stream,
As those, thy long gone primal ages gave,
Unto the world, and still as [[vainly?]] dream
Of Love and Happiness, and fondly deem
That they in after years will grasp the wand
Of Human Bliss, whose rich illusive gleam
Seen from afar but vainly leads them on
Till Youth and health and strength and hope and life are gone.

Tho’ this be so, O! still we’ll grasp the hour
That beams with Love and Hope’s illusive smile
We’ll woo its presence, and its cheerful power
To be around us, tho’ for so short awhile
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 61. Read 10-059, 10-058, 10-055 (manuscript pages 61–63); the conclusion is dated June 1874. “Grave” is inserted above the first stanza. The poem imagines an Indigenous grave and presents a nineteenth-century narrative of Indigenous disappearance. Neither the grave’s identity or age nor the claim of disappearance is independently established by this poem. No tribal identity or precise landmark is supplied.
