pages.family_title: “Apostrophe to the Brazos”
pages.family_text:
Sweet Brazos! Your murmuring waters still wash
your pebbled bank beneath that mountain,
whose summit is crowned by an ancient Indigenous grave—
the grave of one who was his nation’s pride and strength.
Some hundred years have wearily passed
since he was placed in the warrior’s tomb.
What change there has been! What destructive force
has condemned the Indigenous man to an early end,
sweeping him from the earth to make room for the white man.

Yet you flow on as in earlier days,
with the same sounds in your rocky bed.
Rugged cliffs still crown your winding shore;
perhaps an ancient tree still lifts its head.
Except for these, all [[other?]] scenes are gone:
the proud, strong warrior and his dark-skinned bride,
the powerful chief and his trusted horse are dead;
the dwelling is gone, with all the Indigenous man’s pride,
swept away by the passing years, [[words unreadable]] from their changing tide.

Though they are gone, hearts just as loving, brave,
and deeply faithful still beat beside your stream,
as those your distant earliest ages gave
to the world. They dream just as [[vainly?]]
of love and happiness, fondly imagining
that in later years they will grasp the wand
of human happiness, whose rich, deceptive glow,
seen far away, leads them fruitlessly onward
until youth, health, strength, hope, and life are gone.

Even so, let us seize the hour
that shines with love and hope’s deceptive smile.
Let us welcome its presence and its cheerful power
around us, even for so short a time—

pages.title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: twilight and remembered youth
pages.text:
15
Thus still those early scenes which first I knew
Linger on the pages of the shadowy Past
Which as Memory turns its leaves comes to view
In pure unstained colors, which will last
When the bands of Age are round me cast
And earthly joys grow dim and fade away
And Life’s last sands are ebbing fast
And soon to mingle with earth’s common clay
Where all at last must moulder and decay.

How beautiful! when the garish day was done
The sky appeared in twilight’s lovely hue
When the last lingering rays of the glorious sun
With amber streaked the deep heavenly blue
Unto my boyish eyes the glorious view
Seemed but the portals of a heaven on high
Where from the horizon we might spring through
And taste immortal bliss above the sky
With those pure Spirits there which never die.

And as still deeper glowed the tints of night
Upon that horizon’s far distant west.
The stars came forth with their lovely light
And gazed on the earth like Spirits blest
Watching it whilst it calmly sank to rest
From the toil and cares of days passed here
Whose fierce pursuits, pursued with eager zest
By men, seeking for some altitude of power
To dispense to mankind, curses by the hour.

How softly falls, with the calm advance of night
Its mild influences on mans stormy soul!
Erasing the stripes of day, and bearing [[unsought?]]
That boon of Heaven, whose high goal

pages.family_title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: twilight and remembered youth
pages.family_text:
The early scenes I first knew still linger
on the pages of the shadowy past.
As memory turns those pages, they appear
in pure, unstained colors that will remain
when age has bound me,
when earthly pleasures dim and fade,
and the last sands of life run quickly out,
soon to mingle with the earth’s ordinary clay,
where everything must eventually decay.

How beautiful the sky looked in twilight
when the glaring day was over,
and the glorious sun’s last lingering rays
streaked the deep heavenly blue with amber.
To my boyish eyes that splendid view
seemed like the gates of heaven,
through which we might leap from the horizon
to taste immortal happiness above the sky
with the pure spirits who never die.

As night’s colors deepened
on the far western horizon,
the stars emerged with their lovely light
and gazed down like blessed spirits,
watching the earth sink calmly to rest
from the work and cares of days spent here,
from the fierce pursuits eagerly followed
by people seeking high positions of power
so they can dispense curses upon humanity by the hour.

How gently, as the quiet night advances,
its mild influence falls on humanity’s stormy soul!
It erases the day’s wounds and brings [[unasked?]]
that gift of heaven, whose high goal—
pages.family_note: A displaced continuation of “On the Banks of Brushy,” between 10-051 and 10-061. “Wounds” interprets the source’s “stripes”; the uncertain following word remains marked.

pages.title: “On the Banks of Brushy”: childhood sleep and mortality
pages.text:
16
Is fixed where Time’s billows can never roll
Nor reach with their canker and decay
The immortal Spirit’s far magnetic pole
Around which it pursues its eternal way
In the boundless light of an unending day.

At length when all without was calm and still
I would seek in slumber deep for childhood’s dream
Softly lulled to sleep by the lone whip-poor-will
Which sang its sweet song in nights soft beams
And which to my young imaginations seems
A lovely creature sent with pure nameless charms
And matchless beauty, which in the starlight gleams
Brilliant and bright, such as mightily warms
A poets fancy when wrapped in Morpheus’ arms.

How quiet are childhood’s slumbers! how free from all
The stormy dreams of manhood’s feverish sleep!
No wild unrest, no vain ambitions lofty fall!
No withering hopes! o’er which to wake and weep
But all is peace, and soft repose—and sweetly keep
Their star watch o’er the young and tender frame
Now resting in sweet unconsciousness so deep,
That ’twere a pity, it should ever wake to claim
A place again on the rough road to earthly Fame.

Oh! it were better far in our earliest days
Before we learn the torturing way of Sin,
That in Death, should be quenched Life’s loved bright rays
And we, sink into the tomb—though cold within
Should be its cold vault—yet Oh! ’tis there
Through that drear portal, and break the chain
Of icy bondage there—and triumphing in
The death struggle—returned unto Heaven again
Resting the bliss of victory and Death of pain.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 16 follows 10-060 and precedes 10-052. This locates the two manuscript pages displaced from the poem’s earlier scan sequence. The closing stanza is syntactically difficult; its words and line divisions are preserved without rewriting the archival text into smoother theology. The final phrase appears to be “Resting the bliss,” not silently changed to “Tasting.”

pages.family_text:
—is fixed where time’s waves can never roll,
nor reach with their corrosion and decay:
the immortal spirit’s distant magnetic pole,
around which it travels eternally
in the boundless light of an endless day.

At last, when everything outside was calm and still,
I would seek childhood dreams in deep sleep,
softly lulled by the solitary whip-poor-will
singing sweetly in the gentle night light.
To my young imagination, it seemed
a lovely creature endowed with unnamed, pure charms
and unequaled beauty shining in the starlight,
bright enough to stir a poet’s imagination
while asleep in the arms of Morpheus.

How quiet childhood’s sleep is, how free
from the stormy dreams of adult, feverish sleep!
No restless turmoil, no collapse of lofty, empty ambitions,
no dying hopes to wake and weep over.
Everything is peace and gentle rest, keeping
a starry watch over the young, tender body,
resting so deeply in sweet unconsciousness
that it seems a pity it must ever wake
to take its place again on the rough road to earthly fame.

Oh, it would be far better, in our earliest days,
before we learn sin’s tormenting ways,
for death to extinguish life’s beloved bright light
and for us to sink into the tomb, though it is cold within.
Cold as its vault may be, it is there,
through that bleak doorway, that the chain
of icy bondage is broken; triumphing
in the struggle with death, we return to heaven,
resting in victory’s happiness and the end of pain.

pages.title: To Miss M. L. G.: courtship after peace returns
pages.text:
5
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form, as at 10-062]]
To Miss M. L. G.......

Now gentle peace has come again
And every girl wants a man
And every man is in a whirl
Looking around for a girl
Who is to share his after life
As his companion—partner—wife—
And all is bustle and confusion
Around Hymen’s bower—and the allusion,
To anything that ties up two
For life in bonds enduring
In a young chap will never do
That is if he is not a “daring.”

But as each one has some choice above
The ordinary feelings of his mind
I sincerely think the “Elm Grove”
Will fill the Ideal to which I’m inclined.
And I do intend to win
The prize that there is glowing
But doubtless I’ll have opposition in
My endeavors at so doing.
I know of but only four
Who stand opposed to my endeavors
Yet they may puzzle me quite sore
As, They are gentlemanly and clever,
I will mention them in detail
And pardon any digression
That may occur in manner metrical
For this is an allowed transgression.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 5, on a reused military form. Continues through 10-066–10-068, ending with a May 1, 1866 date. “Elm Grove” and the four rivals’ labels are left as the poem presents them; no identities or modern place locations are inferred. Hymen’s bower is an image of marriage. The light, competitive rhetoric does not establish actual engagements.

pages.family_text:
Now gentle peace has returned,
and every girl wants a man,
while every man is in a whirl,
looking for a girl
to share the rest of his life
as his companion, partner, and wife.
Everything is bustle and confusion
around the marriage bower. Any mention
of tying two people together
in lifelong bonds
will not suit a young fellow
unless he is a daring one.

But everyone has a special preference
beyond his ordinary feelings.
I sincerely think “Elm Grove”
will fulfill the ideal I favor.
I do intend to win
the prize shining there,
though I will doubtless face opposition
in my efforts.
I know of only four
who oppose my plans,
but they may give me serious trouble,
for they are gentlemanly and clever.
I will describe them one by one;
please forgive any digression
or irregularity in the meter,
for that is an allowable poetic offense.

pages.text:

[[separate block: preprinted form]]

No | NAME | AGE | ENLISTMENT. WHEN. WHERE. BY WHOM. TERM. | OCCUPATION.

“Elysian’s” claims are old and strong
And await you there a splendid bower
Which you may enjoy ere long
As a patrimonial dower.
But I candidly believe
The owner will never do
For verily he will deceive
Others, and why not you
His claims I’ll admit are old enough
To hold the prize if true enough
But their constancy I doubt
Since I’ve heard the idle chat’s out
In circulation round about.

“Bloomdale” has found a voice to speak
And oft quite oft I hear it squeak;
I fear it not for subtle wit
But once it grasps ’twill never quit
Its hold upon the object sought.
Until the prize is fairly caught.
But there are so many “ifs” and “ans”
And “I’ll come it if I can”
“But when and where to show my love
“I know not or how it to prove
“So as to win the prize of ‘Elm Grove,’

From “Shiloh” loud at times there comes
A brave and beauteous boy
Who to my heart “strikes terror dumb”
And threats to mar for aye my joy.
Oh! that Time’s devouring shafts may fall

“Elysian’s” claims are longstanding and strong,
and a splendid home awaits you there,
which you may soon enjoy
as an inherited marriage portion.
But I honestly believe
the owner will never suit:
he will certainly deceive
others, so why not you?
I admit his claims are old enough
to win the prize if they are faithful enough.
But I doubt their constancy,
having heard the idle gossip
circulating all around.

“Bloomdale” has found his speaking voice,
and very often I hear it squeak.
I do not fear his subtle wit,
but once he takes hold he will never release
the object he seeks
until the prize is securely caught.
Yet there are so many “ifs” and “ands,”
and “I will manage it if I can,”
followed by “When and where should I show my love?
I do not know how to prove it
so as to win the prize of Elm Grove.”

From “Shiloh” there sometimes loudly comes
a brave and handsome boy,
who strikes my heart speechless with fear
and threatens to spoil my happiness forever.
Oh, may time’s destructive arrows fall—

pages.title: To Miss M. L. G.: mock curses and a fourth rival
pages.text:
7
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form, as at 10-062]]
Upon his glowing face!
In Showers thick fast and terrible
And destroy each lovely trace
Of feature that now glowing shines
And leave him halt, lame, sick, unsoond,
With all those woes which swift refines
The failing body for the ground,
Because he leaves his home to mar the joys
Of other and of better boys
Who claim by right the first choice
Of all the maids of syren voice
Who dwell around in the country near
And are to me so very dear
And I can them all in detail love
But best of all the prize of “Elm Grove,”

“Seclusion” too will put in his claim
From his hermitted bowers.
They will get—howies but in name
So I care not for their powers.
Perhaps howies as he damns all
Who fill not his Ideal
His maledictions he may let fall
Upon this glorious rival.
Just let them come and if your feelings
Are wounded by his rough opinion
“His muddy head I’ll be after peeling”
Just as a paddy would an onion.

Yes fly to me, thou dearest maid
And protection I will give,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 7 follows 10-066 and continues at 10-068. “Unsoond” and “howies” are retained as visible nonstandard forms; the precise sense of “howies” is unclear. The extravagant curses and threat are part of a comic rivalry poem, not evidence that a physical attack occurred. “Paddy” is the source’s dated ethnic stereotype.

—upon his glowing face,
in thick, swift, terrible showers!
May they destroy every lovely trace
of his now-radiant features
and leave him limping, lame, sick, and unsound,
with all the troubles that quickly prepare
a failing body for the grave,
because he leaves home to spoil the happiness
of other, better boys,
who claim the right to choose first
among the sweet-voiced young women
living nearby in the country,
all so very dear to me.
I can love every one of them individually,
but most of all the prize of “Elm Grove.”

“Seclusion” will also make his claim
from his secluded retreat.
They will get—[[the meaning of “howies” is unclear]]—only in name,
so I do not care about their powers.
Perhaps [[“howies,” meaning unclear]], since he condemns everyone
who does not meet his ideal;
he may let his curses fall
on this glorious rival.
Let them come! If his harsh opinion
hurts your feelings,
“I will peel his muddy head,”
as an Irishman might peel an onion.

Yes, come quickly to me, dearest girl,
and I will protect you—
pages.family_note: Continues 10-066 and ends at 10-068. The source uses comic exaggeration, unusual words, and an ethnic stereotype; unclear wording is marked rather than softened into an invented meaning.

[[separate block: preprinted descriptive roll and enlistment headings, as at 10-066, with troop category blank]]
Until this form is lowly laid
And I shall cease to live
Enshrined within my heart for aye
Your image shall ever sit
So will you not come and stay
Forever there with it.

My misery is complete on earth
Alone as I am living
My life is a very death
To me no pleasure giving.
Shortly then I know I’ll die
Because no one will me love
The reason I cannot tell why,
Can you fair maid of “Elm Grove”

I loved you at first and now still better
And love you I ever will
This you may see by my letter
Can you love a Verdant Hill?

May 1st 1866

[[separate block: Epigrams, lower left column]]
Epigrams.
If you wish to get a new wrinkle
Upon your brow deeply set
Go over and note the Rip van winkle
There is in Liberty etiquette.

A prayer meeting “is the chief concern”
As every sinner knows
By which he can most quietly learn
How he stands at uncle [[Gid’s?]],

[[separate block: Epigrams, lower right column]]
If you want to get any information
From any Liberty aboriginal
Don’t go to the composition examination
For [[Ben?]] will tell you they are original,

People often go to a frolic or ball,
To seek for enjoyment in general
But there you will find that one and all
For amusement will go to a funeral,

Four separate epigrams occupy the lower part of the page in two columns. Their jokes about Liberty, prayer meetings, compositions, and funerals are reproduced as satire, not as a verified description of a community. Two names remain tentative.

—until this body is laid in the grave
and I cease to live.

May 1, 1866.

Four epigrams:

If you want a new wrinkle
set deeply in your brow,
go and notice the Rip Van Winkle-like old-fashioned habits
in Liberty’s social etiquette.

A prayer meeting is “the chief concern,”

there he can quietly discover
how he stands with Uncle [[Gid?]].

If you want information
from anyone native to Liberty,
do not go to the composition examination:
[[Ben?]] will tell you the compositions are original.

People often go to a party or ball
to find enjoyment,
but there you will find that everyone
goes to a funeral for entertainment.

pages.text:
9
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form, as at 10-062]]
To Miss M. L. G.....

’Tis all in vain you strive and try
And glance about so furtively
And eye each boy that comes in sight
As though ’twas he that did indite
Unto you these Scattering rhymes
Flung out offhand in backwoods chimes
In which was made such abrupt allusion
To “Elysian” “Bloomdale” [[inserted: “Shiloh”]] and “Seclusion,”
And told upon them some very ugly tales
No doubt which made them think they are not whales.

No doubt “Elysian” calls it an outrage
Upon a gentleman of his age
And makes him loudly rave and storm
Against a poor unknown fellow worm.

“Bloomdale” no doubt will cut a figure
Erect his brows and feel the bigger
Simply because I took the notion
To make some slight notices of him.

“Shiloh” no doubt will never know
Who has caused him so much woe
But should the three get together
Lift their heads and raise their feathers
And strut about as big as Aristotle
Having along a big black bottle
Should they then this mortal chance to see
What! oh what!! would become of poor me!
Continued on Page 53
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 9 refers back to the rivals in 10-065–10-068. “Shiloh” is inserted above the line listing them. The page explicitly directs the reader to manuscript page 53 for its continuation. The speaker presents himself as unknown; this is not an author’s signature. “Whales” is retained as written. The continuation has been located at 10-093–10-096 (manuscript pages 33–36); 10-093 explicitly says “Continued from 9th page.” The forward reference here was read as 53 and is retained pending closer numeral comparison.

pages.family_text:
It is no use trying so hard,
looking around so furtively,
and studying every boy who appears
as though he were the one who wrote
you these scattered verses,
tossed off casually in rustic rhythms.
They made such sudden references
to “Elysian,” “Bloomdale,” “Shiloh,” and “Seclusion,”
and told some very unflattering stories about them,
no doubt making them feel less like important “big fish.”

“Elysian” surely calls it an outrage
against a gentleman of his age,
and loudly rages
at a poor, unknown fellow creature.

“Bloomdale” will doubtless make a show,
raise his brows and feel more important,
simply because I decided
to mention him briefly.

“Shiloh” will surely never know
who has caused him so much trouble.
But if the three get together,
lift their heads and ruffle their feathers,
and strut around as important as Aristotle,
with a big black bottle along,
and happen to see this poor mortal—
what, oh what, would become of me?

The manuscript says: continued on page 53.

Social Parties—What Are They?

The Social Parties as practiced by the Native and Adopted citizens of the younger class in this Section are in my humble opinion the most ridiculous amusements which it is possible for intelligent people to practice. Imagine a gathering of thirty or forty young people aged respectively from eighteen to thirty at some place selected for the contemplated performance. Having met and sat about rather indolently for awhile apparently very much embarrassed and seemingly very modest and very fearful of doing something contrary to the rules of Etiquette some venturesome character proposes a “play” The young gents capering select their partners and ere long promenading the floor in a circle by twos to the bewitching strains of “Old Sister Phebe” or “My pretty little love” or some other popular air sung in enchanting style by some one or two vocalists. No conversation worthy the name is ever carried on by any couple, those not engaged in singing keep profoundly silent or indulge in unmeasured laughter at some real or imaginary blunders of some one or more of the party. Tiring of the first or any other play each individual looks for a seat for him or herself, or a drink of water or something else. The girls congregate on one side of the house and indulge in apparently very lively and interesting chat if we are to judge from the many Smiling faces and little giggles which may from time
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 10 continues at 10-071. This is the writer’s satirical criticism, not a neutral survey. The location and date become explicit on the following page: Ellis County, Texas, May 1866. “Native and Adopted citizens” here distinguishes local-born residents and newcomers in the writer’s wording; it is not an identification of Indigenous ancestry. Song titles are transcribed, not attributed to an external version.

pages.family_title: “Social Parties—What Are They?”: a critical account of local gatherings
pages.family_text:
Social Parties—What Are They?

In my humble opinion, the social parties held by younger people in this area, both those born here and those who have settled here, are among the most ridiculous amusements intelligent people could practice.

Imagine thirty or forty young people, aged eighteen to thirty, gathering at a place chosen for the occasion. After they have sat about idly for a while, looking embarrassed, very modest, and afraid of breaking the rules of etiquette, someone ventures to suggest a “play,” or party game. The young men eagerly choose partners, and before long they are walking around the room in pairs to “Old Sister Phebe,” “My Pretty Little Love,” or another popular song, sung in enchanting fashion by one or two singers.

No couple ever carries on a conversation worth the name. Those who are not singing remain completely silent or laugh uncontrollably at someone’s real or imagined mistakes. When they tire of a game, everyone looks for a seat, a drink of water, or something else to do.

The girls gather on one side of the room and apparently enjoy lively, interesting conversation, judging by the many smiling faces and little giggles that may from time—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-071. The amused but disapproving tone belongs to the writer. This text records one person’s view of local social customs.

Having met and sat about rather indolently for awhile apparently very much embarrassed and seemingly very modest and very fearful of doing something contrary to the rules of Etiquette some venturesome character proposes a “play” The young gents capering select their partners and ere long promenading the floor in a circle by twos to the bewitching strains of “Old Sister Phebe” or “My pretty little love” or some other popular air sung in enchanting style by some one or two vocalists. No conversation worthy the name is ever carried on by any couple, those not engaged in singing keep profoundly silent or indulge in unmeasured laughter at some real or imaginary blunders of some one or more of the party. Tiring of the first or any other play each individual looks for a seat for him or herself, or a drink of water or something else. The girls congregate on one side of the house and indulge in apparently very lively and interesting chat if we are to judge from the many Smiling faces and little giggles which may from time

pages.family_title: A Fourth of July school exhibition near Red Oak in 1866
pages.family_text:
July 4, 1866. I spent the day at the school examination and exhibition at Mrs. [[Ray’s?]] school, a mile and a half west of the Red Oak post office.

It was a brilliant affair for Texas at this stage of its intellectual development, surpassing anything of its kind held in this part of the country so far. Nothing spoken or performed on stage was original, however; it all came from the mind of some genius elsewhere.

The passing spectacle ended at eleven at night. Judging by appearances, I suppose everyone went home satisfied, and some were doubtless delighted. But I suppose we have no right to speculate about the secrets of all those fluttering hearts that left the grounds. Perhaps not everything that could be told would be pleasant to hear.

As people say, the “skirmish line” was established, and at least one romantic or marital affair was fully accomplished at this occasion of wit and [[merriment?]]. May it eventually leave everyone satisfied, happy, and content to go their way rejoicing—if not because their hopes have been fulfilled, then at least because they hope for a better day when they can call the [[beloved?]] [[unreadable]] their own, if only temporarily.

Sunshine and shadow are strangely mixed in this [[earthly?]] world. Those happy today may be [[sad?]] tomorrow, and those sad today may be happy tomorrow. It is doubtless [[more pleasant?]] to watch these changes than to [[experience?]] them. We will wait a while and [[ending unreadable]].

pages.text:

A residence of Sixteen years in this portion of Texas (Ellis County) has not made me fall in love with it by any means. ’Tis may be the easiest place to “get along” in of any other—yet the experience which I have had here in common farming life forces me to the conclusion that it is a hard place to make a living. The general mildness of the climate, and [[slowness?]] of the Summer have enervated the inhabitants to such a degree that they do not look forward with the proper foresight in regard to their pecuniary interests. Proper places for deposit of grain are not provided and frequently crops suffer [[deleted: from]] destruction to a considerable extent from this cause alone. We are poorly provided with machinery of all descriptions, There is not half mills enough in the country consequently instead of Competition we have Combination, and exorbitant rates of toll are charged which is detrimental to the farming interests of the country, but we farmers have to submit to an [[illegible]] which we cannot help and any hope [[illegible]] away change. I cite Millers [[illegible]] which [[inflict?]] upon the Community—Other professions do likewise as far as they are able. Self is the governing principle here [[to?]] the exclusion of all other and [[while?]] [[illegible]] [[localities?]] whose competition gives the farming class a chance to realize the full value of their crops from year to year [[would?]] surely be more desirable than [[illegible]] they are much the most [[illegible]].

pages.family_title: Sixteen years in Ellis County and the difficulties of farming
pages.family_text:
Living in this part of Texas—Ellis County—for sixteen years has certainly not made me fall in love with it. It may be the easiest place to “get along,” yet my experience of ordinary farming here forces me to conclude that it is a hard place to make a living.

The generally mild climate and the [[slowness?]] of summer have drained the inhabitants’ energy so much that they fail to plan properly for their financial interests. Proper grain storage is not provided, and crops are often substantially damaged for that reason alone.

We have too little machinery of every kind. There are not even half enough mills in the country. Consequently, we have collusion instead of competition, and excessive milling charges harm the farmers. Yet we farmers must submit to [[unreadable]] that we cannot remedy. [[Part of the argument is unreadable.]] I cite millers [[unreadable]] the community. Other professions act similarly as far as they can.

Self-interest is the governing principle here, [[to?]] the exclusion of everything else. [[Some words are unreadable.]] Places where competition gives farmers a chance to receive the full value of their crops each year [[would?]] surely be more desirable than [[ending partly unreadable]].

pages.title: Home and the ties of childhood
pages.text:
14
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Home

There are many pleasant associations connected with the word Home, It embodies at one group and in one view the leading features of our earlier days. Our first recollections, our first associations our first connections all spring at once to the mind at the mention of that one word. Our recollections of the innocent Sports that beguiled the days of our infancy, when lighthearted and joyous we played amid Sunshine and flowers, inhaling the wild free air and Spirit of nature, careless and gay as the bright plumaged birds which warbled their hymns of praise from every tree, Free as they from the follies and vices of the world nor dreaming of the blight of after years through which we would be called to pass—Our earlier associations with companions joyous as we, which can never be renewed, but which will linger in Memory, as one of the brightest periods of our existence; and to which we can always turn with pleasing emotions—Our earlier connections with parents, brothers, and sisters, fond endearing ties, woven in childhood years, and never to be forgotten, though separated by time and distance, far from the places where they sprung into existence—These remembrances all spring within the mind when Home is mentioned and as we contemplate them through the lapse of years they assume a hallowed purity, which no other scenes or associations can. They are holy because they belong to the past, they are sacred because they are pure and uncontaminated by vile connections, they are the tender ties of early love, mutually enjoyed and mutually reciprocated, they are the holy links which bind the family

pages.family_title: Home and the ties of childhood
pages.family_text:
Home

The word “home” carries many pleasant associations. It brings the main features of our early days together in a single picture. Our first memories, companions, and relationships all spring to mind at its mention.

We remember the innocent games that filled our childhood, when we played happily among sunshine and flowers, breathing nature’s free air and spirit. We were as carefree as the brightly feathered birds singing praise in every tree, and as free from the world’s follies and vices, never imagining the troubles of later years.

We remember our early friendships with companions as happy as ourselves. Those days can never return, but they remain in memory as one of the brightest periods of our lives, to which we can always turn with pleasure. We remember our first relationships with parents, brothers, and sisters: affectionate ties formed in childhood and never forgotten, however far time and distance take us from their beginnings.

All these memories arise when home is mentioned. As we contemplate them across the years, they acquire a sacred purity that no other scenes or associations can have. They are holy because they belong to the past, and sacred because they are pure, untouched by corrupt relationships. They are the tender ties of early love, enjoyed and returned by everyone—the sacred links that bind the family—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-075. The essay idealizes home and childhood; its descriptions do not establish specific biographical events.

pages.text:

band together in bonds of perpetual union.
The influence of such associations will always be felt no matter what may be our course through life, whether wild and dissipated, or gentle and refined, in one case, they will check us in our wayward career, and point to a nobler existence, in the other, they will be an incentive to a continuation in a life of well doing, ennobling our feelings and refining our natures, inspiring in our hearts a spirit of Charity and contentment which will be a perpetual wellspring of happiness to us, which the cares of Life cannot destroy.
Written at the request of a Young Lady
Seclusion Sept 20th 1866.

Sonnet or, Blent Flowers,
Adieu ye bright hopes that so fondly have hovered
Around the light dreams of my earlier days
When with feelings transparent and affections uncovered
I faced the gay world in its meridian blaze
Those visions of joy bright [[deleted: in]] [[inserted: all]] ecstatic Elysian
Have faded before adversity’s cold gaze
And nought now remains but those dreams [[deleted: of]] [[inserted: Life’s elysion]]
Dimly discovered through memory’s dark haze
But still they will linger on those dim distant pages
And occasionally be read when a sunbeam there strays
And fondly remembered as one of those happy ages
That in Childhood and Youth deceivingly plays
But will return not again in life’s varied stages
Although we hope for it in Philosophy’s atherian ways
Seclusion July 1866

pages.family_title: The conclusion of Home and a sonnet on vanished hopes
pages.family_text:
—together in lasting union.

These associations will always influence us, whatever course our lives take. If we become wild and dissipated, they will restrain us and point toward a nobler life. If we are gentle and refined, they will encourage us to continue doing good, improving our feelings and character. They inspire kindness and contentment in our hearts, a lasting source of happiness that life’s cares cannot destroy.

Written at a young lady’s request.
Seclusion, September 20, 1866.

Sonnet, or Blent Flowers

Farewell, bright hopes that hovered so fondly
around the light dreams of my early days,
when, with open feelings and unhidden affection,
I faced the cheerful world at its brightest.
Those blissful visions of joy
have faded before adversity’s cold gaze.
Nothing remains but those dreams of life’s paradise,
dimly seen through memory’s dark haze.
Yet they will linger on those distant pages,
and sometimes be read when a sunbeam falls there,
and fondly remembered as one of those happy times
that childhood and youth deceptively offer.
They will not return at later stages of life,
although we hope for them through philosophy’s airy ways.

Seclusion, July 1866.

pages.title: To W H B on lasting friendship
pages.text:
16
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To W. H. B.....

Though short the time since first we met
The few bright and glowing scenes
That have past I can never forget
While I know what pleasure means.
But to those moments sweetly fraught
That yielded such a pleasant time
I would bestow a passing thought
Penned in idle Scattering rhyme.

To Friendship I would dedicate my verse
(That brightly blooms in darkest hours)
And though it may be rude and coarse
A nobler aim shall direct its powers.

May the friendship we have just begun
Stand the test of after years
“And round our hearts be surely spun”
The chains that pleasure fondly bears,

True Friendship like the gnarled Oak
Firm rooted in the rock
Feel the lightnings deadliest Stroke
And brave the tempests rudest shock,
But when the moaning storms are sped,
And calmly comes the hour of even—
Again it rears its vernal head
Towards the ether vault of Heaven,

Be it ours to brave the lightnings brand
Of malice dark and dread,

pages.family_title: To W H B on lasting friendship
pages.family_text:
To W. H. B.

Though we met only recently,
I can never forget the few bright, glowing scenes
we have shared,
as long as I know what pleasure means.
I would give those sweet moments,
which brought such happiness,
a passing thought
in these casual, scattered rhymes.

I dedicate my verse to friendship,
which blooms brightly in the darkest hours.
Though the verse may be rough and crude,
a nobler purpose will guide it.

May our newly begun friendship
stand the test of future years.
May the bonds that pleasure gladly bears
be woven firmly around our hearts.

True friendship is like a gnarled oak,
firmly rooted in rock:
it feels lightning’s deadliest stroke
and withstands the fiercest storm.
But when the moaning storms have passed
and evening comes peacefully,
it raises its green head again
toward the vault of heaven.

May we withstand the lightning bolt
of dark and dreadful malice—

pages.title: George Douglas on friendship and a later farewell verse
pages.text:
17
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Be it ours to firmly rooted stand
While calumnys storms burst overhead
So when the storms of Life are past
And their fury spent that was given
Friendship will point our way at last
Toward the upper courts of Heaven,

Thus I give to friendship true
Words that can never be lost
Which will be highly prized by you
While you remain at Honors post,
And if you should ever be forsaken
By Loves circle false and fair
Olden emotions will awaken
When you read what I have written here.
Geo. Douglas
Seclusion Nov 18th 1866

[[separate block: separate farewell verse]]
Farewell for now my eyes wax dim,
And I must leave this home so blest
But where I’m gone my thoughts will ever
And on dear [[Matty?]] Farm alight
For ’tis in this secluded spot
That tranquil hours have passed,
Peace to the [[hearts?]] whose happy lot
On earth with thee are cast.
June 27th 1869
[[L?]]

And on dear [[Matty?]] Farm alight
For ’tis in this secluded spot
That tranquil hours have passed,
Peace to the [[hearts?]] whose happy lot
On earth with thee are cast.
June 27th 1869
[[L?]]

To the Y. L. of the L. S.
(Or the gnawing of a bone)

Now gentle girls polite and fair
As I am tonight all alone
I will try and get off some rhyming ware
About a tough and crusty bone.

I am told you have a bone to gnaw
Harder than any heretofore known
The like of it nobody ever saw
It is such a very strange bone.

Every monday morning I understand
All of your faults you have to own
Then lay strong hold with both your hands
And go to gnawing on this bone.

Tewsday comes bright and fair
Yet there is no softness shown
And each moment you busy are
Gnawing away upon this bone.

So you go until Saturday
The trying task all week youve known
Yet you have not gnawed away
One particle of this hard bone.

Then comes the Sabbath pure and bright
Its glories over earth are thrown

pages.family_title: To the Y L of the L S or the gnawing of a bone
pages.family_text:
To the Y. L. of the L. S., or Gnawing a Bone

Gentle girls, polite and fair,
since I am alone tonight,
I will try to produce some rhymes
about a tough and crusty bone.

I hear you have a bone to gnaw,
harder than any ever known.
Nobody has seen its like:
it is such a very strange bone.

Every Monday morning, I understand,
you must confess all your faults,
then grip it firmly with both hands
and start gnawing this bone.

Tuesday comes bright and fair,
but it shows no sign of softening.
You spend every busy moment
gnawing away at this bone.

You continue until Saturday,
knowing this tiresome task all week,
but have not gnawed away
even one particle of the hard bone.

Then the pure, bright Sabbath comes,
its glories spread across the earth—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-079–10-080. The initials and the target of the joke are not identified.

pages.title: The strange bone and a joke about army food
pages.text:
19
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Yet you have to take a double bite
Of this everlasting bone.

I too have been biting something very tough
The like of it I have never known
’Tis neither smooth nor very rough
Possibly it may be your bone?

When I used to be in the army
I ate everything to me thrown
For I knew it could not harm me
Although it was a dry bone.

But I am not so sure about this
For it makes my teeth ache, I own,
And I do not like the bliss
There is in gnawing on this bone.

’Tis different from anything I ever tried
Or anything I have ever known
So I will look over the world wide
To find a name for this bone.

’Tis neither duck nor goose nor chick
Nor of no hog with fat oer grown
But something mighty hard and Slick
So I am sure it is a bone.

’Tis not sheep nor deer nor horse
Nor anything in modern times grown
So I think as a matter of course

pages.title: The bone joke concluded and an album blessing
pages.text:
20
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
It must be of Balaams animal a bone.

So now you have my guess
(And for it I may groan)
So let us rig up a dress
To put upon our poor bone.

I think it should have a just desert
These cold and wintry weathers
So I propose an overshirt
Of genuine Tar and Feathers.
Seclusion. Dec 8th 1866

For an Album,
To grace thy Albums virgin leaf
From the depths of my soul I bring
Some purer thought where Love is chief
An unrestrained votive offering—
I place upon thy Friendships shrine
The heartfelt wish from on high
That for you the brightest suns may shine
And not a cloud oercast thy sky.
May flowers along thy pathway bloom
Of every hue which brightness yields
And hourly shed their sweet perfumes
From myriads of ambrosial fields,
May Love and health and happiness
Be thy lot wherever you go
And you be shorn of loneliness
And the [[obscured: ink blot]] flowing cup of woe.
Feb 12 1867.
Geo.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 20 concludes 10-078–10-079 with an allusion to Balaam’s animal and a proposal of tar and feathers. This is a satirical threat within verse, not evidence that an assault took place. A separate “For an Album” is dated February 12, 1867 and signed Geo. A blot obscures part of the final line.

I bring from the depths of my soul
a pure thought in which love comes first:

bloom along your path,

from countless heavenly fields.

be yours wherever you go.
May you be spared loneliness
and the [[word obscured]] flowing cup of sorrow.

February 12, 1867. Geo.

pages.title: An album poem on remembrance in sorrow
pages.text:
21
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
For an Album,

To grace an Albums virgin page
With thoughts and words both suited
For youthful prime and manly age
Is a task I have not mastered.

But since it is I must appear
With others here on Friendships scroll
I hope I will not be held more dear
If I should possess a deeper soul.

I ask no place in affections name
To remembrance when all is bright
For me it is too high a claim
To gayly seek with feelings light.

But when to you is widely given
Anguish fierce and burning draught
And from your heart is rudely driven
Friends whose health youve freely quaffed.

Oh! then remember one who loves
To [[illegible]] in [[illegible]] lie
One who through life careless roves
Nor breathes for others woes a sigh.
January 1867
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 21. Part of the second line of the final stanza remains unreadable after enlargement. The last line reads “Nor breathes for others woes a sigh”; it is not silently reversed to make a conventionally sympathetic ending. No author or recipient is named.

pages.family_title: An album poem on remembrance in sorrow
pages.family_text:
For an Album

I have not mastered the task
of adorning an album’s untouched page
with thoughts and words suitable
for both youth and mature adulthood.

But since I must appear
among the others on friendship’s record,
I hope I will not be valued more highly
merely for having a deeper soul.

I do not ask affection
to remember me when everything is bright.
That is too great a claim for me
to seek lightly and cheerfully.

But when you are given
fierce anguish and a bitter drink,
and friends whose health you have toasted
are roughly driven from your heart,

then remember one who loves
[[next line partly unreadable]],
one who wanders carelessly through life
and breathes no sigh for others’ sorrows.

January 1867.
pages.family_note: The final stanza may contain irony or difficult wording. Its apparent contradiction is preserved rather than rewritten as an uncomplicated promise of sympathy.

pages.title: To Miss M A A or fair Mary
pages.text:
22
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To Miss M. A. A.

When Heavens blue arch so gracefully bending
Above me brightly glows with loves azure hue
And the mind with sweet thoughts calmly ascending
Along that bright arch turns fair Mary to you.

As the needle with magnet faithfully thrilling
Still points to the pole so steady and true
So the deepest emotions of my hearts fond instilling
Drawn with true magnet fair Mary to you.

And when on the green grassy banks reclining
Of fair Red Oak, listening to its waters flowing there
The entrancing shades, above it so gracefully entwining
Fond Memory turns fair Mary to you.

The voices of waters songsters in those bowers dwellying
My wild restless Spirit does enchantingly woo
But still while I listen to the wild choral ringing
In rapture my heart turns fair Mary to you.

And like the Sunflower its fair face Extending
In the early morn ere it sheds the bright dew
To meet the bold gaze of its bright god ascending
So I open my heart fair Mary to you.

In the morning of Life I am now joyously standing
Before me is spread bright prospects sweet to view
With the gay Charm of Hope my heart is expanding
But they all point at last fair Mary to—you.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 22 continues through 10-084, where it is signed Geo. Douglas, Seclusion, October 15, 1866. Mary is named in the poem; her remaining initials are not expanded. “Red Oak” is named as a watercourse in the poem. Unusual syntax, such as “Drawn with true magnet,” is retained.

pages.family_title: To Miss M A A or fair Mary
pages.family_text:
To Miss M. A. A.

When heaven’s blue arch bends gracefully above me,
glowing with love’s azure color,
my mind rises calmly with sweet thoughts
and turns along that bright arch to you, fair Mary.

As a magnetized needle
points steadily and faithfully to the pole,
the deepest affectionate feelings in my heart
are drawn like a magnet to you, fair Mary.

When I recline on the green grassy banks
of fair Red Oak, listening to its flowing water,
with lovely shades intertwining above it,
my affectionate memory turns to you, fair Mary.

The voices of water and birds in those leafy bowers
enchant and draw my restless spirit.
Yet as I listen to their wild chorus,
my delighted heart turns to you, fair Mary.

Like a sunflower extending its face
in early morning, before the bright dew falls away,
to meet the bold gaze of its rising sun,
I open my heart to you, fair Mary.

I stand joyfully in the morning of life,
with bright, pleasant prospects before me.
Hope’s cheerful charm expands my heart,
but all those hopes finally point to you, fair Mary.
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-083–10-084. The poem names Mary but does not supply her full identity or establish that she reciprocated the writer’s feelings.

pages.title: The plea for Mary’s support
pages.text:
23
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Linked with the future how fondly entwining
Are the tendrils of my heart around the lovely & True
And as the vine on the tree so confidingly reclining
So my affections recline fair Mary on you.

But can I claim for them that substantial supporting
The tree yields the vine succeeding years through
And be securely screened against Cynics rude sporting
May I ever hope for this fair Mary from you!

While my cheek the soft wind of Autumn is fanning
And the forests have assumed the bright Sombre hue
While the beauties of nature I am rapturously scanning
Thought eagerly turns fair Mary to you.

When the bright plumaged birds their harmony swelling
In soft thrilling notes through scattering and few
Then my hearts pure emotions deeply are swelling
To Nature’s wild music fair Mary and you.

And when o’er earth Twilights dusky mantle is spreading
And peacefully we gaze the sky’s [[inserted: deep]] ether blue
Up that star spangled vault my thoughts are oft treading
And Fancy is weaving bright garlands for you.

The treasures of the heart she is modestly wreathing
With the gems of the Soul that lend their bright hue
Over all the Spirit of Affection she’s breathing
And Smilingly waves it fair Mary to you.

That Spirits bright beam my soul is beholding
Imagery paints on it joys brighter far anew
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 23 continues 10-082 and leads to 10-084. “Through scattering and few” is retained as written; it may have been intended as “though.” The closing two lines begin a stanza completed on the next page. The love and hope expressed belong to the speaker, not an established reciprocal relationship.

pages.family_title: The plea for Mary’s support
pages.family_text:
How fondly my heart’s tendrils entwine
around what is lovely and true in the future.
As a vine leans trustingly on a tree,
my affections lean on you, fair Mary.

But can I claim the lasting support
that a tree gives its vine through the years,
and secure protection from a cynic’s cruel mockery?
May I ever hope for this from you, fair Mary?

While autumn’s soft wind fans my cheek
and the forests take on their bright, somber color,
while I gaze delightedly at nature’s beauty,
my thoughts turn eagerly to you, fair Mary.

When brightly feathered birds swell their harmonies
in soft, thrilling notes, scattered and few,
my heart’s pure feelings rise deeply
for nature’s wild music and you, fair Mary.

When twilight spreads its dusky mantle over earth,
and we gaze peacefully into the deep blue sky,
my thoughts often climb that starry vault,
and imagination weaves bright garlands for you.

She modestly wreathes the heart’s treasures
with the soul’s brightly colored gems,
breathing affection over everything,
and smilingly waves the garland to you, fair Mary.

My soul beholds that spirit’s bright beam;
imagination paints still brighter joys upon it—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-084. The family reading smooths unusual syntax while preserving the uncertainty of the speaker’s hopes.

pages.title: George Douglas’s verses to Mary and To the Same
pages.text:
24
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Its rapturous beauties are sweetly unfolding
Yielding their brightness fair Mary to—you.

And still while its halo so beautifully beaming
With a soft lovely light so charming to view
My Soul is entranced with the visions so soft seeming
Yet breathes with devotion fair Mary to you.

Now I yield on thy Shrine Friendships first brightling
’Tis an offering of Faith which is but due
A few simple lines my Soul’s own inditing
From the depths of my heart fair Mary to you.
Geo. Douglas
Seclusion Oct 15th 1866

To The Same,

Oer the Orient sky the bright dawn is Streaming
Rousing Slumbering Nature from its dreamy repose
Through the forests there arises gaily so Screaming
The sweetest reveille from Minstrels gay foes
I spring from my couch—my visions bright seeming
Mingling with Natures in its reality true
Fading are the raptures of the last nights dreaming
Yet a deeper rapture awaits [[inserted: me]] fair Mary in you

The Sun from his bed gloriously is Springing
And up the bright east triumphantly rides
O’er the wide earth his rays gayly he is flinging
That bows in his gaze the loveliest of brides
And the music of Nature, the hymn she is Singing
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 24 concludes 10-082–10-083 with Geo. Douglas’s signature and October 15, 1866 date. “Friendships first brightling” is retained. “To the Same” then begins and continues at 10-085. The unusual wording “Minstrels gay foes” is transcribed as read, without replacing it with a conjectural bird phrase.

—its delightful beauties unfold sweetly,
yielding their brightness to you, fair Mary.

While its halo beams beautifully
with a soft, lovely light,
my soul is entranced by these gentle visions,
yet breathes devotion to you, fair Mary.

I now lay friendship’s first bright offering
upon your shrine: a fitting gift of faith.
These few simple lines are my soul’s own writing,
from the depths of my heart to you, fair Mary.

Geo. Douglas
Seclusion, October 15, 1866.

To the Same

Bright dawn streams across the eastern sky,
waking sleeping nature from its dreamlike rest.
Through the forests rises a cheerful chorus,
the sweetest morning reveille [[source’s phrase about the singers is unclear in meaning]].
I spring from my bed; my bright visions
mingle with nature’s living reality.
The delights of last night’s dreams fade,
but a deeper delight awaits me in you, fair Mary.

The sun springs gloriously from his bed
and rides triumphantly up the bright east,
cheerfully scattering his rays across the wide earth,
which bows beneath his gaze like the loveliest bride.
And nature’s music, the hymn she sings—

pages.title: Birdsong and a heavenly offering to Mary
pages.text:
25
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
In fondest adoration devoted and true
And while I hear its wild melody ringing
Affection then points me fair Mary to you.

In some distant bower I hear the soft cooing
Of the ring dove as it so closely keeps
Watch oer the bride of its hearts early wooing
That dreamily on a neighboring bough sleeps
And I fancy it has not known the hearts deep unresting
That afflicts us when we love the lovely and true
And has never known the ranging hopes of pursuing
As those I have felt fair Mary for you.

Now the lark from [[inserted: its]] dewy nest widely Springing
Soars far up on high oer the green coated plain
And amid the blue heavens sweetly is Singing
In the ear of its Maker natures wild strain,
In his viewless wake, my Soul I am flinging
Robed in a vesture of fair heavenly hue
And with the “music of the Spheres” my Spirit is ringing
Commingling their sweetness fair Mary for you.
Nov 186[[lost: remaining date at right edge]]

From Heavens high portals Angels are descending
Bearing their harps of bright golden hue—
To meet the bright host on Faiths wings ascending
My Spirit traverses the Skys ether blue.
Ten thousand voices in harmony blending
Bequeathed me an offering beautiful and true
Of Love in its brightness, all things Earthly, transcending
And bade me bear it fair Mary to you.
Jan 27–1867

pages.family_text:
—in devoted, faithful adoration.
As I hear its wild melody ring,
affection points me toward you, fair Mary.

In a distant bower I hear a ring dove cooing
as it keeps close watch
over the mate it courted in its early days,
who sleeps dreamily on a neighboring branch.
I imagine it has never known the heart’s deep restlessness
that troubles us when we love someone lovely and true,
or the wandering hopes of pursuing love
that I have felt for you, fair Mary.

Now a lark springs from its dewy nest
and soars high above the green plain,
singing nature’s wild music sweetly
in its Maker’s ear amid the blue heavens.
I send my soul along its invisible path,
clothed in lovely heavenly colors.
My spirit rings with the “music of the spheres,”
mixing their sweetness for you, fair Mary.

November 186[[last digit lost at the edge]].

Angels descend from heaven’s high gates,
carrying bright golden harps.
Rising on faith’s wings to meet that shining host,
my spirit crosses the blue sky.
Ten thousand voices, blending harmoniously,
gave me a beautiful, true offering
of radiant love surpassing everything earthly,
and told me to carry it to you, fair Mary.

January 27, 1867.
pages.family_note: The final stanza has a separate date from the preceding stanzas. Heavenly scenes are poetic imagery, not descriptions of documented events.

25
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
In fondest adoration devoted and true
And while I hear its wild melody ringing
Affection then points me fair Mary to you.

In some distant bower I hear the soft cooing
Of the ring dove as it so closely keeps
Watch oer the bride of its hearts early wooing
That dreamily on a neighboring bough sleeps
And I fancy it has not known the hearts deep unresting
That afflicts us when we love the lovely and true
And has never known the ranging hopes of pursuing
As those I have felt fair Mary for you.

Now the lark from [[inserted: its]] dewy nest widely Springing
Soars far up on high oer the green coated plain
And amid the blue heavens sweetly is Singing
In the ear of its Maker natures wild strain,
In his viewless wake, my Soul I am flinging
Robed in a vesture of fair heavenly hue
And with the “music of the Spheres” my Spirit is ringing
Commingling their sweetness fair Mary for you.
Nov 186[[lost: remaining date at right edge]]

From Heavens high portals Angels are descending
Bearing their harps of bright golden hue—
To meet the bright host on Faiths wings ascending
My Spirit traverses the Skys ether blue.
Ten thousand voices in harmony blending
Bequeathed me an offering beautiful and true
Of Love in its brightness, all things Earthly, transcending
And bade me bear it fair Mary to you.
Jan 27–1867

Dutch Campmeeting 1866.
In 1866 in September
I went to the campmeeting
And as well as I can remember
Received a very cordial greeting
The first of social joys which I took
Was a gentle sprinkling.
Thus I caught a forward look
And of what was coming got an inkling.
’Twas rain a shower and mud a heap
And drabbled dresses plenty
And I got many a sly peep
At tapering ankles from ten to twenty.
The camp accommodations were very poor
And it did not suit the lasses
To have to sit upon the floor
On straw in lieu of grasses.
Grasses they would have preferred beneath a willow
Soft yielding green dewy sparkling ever
And every lass of them a handsome fellow
To twain bright garland posies weaving ever
But alas! the difference, a preacher here
Restraining the free flow of chat
Between the gents and ladies fair
A thing they all would fain be at.
But after a while they bolder grew
And some got in the passage
And what do ye think they did do
When they got the passage?
Why they mixed all up together
In a crowd huddle—

pages.family_title: Dutch Campmeeting in September 1866
pages.family_text:
Dutch Camp Meeting, 1866

In September 1866
I went to the camp meeting.
As well as I can remember,
I received a very cordial welcome.
The first social pleasure I experienced
was a gentle sprinkling,
which gave me a preview
and a hint of what was coming.
There was a shower of rain and heaps of mud,
and plenty of mud-spattered dresses.
I caught many a sly glimpse
of slender ankles, ten or twenty of them.
The camp accommodations were poor.
The young women did not enjoy
sitting on the floor
on straw instead of grass.
They would have preferred soft, green,
dew-sparkling grass beneath a willow,
each with a handsome young man,
[[an awkward line about two people weaving flowers into garlands]].
But here the situation was different:
a preacher restrained the easy conversation
between gentlemen and young ladies,
which they would all gladly have enjoyed.
After a while they grew bolder,
and some went into the passage.
What do you think they did there?
They all mixed together
in a crowded huddle—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-087–10-090. This is comic and sometimes insulting social verse, not a neutral account.

pages.title: Camp meeting conversation and flirtation
pages.text:
27
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
And did not mind a bit the weather
Falling rain or Splashing puddle.
And now and then a softer word
I spect was slyly thrown in
And by the proper person heard
Who never thought it a bit o’ sin.
But this I do not know
I only simply guess it
But they had none to do
A great deal in the way of chat
Betimes they grew more confidential
As they got into a livelier mood
And some things were said potential
Which by the way were very good.
But I did not like the stile of compliments
Which was peped around off from the fence
Yet I do not think any one meant
To give to any other any offence.

There was a brace of widows there
Some ugly and very fat
They could hardly lay claim to being fair
Unless ’twas to that which was past
They eyed the boys and could talk
Upon a string peculiarly their own
Yet they could sit about or take a walk
And be the while entirely alone.
And then there was the handsome young misses
[[Gagging?]] about just in their teens
All made up for glorious hugs and kisses
Which a fellow might get on the sly I ween
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 27 continues 10-086 and leads to 10-088. Unusual syntax and “peped” are retained. The verb before “about” near the bottom is uncertain. Derogatory descriptions of widows and young women are the writer’s language, not editorial judgments.

pages.title: The camp meeting poem on flattery and courtship
pages.text:
28
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
How affectionate they looked so coy and sly
With their bright eyes glancing about
Seeming to say “if you will but try
The kisses you may have with a pout!”
By hokey! the favorite young devil
Who was smart enough to get a few smacks
Should I find him in manner quite civil
I’ll endeavor to walk in his tracks!
I will be all smiles and attention
And specially notice their slightest needs
Do everything that politeness could mention
And think of all things that it cant.
And always with the greatest deference
Will I lift my hat when I speak to them
And always manifest the greatest preference
For any thing to which they take the whim.
To please them so in a loving mood
I will tell them lies by the score
And if this does not do any good
I will tell them twice as many more.
Then if I see their brows gently reproving
I will instantly recant all I have said
And be so affectionate and loving
They will bestow blessings by the forewarning head,
In short I will bend as the willow
To every slight breath of the wind
And do everything in the world to pillow
My head on their bosoms so kind!

But I know there are some peevish creatures
Who long since have lost their lovely features
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 28 continues 10-087 and leads to 10-089. The unusual phrase “by the forewarning head” is retained as read; its meaning is uncertain. The boasts and imagined courtship behavior are part of a comic speaker’s voice, not established actions by an identified ancestor.

pages.family_title: The camp meeting poem on flattery and courtship
pages.family_text:
How affectionate they looked, so coy and sly,
their bright eyes glancing about,
as though saying, “If you only try,
you may get kisses, with a pout!”
By hokey, if I politely encounter
the lucky young devil
clever enough to get a few kisses,
I will try to follow his example.
I will be all smiles and attention,
noticing their smallest needs,
doing everything courtesy could suggest,
and thinking of everything it cannot.
I will always lift my hat respectfully
when I speak to them,
and show the greatest preference
for whatever catches their fancy.
To please them in a loving mood,
I will tell them scores of lies;
if that does no good,
I will tell twice as many more.
If their brows gently reproach me,
I will immediately take back everything I said,
and become so affectionate and loving
that they will shower me with blessings [[ending phrase unclear]].
In short, I will bend like a willow
to every slight breath of wind,
and do everything possible
to rest my head upon their kind bosoms!

But I know there are some irritable creatures
who long ago lost their lovely features—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-089. The manipulative courtship boasts are reproduced as satire, without endorsement or biographical inference.

pages.title: The camp meeting speaker answers his imagined critics
pages.text:
29
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Who will censure me quite severely
For all which I have here said sincerely,
And will dubiously say “he is a devilish scamp
And one too of the most outrageous stamp,
And, the girls should not allow such capers,
But give him at once his walking papers!”
Should some thus talk I can only say
That they have not known in lifes rugged way
The glorious pleasure, the enraptured bliss
That hovers around an endearing kiss
They are such persons as an aged tale avers
Of winning charms or gentle graces devoid
Who have so far gone Lifes journey all alone
To social joys and high vested bliss unknown,
Who have this [[Cythera’s?]] bright congenial shores
Plucked no fruits from its unrivaled bowers
But withered them all beneath a misanthropic Sun
Until their nobler feelings were forever gone
And now they stand upon Lifes verge
Whining to Youth and happiness a mournful dirge.

But when we meet a beauteous girl
The pride and envy of the world
Whose matchless beauty and faultless grace
Displays each lovely feature of form and face
Where from a high and classic brow
The raven tresses fall around a neck of snow,
And from her dark eyes deep lustrous hue
The beaming soul looks unimprisoned through,
He who can these innumered there uniting art
And not feel the fond effect of Cupids dart—
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 29 continues 10-088 and leads to 10-090. The geographic or mythological name before “bright congenial shores” is uncertain; Cythera is a tentative reading only. Several grammatically irregular lines remain as written. The attacks on critics are the speaker’s rhetoric.

pages.title: The camp meeting poem concludes with an imagined embrace
pages.text:
30
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
His soul is dead to all thats fair and dear
And from the most unpropitious climes not a tear
But will sink into an unhonored tomb
Fit sequel to his lifes deep seated gloom.

Ah! when I meet [[deleted: illegible]] maiden fair
With “azure eyes and golden hair”
With moulded limbs elastic tread
With dimpled cheeks and fairy head,
With sunny smiles and nymphly charms
And noble mien my bosom warms
With all those chaste sweet desires
The wand of Love so oft inspires,
And when her yielding hand I clasp
In affections ardent grasp
And gently draw unto my breast
The object where my fondest feelings rest
And meet the glance of the soul lit eye
And hear the short yet deep heaving sigh
While from a puckered lip all fair
Backward flows her waving hair
And with the sweetish of caress
Her living lips to mine she press
Sending thro my deepest soul
Affections springs which spurn control
The wild enchanting raptures tell
Of the wide world exists all in this.
Sept 1866

—has a soul dead to everything lovely and dear.
[[An awkward line concerns harsh circumstances and the absence of a tear.]]
He will sink into an unhonored grave,
a fitting end to his life’s deep gloom.

Ah, when I meet a fair young woman
with “azure eyes and golden hair,”
well-formed limbs and a springing step,
dimpled cheeks and a delicate head,
sunny smiles, graceful charms,
and noble bearing, my heart warms
with all those pure, sweet desires
that love so often inspires.
When I clasp her willing hand
in an ardent, affectionate grip,
and gently draw to my breast
the person who holds my deepest feelings,
meet the glance of her soul-lit eye,
and hear her short but deep sigh,
while her waving hair falls backward
from her lovely, pursed lips,
and with a sweet caress
she presses her living lips to mine,
affection beyond control
rushes through the depths of my soul.
Those wild, enchanting delights suggest
that the whole world exists in this moment.

September 1866.

pages.title: Idle Hours on lost hopes and storms
pages.text:
31
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Idle Hours.

I can for hours watch the tempest fly
And listen to the deep mouthed thunder roar
As they roll in grandeur in the sky
Where all was peace and quiet once before.

And a wild companionship I own
With these fierce scenes of strife,
Now that my serener peace is gone
In the rude blasts of early life.

Once was my sky bright blue and clear
And every hope of pleasure gave
But now alas! all is dull and drear
And fondest hopes lie withered in the grave.

What once was spread with fairest flowers
And where sweetest fruit in prospect gleamed
When pleasure winged the golden hours
And light and life and joy all seemed
To be upon my pathway bright spread
With happiness the vision bright
All fraught with bliss before me laid
In one long line of gleaming light.

I little dreamed of this dark hour
When Peace I’d woo from wildest strife
Or thought I’d subject be to the dark power
Which blasted thus my early life
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 31 continues at the top of 10-092, dated Seclusion, August 23, 1866. “What once” and the unusual syntax of the longer stanza are retained. The poem’s buried hopes and blighted life are figurative statements, not proof of a named bereavement.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours on lost hopes and storms
pages.family_text:
Idle Hours

I can watch the storm for hours
and listen to the deep-voiced thunder,
rolling majestically across the sky
where everything was once peaceful and quiet.

I feel a wild kinship
with these fierce scenes of conflict,
now that my calmer peace has vanished
in the harsh blasts of early life.

My sky was once clear and bright blue,
and every hope promised pleasure.
Now everything is dull and dreary,
and my dearest hopes lie withered in the grave.

What once was covered with lovely flowers,
where the sweetest fruit seemed to lie ahead,
when pleasure gave wings to golden hours
and everything seemed light, life, and joy,
spread brightly along my path—
that shining vision of happiness,
filled with bliss, lay before me
in one long line of gleaming light.

I scarcely imagined this dark hour,
when I would seek peace in the fiercest conflict,
or thought I would submit to the dark power
that has blighted my early life.
pages.family_note: Concludes at 10-092. The imagery expresses sorrow but does not identify its cause.

pages.title: Idle Hours concluded and memories of an oasis in life
pages.text:
32
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
But so it is, with callous heart
I face the world nor fear its scorn
Conscious still that I can bear my part
Though deeper in my bosom press the thorn.
Seclusion Aug 23rd 1866

[[separate block: a second poem, main text continuing into the lower right margin]]
While backward gazing through the lapse of years
A lone oasis in my early life appears
Beautifully verdured and flowery fair
And draped in brightness richly rare
There Sunshine played o’er [[inserted: each]] happy scene
And enchanting beauties shed their silver sheen
Upon the vernal air, in bright relief
To Lifes surrounding wastes of gloomy grief.

Careless I strayed its glorious aisles among
Where mid embowering sweets still sweeter sung
Innocent warblers their soul stirring lays
Adding music’s bliss to each unclouding maze—
Blinded by the beauteous scenes I saw around
Methought these scenes so bright would always abound
That downward in Life’s meandering march
Such beauteous bowers would forever arch
Amid my pathway and lend their brightest hues
To shed a soft delight and milder joys infuse.

But soon the glowing pageant [[inserted: swiftly]] passed
And before me lay Lifes dreary waste
Its scorching sands far spread before the eye
Where fierce Simoons of Hate hurl them on high
Burying beneath its fiercely burning sway
Each nobler passion that might chance to stray
Oft in the desert heart where once sweetly stood
All the purer instincts of the generously good,
But where nought now of pleasures hopes remains
Except the sad Remembrance—“it can ne’er come again!”
Jan 14th 1867
George Douglas

[[separate block: separate verse in upper right margin]]
There is a loneliness of the heart
No words can e’er express
Too deep for Sorrows tears to start
To relieve the aching breast
A joyless motionless [[moodly?]] waste
All dark and drear, forlorn
And every lovely flower thats placed
Upon it hides a poisonous thorn.
G. D.

D. The marginal writing was rotated for reading. “Simoons” denotes the poem’s hot desert winds; the metaphors do not establish travel to a desert. The word before “waste” in the short verse remains uncertain.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours concluded and memories of an oasis in life
pages.family_text:
But so it is. With a hardened heart,
I face the world without fearing its scorn,
still knowing I can bear my part,
though the thorn presses deeper into my breast.

Seclusion, August 23, 1866.

A second poem

Looking back through the years,
I see a single oasis in my early life,
beautifully green and filled with flowers,
clothed in rare, rich brightness.
Sunshine played over every happy scene,
and enchanting beauties cast a silver glow
through the spring air, a bright contrast
to life’s surrounding wasteland of sorrow.

Carefree, I wandered its glorious paths.
Among the lovely bowers, innocent birds
sang still sweeter, soul-stirring songs,
adding music’s happiness to each clear, winding way.
Dazzled by the beautiful scenes around me,
I thought they would always be plentiful:
that, as I followed life’s wandering course,
such lovely bowers would always arch
across my path, lending their brightest colors
to create gentle delight and quiet happiness.

But the glowing spectacle quickly passed,
and life’s dreary wasteland lay before me.
Its scorching sands stretched into the distance,
where hatred’s fierce desert winds lifted them,
burying beneath their burning force
every noble feeling that happened to wander there.
In the deserted heart where once stood
all the generous instincts of goodness,
no hope of pleasure now remains
except the sad memory: “It can never come again!”

January 14, 1867. George Douglas.

A separate marginal verse

There is a loneliness of the heart
that words can never express,
too deep for sorrow’s tears
to relieve the aching breast:
a joyless, motionless, [[uncertain adjective]] wasteland,
all dark, dreary, and abandoned,
where every lovely flower placed upon it
conceals a poisonous thorn.

G. D.
pages.family_note: The three pieces and their dates are kept separate. The sorrow is real as literary expression; its biographical cause is not supplied here.

32
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]

I face the world nor fear its scorn
Conscious still that I can bear my part
Though deeper in my bosom press the thorn.
Seclusion Aug 23rd 1866

[[separate block: a second poem, main text continuing into the lower right margin]]
While backward gazing through the lapse of years
A lone oasis in my early life appears
Beautifully verdured and flowery fair
And draped in brightness richly rare
There Sunshine played o’er [[inserted: each]] happy scene
And enchanting beauties shed their silver sheen
Upon the vernal air, in bright relief
To Lifes surrounding wastes of gloomy grief.

Careless I strayed its glorious aisles among
Where mid embowering sweets still sweeter sung
Innocent warblers their soul stirring lays
Adding music’s bliss to each unclouding maze—
Blinded by the beauteous scenes I saw around
Methought these scenes so bright would always abound
That downward in Life’s meandering march
Such beauteous bowers would forever arch
Amid my pathway and lend their brightest hues
To shed a soft delight and milder joys infuse.

But soon the glowing pageant [[inserted: swiftly]] passed
And before me lay Lifes dreary waste
Its scorching sands far spread before the eye
Where fierce Simoons of Hate hurl them on high
Burying beneath its fiercely burning sway
Each nobler passion that might chance to stray
Oft in the desert heart where once sweetly stood
All the purer instincts of the generously good,
But where nought now of pleasures hopes remains
Except the sad Remembrance—“it can ne’er come again!”
Jan 14th 1867
George Douglas

[[separate block: separate verse in upper right margin]]
There is a loneliness of the heart
No words can e’er express
Too deep for Sorrows tears to start
To relieve the aching breast
A joyless motionless [[moodly?]] waste
All dark and drear, forlorn
And every lovely flower thats placed
Upon it hides a poisonous thorn.
G. D.

pages.title: The anonymous courtship poem resumes with Seclusion
pages.text:
33
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Continued from 9th page.
But amid all this confusion
What has became of “Seclusion”?
I saw him on the fourth of July
Slipping about rather sly
Squinting first at this then that one
For the world like a chap undone.
And—list! oh ye many Stars and
I saw him close beside Miss McFarland
And at that time I’ve “hearn tell”
He was seen to fan Miss Maggie Bell.

But still I say tis all in vain howies
You may around about you peer
And strive to find out my incog
Safe I fire from behind a log
And hit them all a few times more
Until they fume as neer they fumed before
I care not, let them fret and roar
And use their voices till their throats are sore
The only satisfaction that I have
Is to see my fellow mortals rave.

But I felt myself vastly flattered
When oer those pages Freely plastered
And pronounced me with decision sage
The greatest poet of the modern age.

When first I heard this lofty eulogium
Upon my merits—the glorious vision
Of Fame undying—transport elysium
Shot through my heart with unrivalled precision

pages.title: The comic poet’s disappointed hopes for Kitty and Laura
pages.text:
34
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Which made me feel like a modern Pope
And bade me for eternal honors hope.

But unto you before whom poets bow
With deep heartfelt adoration
Will you listen at me now
While I narrate a sad narration.
This fond heart at last is broken
“Because no one will me love”
Although the words which I have spoken
Were inspired from above.

Once I thought I would write a ditty
To the handsome pleasant little Kitty
But as the lines I began to trace
There came along one Samuel Pace
And with his earnest gesticulations
Spoilt all my handsome calculations
So I had to seek for a new bower
To try again my magic power
Which by the way is not so magical
As has been fully proved by all.

Next in my view came Pleasant hill
In all its glory blooming still
And I thought I could neer be dreary
While there smiled a lovely Laura,
So with the best of all my art
I bound up my shattered heart
And dressed it in the gayest smiles
That ever bloomed on earth the while,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 34 continues 10-093 and leads to 10-095. Kitty, Samuel Pace, Laura, and Pleasant hill are named in the verse, but their identities and the literal truth of the romantic competition are not established. “A modern Pope” is a literary allusion in a boast about poetry; no external attribution is asserted.
