pages.title: Sammy wins Laura in the poem’s mock campaign
pages.text:
35
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
And thought to offer on her altar
A love that would never never falter,
But alas! for all my speculations
How they are spoilt by oppositions.

For you see at last there came
The backward bashful modest Sam
And urged his suit with so much ardor
That I seriously thought of gunpowder,
But I knew if I wrought his ruin
’Twould be also my own undoin,
So I acted fairly on my part
But Sammy won dear Lauras heart
And left me like a lamb shorn
Out in the cold my loss to mourn.

Before the Delphine Shrine I could bow
And plead my cause with ardor now
But I have not the will [[deleted: to charge]]
To charge against strong Prospect Hill.
Two Generals are entrenched there
Within the hearts of the lovely Fair
And a poor Corporal has no chance
To force them out with spear or lance,
But must at once raise the siege
And seek another nearer leige.

Go where I will where can I find
One more suited to my mind?
Than you fair maid? whose purest love
Is gently distilled from above
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 35 continues 10-094 and leads to 10-096. “Delphine” and “leige” are retained as written. Generals, corporal, gunpowder, and siege belong to the courtship metaphor and do not establish military ranks or a violent incident. The poem claims Sammy won Laura’s heart; this is not a marriage record.

pages.title: The courtship poem ends with a plea and two epigrams
pages.text:
36
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
The noble passions that to thy heart is given
Are but affections Strayed from Heaven
And upon natures own bestown that heart of thine
Receives direct a gift divine.
Can it be wrong for me to seek
That love, of which I scarce dare speak?
Oh no! that which is to mortals given
Should be by mortals owned although from Heaven.
July 30th 1866

[[separate block: two short verses below]]
If it be true that all still waters
Indicate a deep hole
I suppose an old maids clatter
Betokens a mighty shoal.

“Married life is a great source of happiness”
Designing Sapheads conjecture
But they [[deleted: illegible]] will change their minds soon I guess
“When they receive a curtain lecture!”

pages.title: Idle Hours on childhood innocence
pages.text:
37
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Idle Hours.

The first the fondest purest hopes
Of Lifes bright sunny hour
Bloom fresh within a narrow scope
Like Springs bright vernal flower.

Then does the mind expanding glow
Beneath a genial Sun
And joys bright perennial flow
Yet still their source is one.

That source is guileless innocence
By the infant heart expressed
Breathing a holy sweet incense
Upon its mothers breast.

And angels hover oer its way
On Spirit wings afar
To turn each else baneful ray
That its purity might mar.

And weeping oer each wayward thought
That Springs within its mind
Lest all thats lovely comes to nought
Which speaks its will divine,

But alas! what are Angels tears?
Or what can they avail?
When through the blight of after years
We read the hearts sad tale.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 37 continues at 10-098, dated Seclusion, August 26, 1866. The poem’s infant, mother, angels, and later despair are generalized images. No particular child or mother is identified.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours on childhood innocence
pages.family_text:
Idle Hours

The first, dearest, purest hopes
of life’s bright, sunny hour
bloom freshly within a small world,
like a bright flower in spring.

The growing mind then glows
beneath a kindly sun,
and bright joys continually flow,
yet all come from a single source.

That source is innocent simplicity,
expressed by the infant’s heart,
breathing like sweet, sacred incense
upon its mother’s breast.

Angels hover over its path
on distant spiritual wings,
turning aside every harmful ray
that might spoil its purity.

They weep over each wayward thought
that arises in its mind,
fearing that all its divine loveliness
might come to nothing.

But alas, what are angels’ tears?
What can they accomplish
when, through the troubles of later years,
we read the heart’s sad story?
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-098. This is a philosophical poem, not evidence of a specific childhood or death.

pages.title: Idle Hours concludes with grief for lost innocence
pages.text:
38
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Of hopes once bright now faded gone
With happier hours past by
Leaving the heart a hardened stone
With all affections fountains dry.

And Disappointment too deeply written
Upon Lifes dreary page
And earlier joys forever smitten
And withering in declining age,

With life a blank, and Sorrow stamped
Upon the wrinkled brow
And Memory embittered damped
With scenes of by gone woe.

And dark Despair still hovering oer
The shattered wreck of Man
Nor hope can lend upon Times shore
One ray to cheer him on again.

Then what avail are angels tears
Since we must suffer so
And reap through succeeding years
Succeeding fields of woe?

Oh! it is best in Childhoods time,
To find an early grave
And return to Heaven undimmed
The jewel which it gave!
Seclusion Aug 26th 1866
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 38 concludes 10-097, dated August 26, 1866. The final stanza imagines an early grave as preserving childhood innocence. It is literary and religious reflection, not a death notice or evidence that a particular child died.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours concludes with grief for lost innocence
pages.family_text:
It tells of hopes once bright, now faded and gone,
with happier hours behind them,
leaving the heart a hardened stone
and every spring of affection dry.

Disappointment is written too deeply
upon life’s dreary page.
Earlier joys are struck down forever,
withering as age advances.

Life is empty, sorrow stamped
upon a wrinkled brow,
and memory embittered and weighed down
by scenes of past unhappiness.

Dark despair still hovers
over the shattered human wreck.
On time’s shore, hope can offer
no ray to encourage him again.

What use, then, are angels’ tears,
if we must suffer this way
and harvest, year after year,
successive fields of sorrow?

Oh, the speaker says, it is better in childhood
to find an early grave
and return to heaven, still undimmed,
the jewel that heaven gave.

Seclusion, August 26, 1866.

pages.title: Idle Hours at sunset beside a stream
pages.text:
39
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Idle Hours,

The Sun was sinking in the west
Deep in an azure sky
Nature slowly retiring to rest
Hymned its music far on high.
Forth from a cozy fireside I
Strayed alone in musing mood
Down near a Streamlet murmuring by
A deep and Solitary wood.
And passions hot my bosom fired
O’erwing my senses in headlong speed
Ambition urged to win the admired
And gain a heart the wished meed,
A wreath of beauty yet afar
On lifes uncertain Sea,
Yet none the less a glorious star
Tho’ veiled in deep uncertainty.

I tracked upon Lifes future road
My devious way unto the prize
Where I could lay my heart felt load
Of Love before her Soul-lit eyes;

’Tis sweet to look adown the tide of Time
And see awaiting glories shine
’Tis sweet to hear their voices chime
And fancy their blending beauties mine.
’Tis sweet to think that I may win
A heart my weary way to cheer
Through hours of Darkness intervene—
A Starless night’s monotonously drear,
Continued on page 52
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 39 has a continuation reference read as page 52. The writer imagines winning an unnamed beloved’s heart; this is hope, not proof of a relationship. Some grammar is irregular and has not been silently repaired in the reference transcript. The continuation is at 10-112 (manuscript page 52), which explicitly refers back to page 39, and then 10-113.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours at sunset beside a stream
pages.family_text:
Idle Hours

The sun was sinking in the west
into a deep blue sky.
Nature slowly retired to rest,
singing its music high above.
I left a cozy fireside
and wandered alone in a thoughtful mood,
down near a murmuring stream
beside a deep, solitary wood.
Hot passions fired my heart,
racing ahead of my senses.
Ambition urged me to win the woman I admired,
and gain her heart as my desired reward:
a wreath of beauty still far away
on life’s uncertain sea,
yet no less a glorious star
though hidden by deep uncertainty.

I traced my winding course
down life’s future road toward that prize,
where I could lay my heartfelt burden
of love before her soul-lit eyes.

It is sweet to look down time’s current
and see awaiting glories shine,
to hear their voices harmonize
and imagine their combined beauty as mine.
It is sweet to think I may win
a heart to cheer my weary journey,
though dark hours come between us,
like the monotonous gloom of a starless night.

The manuscript directs the reader to page 52.

pages.title: An apology to Miss M L G for the anonymous rhymes
pages.text:
40
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To Miss M. L. G.....

Throughout the livelong day amid the crowds
I patient sat and listened to the thundring words
Of a long sermon delivered to the sinners
Who were kept in the heat without their dinners.

It may be well for Christian folks to fast
But feed the sinners if you would keep them to the last
Lest they become uneasy and run away
And get no Salvation on that day.

But Saint and Sinner vanished from my mind
And the good preacher with his words so kind
When low amid the crowded clan
Some idle vacant whisperings ran,

That you were offended like the Nation
At an anonymous Communication
Which had been dished up in rhyme
And forwarded to [[lifless?]] rhyme thrice.

And you thought the author of the rhyming clatter
Had surely overdone the matter
And in his Simple little Song
Had piled it on rather Too Strong.

I am misfortunes favorite child
For all my noblest hopes are foiled
By my impassioned nature drives
My Sentiment thoughts I fondly pen
So ever tho I Strike on the lyre
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 40 continues at 10-101, dated August 15, 1866. The line about forwarding the rhyme contains uncertain or awkward wording. “By my impassioned nature drives” and the final lines are retained despite irregular syntax. This poem refers to the recipient’s reported offense at anonymous verses; it does not establish the identities behind the earlier sobriquets.

pages.family_title: An apology to Miss M L G for the anonymous rhymes
pages.family_text:
To Miss M. L. G.

All through the long day, among the crowd,
I sat patiently listening to the thunderous words
of a long sermon addressed to sinners,
kept in the heat without their dinners.

Fasting may be good for Christian people,
but feed the sinners if you want them to stay until the end,
lest they become restless and run away
without receiving salvation that day.

But saint, sinner, and the kindly preacher
all vanished from my thoughts
when quiet, idle whispers
ran through the crowded gathering.

They said you were terribly offended
by an anonymous communication,
served up in rhyme
[[an unclear line about its being forwarded three times]].

You thought the author of the noisy rhymes
had certainly gone too far
and, in his simple little song,
had laid it on much too strongly.

I am misfortune’s favorite child,
for all my noblest hopes are frustrated.
[[An awkward line describes my passionate nature.]]
I fondly write down my sentimental thoughts,
yet whenever I strike the lyre—

But feed the sinners if you would keep them to the last
Lest they become uneasy and run away
And get no Salvation on that day.

But Saint and Sinner vanished from my mind
And the good preacher with his words so kind
When low amid the crowded clan
Some idle vacant whisperings ran,

That you were offended like the Nation
At an anonymous Communication
Which had been dished up in rhyme
And forwarded to [[lifless?]] rhyme thrice.

And you thought the author of the rhyming clatter
Had surely overdone the matter
And in his Simple little Song
Had piled it on rather Too Strong.

I am misfortunes favorite child
For all my noblest hopes are foiled
By my impassioned nature drives
My Sentiment thoughts I fondly pen
So ever tho I Strike on the lyre

pages.title: The anonymous poet offers an apology
pages.text:
41
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
And always overshot the mark,

I every passion in one effort fling
And aim to reach the goal at one bold Spring
So ever thus my fondest hopes I blast
By being just a little bit too fast.

I am extremely sorry and would apologize
For having written to you in this wise,
If I knew how—but I cannot claim
The honor of approaching you by name.

But if I thought I could win your partial favor
I would throw off my disguise and endeavor
To rush to your presence half annihilated by fear
And plead my case like a Lawyer at the bar.

I would not have any words to retrace
And speak the whole truth in their place
Unless I supply some new compliment
With deeper feelings fully blent.

I would not hurt your feelings for the world
(Allow me to except one lovely girl).
And would humbly humbly apologize
And hope to read my pardon in your eyes.

When I write to you again
I will select a nobler Strain
[[deleted: To descend]] And invoke the Parnassian Nine
To descend and my vulgar thoughts refine,
Aug 15th /66

pages.title: Invocation dedicated to Miss M L Green perhaps
pages.text:
42
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Respectfully Inscribed to Miss M. L. [[Green?]]
Invocation

Come ye heavenly Sister band
From Parnassus height
Come and with the starry brand
Of Inspiration my pen relight
Come let the thoughts of Heaven refined
Flash through my heart inspire my mind
With all those feelings pure and bright
Which emanate from the source of light.
Let no corruptive thought their powers blend
With these true words I dedicate to a friend
But let the noblest sentiment that ever rose
In the human breast descend from the Stars
Nor lose upon their lengthy flight
The Stamps of Heavens refulgent light
But let them glow transcendentally fair
As ever they did within their native Star
Ere baser Passions taught the human heart
To act the lie or show deceptions art.

Yes, Pure Friendship demands a nobler offering
Than aught that earthly treasure E’er can bring
Something pure which flows from heart to heart
Which wit with all its Schemes cannot impart;
But bears upon its face the impress of the Soul
Which friend to friend from time to time may candidly unroll
And now upon fair Friendships Shrine
I place this Simple offering of mine,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 42 continues at 10-103, dated Seclusion, August 21, 1866. The dedication appears to give the surname Green, but the letters after the capital are indistinct; it remains a tentative reading. The nearby poems use M. L. G. and may concern the same person, but the full identity is not established. The classical invocation is literary imagery.

pages.family_text:
Respectfully inscribed to Miss M. L. [[Green?]]
Invocation

Come, heavenly sisterhood of Muses,
from the heights of Parnassus.
Come with inspiration’s starry torch
and rekindle my pen.
Let heaven’s refined thoughts
flash through my heart and inspire my mind
with all the pure, bright feelings
that come from the source of light.
Let no corrupting thought mingle its power
with these true words I dedicate to a friend.
Let the noblest feelings ever held
in a human heart descend from the stars.
May their long journey never dim
the imprint of heaven’s radiant light.
Let them glow as wonderfully fair
as they did in their native star,
before baser passions taught the human heart
to lie or practice deception.

Yes, pure friendship deserves a nobler offering
than earthly treasure can provide:
something pure that flows from heart to heart,
which cleverness and all its schemes cannot give.
It bears the soul’s imprint,
which one friend may honestly reveal to another.
On the shrine of fair friendship,
I now place this simple offering—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-103. The surname in the dedication is tentative; it should not yet be added to the family tree as certain.

pages.title: Trust as the strongest bond of friendship
pages.text:
43
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
’Tis Confidence, the first flower in the wreath of Love
Which I now bestow a boon drawn from above
Inspired by Heaven in thy Stainless truth,
(The noblest gift now owned by mortal youth)
Accept it, for within it lies
The strongest links in Friendships holy ties.

Then will the Social joys live again
And within our hearts supremely reign
And base Detraction hurled from his high seat
Into the dust and trampled ’neath our feet
Can rise no more in a hideous form
To shake our trust or mar our joys so warm,
Joys which will in long succession rise
And date their birthright from the skies
And through successive ages roll
The light of life, the adamant of the soul
Strengthening through succeeding years
Erasing darkening doubts, dispelling gloomy fears.

A Panacea for all human woes
Which the unwilling future may disclose
Leaving Nature in its purest mood
When with pulses high and madly bounding blood
The human breast by contending passions wildly driven
Exiles Mercy from its home, defying Heaven
Heaven with all its deep emotions pure
Which requires no grosser props our to insure
Through our downward march to Lifes ending scene
Noble thoughts divine, deep, bright, and serene.
Seclusion August 21st 1866
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 43 concludes “Invocation” at 10-102. The date is August 21, 1866. “Which requires no grosser props our to insure” is awkward wording retained as read; the family version gives its apparent general sense without inventing a missing object. “Adamant” is used as a metaphor for something enduring or unyielding.

pages.family_title: Trust as the strongest bond of friendship
pages.family_text:
—trust, the first flower in love’s wreath,
which I give as a gift from above,
inspired by heaven and your spotless truth,
the noblest gift a young person can possess.
Accept it, for it contains
the strongest links in friendship’s sacred bonds.

Then the pleasures of companionship will live again
and reign within our hearts.
Base slander, thrown from its high seat
into the dust and trampled underfoot,
will never again rise in a hideous form
to shake our trust or spoil our warm happiness.
Those joys will follow one another for years,
claiming their birthright from the skies.
They will continue through successive ages,
the light of life and the soul’s enduring strength,
growing stronger through the years,
erasing dark doubts and driving away gloomy fears.

They are a cure for every human sorrow
that the reluctant future may reveal,
leaving nature in its purest state.
Even when high pulses and racing blood,
driven by conflicting passions,
banish mercy from the heart and defy heaven,
heaven still holds pure, deep feelings
that need no coarse support [[wording uncertain in sense]].
May they sustain, through our journey to life’s end,
thoughts that are noble, divine, deep, bright, and serene.

Seclusion, August 21, 1866.
pages.family_note: This is a modern rendering of the poem’s argument about trust and friendship. Irregular wording is preserved in the reference transcript.

pages.title: Written on the death of Robert D Andrews
pages.text:
44
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Written on the death of
Robert D. Andrews,

I stood beside his Soulless clay
And coffined breast
And saw the hopes of yesterday
In death’s robe drest.
I heard the solemn service read
The funeral rite
The last tribute to the noble dead
Shrouded in white.

“Before us lays his mortal form
His Spirit fled
“His voice our hearts no more will warm
For he is dead.
“Though gone and we shall see no more
Him that we love
“Yet One has passed on before
To Heaven above,
“That One has borne the shameful cross
On Calvary,
“He rejects alone the worthless dross
Of mortality,
“The Soul, the Gem, that Heaven gave
So pure and bright
“Shall safely pass beyond the grave
To realms of light.
“Upon its threshold we may meet
To part no more
“And those we’ve loved shall sweetly greet
Us on that Shore,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 44 begins an elegy continued through the upper part of 10-106, where it is signed George Douglas and dated Seclusion, December 24, 1866. The heading names Robert D. Andrews. The poem records a funeral and later calls him a friend and companion of the speaker’s youth; it does not give an age, kinship, burial location, or precise date of death. Quotation marks indicate a passage voiced as a funeral address, not a verified verbatim sermon.

pages.family_title: Written on the death of Robert D Andrews
pages.family_text:
Written on the Death of Robert D. Andrews

I stood beside his lifeless body
and his breast enclosed in a coffin,
and saw yesterday’s hopes
dressed in death’s clothing.
I heard the solemn funeral service,
the last tribute to the noble dead,
who lay shrouded in white.

“His mortal body lies before us;
his spirit has departed.
His voice will no longer warm our hearts,
for he is dead.
Though he is gone and we shall see
our loved one no more,
One has gone before him
to heaven above.
That One carried the shameful cross
on Calvary.
He rejects only the worthless remainder
of our mortal existence.
The soul, the jewel heaven gave,
so pure and bright,
will pass safely beyond the grave
into realms of light.
We may meet at their threshold
and never part again.
Those we have loved will warmly greet us
upon that shore—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-105–10-106. This is a named memorial poem, but its composition date should not be substituted for Andrews’s death date.

pages.title: A friend and companion of the poet’s youth
pages.text:
45
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Slowly the Shroud around him wound
Its spotless folds
Then deep was laid beneath the ground
Affections holds.
Friend and companion of my youth
Though death has come
It could not blast the lovely Truth
That bore thee home.
Though we shall meet no more on earth
Thy memory
In my hours of wildest mirth
Shall sacred be.
“And though I run Lifes mad career
Wild as the wave,”
I’ll pause, and drop, fond Friendship’s tear,
Upon thy grave.
When Spring in beauty bright shall come
And robe the trees,
The rose shall shed its sweet perfume
Upon the breeze.
The daisy on the verdant lea
Shall sweetly blow
And Natures wildest minstrelsy
Joyously flow.
No more with thee shall these bright scenes
Pass in review
For all that earthly pleasure means
Has passed from you.
No more with thee we’ll greet the morn
When carols sweet
On fragrant winds to Heaven are borne
An offering meet
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 45 continues the elegy for Robert D. Andrews at 10-104 and leads to 10-106. “Affections holds” is the awkward phrase as read. The poem explicitly says “Friend and companion of my youth”; it does not say cousin, brother, or another kinship.

Slowly the spotless shroud
wrapped its folds around him.
Then affection’s beloved one
was laid deep beneath the ground.
Friend and companion of my youth,
though death has come,
it could not destroy the beautiful truth
that carried you home.
Though we will never meet again on earth,
your memory will remain sacred,
even in my most carefree hours.
“Though I pursue life’s wild course,
as restless as the waves,”
I will pause to shed friendship’s affectionate tear
upon your grave.
When spring returns in bright beauty
and clothes the trees,
the rose will release its sweet perfume
upon the breeze.
Daisies will bloom sweetly
in the green meadow,
and nature’s wild music
will flow joyfully.
We will no longer share
these beautiful scenes,
for every earthly pleasure
has passed away from you.
We will no longer greet the morning together,
when sweet songs rise to heaven
on fragrant winds,
a fitting offering—

pages.title: George Douglas’s farewell to Andrews and Ad idem
pages.text:
46
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To Natures God, who rules above
In purity
The Universes, with the Laws of love
Through eternity.
With thee no more will we hear
These raptures rise
And in their inspiration clear
Ascend the skies,
For thou art gone, beyond Death’s gloom
In Heaven to dwell
And I can but breathe upon thy tomb
A last farewell.
Seclusion Dec 24th 1866
George Douglas

Ad idem,
Oh! come with me to a lone graveyard
Where the oak trees wave their stately boughs
Where the sunshine on the soft greensward
And the daisy in its beauty blows.

Where warbling birds on their brilliant wings
Hymn their sweetest notes in the forest near—
Where the heart melted by soft reflection springs
Heavenward through the deeply sorrowing tear,

Oh come! and kneel by a fresh made mound
Where the violet never has bloomed
Lowly bend over the damp cold ground
Where the early dead is deeply entombed
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 46 concludes 10-104–10-105, signed George Douglas, Seclusion, December 24, 1866. “Ad idem” introduces a separate poem on the same subject, continuing at 10-107. The graveyard is described but not named. “Where the sunshine” is retained without supplying an absent verb.

—to nature’s God, who rules the universes
from above in purity,

On the Same Subject

Come with me to a lonely graveyard,
where oak trees wave their stately branches,
sunshine lies on the soft green turf,
and daisies bloom in beauty.

There brightly winged birds
sing their sweetest notes in the nearby forest.
The heart, softened by quiet reflection,
rises toward heaven through deeply sorrowful tears.

Come and kneel beside a newly made mound,
where violets have never yet bloomed.
Bend low over the damp, cold earth,
where someone who died young lies deeply buried.

pages.title: Ad idem concludes with Courtesy and truth
pages.text:
47
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Drop here a tear with the broken hearted
That live to mourn the loved and lost
And the cherished hopes death has thwarted
With the blasting blight of its early frost.

In affection weep! oer Sundered ties
Woven in lifes bright early may-morn.
Weep for the one that now lowly lies
Where the pain racked heart ne’er may mourn.

His hopes his joys and prospects are past
Like the dews of the morning swiftly away—
Too bright was that heart—it could not last
Through the withering scenes of ensuing day.

Oh sincerely weep! oer the one that has gone
For the melting Soul by tears is refined
And as each pearly drop brightly flows on
The heart gently expands to receive the divine.

Oh sincerely weep! for the record on high
Against the heart by sin earthly defiled
Is gently removed by the deep heaving sigh
And wins back the joy—Heaven reconciled.

Oh sincerely weep! ’tis a tribute but due
To the associate of our earlier youth
A noble companion devoted and true
Whose burning motto was “Courtesy and truth”
Jany 5th /67
Geo. D.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 47 concludes the second memorial poem begun at 10-106. Signed Geo. D., dated January 5, 1867. “Courtesy and truth” is presented as the deceased companion’s motto in the poem. In context the subject is associated with the preceding Robert D. Andrews elegy, but his name is not repeated here. Religious statements express the poet’s belief.

pages.family_text:
Shed a tear here with the brokenhearted,
who remain to mourn those loved and lost,
and cherished hopes defeated by death’s
blighting, untimely frost.

Weep affectionately over broken bonds
woven in life’s bright early spring.
Weep for the one who now lies low,
where his suffering heart can no longer mourn.

His hopes, joys, and prospects have passed
as quickly as morning dew.
That heart was too bright to endure
the withering scenes of the coming day.

Weep sincerely for the one who has gone,
for tears refine the softened soul.
As each pearly drop flows,
the heart gently opens to receive the divine.

Weep sincerely, for the heavenly record
against a heart stained by earthly sin
is gently removed by the deep sigh,
winning back the joy of reconciliation with heaven.

Weep sincerely: it is a fitting tribute
to the companion of our early youth,
noble, devoted, and true,
whose ardent motto was “Courtesy and truth.”

January 5, 1867.
Geo. D.

pages.title: Varying Moments from delight to darkness
pages.text:
48
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Varying Moments,

Oh! there are moments when we rove
Imaginations delights among
Softly inspired by nobler love
And rapt in joyous song

Oh! there are moments, when we give
Our purest noblest thought
To the higher aim, for which we live
The aim for us with blood bought,

These moments beam with soft delight
Unknown to darker hours,
Shedding a bright yet transient light
O’er this dark way of ours.

Shadowing forth a happier day
Of peace and quiet rest!
When in fairer fields we may stray
By flowers and Sunshine blest!

When the Soul expanding will inhale
The perfume of purer joys
Than those which round us now exhale
From ruder passions gross alloys.

But soon! oh too soon is past!
These visions of brighter days
And darker moments are gathering fast
Through which no sunbeam strays,
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 48 continues at 10-109. The poem contrasts spiritual joy with bitterness and human reasoning. Religious imagery is preserved as the speaker’s belief; the line about an aim bought with blood is not a record of a specific injury or battle.

pages.family_title: Varying Moments from delight to darkness
pages.family_text:
Varying Moments

There are moments when we wander
among imagination’s delights,
gently inspired by a nobler love
and absorbed in joyful song.

There are moments when we give
our purest, noblest thoughts
to the higher purpose for which we live,
a purpose bought for us with blood.

Those moments shine with a gentle delight
unknown to darker hours,
shedding a bright but passing light
upon our dark road.

They foreshadow a happier day
of peace and quiet rest,
when we may wander in lovelier fields,
blessed by sunshine and flowers.

Then the growing soul will breathe
the fragrance of purer joys
than those that now surround us,
mixed with the coarser elements of passion.

But all too soon those visions
of brighter days have passed.
Darker moments quickly gather,
with no sunbeam passing through them.
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-109. The poem speaks in general terms about changing moods and spiritual hope.

paragraphs.text:
48
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Varying Moments,

Oh! there are moments when we rove
Imaginations delights among
Softly inspired by nobler love
And rapt in joyous song

Oh! there are moments, when we give
Our purest noblest thought
To the higher aim, for which we live
The aim for us with blood bought,

These moments beam with soft delight
Unknown to darker hours,
Shedding a bright yet transient light
O’er this dark way of ours.

Shadowing forth a happier day
Of peace and quiet rest!
When in fairer fields we may stray
By flowers and Sunshine blest!

When the Soul expanding will inhale
The perfume of purer joys
Than those which round us now exhale
From ruder passions gross alloys.

But soon! oh too soon is past!
These visions of brighter days
And darker moments are gathering fast
Through which no sunbeam strays,

pages.title: Varying Moments questions human systems of thought
pages.text:
49
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Moments of Bitterness, deep and dark
When wither each holier aim;
Aims that rise as twere Spark by Spark
From a lone and dying flame.

These bitter moments congeal the Soul
And cramp its warm desires
Yet their way they onward roll
Like fierce consuming fires,

Fed by man with his isms wild
That rack the brain, the Senses whelm,
Distracting from his way each tender child
That does not know who guides the helm!

Oh! man, that tryest to lead the way
Through Lifes temptations scenes,
Canst thou, pour into a heavenly ray
And tell us what it means?

Canst make the darkened Spirit light
Remove each load of care,
And give us hopes forever bright
While we may wander here?

Do not thy isms blur each page
Of Light that to us is given?
Do not thy isms augment with age
And shut out the light of Heaven?
June 14th /67.
Geo. D.
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 49 concludes 10-108, signed Geo. D., June 14, 1867 as read. The repeated word is “isms,” a general attack on human systems or doctrines, not a named creed. “Pour into a heavenly ray” is awkward wording retained in the reference transcript.

pages.family_title: Varying Moments questions human systems of thought
pages.family_text:
These are moments of deep, dark bitterness,
when every higher purpose withers:
purposes that rise spark by spark
from a lone, dying flame.

Such bitter moments freeze the soul
and constrain its warm desires,
yet roll onward
like fierce, consuming fires.

People feed them with their wild “isms,”
which torment the mind and overwhelm the senses,
leading every trusting child astray
who does not know who steers the ship.

Humanity, you who try to lead the way
through life’s temptations,
can you shed a ray of heavenly light
and tell us what it means?

Can you brighten the darkened spirit,
remove every burden of care,
and give us lasting, radiant hopes
while we wander here?

Do your systems not blur every page
of the light given to us?
Do they not multiply with age
and shut out heaven’s light?

June 14, 1867.
Geo. D.

pages.title: An album as a keepsake of absent friends
pages.text:
50
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
For an Album,

When young we treasure up some sacred Ties
Of Lifes bright morn while all is gay
Some garlands gathered ere the dewdrop dries
Of beautys smile, too soon to pass away.

We twine them in a pure and fragrant wreath
And lay them on the heart in Friendships name
And note how swift the sable wings of death
Sweeps from us those flowers we loved to claim.

In after days we sadly weep alone
Oer those withered gems of earlier years
Which leads the Memory back to loved ones gone
Who left us to loneliness and tears.

These treasures are some thoughts to virtue given
And traced upon an Albums spotless page
By Youths careless heart ere by Sorrow driven—
Or claimed by Death for his tutelage.

So oer this page I now careless strew
Some idle thoughts which may yet recall
Unto thy Memory one you knew
But who ah! too soon perhaps didst fall.

Perhaps a lone tear from thine eye may start
While thinking on his joyless career
And a deep sigh escape thy tender heart
To mingle with that gently flowing tear.
February 1867
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 50, dated February 1867. No author or recipient is named. The closing lines imagine the writer’s future death; they are not evidence that he died then. Grammatical forms such as “didst fall” are retained.

pages.family_title: An album as a keepsake of absent friends
pages.family_text:
For an Album

In youth we treasure sacred bonds
formed in life’s bright, cheerful morning,
like garlands gathered before the dew dries
from beauty’s smile, which will pass too soon.

We weave them into a pure, fragrant wreath
and lay it on the heart in friendship’s name.
Then we see how quickly death’s dark wings
sweep away the flowers we loved as our own.

In later days we sadly weep alone
over those withered jewels of earlier years,
which lead memory back to departed loved ones
who left us lonely and in tears.

These treasures are virtuous thoughts
written on an album’s untouched page
by youth’s carefree heart, before sorrow pursues it
or death claims it for instruction.

So I casually scatter across this page
some idle thoughts that may someday recall
to your memory someone you knew,
who perhaps fell all too soon.

Perhaps a solitary tear will start from your eye
as you remember his unhappy life,
and a deep sigh will escape your tender heart
to mingle with that gently flowing tear.

February 1867.
pages.family_note: An album verse about memory and anticipated loss. Its imagined future death is not a dated death record.

pages.title: Farewell to Irene
pages.text:
51
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Song
Farewell! Irene the parting hour
Has come, and I must away
But back to you my cherished flower
Memory will love to stray.
Broken hopes around me lying
Speak of brighter scenes now gone
And brighter prospects slowly dying
Warn of sadness coming on.

Farewell Irene! we may never
Meet while we live above
But oh! Times scythe cannot sever
From my heart the one I love!

Oh! I regret to leave you Irene
And sunder every sacred tie
That has twined like the ivy green
Where the charms of virtue lie
But pleasant hopes do not abound
But to die mid scenes of Strife
And Fate between has darkly frowned
Blighting all my early life.

Alone I’ll wander oer the earth
Far from scenes I’ve loved too well
In pleasures throng I’ll seek for mirth
To check sorrows rising swell.
Scenes of the past! Oh fade away
And new hopes my bosom charm
Careless onward let me reckless stray
Heeding nought that breathes of harm.
Feby 1867
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 51, dated February 1867, titled Song. Irene is explicitly named, but no surname, signature, tune, or proof of a real relationship is supplied. “While we live above” is retained, even though its sense is unusual. This may be original or copied verse; attribution beyond the manuscript is not established.

pages.family_title: Farewell to Irene
pages.family_text:
Song

Farewell, Irene: the hour of parting
has come, and I must go.
But memory will gladly wander back
to you, my cherished flower.
Broken hopes around me
speak of brighter scenes now gone,
and brighter prospects slowly dying
warn of sorrow still to come.

Farewell, Irene! We may never
meet again while we live “above.”
But time’s scythe cannot cut
my loved one from my heart.

I regret leaving you, Irene,
and breaking every sacred bond
that has wound like green ivy
around virtue’s charms.
Pleasant hopes flourish
only to die amid conflict.
Fate has frowned darkly between us,
blighting my early life.

I will wander the earth alone,
far from scenes I loved too well,
seeking merriment among pleasure’s crowds
to restrain sorrow’s rising tide.
Scenes of the past, fade away!
Let new hopes charm my heart.
Let me wander carelessly, recklessly onward,
heedless of anything that threatens harm.

February 1867.
pages.family_note: A literary farewell addressed to Irene. The page does not establish her identity or whether the song recounts the writer’s own experience.

pages.title: Idle Hours continued in imagination’s fields
pages.text:
52
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Continued from page 39
’Tis Sweet to rove in fancys fields
Amid her beauteous flowers
Where glowing thought rich treasure yields
In brightness thro successive hours,
’Tis sweet to hold communion fond
With nature wild and free
And feel the magic influence of her wand—
Imaginations boundless Ideality.

Oh Imagination! parent of my sweetest joys
I yield to thee, the homage of the heart,
Your brightest visions no corruption cloys
With guileful stains of [[inserted: dark]] Reality’s art,
You lead me far amid gayest fields
Where perennial Summers brightly beam
You to my heart the sweetest blisses yield
That in tasting more—still sweeter seem.

Oh! patron goddess of my happier hours!
With thee I fondly love to stray
For thou is spread the fairest sweetest flowers
Upon my thorn hedged meandering way!
My visions in sweetest odours drest
Leap forward on sunny landscapes fair
That with beautys brightest smiles are blest
And loveliness exquisitely rare,
The cankering Cares of Fact evanish
Before thy approaching lovely face
Back to oblivion, their hideous forms, you banish
And to unstained Joys give a glowing place
Welcome then! hand in hand we’ll wander
Adown the warping Stream of Time
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 52 explicitly continues page 39 (10-099) and leads to 10-113. The unusual forms “thou is spread” and “warping Stream” are retained. The insertion “dark” is visible above the line about Reality. The goddess is a personification of imagination, not an identified woman.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours continued in imagination’s fields
pages.family_text:
Continued from manuscript page 39

It is sweet to wander through imagination’s fields
among her beautiful flowers,
where glowing thoughts yield rich treasures
brightly through successive hours.
It is sweet to commune affectionately
with wild, free nature,
and feel the magic influence of her wand:
imagination’s boundless world of ideals.

Imagination, source of my sweetest joys,
I offer you my heart’s homage.
No corruption spoils your brightest visions
with the deceptive stains of dark reality.
You lead me far into cheerful fields
where endless summers shine.
You give my heart the sweetest joys,
which grow sweeter the more I taste them.

Patron goddess of my happier hours,
I love to wander with you.
You scatter the fairest, sweetest flowers
along my thorn-lined, winding path.
My visions, clothed in sweet fragrances,
leap forward across lovely sunny landscapes,
blessed by beauty’s brightest smiles
and rare, exquisite loveliness.
The gnawing cares of fact disappear
before your approaching, lovely face.
You banish their hideous forms to oblivion
and make a glowing place for unsullied joy.
Welcome, then: hand in hand we will wander
down time’s twisting stream—
pages.family_note: This resumes 10-099 and continues at 10-113. The text personifies imagination and contrasts it with the cares of fact.

pages.title: Idle Hours concluded and a later satire
pages.text:
53
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
And gather as we go from each meander
Its sweetest joys to mingle in our rhyme,
Jan. 5th /67
Geo. D.

[[separate block: later satirical verse]]
Alas! My old flame has faded
The bloom from her cheek is now gone
And her classic brow is now shaded
By tresses of Beauty=nary one=
And dull and lifeless is her tread
As she slowly pines her old maids bed.

The light from her eye has departed
Like the gleam of a star in a fog
And instead of poetically sighing brokenhearted
She simply grunts like a hog,
The music of her voice has long gone by
And no more can she heave affections sigh.

Calmly she marches on lifes way
With her old man by her side
And she has at times a good deal to say
To make the old fellow provide
For herself and the young little graces
Now coming around with surly faces.
May 1869
pages.editorial_notes: The first two lines complete Idle Hours, read 10-099, 10-112, 10-113; they are signed Geo. D., January 5, 1867. A distinct, unsigned satirical poem follows, dated May 1869. Its insults and references to an old maid, an old man and children do not establish anyone’s marriage or family. The apparent contradiction is retained.

pages.family_title: Idle Hours concluded and a later satire
pages.family_text:
Idle Hours, conclusion

And gather, as we pass each bend,
its sweetest joys to mingle in our verse.
January 5, 1867. Geo. D.

Separate satire, May 1869

Alas, my old flame has faded.
The bloom has gone from her cheek,
and not one beautiful tress
now shades her classical brow.
Her step is dull and lifeless
as she pines in her old maid’s bed.

The light has left her eye
like a star’s gleam lost in fog.
Instead of sighing poetically with a broken heart,
she simply grunts like a hog.
The music has long gone from her voice;
she can no longer breathe affection’s sigh.

She calmly marches through life
with her old man beside her.
She sometimes has plenty to say
to make the old fellow provide
for her and the little “graces”
now gathering around with surly faces.

May 1869.
pages.family_note: The first poem ends here. The second is an unkind literary satire with no named subject; it is not reliable biographical evidence about the writer or his family.

pages.title: Farewell to earthly joys, addressed to Miss M. A. A.
pages.text:
54
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Respectfully Inscribed to Miss M-A-A.
Farewell! ye joys of earth farewell
Upon lifes threshold we must part
I would not try again your syren spell
I would not risk a broken heart.

Farewell ye joys! a long farewell!
No pleasures now I claim
I’ve learned your fleeting [[age?]] too well
I’ve learned ye live but in the name.

Farewell! with sadness still I speak the word
Your visions lured me on too far.
Yet still they tremble oer Memorys Chord
And softly start the glistening tear.

Farewell! tis wrong to mourn the decay
Of visions false yet bright
Yet without you Lifes dark way
Is but a weary, weary night.

But shall I woo bright Fancys gleam
My darksome way to light?
Which sparkles like a meteor beam
Amid the darkness of the night.

And shines resplendent from afar
A beacon reared on high
Like the glorious Morning Star
Beaming from an early sky
pages.editorial_notes: Manuscript page 54 continues at 10-115. The recipient is given only by initials; no surname is expanded. One faded word in the second stanza is tentative. The poem’s despair is a literary expression, not proof of a particular broken engagement.

pages.family_text:
Respectfully inscribed to Miss M. A. A.

Farewell, joys of earth, farewell.
We must part at life’s threshold.
I will not try your enticing spell again
or risk a broken heart.

Farewell, joys: a long farewell!
I now claim no pleasures.
I have learned too well how fleeting you are;
I have learned that you exist in name alone.

I still speak “farewell” with sadness.
Your visions drew me onward too far.
They still vibrate on memory’s chord
and gently bring a glistening tear.

It is wrong to mourn the fading
of visions that were false, yet bright.
But without you, life’s dark road
is only a weary, weary night.

Shall I seek imagination’s bright gleam
to light my dark road,
sparkling like a meteor
in the darkness of night?

It shines brilliantly from far away,
a beacon raised on high,
like the glorious morning star
shining in an early sky.
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-115. The family rendering gives the apparent sense of the faded line about fleeting joy; the uncertain word is marked in the reference transcript.

pages.title: Imagination offers relief from sorrow
pages.text:
55
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Yes I may woo that beauteous ray
And court its brightness for awhile
To shine upon my lone dark way
With its bright illusive smile

For while that beam resplendent shines
My soul leaps forth along its trace
And thought swift treads those burning lines
Across the trackless realms of Space

Then! then ye Visions! then your power
My spirit captive leads
Then your bright illusions rule the hour
And my breaking heart no longer bleeds

I catch bright Fancys glorious ray
That sheds those dreams of wild delight
And for awhile my darksome way
Shines fair in bright effulgent light

Then flowerets yield their sweet perfumes
From myriads of ambrosial bowers
And Pleasures wand with hope illumes
Each [[illegible]] moment of the golden hours

And aromatic breezes [[illegible]] rove
These ideal fields among
And bears from out each sainted grove
Its spicy fragrance swift along.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 10-114. Two short faded passages remain unread. The following scan starts Visit to Siloam, a different poem; a further continuation of the present poem should not be assumed from physical adjacency alone.

pages.title: Visit to Siloam
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Visit To Siloam.

Twas on the first of Brumaire,
(I like to be particular as to time
So no matter when I go or where
I will always know the occasion of my rhyme.)
Twas on the first of Brumaire
As I was just going to say
That I brushed my shoes and sleeked my hair
And promised myself a happy day.
A western wind blew fresh and fair
The morning clouds soon dispelled
And as I faced the bracing air
Its wild free spirit I inhaled.

I mounted on a trotting horse
And through the mud swiftly sped
Unto Siloam I bent my course
With poesy running in my head,
Upon its grounds at length arrived
And tied my steed unto a tree
Then looked around at how things were contrived
And to see such things as were to see.
My heart beat high with hope elate
While every thing propitious smiled
With satisfaction I scanned my fate
And with Hope the sunny hours beguiled.
While stumping round through its verdant shades
Oer heaps of logs and now and then a slab
I came upon some of my old comrades
Privately enjoying a lone confab.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues at 10-117. “Brumaire” is the word written, not silently converted to a modern date. The precise location of Siloam is not established here. The poem describes a social outing and should not be treated as a verified itinerary.

pages.family_title: Visit to Siloam
pages.family_text:
Visit to Siloam

It was on the first of Brumaire—
I like to be precise about time,
so whenever or wherever I go,
I will remember the occasion for my verse.
It was on the first of Brumaire,
as I was about to say,
that I brushed my shoes and smoothed my hair,
promising myself a happy day.
A fresh, fair west wind blew,
soon dispersing the morning clouds.
As I faced the invigorating air,
I breathed in its wild, free spirit.

I mounted a trotting horse
and hurried through the mud,
heading toward Siloam
with poetry running through my head.
At last I reached its grounds
and tied my horse to a tree.
I looked around at the arrangements
and at whatever there was to see.
My heart beat high with joyful hope;
everything seemed promising.
I considered my prospects with satisfaction
and passed the sunny hours hopefully.
Stumbling through the leafy shade,
over heaps of logs and an occasional slab,
I found some old companions
having a private conversation.
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-117. The source calls the date “the first of Brumaire”; no calendar conversion or identification of Siloam is asserted.

Twas on the first of Brumaire,
(I like to be particular as to time
So no matter when I go or where
I will always know the occasion of my rhyme.)
Twas on the first of Brumaire
As I was just going to say
That I brushed my shoes and sleeked my hair
And promised myself a happy day.
A western wind blew fresh and fair
The morning clouds soon dispelled
And as I faced the bracing air
Its wild free spirit I inhaled.

I mounted on a trotting horse
And through the mud swiftly sped
Unto Siloam I bent my course
With poesy running in my head,
Upon its grounds at length arrived
And tied my steed unto a tree
Then looked around at how things were contrived
And to see such things as were to see.
My heart beat high with hope elate
While every thing propitious smiled
With satisfaction I scanned my fate
And with Hope the sunny hours beguiled.
While stumping round through its verdant shades
Oer heaps of logs and now and then a slab
I came upon some of my old comrades
Privately enjoying a lone confab.

pages.title: Siloam companions and courtship banter
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
“What ho! my comrades are ye here?
“I give you a cordial greeting
“But I dont see how you could stir
“So far from home just for a meeting.
“I’m rather inclined unto the notion
“That there is some prime moving cause
“And that you feel some kind of emotion
“Set in full blast by Cupids laws?

Slowly at length spoke Prospect Hill
“You are right about the emotion
“And you may have it by whose laws you will
“To us works out no ‘motion’
“I’m told the virgins of our Shrine
“To day are coming to Siloam
“One Sylph-like girl I’ll claim as mine
“And with the rest you may freely roam.

As thus he spoke I keenly watched
Each varying emotion on their faces
That wrinkled up like a stick notched
In some half a dozen places.

Then Prospect Junior smilingly replied
“To all I came here at Siloam
“To rein up to the grey pony’s side
“And quietly escort him home.

Thus I to him, “may you no ill betide
“I would not do it for money
“For you will be sure to ride
“Home with a Parsons Honey.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 10-116. Prospect Hill and Prospect Junior appear as literary names or nicknames, not identified persons. Some quotation marks are opened on successive lines without closing marks; their form is retained. “To all I came here at Siloam” is awkward but retained. The next scan opens mid-thought; continuity across the transition is not established.

pages.family_title: Siloam companions and courtship banter
pages.family_text:
“Hello, companions! Are you here?
I greet you warmly,
but cannot see why you would travel
so far from home merely for a meeting.
I rather suspect
some stronger motive:
an emotion set fully in motion
by Cupid’s laws.”

At last Prospect Hill spoke slowly:
“You are right about the emotion.
Assign it to whichever laws you please;
it brings us no ‘motion.’
I hear the young women of our shrine
are coming to Siloam today.
I will claim one graceful girl;
you may wander freely with the rest.”

As he spoke, I watched closely
the changing expressions on their faces,
which wrinkled up like a stick
notched in half a dozen places.

Then Prospect Junior smiled and replied:
“I came here to Siloam
to draw up beside the gray pony
and quietly escort him home.”

I answered, “May no harm come to you!
I would not do that for money,
for you are sure to ride home
with a parson’s sweetheart.”

pages.title: Sorrow over interrupted social pleasures, and Love
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Yet no pen can describe the depth of our wo
Since from the regions of darkness that curtain has strayed.

“Oh! Euroclydon of Sorrow! that has spread oer our sky,
May the Sunshine of! softness dispel thy dark gloom.
That we may gaze once more far upon high,
To where our bright stars the social Heavens illume;

“Then will be restored all the bliss we desire
Permission to yield our devotion again
On the Shrine that we love, we can ask no higher
Enjoyment than this in this low world of pain.

“Flow on ye bright waters no more will I sing
To thy limpid clearness the tale of our woes
Perhaps future years brighter hours may bring
And in Pleasures lap we may (?) sweetly repose.
Geo. D.
Seclusion Nov 4th 1866

[[separate block: short poem]]
“Love” is a fragrant flowering bud
That for awhile delights the young
They gaze upon its rosy blush
While pulse is high and pleasure strong.
But its glowing beauties please not long
Their eyes soon turn to solid charms
The fickle Goddess breathes a parting song
And dies within pure friendships arms.
Dec 1866
Geo. D.
pages.editorial_notes: The first poem begins mid-thought and is signed Geo. D., Seclusion, November 4, 1866. Its social imagery may connect with Visit to Siloam (10-116–117), but intervening wording has not been securely located. “May the Sunshine of! softness” is retained as written; the source’s parenthesized question mark after “may” is original, not an editorial uncertainty. A separate verse on love and friendship is signed Geo. D., December 1866. Euroclydon is used as storm imagery, not an account of an actual storm.

pages.family_title: Sorrow over interrupted social pleasures, and Love
pages.family_text:
No pen can describe the depth of our sorrow
since that curtain strayed from the regions of darkness.

Storm of sorrow spread across our sky,
may the sunshine of gentleness disperse your gloom,
so we may once more look far upward
where our bright stars light the social heavens.

Then all the happiness we desire will return:
permission to offer our devotion again
at the shrine we love. We could ask no greater
pleasure in this lowly world of pain.

Flow on, bright waters. I will no longer sing
the tale of our sorrows to your crystal clarity.
Perhaps future years will bring brighter hours,
and we may (?) rest sweetly in pleasure’s lap.

Geo. D. Seclusion, November 4, 1866.

Separate verse

Love is a fragrant flowering bud
that delights the young for a while.
They gaze at its rosy blush
while their pulse is high and pleasure strong.
But its glowing beauty does not please for long;
their eyes soon turn to more lasting attractions.
The fickle goddess sings a farewell
and dies in pure friendship’s arms.

December 1866. Geo. D.
pages.family_note: The first passage starts in the middle of a poem. Its relationship to the preceding Siloam verses is possible, but not certain. The question mark in “may (?)” belongs to the manuscript.

pages.title: To Miss Mat. A. on truth and affection
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
To Miss Mat. A.
As o’er that brow so pensive calm pure
I fondly gaze with ardor beaming eye
I read with Prophetic inspiration clear
Some pure lineaments strayed from Paradise.

And lighted on this stormy world below
Still blooming fair in firmest purity
The loveliest gift Heaven [[deleted: could]] could e’er bestow
From the vast bounds of its immensity.

That gift is Truth, the donor Heaven
And you fair girl the recipient are
Of the noblest boon to mortal given
Which e’er inhabited this lowly sphere.
July 1866
Geo. D.

Ad idem
The remembrance of when last we met
Still fills my heart with pleasure.
And I never never shall forget
You who are my only Treasure.

The emotions then that thrilled my breast
Holy and pure—yet unspoken
Are burning yet and will not rest
Forming links ne’er to be broken.

Links of affection pure unstained,
By deep Designs dark alloy
Pure as e’er has been attained
Pure as the purest earthly joy.
pages.editorial_notes: The first poem is addressed to Miss Mat. A. and signed Geo. D., July 1866. “Ad idem” introduces another poem to the same subject, continued at 10-120. The initials and shortened name are not expanded; a real courtship or engagement is not established. The overwritten first occurrence of “could” is treated as canceled.

pages.family_title: To Miss Mat. A. on truth and affection
pages.family_text:
To Miss Mat. A.

As I gaze affectionately, with shining eyes,
at your thoughtful, calm, pure brow,
I see, with clear prophetic inspiration,
pure features that have wandered from paradise.

They have alighted on this stormy world,
still blooming beautifully in steadfast purity:
the loveliest gift heaven could ever offer
from the vast reaches of its immensity.

That gift is truth; heaven is its giver.
You, fair girl, are its recipient:
the noblest gift bestowed on any mortal
who has lived in this humble world.

July 1866. Geo. D.

To the same

Remembering our last meeting
still fills my heart with pleasure.
I will never, never forget you,
my only treasure.

The feelings that then thrilled my heart,
holy and pure but unspoken,
still burn and will not rest,
forming bonds never to be broken.

These are bonds of pure affection,
unstained by the dark mixture of hidden designs,
as pure as has ever been achieved,
as pure as the purest earthly joy.
pages.family_note: The second poem continues at 10-120. “Mat. A.” is the manuscript’s form; no full identity is asserted.

pages.title: Enduring affection and two irreverent epitaphs
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Oh! maiden fair, you know not the tie
That round my heart is hourly twining
You knownot the feelings which burie lie
For Loves rolls deep divining.

Feelings which will linger long
When Youthful bloom has faded
Glowing still bright and strong
Tho’ by Age darkly shaded.
December 1866.
Geo. D.

Epitaph,
Draw near and drop a pious tear
Beside this monumental stone
For the bones which now moulder here
Were once a mighty living Bore.

Epigram.
Oh! what a pity! man should waste
So much good time upon a stone
Simply at last to have it placed
Above a foully rotten Bone!
pages.editorial_notes: The first two stanzas complete Ad idem at 10-119, signed Geo. D., December 1866. The irregular wording “burie lie / For Loves rolls deep divining” is retained; its exact sense is uncertain. Two distinct short satires follow. Neither identifies a deceased person or grave.

pages.family_title: Enduring affection and two irreverent epitaphs
pages.family_text:
Fair maiden, you do not know the bond
that winds around my heart each hour.
You do not know the feelings buried there,
deep within love. [[The original wording is irregular; this is its apparent sense.]]

These feelings will linger long
after youth’s bloom has faded,
still glowing brightly and strongly,
though darkened by age.

December 1866. Geo. D.

Epitaph

Come near and shed a pious tear
beside this memorial stone.
The bones now decaying here
were once a mighty living bore.

Epigram

What a pity that people waste
so much good time on a stone,
only to set it at last
above a thoroughly rotten bone!
pages.family_note: The first poem continues 10-119. The two epitaphs are anonymous satires, not records of a named person’s death.

pages.title: Hours of Bitterness: remembered pleasures
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Hours of Bitterness.
Oh there are moments when the past
Comes oer me as a dream
The scenes of youth—too bright to last
That shed [[illegible]] a flickering gleam,
Of happiness o’er my saddened heart
Where not a ray of light now strays
That could a moments bliss impart
But what would ere the instant fade.
I’ve grasped at Pleasures lively host
That in swift groups swept by
I’ve mingled in its wildest boast
With pulses madly bounding high;
I’ve seen its charms before me spread
In bright succession far
I’ve felt its influence when it led
My way from Star to Star,
Of Beauty that so brightly reigned
Queen of every idle heart
That blindly knelt in her bright train
The centre of gay folly’s mart.
I’ve seen the smiles of eager joy
Play on the rosy lips
Unstained by Arts deep dark alloy
That Hope’s sweet fountains sips.
I’ve seen the fondly loving eyes
Meet eyes that loved again
I’ve heard the softest earliest sigh
Of the heart by Cupid slain.
I’ve felt the hopes which fire the blood
When prospective joys appeared,
pages.editorial_notes: Begins a long poem continued through 10-128; read in consecutive scan order, rotating 10-123. The present page is undated and unsigned. A faded portion of the fourth verse line remains unread. “But what would ere the instant fade” and “wildest boast” are retained as read.

pages.family_title: Hours of Bitterness: remembered pleasures
pages.family_text:
Hours of Bitterness

There are moments when the past
comes over me like a dream:
scenes of youth, too bright to last,
which cast [[unreadable wording]] a flickering gleam
of happiness over my saddened heart.
No ray of light now enters there
to give a moment’s joy
without fading in that very instant.
I have reached for pleasure’s lively company
as it swept past in swift groups.
I have mingled in its wildest boasting,
my pulse beating madly and high.
I have seen its attractions spread before me
in a bright, distant succession.
I have felt its influence lead me
from star to star of beauty,
which shone brightly as queen
of every idle heart that blindly knelt
among her brilliant followers,
at the center of cheerful folly’s marketplace.
I have seen smiles of eager joy
play on rosy lips,
untainted by deceit’s dark influence,
drinking from hope’s sweet fountains.
I have seen fond, loving eyes
meet eyes that returned their love.
I have heard the first, gentlest sigh
of a heart struck down by Cupid.
I have felt the hopes that quicken the blood
when future joys appear—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-122. The poem’s speaker describes remembered emotions; unnamed romantic figures are not assigned identities.

pages.title: Hours of Bitterness: hopes that vanish
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
I’ve felt the influence of a gayer mood
When songs of revelry were heard.
But what were they, a moment bright
A minute like a flickering spark
That upward leaps from a lone light
Then dies and leaves all doubly dark.

I’ve seen the hopes of Life decay
Ere morning dews were dried
I’ve felt my joys low with’ring lay
Like garlands in the desert wide;
All I have loved with trusting heart
All I have hoped in early days.
I’ve seen before me fast depart
Like dews in mornings gaze.
I’ve tried to win those pearly dews
To keep within my heart
I’ve hoped a gentler spirit to infuse
With their pure and guileless art.
I’ve tried to gather [[deleted: sweetest]] fragrant flowers
That bloomed my way along
To intertwine with happier hours
And interweave in joyous song.
Before my touch those dew drops bright
Fled like morning mists away
When the suns bold beaming light
Proclaimed the Advent of the day.
Those fragrant flowers of loveliness
Like Snowflakes on the sea
Reclined an instant on my breast
Then swelled its storminess.
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 10-121 and leads to 10-123, which is inverted in the PDF. The canceled word before “fragrant” is retained as an editorial deletion. The closing metaphor is “Then swelled its storminess,” not an assertion about an actual sea voyage.

pages.family_title: Hours of Bitterness: hopes that vanish
pages.family_text:
I have felt a more cheerful mood
when songs of revelry were heard.
But what were those pleasures? A bright moment,
a minute like a flickering spark
that leaps upward from a lonely light,
then dies, leaving everything twice as dark.

I have seen life’s hopes decay
before the morning dew dried.
I have felt my joys lie low and withering,
like garlands in a vast desert.
Everything I loved with a trusting heart,
everything I hoped for in early days,
I have seen quickly depart before me
like dew beneath the morning sun.
I tried to capture those pearly drops
and keep them in my heart,
hoping their innocent purity
would inspire a gentler spirit.
I tried to gather fragrant flowers
blooming along my path,
to entwine with happier hours
and weave into joyful song.
Before I could touch them, those bright drops
fled like morning mist
when the sun’s bold, shining light
announced the arrival of day.
Those fragrant flowers of loveliness,
like snowflakes upon the sea,
rested for an instant on my breast,
then increased its storminess.

pages.title: Hours of Bitterness: loneliness and lost hopes
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form; page read after 180-degree rotation]]
Where e’er I turn for solid charms
Where e’er I look with brighter hopes
There is nothing which my bosom warms
Or my hearts deep fountain opes.
I’ve tried in vain from Purity
To win her gems of priceless worth
To wrench them from Adversity
To illume my way on earth,
Deeper in the dark recess
Of the Souls night I’ve plunged my way
And only found that nothingness
Within its dreary portals lay.
A chaotic void filled with gloom
And stormy passions darkly driven
Where light and beauty ne’er can come
Or stray a single breath of Heaven.

Oh! the dark thoughts which rack the mind
When lowering hours of loneliness
Around me hover, and leave behind
Emotions I can ne’er express.
Scenes and early visions bright
Fade like morning dews away
Hopes which shed a holy light
Akin to Heavens benignant ray
Perish too, amid the wreck
Of Human aims, which “dying fall”
Nor in descending meet a check
To save from total ruin all—
I’ve turned and wept to see them go
And leave my heart all desolate.
pages.editorial_notes: The scan is inverted; transcription follows a 180-degree rotation. Continues 10-122 and leads to 10-124. The quotation marks around “dying fall” occur in the manuscript; no external literary attribution is established here.

pages.family_title: Hours of Bitterness: loneliness and lost hopes
pages.family_text:
Wherever I turn for lasting attractions,
wherever I look with brighter hopes,
nothing warms my heart
or opens its deep fountain.
I have tried in vain to win
purity’s priceless jewels,
to wrest them from adversity
and light my earthly path.
I have plunged deeper into the dark recesses
of the soul’s night,
only to find that nothingness
lay inside its dreary gates:
a chaotic void filled with gloom
and dark, storm-driven passions,
where light and beauty can never enter,
nor a single breath of heaven stray.

The dark thoughts tormenting the mind!
When threatening hours of loneliness
hover around me, they leave feelings
I can never express.
Bright early scenes and visions
fade like morning dew.
Hopes that shed a holy light
like heaven’s kindly ray
also perish amid the wreck
of human aims, which “dying fall,”
meeting no restraint as they descend
to save them all from total ruin.
I have turned and wept to see them go
and leave my heart completely desolate.

pages.title: Hours of Bitterness asks where relief can be found
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
I would recall them now—but Oh!
’Tis the relentless hand of Fate,
And who can change its stern decrees?
When once the signet ring is set?
We must submit though [[deleted: ’tis desperate]] [[inserted: robbed of ease]]
And learn to suffer sorrow yet.

When will the cup of Wo be full?
When will the Demon Misery rest?
When will Dejection cease to pull
Contentment from the wearied breast?
When will Oblivions gloomy shades
Wrap the Past in endless night?
When will the blackened fiends of Hades
Cease to lower the Spirits light?
Are there no hours we may expect
To bring Sunshine and bright relief?
Are there no guides that can direct
A heart from the perennial grief
Of dying Hopes? ere Life begins
To be an earnest here on earth
Before the Spirit halfway wins
The form of that which gave it birth?
Are there no scenes that may bloom
Towards Life’s dismal closing days
That will shed a rich perfume
Of sweetness in its dying maze?
Are there no joys which swell the breast
Some purer hours unto us given
Before we find the final rest
Prepared for [[deleted: us]] [[inserted: some]] in Heaven?
It seems as though all Earth were dark
And we blind wanderers below
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 10-123 and leads directly to 10-125. Two revisions are visible: “robbed of ease” replaces canceled wording, and “some” replaces “us” in the line about heaven. The latter change matters to the poem’s subsequent discussion of competing salvation doctrines. The canceled phrase in the first revision is read as “’tis desperate.”

pages.family_title: Hours of Bitterness asks where relief can be found
pages.family_text:
I would bring those hopes back now—but, oh,
this is fate’s relentless hand.
Who can change its stern decrees
once the seal has been set?
We must submit, though robbed of ease,
and learn to suffer further sorrow.

When will the cup of sorrow be full?
When will misery’s demon rest?
When will dejection stop pulling
contentment from the weary heart?
When will oblivion’s gloomy shadows
wrap the past in endless night?
When will the darkened fiends of Hades
stop dimming the spirit’s light?
Can we expect no hours
of sunshine and bright relief?
Are there no guides to lead
a heart away from the lasting grief
of dying hopes, before life
has even begun in earnest on earth,
before the spirit has halfway attained
the form of that which gave it birth?
Are there no scenes that might bloom
toward life’s dismal closing days,
shedding a rich fragrance of sweetness
in its dying confusion?
Are there no joys to fill the heart,
no purer hours given to us,
before we find the final rest
prepared for some in heaven?
It seems the whole earth is dark
and we are blind wanderers below—

pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Travelling—Where? without a mark
By which we might surely go—
Travelling in thro’ doubt and gloom
Thro’ cankering cares on every side
Behind, before, contentions loom
And darkly rolls their murky tide;
In vain for peace and sweet repose
We gaze around with eager eyes
And hope amid surrounding woes
To see a ray of pleasure rise—
Each distant scene which promise gives
Of happiness in future days
Alone in Fancy faintly lives
And passes as the Summer haze;
A moment bright it shines afar
With varied brilliancy on high
Glowing as a meteor star
Amid the blackness of the sky
And as quickly too it expires
Amid the stillness of the night
And backward hope as swift retires
As it advanced to meet the light.
Oh! even thus we hourly stand
Twixt hope and fear, twixt joy and pain.
Oft as we feel the heart expand
As oft we feel it contract again!—
Hark! a strange sound arrests the ear
Borne on the swiftly passing gale.
Hark! it rings again loud and clear
And faintly echoes down the vale!
“Lo! here is rest”, it is a voice
Breaks on the stillness of the gloom,

by which we could surely find our way,
traveling through doubt and gloom,
through gnawing cares on every side.

for peace and sweet rest,
hoping amid surrounding sorrow
to see a ray of pleasure rise.
Every distant scene promising
happiness in future days
lives faintly in imagination alone
and passes like summer haze.
For one bright moment it shines far away,
with changing brilliance above,
glowing like a meteor
in the blackness of the sky.
Just as quickly, it disappears
in the stillness of night,
and hope retreats as swiftly
as it advanced toward the light.

between hope and fear, joy and pain.
Whenever we feel the heart expand,
we feel it contract again.
Listen! A strange sound catches the ear,
borne on the swift-passing wind.
Listen! It rings again, loud and clear,
echoing faintly down the valley:
“Here is rest!” A voice
breaks the gloomy silence—

pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
“Lo! here is rest!” Oh! man rejoice
“And to the living fountain come,
“Here is a balm for every wound
“Which mortal bosoms deeply bear.
“By Faith alone it may be found
“Alone secured by humble prayer,
“Know of yourselves ye are undone
“And totally depraved on earth
“Of redeeming powers you have none
“Until you taste the second birth;
“But when you’ve passed from Natures night
“Wherein ye hourly doubting stand
“Into the marvellous Spirits light
“That leads unto a better land,
“Then Heaven’s glories are thine own
“In all their spotless purity
“And before the great Eternal Throne
“You will rejoice thro’ eternity.
“This is the way and this alone
“All others lead to gloom beneath
“Accept it now the precious boon
“Before you taste the second death!

“Lo! here is rest!” again we hear
From another side the syren tone
In melodious sweetness it greets the ear
With a softer cadence before unknown,
“Lo! here is rest for you oh man
“Redemption free is shed abroad
“Come and take ye glorious stand
“Cast aside your sinful load
“Believe that One has borne a Cross

pages.family_text:
“Here is rest! Rejoice, humanity,
and come to the living fountain.
Here is a balm for every wound
that human hearts bear deeply.
It can be found by faith alone,
secured only through humble prayer.
Know that by yourselves you are lost,
totally depraved on earth.
You have no power to redeem yourselves
until you experience a second birth.
But once you have passed from nature’s night,
where you stand doubting hour by hour,
into the Spirit’s marvelous light
that leads to a better land,
heaven’s glories are your own
in all their spotless purity.
Before the great eternal throne
you will rejoice for eternity.
This is the way, and the only way;
all others lead to the gloom below.
Accept this precious gift now,
before you taste the second death.”

“Here is rest!” Again we hear
the enticing voice from another direction.
It greets the ear with melodious sweetness,
a softer cadence unknown before:
“Here is rest for you, humanity.
Free redemption is spread abroad.
Come and take your glorious stand;
cast aside your burden of sin.
Believe that One bore a cross—

pages.family_title: Hours of Bitterness: obedience and predestination
pages.family_text:
“Up Calvary’s rugged slope
to free humanity from sin’s dark impurities.
Believe, humanity: believe and weep.
Weeping, bow at his command
beneath the flowing, crystal water,
then rise clothed in robes of life.
For this the mighty Savior died.
On high he stands to plead the case
of those who claim his favor
by willingly obeying his laws,
seeking ‘another name.’
Only this way can rest be found.
For the many hungry, waiting souls,
false teachers will always abound
while time’s tide rolls darkly onward.”

Again we hear a different voice
ringing through the murky air:
“Know, humanity, first and last,
what heaven has promised you here.
It was determined from the earliest hour
when creation came into being:
some would rise in spiritual power
and be heaven’s chosen on earth.
Saved by the great sacrifice,
they need not fear dark sin,
for through it heaven’s paradise
is theirs beyond this world of care.
But some, through the endless night
of misery and dark despair,
excluded from redemption’s light,
must bear heaven’s curse—
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-128. The family reading smooths an irregular line about hungry, waiting souls. The theological statements belong to contrasting voices staged by the poem.

pages.title: Hours of Bitterness rejects contradictory sectarian claims
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
“For them no sacrifice was made
“By Heaven’s own Eternal grace,
“But [[inserted: they]] must bear the curse that’s laid
“On Adam’s fallen erring race,
“’Tis all in vain they plead for life
“And happiness beyond the tomb
“If they are predestined for strife
“And mis’ry in the world to come.
“Oh! thus ’tis said—and thus ’twill be
“As sure as Heaven rules on high
“This is the law laid down—and ye
“Must accept it—nor ask why.

Where shall we go—whom shall we hear
Whom believe and trust in all?
Each offers rest from every fear
Each says the other sure must fall.
Where is one ray of light thats shed
Amid surrounding darkness drear,
But what another cloaks in dread
Each glowing scene it makes appear?

“We’ll let them go—they all are wrong
All narrowminded, partial, blind.
Their brightest Creeds—are an old Song
In Sectarianism deep refined.
We’ll let them go—their Sophistry
Serves but to lead the mind astray
And to all but Hypocrisy
They are false—false every way.”
February 1867
pages.editorial_notes: Concludes Hours of Bitterness (10-121–128), dated February 1867, without a signature on this page. The final quotation rejects the conflicting teachers and their sectarian creeds. This is a critique of those claims, not sufficient evidence by itself that the author rejected all religious belief. Horizontal separators in the manuscript distinguish the three movements reproduced as paragraphs.

pages.family_text:
“For them no sacrifice was made
through heaven’s own eternal grace.
They must bear the curse laid
upon Adam’s fallen, erring race.
They plead in vain for life
and happiness beyond the grave
if they are predestined for conflict
and misery in the world to come.
So it is said, and so it will be,
as surely as heaven rules above.
This is the law laid down;
you must accept it without asking why.”

Where should we go? Whom should we hear?
Whom can we believe and trust through it all?
Each offers rest from every fear;
each says the other must surely fail.
Where is a ray of light shed
amid the surrounding dreary darkness
whose bright scene another teacher
does not shroud in dread?

“We will leave them: they are all wrong,
narrow-minded, biased, blind.
Their brightest creeds are an old song,
refined into deep sectarianism.
We will leave them. Their deceptive reasoning
only leads the mind astray.
They are true to nothing but hypocrisy;
they are false in every way.”

February 1867.
