pages.title: Blue eyes imagined during a storm
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
[[Blue Eyes?]] [[illegible]]

The blustering rain loudly rattles on the roof
Around the gables sadly sighs the wind
And as I gaze into the fast thickening woof
Of darkness far without all grows dark within.

Then I turn me to Imagery’s fair skies
Where not a cloudlet dims the azure scene
Where far stretched before my raptured vision lies
Wreaths of Beauty shedding o’er all a lovely Sheen.

And in my fancied visions oft I meet
The angelic gaze of eyes of heavenly blue
With wildest transports their sweet glances I greet,
A holy rapture which pervades my being through.

Affection’s purest strongest flame is kindling then
Flowing in a tide of purest holiest Love
And in fancy’s visions oft again and again
I clasp unto my heart this Angel from above.

Aye! aye! I love that pure and spotless form
For that blue eye in which the deep Soul loves to dwell
They are the gates through which the heart pure and warm
With ebb and flow betrays affections deepest swell.

Oh! yes I love that noble generous nature which
Betrays itself in those eyes of heavenly blue
Though placed forever beyond my farthest reach
In Fancy’s fairest fields, that Spirit I may woo.
February 1867
pages.editorial_notes: The heading is badly faded: “Blue Eyes” is tentative and remaining title wording unread. Dated February 1867, with no visible signature or named recipient. The poem explicitly locates the encounter in imagination; it does not identify a partner or establish a relationship.

pages.title: Oh! Let Me Forget: childhood and vanished hopes
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Oh! let me forget! In answer to—“Forget; Oh! never!”

Oh! let me forget the [[inserted: early]] scenes of my childhood
When careless I strayed brightest flowers among
On the hills, in the valleys, by the stream in the wildwood,
Inhaling their fragrance all the day long
When my young heart expanded in the bright sunshine
That fed the sweet flowers budding around
And inhaled the pure emotions of the noble and divine
Which haunted the ear at each joyous heart bound.
Oh! let me forget!

For those scenes in their brightness in Memory lingers
Contrasting so vividly with with the dark gloom around
Like the voices of Some distant melodious singers
Which reaches us at times with a heavenly sound
Which partakes not of earth in its mellowing sweetness
But seems to proceed from a holier Sphere
And with the rich bursts of its metrical sweetness
Shows us the discords we always have here.
Oh! let me forget!

Oh! let me forget the hopes I have cherished
In boyhoods bright morn, when all was so fair
Ah! little I then thought they all would have perished
And melted away like the mirage in air.
But they have gone and all that was blooming
Has rapidly faded before my eager gaze
Which once was so brightly and sweetly illuming
My varied wanderings in Lifes dreary maze
Oh! let me forget!
pages.editorial_notes: Continues at 10-131–132, where it is dated February 1867. The title explicitly answers “Forget; Oh! never!” but no author of that earlier piece is given. Repeated “with with” and other grammatical irregularities are retained. The poem is unsigned on these pages.

pages.family_title: Oh! Let Me Forget: childhood and vanished hopes
pages.family_text:
Oh, Let Me Forget!
In answer to “Forget? Oh, never!”

Let me forget the early scenes of childhood,
when I wandered carelessly among the brightest flowers:
on hills, in valleys, beside the stream in the woods,
breathing their fragrance all day long.
My young heart expanded in the bright sunshine
that nourished the sweet flowers budding around me,
and breathed in pure feelings of nobility and divinity,
which filled the air at every joyful heartbeat.
Oh, let me forget!

Those bright scenes linger in memory,
contrasting vividly with the dark gloom around me,
like voices of distant, melodious singers
that sometimes reach us with a heavenly sound.
Their mellow sweetness seems unearthly,
as though it came from a holier realm.
The rich bursts of their rhythmic sweetness
reveal the discord always present here.
Oh, let me forget!

Let me forget the hopes I cherished
in boyhood’s bright morning, when everything was fair.
I scarcely imagined they would all perish,
melting away like a mirage in the air.
But they are gone. Everything that bloomed
has quickly faded before my eager eyes:
everything that once so brightly and sweetly lit
my wanderings through life’s dreary maze.
Oh, let me forget!
pages.family_note: Continues at 10-131–132. The named poem being answered has not been independently identified.

pages.title: Oh! Let Me Forget: leaving home and the horrors of war
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
Oh! let me forget the sad tears when I parted
From home and its charms which I loved so well
And the fond friends whom I left there broken-hearted
When I spoke as I thought my last sad farewell.
To go to that war whose Tocsin was ringing
The death knell to thousands in our lovely land
And from its distant bounds was rapidly bringing
Those daring heroes the shock to withstand.
Oh! let me forget

Oh! let me forget the muskets horrid rattle
Where brothers [[inserted: contending]] against brothers fell
And the cannon’s loud roar in the din of the battle
Portraying on earth a miniature hell.
Where Death proudly riding rode on the breeze
And fiendishly hurled his darts In the plain
Or where the dark waves of the deep heaving Seas
Her fiercely cast them again and again.
Oh! let me forget

Oh! let me forget those dark scenes of horror
Which harrowed the soul with visions of dread
And darkly foreboded that each coming morrow
Would add a new list to the nations of dead,
And the dark robe of crime gathering o’er us
Racked the sad heart where the gospel light shone
And with the prospect of oppression ever before us
Prepared us to yield ere life was all gone.
Oh! let me forget!

Oh! let me forget the maid to whom I plighted
The wild romantic feelings which burned in my breast
And those heavenly ties which hourly invited
pages.editorial_notes: Continues 10-130 and leads to 10-132. The war is not named, nor are battles, dates of service or the woman in the final stanza. In the collection’s context the Civil War is a plausible referent, but this unsigned literary passage alone does not document a particular combat experience. “Her fiercely cast them” is retained as read, with uncertain syntax; the family version gives its apparent sense.

Oh, let me forget!

Let me forget the muskets’ terrible rattle,
where brothers fell fighting brothers,
and the cannon’s loud roar amid battle’s din,
portraying a miniature hell on earth.
Death rode proudly upon the wind,
fiendishly hurling darts over the plain,
or casting them fiercely again and again
over the dark waves of the swelling seas.
Oh, let me forget!

Let me forget those dark, horrifying scenes
that tormented the soul with dreadful visions,
foretelling that every coming day
would add a new list to the nations of the dead.
The dark robe of crime gathering over us
tormented the sad heart where the gospel’s light shone.
With oppression always looming before us,
it prepared us to yield before life was completely gone.
Oh, let me forget!

Let me forget the woman to whom I pledged
the wild, romantic feelings burning in my heart,
and those heavenly bonds that continually invited—

pages.title: Oh! Let Me Forget ends with grief and memory
pages.text:
[[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]]
My wild erring Spirit to sweet moments of rest
For the charms which encircled her, brought pain at the parting
And saddens the long hours through each returning day
And too often ’neath my eyelids the pearly tear starting
Stains with effeminacy manhood’s stern way.
Oh! let me forget!

Oh! let me forget the varied Past and its pleasures
Which never, never again in life can return
With its hopes and its joys, and the hearts deepest treasures
Which all moulder now in the Sepulchres urn.
Like the Storm shivered tree alone on the heath
Far from its mates in the forests so fair
I stand and view my branches low scattered in death
And pour my lament on the wild desert air.
Oh! let me forget!
February 1867.

with its hopes, joys, and the heart’s deepest treasures,

far from its companions in the beautiful forest,

and pour my lament into the wild desert air.
Oh, let me forget!

pages.title: A portrait in verse, dated May 31, 1861
pages.text:
She was not very beautiful if it be beauties test
To [[deleted: with]] a Clasic model when perfectly at rest;
And She did not look bewitchingly if witchery it be
To have a forehead and a lip Transparent as the sea.
The fashion of her gracefulniss was not a followed rule
And her [[effervescent?]] sprightliness was never learnt at School
And her words were all peculiar like the faeries [[inserted: fabled]] dialect,
And her tone was ever Sweetest midst the cadences of grief.
Said I she was not beautiful? Her eye upon your sight
Broke with with the lambent purity of planetary light;
And an intellectual beauty like a light within a vase,
Touched every line with [[deleted: beauty]] [[inserted: glory]] of her animated face.
Written May 31st. 1861 By [[Lizzie?]] Douglas
pages.editorial_notes: The separate sheet is sideways in the PDF and is read after clockwise rotation. The name after “By” is tentatively Lizzie Douglas, not assigned to George Douglas. “Written” may refer to copying rather than composition; original authorship has not been verified. An apparent canceled “with,” a correction within “effervescent,” the inserted “fabled,” and the substitution of “glory” for “beauty” are preserved. The irregular line “To a Clasic model” and repeated “with with” are retained. The woman described is unnamed.

pages.family_title: A portrait in verse, dated May 31, 1861
pages.family_text:
She was not very beautiful, if beauty is judged
by a classical model perfectly at rest. [[The source’s second line is incomplete or irregular.]]
She did not look bewitching, if enchantment means
having a forehead and lips transparent as the sea.
Her grace followed no prescribed rule;
her lively sparkle was never learned at school.
Her words were distinctive, like the fairies’ fabled language,
and her voice was always sweetest in the cadences of grief.
Did I say she was not beautiful? Her eyes met yours
with the softly shining purity of planetary light.
An intellectual beauty, like a light within a vase,
touched every line of her animated face with glory.

Written May 31, 1861, by [[Lizzie?]] Douglas.
pages.family_note: The signature’s first name is tentative. “Written” does not establish original composition: this could be a copied poem. The subject is not identified.
